News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” added the ASA, who launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

Voy said the ads were retracted while the investigation was underway, adding that they will not run them again.

Dr Earim Chaudry, Chief Medical Officer at Voy, said: “Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance”.

News.title: Saucepan racks, fitted sheets and dehumidifiers: Your tricks for drying laundry in winter
News.content:
As temperatures drop and laundry piles up, drying clothes indoors can become a headache. But when Laura de Barra gave her verdict on the best heated clothes airers, Telegraph readers had a lot to say. So, we asked you what works in your homes.

While some of you have relied on heated airers for years, others have found a standard clothes horse or an overhead airer paired with a dehumidifier preferable. Several of you argue that you can’t beat the efficiency of a tumble dryer.

Here are your tried and tested tips...

Heated airers

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.



After seeing a review for the Lakeland heated airer printed in The Telegraph in 2008, Clive Ruffle, 67, from Surrey, felt enticed to buy one. “It had a price offer and a coupon to send to the newspaper,” he recalls.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

The options to fold the airer away flat and use only half of it, where one side is folded down, are the two major features that attracted Clive to the product.

“The drying speed is good, and we’ve never felt frustrated by it,” he says. “The heated bars are very effective and if we choose to heat, clothes are usually done in the day. They take a bit longer without the heater.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

For a more affordable option, Caroline Morrell, 65, from Greater Manchester, recommends buying a tiered Minky heated clothes airer, which she uses with a Beldray cover.

News.title: ‘I lost my family when I contracted HIV’: why virus is still taboo in Iraq
News.content:
Hassan Mehdi never imagined that telling his family he had contracted HIV would cost him his home and his family.

The initial symptoms of the virus weren’t too worrying: a skin allergy, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes in his neck. The dermatologist told Mehdi, not his real name, that he was probably suffering from a seasonal allergy. But he then began to think about his dating and sexual history and did an HIV test at home. A faint line appeared, indicating it was positive. “I tested once again at home and got the same result,” he said.

His worst fears were then confirmed by doctors at a public HIV centre.

“Mentally and psychologically, I collapsed,” Mehdi told The Telegraph, his voice thick with pain. “I decided to take a break and leave my job as a graphic designer, and I shut myself in my room.”

The doctor urged Mehdi to tell his family about the diagnosis. He also asked him to sign a paper promising to disclose his status if he married, not to stop treatment and not get a tattoo. It also warned that he could face legal consequences if someone accused him of spreading the virus.

When he finally broke the news to his mother, he hoped she would support him. But instead, he was met with hostility.

He said: “After informing my mum, she started to spread the news with my relatives, and they warned her that if I stayed at home and mixed with them, I would infect them all. Additionally, my elder brother heard and told me: ‘If I see you in the street or anywhere else, I will kill you.’ That was the last sentence I heard from him before I packed my bag to leave home forever,” he said.

“I lost my family when I told them I had HIV,” he adds. “To a religiously extreme family, HIV/Aids is taboo,” he added.

To fight the virus and adjust to a new life away from the town where he grew up, he immersed himself in gym workouts, a strict diet, and his treatment regimen. Close friends, social gatherings, and special cultural events became his sanctuary.

News.title: Bosses ‘increasingly reluctant’ to hire as employment costs soar
News.content:
Job vacancies fell to their lowest level in 12 years outside the pandemic as employers braced for the impact of the Government’s workers’ rights reforms.

Vacancies dropped by 22,000 to 690,000 in the three months to October, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This was the lowest since February to April 2021 – and the worst performance since the three months to September 2014 when taking out the impact of Covid lockdowns.

Bosses are grappling with higher employment costs in addition to the Government’s looming deadline to implement the Employment Rights Act on Jan 1. Under the changes, a cap on claims for unfair dismissal will be scrapped and the time a worker needs to have been employed before they can make a claim will be cut from two years to six months.

Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “The problem isn’t that businesses are firing workers. It’s that they’re increasingly reluctant to hire them.”

Sports.title: Chelsea snatch late winner vs PSG to move top of WCL table
Sports.content:
Veerle Buurman's late winner snatched a late 1-0 win for Chelsea against Paris Saint-Germain to move them to the top of the Champions League table.

Sonia Bompastor's side looked as if they were heading to back-to-back goalless draws, following the 0-0 draw with BK Hacken last time out in Europe, until Buurman was able to bundle her effort home at the near post in the 88th minute.

The hosts had been the dominant side throughout but were thwarted by Katarzyna Kiedrzynek on more than one occasion.

Alyssa Thompson had come close to breaking the deadlock just before the break after seeing her initial shot and follow-up effort smothered by Kiedrzynek.

Image: Alyssa Thompson went close for Chelsea

The corner for Buurman's timely winner arrived after the PSG goalkeeper got down well to her right to keep Sjoeke Nusken's header out.

Lucy Bronze's delivery and a slight touch on the way through sparked panic among the PSG defence and it was Buurman who reacted first to sweep home the winner, sending her side to the top of the table with one league phase game to go.

The Blues remain unbeaten in Europe, winning three of their five games so far, and are well placed to qualify for the last 16 through the top four automatic qualification spots. They face OH Leuven in their final game, where they will go into it as strong favourites.

Bompastor praises resilient team performance

Chelsea boss Sonia Bompastor speaking to UEFA:

"I like the resilience from my team. Believing until the end of the game we could score that important goal and it was really important for us to win tonight.

"What I like in my team and squad is the fact they are really flexible; they are really open-minded to changing systems sometimes, adapting to what is happening on the pitch.

"They understand really quickly. I think it was good for us to be able to change, to go to a back four. We wanted to have the width to destabilise them more than we did in the first half."

On her side potentially finishing in the top four: "We knew we had two games left and getting two wins will help us to probably secure top four.

"So we still have things under control and that was why it was really important for us to win."

Buurman on 'important' win for Chelsea

Chelsea defender Veerle Buurman speaking to Disney:

"It was really important we scored the goal. Winning and three points was really important, especially after the last Champions League game where we drew against Hacken.

"A good team performance. We tried really hard and that I can score a goal is really important for the team."

Walsh: We are in a good place in WCL

Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh speaking to UEFA:

"We spoke about it before the game about wanting to finish the evening on top. We are in a good spot going into the last game.

"It was a massive win. It was tough for us tonight. They defended really well and they're aggressive.

"It was a difficult game physically but to get the win was really important. Hopefully it will push us into the top four."

Key moments from The Cherry Red Records Stadium

43: SO CLOSE! Thompson has an initial shot and a second effort saved by Kiedrzynek from close range.

53: SAVE! Kanjinga makes space to shoot, but Hampton keeps her effort out at the near post.

67: CLOSE! Buurman meets the corner and glances her header towards goal but it is saved by Kiedrzynek again.

86: ANOTHER SAVE! Nusken's header looks destined for the bottom corner until Kiedrzynek dives to claw it away.

87: GOAL! Chelsea finally break the deadlock as Buurman scores late winner at the near post.

Sports.title: Cadillac confirm Bottas to stay with team for 2027
Sports.content:
Cadillac have confirmed Valtteri Bottas will stay on at the team for the 2027 Formula 1 season, ending speculation about the Finnish driver's future.

Bottas returned after a year's absence from the grid for this season, Cadillac's first in the sport, as one of two hugely experienced drivers for the all-new American team's first line-up alongside Sergio Perez, who signed a contract extension last month until at least 2029.

But, Bottas' future has been up in the air recently as Cadillac pushed for American Formula 2 driver Colton Herta to earn a Formula 1 super licence, which he secured two weeks ago, by running him in practice sessions.

The team have committed to Bottas for another year though, citing the 37-year-old's "extensive Formula 1 experience, technical insight and race-winning pedigree to the team".

"To whom it may concern, I'm staying!" said Bottas, in reference to his team radio after winning the 2019 Australian Grand Prix with Mercedes.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come, I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas talks about why he decided to cycle from Malaysia to Singapore between those two races

Newcomers Cadillac are yet to score a point in their maiden campaign but Bottas is ahead of Perez in the Drivers' Championship due to countback, as his 13th place result at the Chinese Grand Prix is the team's highest result.

But, Perez has generally outpaced his team-mate which, with the links of Cadillac potentially keen for an American driver in Herta, led to speculation about Bottas' future.

Cadillac F1 CEO Dan Towriss said: "Valtteri's experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team.

"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1. On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."

Cadillac say they will announce their 2027 F1 reserve and test drivers in "due course".

Rafael Camara Audi Nico Hulkenberg Gabriel Bortoleto Williams Carlos Sainz Alex Albon Aston Martin Fernando Alonso Lance Stroll Cadillac Sergio Perez Valtteri Bottas

Just one seat left to be filled on 2027 F1 grid

With Bottas' future secured and Racing Bulls confirming last week that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will be their line-up once again in 2027, only Haas are yet to complete their driver pairing for next year.

Last month, Haas announced Rafael Camara will drive for the team in 2027, having already made an early F1 debut in Brazil and will compete again this weekend in Las Vegas, after Esteban Ocon was dropped following a dispute at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

But, Oliver Bearman has not been confirmed, although is expected to keep his seat once a "few bigger-picture things that we're working on" have been resolved according to the British driver.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu dismissed speculation around Oliver Bearman last month

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu furiously dismissed reports claiming that contract extension talks with Bearman are being held up by the British driver demanding a £5m annual salary.

"I have no idea where that comes from," he said in Mexico.

"I've experienced this sometimes this season as well. People say there's no smoke without fire but really some people will invent a story."

Sports.title: CME Group Tour Championship: Can Hull and Woad stop Korda?
Sports.content:
Who will be crowned the LPGA Tour’s Race to the CME Globe Champion? Who can stop Nelly Korda from winning? Can Brits Charley Hull and Lottie Woad claim victory? We get you up to speed ahead of this week’s LPGA Tour 2026 season finale, live on Sky Sports.

What is the CME Group Tour Championship?

The CME Group Tour Championship is the final event in the LPGA Tour's season-long points race.

Throughout 2026, players have competed in the LPGA Tour's points competition, the Race to CME Globe.

The top 60 players on the Race to CME Globe Points List are invited to feature at this weekend's event and the player who wins the 2026 CME Group Tour Championship will be crowned the Race to CME Globe champion.

Where is the CME Group Tour Championship held?

The tournament is held at the Tiburon Golf Club at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Resort in Naples, Florida.

The course has hosted the tournament since 2013.

Who can beat Korda?

It is the second time in consecutive years that Korda has arrived at the CME Group Tour Championship sitting at the top of the Race to CME Globe standings.

The American has already been crowned the Rolex Player of the Year, with three events to spare, but has never won the Race to CME Group Tour Championship. A first title this week would see her qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame.

Standing in her way is a field of the LPGA Tour's best players, including two-time CME Group Tour Championship winner Jeeno Thitikul, who arrives in Florida having won four times on the LPGA Tour this season.

Miyu Yamashita, who has three wins on the LPGA Tour in 2026, enjoyed a strong finish to her season, winning twice while placing inside the top 10 three times in her last six events.

Haeran Ryu, who clinched back-to-back majors at The Amundi Evian Championship and the KPMG Women's PGA Championship, also comes into this event off the back of a fine vein of form, finishing tied-second and tied-third in her last two starts.

What Brits are playing?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After the AIG Women's open Charley Hull said she didn't see Korda as her rival

Hull clinched the first LPGA Tour title of her career at this event back in 2016, so she certainly knows how to win at Tiburon Golf Club.

It's been a great year for Hull, who won the Solheim Cup with Team Europe in September and placed inside the top 10 at five LPGA Tour events. She'll no doubt want to end the season in style with a win.

Woad is the only other English player in the field. She too has enjoyed an excellent year, winning the Kroger Queen City Championship in May and finishing tied-ninth at last week's The ANNIKA, marking her seventh top-10 finish of the season.

A total prize purse of £8.33m ($11m) is up for grabs, with the winner set to take home a £3.03m ($4m) cheque, the biggest cash prize in the history of women's golf.

The runner-up is also set to receive £757,423 ($1m).

Sports.title: Sober Glory storms to victory over Old Park Star on chase debut
Sports.content:
Sober Glory turned the tables on Supreme Novices’ Hurdle conqueror Old Park Star to make a faultless chasing bow in the Golwg Gwendraeth Beginners’ Chase at Ffos Las.

One of the most eagerly-anticipated showdowns of the early season as the dry spell forced the exciting duo to west Wales, the main protagonists were immediately to the fore with Philip Hobbs and Johnson White's Sober Glory the more sure-footed of the duo in the early exchanges.

There was little to separate the pair as a fine leap four out brought the Nico de Boinville-ridden Old Park Star alongside, but Ben Jones soon reclaimed the advantage in the home straight aboard the 5-4 second favourite.

With the gap growing all the way up the home straight, the Cheltenham Festival runner-up gained revenge over Nicky Henderson's 4-5 favourite, sauntering to an impressive nine-and-a-half length opening victory over fences.

Co-trainer White said: "It was a very pleasing performance jumping wise and there was a few novicey mistakes, but that is understandable for a first run over the bigger obstacles.

"I was delighted with the authority in which he won the race and he had a very good horse a good few lengths behind.

"His schooling has been very good all autumn, but you still have to go out and put that into practice on the course. Ben Jones says he's only going to get better with experience, but that has to be a very nice starting point.

"There is very few parts you could be disappointed with there. He's jumped well, travelled nicely and he's beaten good opposition so it's a very encouraging start to the season."

BOYLE Sports cut Sober Glory to 7-2 joint-favourite for the Arkle alongside Dan Skelton's Kabral du Mathan and while Hobbs and White will work a path back from that Cheltenham Festival event, they could clash early next month at Sandown in the Henry VIII Chase.

White added: "We'll get him home and reassess, but I think you have to aim at the Arkle and work back from there. Sandown would certainly be one of the races on the agenda along the way."

One horse who will not be in Esher on December 5 is Old Park Star after he faded into third, with Henderson left in "shock" after the six-year-old bled as his four-race winning streak came to an end.

"He's broken a blood vessel and bled so that explains it and it's a not just a bit of a shock, but a huge shock," said the Seven Barrows handler. "These things do happen, but we always just pray to God they don't but it has and it is as simple as that.

"It explains things but does create a massive headache. It's a blow when it happens to one like him and at the moment it is just a massive shock really.

"We'll get him back but he obviously won't be going to the Henry VIII which was the race we were trying to get him ready for. We've got the problem and now we have to try and resolve it - we will do our best."

Sports.title: Manchester United’s infamous 1974 relegation is a warning from history
Sports.content:
In many ways, there are striking parallels between the Manchester United relegated in 1974 and the Manchester United sitting in the relegation zone at this stage of the season for the first time in 40 years. A legendary manager leaves, his shadow remains; with boardroom dithering and uncertainty, his replacements churn and burn as the club slide over several years.

Sir Matt Busby stepped aside as manager of the 1968 European Cup-winning side, but stayed on as a director, just as Sir Alex Ferguson did, watching from the Old Trafford directors’ box as successors tried and failed.

In the six years after being crowned kings of Europe, United turned to Wilf McGuinness, Busby stepped in temporarily to keep them up, then Frank O’Farrell was appointed before they landed on Tommy Docherty, who experienced the ignominy of taking them down.

In the past eight years, United have sacked José Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjær, Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and now Michael Carrick.

View image in fullscreen Tommy Docherty took an old and disjointed Manchester United down to the old Second Division … then back up at the first attempt. Photograph: Robert Stiggins/Getty Images

How did the United of 1974 go down? Most outsiders believed they were too big to fail. Inside the club, though, they sensed the direction of travel. After a heavy defeat at Crystal Palace in December 1972, Busby offered Docherty the job in the Selhurst Park boardroom. “There’s a lot of trouble in the camp,” Busby said. Docherty was doing well as Scotland manager and took a few days to mull it over, but decided he couldn’t turn down the opportunity.

When Busby called him on the Sunday evening, he accepted. “You know it won’t be easy?” Busby said. “It’ll be like turning an oil tanker round, only bigger.” He added: “You might find yourself having to take a step back in order to take a leap forward.” Docherty wrote in his autobiography, The Doc, that at the time he never believed Busby was alluding to relegation.

Docherty was given free rein for a rebuild. The day after his appointment, he signed George Graham from Arsenal for £120,000, a sizeable fee at the time. Alex Forsyth followed from Partick for £100,000 and Docherty pulled off a coup when he persuaded Lou Macari to join bottom-of-the-table United instead of Liverpool for £200,000.

View image in fullscreen George Best made his final appearance for Manchester United against Queens Park Rangers at Loftus Road on New Year’s Day in 1974. Photograph: Wesley/Getty Images

The giants of the previous era were moved on. In February, Bobby Charlton told him that, at 37, it would be his last season. Other big names wanted to stay, but Docherty felt a reset was needed. “The Manchester United team that had won the European Cup in 1968 was without a doubt a great team, but many members of that side had been allowed to grow old together,” he wrote.

“I knew what I had decided would prove very unpopular with many people but it had to be done. I set out my stall to end the United careers of among others Denis Law, Tony Dunne, Pat Crerand and David Sadler.”

George Best, who had retired once but returned under Docherty, played his last game on New Year’s Day 1974 after repeatedly turning up late. The most controversial departure was Law, who was allowed to join Manchester City.

Having taken over with United bottom, Docherty kept them up in his first season and was emboldened to continue his clearout. Thirteen players were released that summer. But halfway through the following season they were facing relegation again and a lack of goals cost them. At one stage, the joint-top scorer was Alex Stepney, with two penalties. He was the goalkeeper.

Relegation was confirmed on the penultimate day as they lost to City, a defeat made all the more painful by Law back-heeling the late winner. Docherty was interviewed on the Old Trafford pitch and asked, in a scene replayed in TNT Sports’ Too Good To Go Down, whether the club would drift into obscurity. “No, there’s no danger,” he said. “We could wash the jerseys here and hang them out to dry and you’d get 15,000 people standing watching them do so.”

Despite the bravado, Docherty was expecting the sack when he met Busby a few days later. Instead, Busby handed him a case of champagne, reminded him of the oil tanker and told him to set to work getting them back up.

Docherty’s prediction proved right: the brand was far bigger than the division they played in. In the Second Division, Old Trafford averaged crowds of more than 47,000 – the biggest in the country – and their away support descended on towns and cities and routinely outnumbered the home contingent.

View image in fullscreen Stuart Pearson, who scored 17 goals for United during 1974-75 as they won the Second Division, celebrates against Blackpool on the last day. Photograph: Harry Ormesher/Popperfoto/Getty Images

Docherty bought young and hungry, targeting players with a point to prove, including Steve Coppell from Tranmere, Stuart Pearson from Hull and Jim Holton from Shrewsbury. The direct, attacking football synonymous with United returned and the Scot shaped a fearless 4-2-4 formation.

Crowds grew after they came straight back up and for a while United were on course to become the fifth side to win the First Division after promotion, but finished third and also reached the FA Cup final, losing 1-0 to Southampton. That shows the stark differences between then and now.

The gap between the first and second tiers was narrower. United did not lose a gargantuan broadcast deal when they went down. They were not saddled with debt by their owners. Their wage bill was not tied to Champions League qualification. Players were not on long contracts and were easier to buy and sell. There were no disruptive agents. Fans were more patient.

If lessons of the 1970s are not heeded soon, the fallout could be infinitely more painful.

Sports.title: Veerle Buurman scrambles late WCL winner to push blunt Chelsea past PSG
Sports.content:
Chelsea were made to work hard for three Champions League points against a resilient Paris Saint-Germain side but their patience paid off, Veerle Buurman squeezing the ball in at the near post to put them, temporarily at least, at the top of the table in the league phase.

Buurman had stolen the show in Chelsea’s defeat of Manchester City at the weekend, coming on 12 minutes in and nullifying Khadija Shaw’s threat to be named player of the match, and she was the hero under the lights with Chelsea doing everything but score prior to her goal.

“She is a top, young talent and is so mature on and off the pitch,” said Sonia Bompastor. “She is a confident player and a really complete player.”

Bompastor’s side were frustrated by Häcken last week, held to a 0-0 draw by the Swedish side and falling out of the top four automatic qualification places. There was a desire to put things right at AFC Wimbledon’s stadium and they did just that, albeit in not the prettiest of encounters.

“Sometimes in football you need to find a way to win and the result tonight was really important for us,” said Bompastor.

Quick Guide WCL roundup: City subs Hemp and Shaw see off Häcken Show Lauren Hemp and Khadija Shaw both scored off the bench to earn Manchester City a 2-0 Women’s Champions League victory over Häcken in Gothenburg. The first half ended goalless with City's best chances coming just before the break. Aoba Fujino was put through on goal but she hit her effort straight at Häcken keeper Jennifer Falk, who made saves from Grace Clinton and Rebecca Knaak to keep the hosts on terms at the interval. Hemp and Shaw were both introduced at half-time by Andrée Jeglertz, and the England winger opened the scoring after 55 minutes. It was a fortuitous breakthrough, with Emma Östlund's clearance ricocheting off Hemp's shin and into the net [pictured]. Mary Fowler appeared to have added a second soon after, but her strike was ruled out for offside against Yui Hasegawa. Soon after Hemp was denied her second goal when her shot hit the post, she turned creator by passing to an onrushing Shaw, who tucked home for City's second in the 77th minute. The visitors could have had a third, but Falk saved Fowler's stoppage-time penalty after a VAR intervention. Signe Bruun also made the difference off the bench on Wednesday, scoring two late goals as Real Madrid wore down 10-woman Internazionale to win 3-1. The Danish forward put Madrid ahead five minutes of time before adding a late penalty to secure all three points. Lineth Beerensteyn got the hosts off the mark in Madrid after 28 minutes, and Inter faced an uphill battle after Karolina Vilhjalmsdottir was sent off three minutes before the break. The visitors got an unexpected equaliser when Michela Cambiaghi headed in from a corner, and held on until Bruun's late double. City and Real Madrid are both unbeaten after five league phase games, winning two and drawing three matches each as they bid to finish in the top four and avoid the playoffs. Juventus join them on nine points after late goals from Annamaria Serturini and Matilde Pavan earned a 2-0 home win over Leuven. PA and Guardian sport Photograph: Declan Lloyd/Manchester City FC Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

PSG had lost 2-1 at home to Bayern Munich after three draws and one win in the competition before their trip to London. Denied a point late on, they remain 10th and dangerously close to slipping out of the playoff places with one game to play.

Chelsea had been thrillingly gutsy and diligent in their 1-0 win over City on Saturday and against PSG they were similarly solid at the back, but they lacked spark in attack. Ellie Carpenter became the focal point of their forward play from the right, with the striker Melvine Malard injured in the game against City.

PSG nullifying the threat of Carpenter blunted Chelsea, and despite their dominance of the ball, amassing 64% possession in the first half, Chelsea struggled to carve a way through the visitors’ backline. They had seven attempts on goal to PSG’s six at the break, despite 33 attacks to 10.

Chelsea have historically performed well against PSG, winning three of their four Champions League meetings prior to this penultimate fixture of their league phase campaign. In the 2018-19 quarter-finals they earned a 2-0 home win and, after a 2-1 away defeat, progressed to the semi-finals; in the 2022-23 season they won both group meetings with an overall score of 4-0.

The visiting team’s first attempt on target arrived after the break, with Merveille Kanjinga forcing a near-post save from Hannah Hampton. While Chelsea still dominated, PSG had more forays forward in the second half.

View image in fullscreen Aggie Beever-Jones is beaten to a header by her Chelsea teammate Wieke Kaptein (right) in what was a close game against PSG. Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty Images

Erin Cuthbert, Maika Hamano and Lucy Bronze arrived at the hour mark as the home team sought to deal the killer blow their dominance required. It increasingly felt like it would take something special to break the deadlock, akin to the sublime effort that Sandy Baltimore had delivered against City.

Aggie Beever-Jones was replaced by Sjoeke Nüsken late on and the German instantly made a difference, forcing a sublime save from Katarzyna Kiedrzynek. The breakthrough came from the resulting corner, and it was far less sublime than Saturday’s effort, Buurman somehow squeezing the ball in at the near post after PSG failed to clear Cuthbert’s ball in.

“The main feeling is one of frustration,” said the PSG manager, Paulo César. “We defended well, we just lacked a bit of clarity on the transition and I have mixed feelings. I’m proud of my team but it shows that there are very fine margins that we need to rival a big team like Chelsea.”

Ultimately, the goal was the bit of luck Chelsea needed and they look increasingly formidable.

Sports.title: Leicester part ways with BC Game after sponsor’s partnership with porn actor
Sports.content:
Leicester City have ditched their front-of-shirt sponsor, BC Game, after the cryptocurrency casino’s partnership with a porn actor sparked a fan backlash. BC Game, an offshore company registered in Belize that is unlicensed to operate in the UK, had been Leicester’s main sponsor since 2024.

This month BC Game named Eva Elfie a brand ambassador, leading the Foxes Trust, Leicester’s supporters’ trust, to highlight the “devastating impacts” caused by gambling and pornography. On Wednesday the club said they prematurely ended their agreement with the online betting firm after they “recognised our differing commercial priorities”.

It is understood Leicester directly raised concerns with BC Game about the implications of their deal with Elfie, a Russian porn actor who BC Game said had “an established presence in gaming communities”. Leicester’s deal with BC Game, which began in July 2024, was due to run until the end of the season.

The trust had previously outlined concerns about the club’s partnership with BC Game. In a statement responding to the partnership this month, they said: “From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting company we felt Leicester City were ditching its values.

“Now throw into the mix that BC Game have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content. Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?”

Leicester, who visit Huddersfield in League One on Saturday, said supporters who purchased a shirt featuring BC Game branding within the past 28 days are able to exchange the shirt or are eligible for a full refund. The club added they would pay for the postage of returns via standard delivery.

Leicester remain for sale, with the club’s Thai owners, King Power, also seeking to sell their stadium, training base and women’s team.

In an unrelated development, the former Chelsea technical director Michael Emenalo is working as an adviser to the club, who are 11th in the third tier. Emenalo is among a team of Deloitte consultants Leicester say they have enlisted to “assess its current operations and inform its future strategic planning”.

Sports.title: USWNT squad: Emma Hayes names veteran group for Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier
Sports.content:
In the two years since the Paris Olympics, Emma Hayes has thoroughly tested fresh faces and new combinations, gathering a considerable amount of data about the US women’s national team. It’s been a thorough process, with 33 players earning their first caps since Hayes assumed the post, to bring her roster of options to 61 players.

At last, the main event is nearing. On 27 November, the United States will enter the Concacaf W Championship with a clear objective: beat El Salvador. Winning the whole thing is nice, of course, and the USWNT have done so in nine of the tournament’s 11 installments to date. But by far the most important game on that journey is the first one, that quarter-final date with clear stakes: overcome El Salvador, or rely on a playoff to reach next summer’s World Cup.

On Wednesday, Hayes acknowledged that the way El Salvador are expected to set up – in a low-defensive block, looking to disrupt the US’s ability to control the game – will pose a different challenge than recent friendlies against fellow World Cup hopefuls Spain and Brazil.

“It’s a much different game to the previous games you’ve just played in, and transitioning your thinking process, especially tactically,” Hayes said after announcing her squad. “We’ll still have to build up against an aggressive press, but we’re going to have to break down a team that will sit and defend the box with numbers. I do think we have been working on that as a team, but we might not have experienced that for a number of camps. So, switching into that and reminding our team of the key things in which that has to come through, in the way we train and the types of training we do.”

Hayes’s 23 selections for the tournament suggests what her preferred core may look like for the remainder of the cycle. Only four outfield players on her roster arrive with fewer than a dozen caps: midfielder Croix Bethune (seven), who sent the Kansas City Current to the NWSL championship last weekend with a brilliant curling free-kick, plus defenders Kennedy Wesley (nine), Kate Del Fava (one) and Evelyn Shores, who becomes only the second uncapped USWNT player selected for a World Cup qualifier (following Taylor Flint, née Kornieck, 2022).

Eight players from Hayes’s Olympic gold medal squad remain in the fold, including the star attacking trio of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Sophia Wilson. Sam Coffey returns after an injury prevented her from joining the team in the previous window, while Naomi Girma misses out due to persistent muscle issues. Claudia Dickey, Mandy McGlynn and Phallon Tullis-Joyce will continue to vie to start in goal, continuing their open competition following Alyssa Naeher’s retirement.

The average age of this roster is 26.1, with only two players (Lindsey Heaps and Rose Lavelle) at least 30. With an average caps tally of 40.7 per player, Hayes will be looking to her veteran options for the crucial one-off qualifier – especially with the team convening just two days before the quarter-final.

“I think this, for us, qualifying for a major tournament first and foremost,” Hayes said. “I’ll be leaning on our experienced players. They know how to do this, and they’ve been with us the longest to be able to deliver that, and I think for the less experienced players, have had a good body of work in the last couple of years.”

The Concacaf W Championship doubles as qualifying for both the 2027 Women’s World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. All four semi-finalists will be guaranteed a spot in the World Cup, and the top three finishers will also qualify for the Olympics field. (The US have a place at LA 2028 automatically as hosts). The losing teams in the quarter-finals will compete against each other for Concacaf’s two spots in the inter-confederation playoffs, which are scheduled for February in Morocco.

As the first competitive games for the US since that gold-medal summer of 2024, the business end of the bracket will provide vital tests against regional rivals. Jamaica project as the favorite to face off in the semi-final should both teams advance, a stern test for a center-back corps operating without Girma and Emily Sonnett. A potential final could pit Hayes’s side against long-time rival Canada or Mexico, a program that has rapidly risen in stature this decade and hopes to make a first Women’s World Cup since 2015.

All of that is a matter for another day. Until then, the US will do what’s necessary to avoid what would be an unprecedented catastrophe: missing a World Cup.

“We know what we need to do,” Hayes said. “We need to just make sure we come into camp with really clear mind about those things. Focus on the game in front of us. That’s the next one. always say this: our identity is not defined by results. Being able to lock into what that identity is really quickly after a gap between lots of NWSL club games is really important when you only have a two-day build before the game.”
