Sports.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
Sports.content:
The awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but.

Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry.

There also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian.

Multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups.

“There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran says. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.”

In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal.

The impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup.

Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier.

Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US.

The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment.

Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game.

View image in fullscreen The 2026 World Cup final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history. Photograph: Lars Baron/Getty Images

Having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026.

The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents.

“Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” says François Godard, an independent media analyst. “And one-off events such as World Cups do not generally do particularly well for subscription services, who want year-round content.

“Fox in particular needs the World Cup and is heavily associated with it. They are the smallest of the legacy broadcasters and are reliant on sport, as well as news. Having said that, the market for sport amongst streamers is far more competitive in the US than in Europe. Netflix, Amazon and YouTube have all bought NFL rights, while Apple is investing heavily in Formula One, so I wouldn’t rule any of them out.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Fortnightly Sign up to The Hotspot A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Adam Kelly, president of the global sports marketing agency IMG, has a seat at the table at many rights negotiations and has long predicted the rise of the streamers, viewing the 2030 World Cup as the potential tipping point when a premium event could be exclusively bought in a major market by a streaming service for the first time. IMG has the rights to sell more than 70 global sports organisations, including the Premier League, World Rugby and Wimbledon.

In addition to the exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups, Netflix has secured exclusive 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. It must sublicense all of the Spanish national team’s matches, both semi-finals and final and at least one match per day to a domestic free-to-air broadcaster to comply with government regulations.

“These entities are the future of broadcasting, as they are the best companies in the world at turning attention into earnings,” Kelly says of the streamers. “Their model allows them to monetise better than their rivals due to their size, scale and the high consumption levels of their customers.

“Netflix in particular has built a sophisticated and lucrative advertising platform. They have the back-office capability and 2027 would provide a perfect test run. If they’re successful in the tender for the World Cup it shows they are potentially the future of sports broadcasting.”

Netflix’s diversification into an advertising business, which brought in $1.5bn last year with projections of $2.7bn this year, puts it ahead of Apple TV and Amazon and well placed to make a profit from an undertaking as large as broadcasting a men’s World Cup. The lack of stipulations in the US for free-to-air coverage makes this tender particularly attractive to Netflix, although if successful it could make some matches available to non-subscribers for promotional purposes, as Apple TV has done with Major League Soccer.

“As a company, Netflix’s unique offering is exclusivity, so why would they hand that to their rivals?” another broadcast source said. “There are no regulations in the US preventing exclusivity so I would expect Netflix to bid for and retain every game if they win.”

Given recent reports that Netflix is exploring tabling an offer for NBC Universal after withdrawing its $85bn bid for Warner Bros last year, a future partnership with a linear network cannot be ruled out if it is successful. Some sources have even suggested that the tender has been timed deliberately to attract a competitive bid from Netflix, as the streamer is short of sports content to promote during the 2027 Women’s World Cup. Others argue that Fifa would have been better advised waiting to build further on the interest created by that tournament.

The NFL’s decision to pause its media rights process as it seeks an early renegotiation of contracts that are due to run to 2034 is likely to have played a part in the timing, creating a window of opportunity for Fifa to go to market. While a second round of bidding is possible after Thursday’s opening round, the outcome is expected to be known within the next few weeks and could present a bounce for Gianni Infantino as he continues his presidential re-election campaign.

Sports.title: ‘When I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West’: the two lives of Bromley footballer Omar Sowunmi
Sports.content:
“I was walking down the street one day and someone came up to me and said: ‘I think you should be a model,’” the Bromley defender Omar Sowunmi says. He was already living out many people’s dreams as a professional footballer but was able to assume an alter ego in the world of fashion. There are few parallels between the grind of lower-league football and Milan fashion week but the 31-year-old is adept in both worlds.

Sowunmi’s dual career mixes trips to Doncaster with visits to Paris. On Saturday Bromley travel to Reading under their new manager, Karl Robinson, as they attempt to move off the bottom of League One and the centre-back is clear where his focus lies even after his chance encounter with a model agency employee expanded his horizons.

“I’d get asked to go to a job or I’d even get booked for a job and they’d be like: ‘Oh, we want you to come to Germany for three days,’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to say: ‘I can’t do it, my priority is football.’ As fun and different as [modelling] is, it’s not my main job. Football was my priority and is my priority.

“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done modelling. Going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris fashion week with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level that I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened.”

View image in fullscreen Omar Sowunmi on the catwalk at London fashion week in September. Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for Natasha Zinko x OnlyFans

Sowunmi takes a pilates class twice a month in the five-star Nobu hotel in central London. He is an imposing presence at 1.98m (6ft 6in) tall and grimaces through the session as his muscles are put to the test to keep him in shape for both his professions. It helps him to battle robust strikers and appear on social media as part of modelling campaigns. “Two days ago one of my current coaches said: ‘You popped up wearing a coat on my Instagram the other day. Can you get me one?’” Sowunmi says. “But I had to explain that it doesn’t really work like that.”

Sowunmi’s career path since he left his first club, Ipswich, without making an appearance has been that of a true lower-league player, taking in spells at Yeovil, Colchester and – between two stints with Bromley – Sutton. On the catwalk, he has rubbed shoulders with some of the biggest names in the industry while promoting designer brands and plans to continue doing that once he retires from the day job. He uses social media not only to post videos and images from photoshoots but to show the reality of life as a footballer.

View image in fullscreen Pilates helps Omar Sowunmi in both his lines of work. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

“The fans and everyone that watches you on Saturday or Tuesday or whatever day you’re playing, they get to see you for 90 minutes and they don’t see the full dedication that goes into being a professional footballer,” Sowunmi says. “We’re away from our families for two days [for away games]; we’ll train on the Friday then leave, maybe have a seven-hour coach journey. We’ll have stuff to do at the hotel, stretching sessions, pool sessions, nutrition. We’ll wake up and we’ll have more stuff to do and it’s that whole buildup that I kind of want to show them and give them an insight into what we do.”

Last season Sowunmi helped Bromley gain promotion to third tier for the first time. The step up has been difficult, costing the long-serving manager Andy Woodman his job. “It’s been tough, as you can tell by the league position,” Sowunmi says. “It’s a completely different league. It’s taken a lot of the players by surprise, the difference between League One and League Two, but we’re grinding, we’re working hard and I’m sure it will turn for us.”

View image in fullscreen Omar Sowunmi scores Bromley’s third goal in May’s 3-1 victory over Walsall – the day they secured the League Two title. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

A carefully curated moustache sits atop Sowunmi’s lip to raise money for Movember. He is speaking at a charity event on Wednesday to highlight the importance of mental health, a subject close to his heart since his best friend took his own life. “It’s something that is really deep in my heart just being a voice for people and trying to help make a difference in any way that I can,” Sowunmi says. “I was actually on an away trip and I received a call from his dad to give me the news.

“Everyone was asking me what was wrong on the bus and that I wasn’t really speaking to anyone and then I think when we got home it was a four-, five-hour journey. The manager took me to the side and got me to open up to him a little bit. Looking back that actually helped a lot, so I thought if I can help someone to speak to someone or know that it’s fine to speak to someone then I’m definitely here for it.”

Sports.title: Fifa’s World Cup TV rights documents indicate hydration breaks to stay in 2030
Sports.content:
Fifa’s tender documents for TV rights for the 2030 World Cup include a provision for broadcasters to sell adverts during hydration breaks in a strong indication the controversial ­stoppages will be retained.

A three-minute break midway through each half was introduced for the first time at all 104 matches at last summer’s World Cup in the interests of player welfare, a radical move that also provided a commercial boon for broadcasters, particularly the rights holders in the United States, Fox Sports and Telemundo.

Fifa insists it has yet to decide whether hydration breaks will be used at the 2030 tournament, which will take place largely in Morocco, Spain and Portugal but will also feature three matches in South America, but the Guardian has learned the possibility and potential commercial benefits are flagged to broadcasters in the tender documents.

The global governing body has awarded World Cup rights to ­Netflix in Spain and to the public service broadcaster SBS in Australia, and the sales process for the US and Puerto Rico is continuing, with Thursday the deadline to bid.

The tender documents are also understood to reference cooling breaks, a welfare mechanism used by Uefa whereby play is stopped for between 90 seconds and three minutes if the on-field temperature reaches 28C.

Fifa sources told the Guardian the tenders were designed to cover all potential options.

Fifa used cooling breaks on an ad hoc basis before triggering the wholesale adoption of hydration breaks for the 2026 World Cup, despite 31 of the 104 games being played in climate-controlled stadiums, after high temperatures led to stoppages in about 60% of matches at the 2025 Club World Cup in the US. Fifa said the move was to protect the integrity of the World Cup by ensuring all matches were played in the same conditions, although there were also major commercial benefits for broadcasters.

The Hollywood Reporter reported last summer that hydration breaks were generating between $2m and $9m in advertising revenue a game, leading to claims that Fox brought in an estimated $250m.

Fox’s overall advertising yield from the tournament was $835m according to the media sales analyst Guideline, almost double the $485m rights fee paid to Fifa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Fifa did not benefit financially last summer but the expectation of hydration breaks being included could drive up prices for 2030. The US rights are expected to fetch between $1.5bn and $2bn (£1.14bn-£1.52bn) in an auction that will feature bids from Netflix and all of the streaming services alongside traditional broadcasters.

Fifa declined to comment.

Mandatory hydration breaks will not be used at next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil, where temperatures are forecast to be cooler than they were in many cities at this year’s men’s tournament.

Sports.title: Overlap, underlap or sit back? How Premier League teams use their full-backs
Sports.content:
Overlapping. Underlapping. Inverted. Traditional. The role of full-back has evolved dramatically. Once a defensive-first position that provided some auxiliary attacking support, the role has developed into something far more multifaceted.

Just ask right-back Ben White, who – with Riccardo Calafiori on the left – has been an important figure in Arsenal’s superb start to the campaign. Talking a few years ago, he said: “Playing full-back the way [Mikel Arteta] wants is completely different to any other manager. To play full-back for him, you’ve got to be a centre-midfielder, a centre-back, a winger and a No 10.”

Between them, White and Calafiori have contributed to six goals for Arsenal already in the Premier League this season (White: three assists; Calafiori: one goal, two assists). No other defender has registered more than three goal involvements so far. The Arsenal duo are a great illustration of the impact full-backs can have. But, with the position more demanding than ever before, how does each Premier League team deploy theirs?

Where do full-backs take their touches?

The graphic below shows the average height and width of the touches of each Premier League team’s full-backs, sorted from highest average position to lowest. The most obvious takeaway is that Arsenal’s full-backs have the highest average touch location of any Premier League side this season, coming 58.2 metres from their own goal.

That is a reflection not only of Arsenal’s territorial dominance, but also the license White and Calafiori are given to push into the attacking line. White averages 3.4 touches in the opposition box per 90 minutes, the most of any full-back or wing-back in the division. Calafiori ranks third, with 2.9.

Arsenal’s full-backs also have the narrowest average touch locations of any team, emphasising how far they have moved away from the traditional full-back role of maintaining width. Instead, they are encouraged to drift inside and operate in central areas.

Tottenham also deploy their full-backs extremely high up the pitch. For most of the campaign, that has been Archie Gray at right-back and Andy Robertson on the left. Of course, analysing a player’s influence is not limited to what they do on the ball. Thanks to Opta Vision, we can also track what they do without it.

Gray is particularly noteworthy, given his exceptional work rate. He ranks first among Premier League full-backs for underlapping runs, both in total (23) and per 90 minutes (2.9), and also ranks fourth for overlapping runs per 90 (1.8). That shows the benefit of deploying an attack-minded player at full-back, with Gray showing energy and an ability to get beyond the ball and offer another option in the final third.

Robertson is no slouch on the opposite flank, either. The 32-year-old ranks seventh for underlapping runs per 90 minutes (1.4) and sits inside the top 20 for overlapping runs per 90 (1.1). He has also received more passes ending in the final third (159) than any other full-back.

It might be more of a surprise to see Coventry’s full-backs play so high, given they have not dominated the ball at all (39.1% possession, second-lowest) and they start their attacks from deep (40.2m away from goal, sixth-lowest). It is, however, something they did to good effect in the Championship last season (average height of 56.8m, sixth-highest).

Frank Lampard has also used a back five at times, which means his wing-backs naturally play higher up, but he has been brave with pushing his defensive line up in general. Coventry have provoked the second-most offsides of any team so far (30).

That has allowed Milan van Ewijk and Jay Dasilva to push forward on the flanks. The pair have each created eight chances, with only Jack Rudoni (12) creating more for the Sky Blues.

Dasilva is a particularly important outlet down the left. He takes his touches higher up the pitch than any other full-back in the division, and Coventry have created 42.2% of their open-play chances down his side, the highest proportion of any Premier League team.

Wing-backs v full-backs?

It makes sense that Nottingham Forest and Leeds also see their full-backs touch the ball high up the pitch, given they are two of the biggest users of wing-backs. That pair are two of just four teams that predominantly play with wing-backs, with the back three/five becoming a rare breed in the modern Premier League.

For Leeds, Jayden Bogle has been particularly influential going forwards. He has made more runs ending in the opposition box than any other full-back this season. They’ve come at an average of 3.9 per 90 minutes, the second-highest rate in the division, behind only Nico O’Reilly, who has played just 54.3% of his minutes at full-back.

Crystal Palace, meanwhile, are feeling the effects of losing the influential Daniel Muñoz. Despite playing solely with wing-backs, they have gone from having the highest average full-back positioning in the Premier League in 2025-26 to sitting below the league average this season. Muñoz was relentless in his work up and down the right flank last term, and his absence has clearly affected the extent to which Palace are able to push their right-sided wing-back up in those wide areas.

The Colombian is now at Nottingham Forest with his former manager Oliver Glasner. They have gone from having the fifth-lowest average touch location for their full-backs to the fourth-highest. That is not only down to Muñoz, but having someone who is able to put in consistent lung-busting runs – he is behind only Ipswich Town’s Leif Davis for the average length of his off-ball runs – helps a lot.

We can’t talk about the league’s most energetic full-backs without mentioning Adrien Truffert, who has continued where he left off last season. The Frenchman is the overlapping king, making more of those runs than any other full-back in the division (23). That comes after he made almost twice as many overlapping runs as any other player across the entire league last season. His manager, Andoni Iraola, may be gone, but he’s clearly got the same license to bomb on from Bournemouth’s new head coach, Marco Rose.

Continuity or change?

Iraola is now at Liverpool, and his full-backs are one of the most asymmetric duos in the league. Milos Kerkez – just as he did at Bournemouth under Iraola – has freedom to push forward and is one of the biggest overlappers in the league, completing 15 such runs thus far. On the other side, Ronald Araújo – who is more of a converted centre-back – plays a far more reserved role.

Manchester City are a curious case. Despite averaging the most possession in the division (65.4%), completing the most passes per game (566) and recording the highest territorial dominance, as measured by field tilt, Enzo Maresca’s team do not use their full-backs in advanced areas to exert that dominance.

Their average full-back touch location is 53.1 metres from goal, making them the fourth-deepest team in the division. That is a huge contrast from Pep Guardiola’s last season, when City ranked third-highest for average full-back positioning. There are plenty of ways to play full-back in the Premier League, but the growing importance of the position is the same for every team.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: The six biggest bombshells in Cameron Bancroft's damning Sandpapergate verdict that tore Australia apart: How Steve Smith will now be hounded, the brave voice they all ignored... and how two English cricket figures are mired in scandal
Sports.content:
Just five days after Pat Cummins addressed the public with the intention of closing the uncomfortable rub of Australian cricket’s sandpaper chapter once and for all, Cameron Bancroft threw the book at the entire Test squad and its entourage.

Enraged by Cummins’ hour-long sermon last Friday, proclaiming his own innocence, Bancroft took to the pages of the West Australian to eviscerate the argument that three players alone knew of the ball-tampering ploys of 2017-18 in a 4,500-word response.

Usman Khawaja’s chronology of events in his recently-released autobiography Sabr had lightened his burden, but ‘the final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference,’ he revealed. ‘It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.’

Perhaps pre-empting what was to follow later on Wednesday, Cricket Australia attacked the issue for the first time since the scandal’s second coming aired earlier this month, promoting an in-house amnesty for those involved during the South Africa tour of 2018 to provide their recollections.

If this was designed to neuter an arsenal of testimony that features David Warner and Chadd Sayers aligning to that of Khawaja, it was like firing a popgun at someone armed with a bazooka.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg (left) announced the new forum in Hobart just hours before Cameron Bancroft's bombshell

For the force of Bancroft’s allegations has turned up the heat on the governing body to upgrade an independent forum into a new probe and for Cummins to revisit the conversation, having dismissed Khawaja’s words as ‘complete and utter nonsense.’

Here are the key takeaways from his bombshell essay...

Now the heat is on Smith and Cummins

Bancroft says he will attend the forum but has ‘reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth.’

And that rather than continuing to hold his tongue, perpetuating the theory that then captain Steve Smith, Bancroft himself and Warner were the sole perpetrators in the ball-tampering scandal, he believes it is important that the country’s cricket-loving public are given transparency.

Bancroft played 10 Tests for Australia but just two were after the sandpapergate scandal

Pat Cummins (left) and Steve Smith will now face questions after Bancroft's claims

Of receiving a nine-month ban and a permanent smear on his reputation as the tamperer-in-chief eight years ago, Bancroft wrote:

‘This was a burden which was heavier than my capacity and I took the bullet for everybody, and it was my choice.

‘However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.

‘It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.

‘When I was questioned during Cricket Australia’s investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account. I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

‘I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.’

Bancroft’s sharing of the finer details will intensify pressure on others to confirm or deny his portrayal of events, with Smith certain to be hounded by questions on his return from his New York home to play for New South Wales this weekend.

As for Cummins? His series of denials over knowledge of sandpaper entering the field of play, stretching back to the original inquiry including putting his name to a joint letter - alongside those of fellow attack members Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon - refuting it in 2021, and culminating in last week’s press conference, will not make this go away.

He must surely now reconsider his position as Australia’s captain.

How Bancroft felt forced into abetting senior stars

Bancroft backed Khawaja’s allegation in Sabr that Australia were doctoring the ball throughout the 2017-18 Ashes by lifting the quarter seam, an illegal tactic to encourage reverse swing.

‘I remember during my first Test match being instructed, along with other members of the team, to push the quarter seam of the ball together after the team took a wicket,’ he recalled, reflecting on how doing anything to gain an advantage over the opposition had been normalised within the Australian team environment.

David Warner (left), Bancroft and Smith were the only three players punished for their role

And so, according to Bancroft, when Warner - who had been in charge of the ball during the 4-0 win over England - suggested sandpaper could be used to rough up one side of the ball in the second Test versus South Africa in Port Elizabeth, he took over the role.

Having entered the match with a 1-0 series advantage, Australia were dismissed for 243 and had seen South Africa close to within 90 for the loss of two wickets by tea on the second day.

Cue the team talk in which Warner’s proposal was aired..

‘I was asked whether I could carry out the task. I felt uncomfortable and compromised. I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating.'

‘But I also saw an opportunity to contribute. I was a youngster playing in his seventh Test match. If you asked me to run through a brick wall at that time I would have.

‘That’s how naive and impressionable I was. I just wanted to be accepted by my teammates beyond the runs and catches I took. This was an opportunity for that.’

Inexperienced in such practice, Bancroft - then 25 - said he looked for reassurance.

‘I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough. All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.’

The moment umpires confronted Bancroft at Cape Town over his use of sandpaper on the ball

Australia took four wickets for 28 runs during the evening session. St George’s Park is a ground renowned for reverse swing due to its warm cross breeze, but this was a particularly fruitful session for the tourists’ attack.

The fact that Bancroft thought he was giving his side an advantage emboldened him to tamper with the ball habitually in the field from that point in what was a second Test defeat until being caught in Cape Town.

The coaches in England implicated in the crime and cover-up...

‘I remember bowling coach David Saker being involved in those conversations. Coach Darren Lehmann was also present.'

In Bancroft's account of the tea-time plot he also claims that after being rumbled by the television cameras shoving the sandpaper down his trousers at Newlands, Australian 12th man Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break with clear instructions.

‘He said to me: “I think it’s time I take that off you now”. And Pete was doing his job after Boof (Lehmann) shouted to him on the walkie talkie “get the f***ing sandpaper off Bangers now”.’

This version of events contradicts the one logged in CA’s 2018 inquiry which logged Lehmann as having said: ‘What the hell is going on?’ Or words to that effect.

‘It has been documented that a coach approached me during our fielding innings telling me that I needed to do more with the sandpaper on the ball to get it to swing. That coach was David Saker and it is true.’

Furthermore, he said Saker was the one who instructed him not to mention sandpaper back in the post-Cape Town media conference.

Australia's bowling coach David Saker went on to work with Ben Stokes at England

This leaves English cricket in something of an awkward spot. Daily Mail Sport is aware that Northamptonshire quizzed Lehmann - who has consistently distanced himself from the scandal - over his involvement when interviewing him for the position of head coach two years ago.

They were satisfied with his response then, and were unconcerned when it re-surfaced recently. Happy with his transformation of the club’s fortunes - they won the Twenty20 Blast for a third time last summer - they extended his initial two-year contract until the end of the 2027 season.

Saker, meanwhile, has worked as England’s fast bowling coach on multiple occasions either side of the sandpaper affair, finishing on the winning side of the Ashes divide in both 2010-11 and 2013 during his initial spell and returning, after leaving his Australian team post in February 2019, on multiple consultancies in the past four years, starting with the Twenty20 World Cup win in 2022, and also including the 2023 and 2025-26 Ashes.

Saker’s most recent assignment was with Brendon McCullum’s white-ball team in Pakistan last month, but the ECB are not intending to use him in the near future.

Lehmann is said to have left his commentary position with ABC radio at England’s win over Australia in Hobart early to consider a response to the allegations.

Northamptonshire quizzed Darren Lehmann before appointing him in 2025

The lowdown on how they tried to get away with it

Bancroft elaborated on the timing of his actions, touched upon in Khawaja’s book, evading suspicion by working outside of TV’s glare.

‘When we returned to the field after the break, the umpires would leave the ball on the outfield, a short distance away from the boundary line. From a broadcast perspective we knew that the cameras didn’t pan onto us as a team until we were about halfway out.'

'This was because the country logos would pop up on the telecast as an intro to the session. This is common practice. We’ve seen this before. Dave (Warner) explained to me why that presented an opportunity. It was also what seemed to be the safest time to do it. Others in the group agreed and gave their opinions on this.’

Such detailed communication about the 30-second windows in which they could operate to avoid detection highlights the depths the Australian team had delved in creating their win-at-all-costs culture.

Traditional methods of trying to get the ball to deviate through the air - of polishing it on trousers with the use of then permitted agents like saliva or sweat - had been ditched just a third of the way into a Test.

And what Bancroft says had been a team culture of fiddling with the quarter seam against Joe Root’s England on home soil weeks earlier had descended into something much more devious.

A brave dissenting voice that everyone ignored

‘Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening. I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

‘I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up. Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.’

Referring to an Australian team meeting on the third morning at Port Elizabeth, Bancroft is talking about media manager Hutchison who left the organisation in April 2018, just days after Lehmann resigned as Australia coach. She has since held positions with Swimming Australia and in Australian rules football.

Australia's former media manager Kate Hutchison with Shane Watson (left) and Xavier Doherty

Usman Khawaja reopened the wounds of sandpapergate with his autobiography

The death knell for Bancroft's international career

‘My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019.

‘I believed that, with time, my performances and conduct might earn me another opportunity to represent Australia.

‘Selection is complicated. There are cricketing reasons, competing players, different conditions and decisions that I have not been part of. For many years I believed I would be selected because I trusted the selection process.

‘But I would be lying if I said I had never wondered whether the unresolved tension surrounding these events in South Africa had played a part.’

Indeed, following two underwhelming performances at the start of the 2019 Ashes, the 33-year-old has finished within the top six Sheffield Shield run scorers for four of the past six seasons and is sixth this year too after four appearances for Western Australia.

Yet whatever he goes on to achieve on the field, it is for his damning revelations off it that he is destined to be remembered.

Sports.title: NFL slams 'inappropriate and offensive' Hitler joke about Patriots coach Mike Vrabel's mustache
Sports.content:
The NFL has publicly rebuked Pro Football Talk's Mike Florio over his controversial comment about Mike Vrabel and the mustache he grew before the New England Patriots' recent trip to Germany.

The Patriots suffered a 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Munich, which was the team's third in its last five games, and Vrabel has naturally been the target of criticism in the days since. Some of that criticism touched upon Vrabel's new mustache.

'If you're in Germany, you've got to be careful trimming that thing,' Florio said during a recent PFT Live podcast.

Florio's producer, Gary Carter, took issue with the joke, which many interpreted as a reference to Hitler's infamous mustache.

'It's funny, Gary. It was 80 years ago. Let us have some fun for crying out loud,' Florio said in response.

Now Jeff Miller, the NFL's EVP of communications, public affairs and policy, has weighed in, calling the comment 'inappropriate and offensive' in a statement provided to Front Office Sports.

New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel pictured at a press conference on Sunday

NFL Insider Mike Florio seemingly made an Adolf Hitler joke at Vrabel's expense

The 61-year-old Florio did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's request for comment. A former West Virginia lawyer, Florio has been covering professional football since the early 2000s.

His comments went viral on social media, with many fans ripping into him for the distasteful on-air remark.

Meanwhile, it was a disastrous trip to Europe for Vrabel and the Patriots, who are now 5-5 and in danger of falling out of the playoff picture.

To make matters worse, quarterback Drake Maye appeared to suffer a season-ending injury after getting sacked by Lions star Aidan Hutchinson.

After receiving medical attention, Maye headed straight for the locker room. He was initially questionable to return before being ruled out of the game a short while later.

Patriots quarterback Drake Maye is set to undergo further tests on an apparent ankle injury

Speaking after the game, Vrabel offered an update on Maye amid major concern from Patriots fans over the extent of the injury: 'Obviously [he] wasn't able to finish the game, so we'll have to get some more tests run when we come back what it ends up being, the severity of whatever injury he has.'

NFL Insider Adam Schefter later added that Maye will undergo those 'additional tests' once the team returned to Foxborough.

The Patriots now welcome their Week 11 bye, which could help provide extra recovery time for the 24-year-old signal-caller.

New England returns to action on November 29 against the Los Angeles Chargers.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino's Man United rallying cry: New boss promises fans it will be a 'SPECIAL' season - despite club sitting in drop zone - as he gets straight to work after flying from US
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino's Man United rallying cry: New boss promises fans it will be a 'SPECIAL' season - despite club sitting in drop zone - as he gets straight to work after flying from US

Mauricio Pochettino has issued a rallying cry to Manchester United supporters, promising that this is going to be a 'special season' despite their dismal start which sees them 18th in the Premier League with just one win from their opening 10 games.

The new Red Devils head coach landed in Manchester on Wednesday morning, hopping straight off a private jet to meet his new players, hours after leading the USA in his final game as their boss.

And during a busy first day among his new surroundings, the Argentine sent a direct message to the club's fanbase as he preached for unity.

'Hi Reds, here's it's Mauricio Pochettino,' he said via a video posted on United's X account at 7.15pm on Wednesday evening.

'I am looking forward to meeting you guys. I hear so many good things about you.

'I hope we bring all the happiness working together and connecting together.

Mauricio Pochettino addressed Manchester United fans directly on Wednesday evening after starting work officially as their new head coach

The new Red Devils head coach has promised a 'special season' in a direct message to fans

Pochettino poses at his unveiling with United director of football Jason Wilcox on Wednesday

'This is going to be a special season to support and to make our players to fight on the field and to get the results that we deserve.'

In a second message in his native Spanish, Pochettino expanded further: 'This message is about being united, like the name Manchester United. We all need to work together.

'I hope to bring the happy moments that this club deserves and create the unity that every team needs so that the players can be at their best on the pitch.'

Those messages came less than eight hours after arriving in England. He landed in Manchester at 11.32am on Wednesday and immediately headed to their Carrington training base where he took a tour and met players and staff.

Speaking to the club's media channels earlier on Wednesday, Pochettino said: 'Thank you so much, I'm very excited to be here. It's an honour, it's a privilege to be in this amazing club. I'm looking forward to starting work.'

The club then officially welcomed the new manager on their website, writing: 'Mauricio Pochettino has officially started work as Manchester United head coach, marking the start of a dream role for the Argentinian.

'Pochettino is joined at United by a team of loyal staff he has worked with at Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and USA. Join us in welcoming Jesus Perez, Miguel D’Agostino, Toni Jimenez, Alec Scott and Sebastiano Pochettino.'

Pochettino had made a promise to end Man City's dominance as United manager in his last interview as United States national team coach on Tuesday evening.

He took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet chartered by the club after his final match on American soil, which saw the US beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati.

But before becoming airborne, Pochettino had time for a final statement Stateside, after being taunted that 'Manchester is blue, and will always be blue' by one of his interviewers.

View this post on Instagram

Earlier on Wednesday, Pochettino made his way to Carrington straight after landing in Manchester, meeting players and staff and taking a tour

The Argentine took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet last night and landed at 11.32am

The manager shared a picture from his journey as he prepared to touch down at the airport (Source: Instagram/Mauricio Pochettino)

'No way,' he shook his head. 'You will see.'

'Give me time. Give me time and then that - that's going to change.'

Pochettino also shared a poignant farewell message to his US set-up, days after breaking down in tears in a press conference ahead of his penultimate time in charge.

Man United fans may also have been pleased to read of Pochettino's new-found love of John Denver's song Country Roads in his goodbye message, a song which is played before kick-off at Old Trafford.

'It is never easy to say goodbye, especially after everything we experienced together.' Pochettino captioned a carousel of photos of his time in the role. 'I always wanted the opportunity to coach in the USA, and I was very happy to have this chance with the national team. Two incredible years, with so many great moments and experiences that will stay with me always.

'From the challenges we faced at the Gold Cup to the excitement of the USA hosting the World Cup, and now finishing our time by reaching the semi-finals of the Nations League, I am proud of what we achieved.

'When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team. Not everything in football can be measured by results, and I believe we have helped build something important for the future of soccer in this country.

The plane believed to be carrying Pochettino and his staff was hired by Manchester United

'This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally. I have discovered a wonderful country, made new friends and enjoyed so many of the traditions. Every time I hear Country Roads, I will forever think of all of you with a smile.

'Thank you to the players, staff, everyone at (the US national team) and all the supporters. Especially to those who believed in us and gave us this opportunity.

'Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.

'I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves. Thank you USA.'

Pochettino had previously explained his emotions as stemming from how difficult the decision had been to leave the national team and re-start at Old Trafford.

‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he said on Friday. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay.

‘I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'

Man United first made contact with Pochettino following their breathless 4-4 draw against Aston Villa in their last match before the international break.

The Man United hierarchy had previously given former head coach Michael Carrick a stay of execution amid a worrying start to the season, but as they prepared to head into the two-week pause in the relegation zone, the board became keen to make a change.

An agonising wait for Carrick followed, with the club legend taking training for multiple sessions at the start of the week as his future was openly mulled by executives including CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

After the duo returned from Monaco, where they had flown to speak to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe about Carrick's future, the 45-year-old was finally dispatched last Thursday morning.

In their statement regarding Pochettino's arrival on Wednesday, United also confirmed the exits of Carrick and Co, writing: 'The club can confirm the departures of Travis Binnion, Jonny Evans, Steve Holland, Craig Mawson and Jonathan Woodgate alongside Michael Carrick.

'We would like to thank the group for their total commitment, dedication and professionalism, and we wish them all good luck for the future.'

Pochettino's United States farewell match went off in pitch-perfect style, which allowed thoughts to quickly move to the next task at hand after the final whistle.

Christian Pulisic helped make sure that Pochettino's reign in charge ended on a high note

The manager will now focus his attentions on getting Man United out of the relegation zone

'When you finish the game, you start in your mind to think about different things,' Pochettino said after the win. 'Of course, it's tough because it's emotional. Because I really love these guys, and I love the players. I love the staff. I love the fans and everything.'

Travelling with Pochettino were outgoing USMNT first-team coach Miguel D'Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott, while his assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez as well as Pochettino's son and fitness coach Sebastiano have already begun preparing for Sunday's matchup with Liverpool at Anfield.

Man United paid a staggering £10million to cleave Pochettino and his staff away from the United States, after the head coach signed a new contract with the national team in the wake of this summer's World Cup.

The quick turnaround means Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty. Furthermore, he is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference around lunchtime on Friday.

Before boarding his flight, Pochettino not only waved to his adoring fans, but took a photo with staff and players on the pitch in Cincinnati.

'It's impossible not to cry, but that is because we care about the people and the people care about us,' he told reporters. 'When that happens, it's normal to show your emotions, no? Because we are human. We are no robots.'

Sports.title: Lionesses star Chloe Kelly cuts a glamorous figure in see-through dress at GQ awards night - hours after being left out of the England squad again
Sports.content:
Lionesses star Chloe Kelly cuts a glamorous figure in see-through dress at GQ awards night - hours after being left out of the England squad again

Lionesses and Arsenal star Chloe Kelly stole the show at the GQ Men of the Year Awards on Tuesday night, going braless in a see-through dress just hours after missing out on Sarina Wiegman's latest England squad.

The two-time Euros and Champions League winner arrived on the red carpet in a long-flowing navy dress, showing off her toned body and glamorous long blonde hair. She was joined by former England stars Mary Earps and Alex Scott.

Kelly was once again left out of Wiegman's selection for the play-offs against Ukraine due to a hamstring injury, as the winger's battle to make the plane for next summer's World Cup continues.

Wiegman announced her squad on Tuesday morning, turning to England's younger generation for the double-header against Ukraine.

Izzy Goodwin is the latest emerging talent to receive a call-up to the Lionesses squad, after Lexi Potter, Erica Meg Parkinson and Freya Godfrey won their first caps in the previous round against Greece.

The 23-year-old London City Lionesses striker scored the equaliser against Kelly's Arsenal last weekend at the Emirates, with the home side dropping points yet again.

Chloe Kelly looked glamorous in a long-flowing navy dress at GQ Men of the Year 2026

The 27-year-old missed out on Wiegman's England squad for the second time in a row

Arsenal have had an underwhelming start to the season, with just three wins in 10 games, and they currently sit in sixth place in the WSL table.

Kelly was dropped for the first time by Wiegman for the previous qualifiers against Greece, alongside fellow forward Ella Toone.

'The main reason is that I think the levels weren't what I expect from them on the pitch,' Wiegman explained at the time.

Toone has returned to the latest squad, with Wiegman praising her reaction to being dropped last time out.

'She responded really well (to being dropped last camp),' Wiegman said: 'Working really hard, she came in and was ready straight away. Going back to club she's done well and that's what has been fed back to me, too.'

As for Kelly, however, it has since been confirmed that she has been struggling with a hamstring injury which has kept her from competitive first-team action since the end of September.

The winger has started just one game for Arsenal, a 0-0 draw with Crystal Palace, and has not registered any goals or assists. She has yet to complete 90 minutes in the WSL this season.

She was previously omitted from Wiegman's squad in 2025 for a lack of playing time as she fought with Mary Fowler for minutes - a disappointment that inspired her move to London from Manchester City.

Kelly was joined by former Arsenal and England legend Alex Scott

Kelly has been battling a hamstring injury that has plagued her since the end of September

Known for showing up in big moments, it was a gamble that paid off and Kelly scored the winning penalty against Spain to win Euros 2025, earning her the nickname Chloe 'clutch' Kelly.

Now, she faces fierce competition from new German signing Lisa Baum, with other talented wingers Caitlin Foord and Olivia Smith refusing to roll over.

Kelly will have to steal the spotlight yet again to get a glimpse of Wiegman's England side.

Sports.title: Legendary commentator MARTIN TYLER on taking the Premier League plunge in 1992, Arsene Wenger's fury, his love of Woking - and THAT Sergio Aguero moment
Sports.content:
Legendary commentator MARTIN TYLER on taking the Premier League plunge in 1992, Arsene Wenger's fury, his love of Woking - and THAT Sergio Aguero moment

Two football images adorn the walls of Martin Tyler’s new home or at least they will when everything is in order.

Tyler has recently moved house and the large, framed photograph of Teddy Sheringham scoring for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool, the only goal of the first Premier League game broadcast live by Sky is still on the floor by the front door.

From wherever it ends up, it will project a moment in time when everything changed for Tyler, having walked away from a steady job at ITV and taken a leap of faith as lead commentator for the new satellite channel.

'A new frontier,' admits Tyler, the undisputed ‘Voice of the Premier League’ by the time he left the role at Sky, more than 30 years later.

'We didn’t know where it would take us, so that was a special day. Feeling a bit like a pioneer. Wondering whether we were all on a fool’s errand. Some people turned down the job I accepted because of the risk. My kids were four and two at the time.

'We used to travel to the games by train in those days, and we would look out of the window and count the satellite dishes as we passed through a big town. We didn’t know whether it was going to work. I wasn’t sure anybody would be watching.

Legendary football commentator Martin Tyler has released a book: TALES FROM THE GANTRY

Tyler was the undoubted 'Voice of the Premier League' by the time he left Sky Sports in 2023

'It was slow off the ground and there was a feeling within the game against live football, that people wouldn’t go to the games if they were televised live, and it ended up the opposite. Attendances have gone up, an amazing paradox. Now you can’t get a ticket.'

Televised football has come a long way since Tyler’s first commentary game, Southampton v Sheffield Wednesday in the old Division Two in 1974, shot with just four cameras for Southern Television.

'Now if you don’t have 24 cameras you can feel a bit short-changed,' he laughs. 'I worked at ITV for about 17 years, most of it commentating and you would get a crew on match day who had been doing Coronation Street or Emmerdale Farm in the week and a match director from light entertainment.'

The Premier League has come a long way, too. Some might argue too far. It has led football from its roots as the working man’s game to a place where clubs are owned by nations states and mired in the legal complications of the Manchester City case.

Tyler wants to reserve comment on City’s financial offences until sentencing is passed, aware he is inextricably bound to their success because of his iconic commentary for Sergio Aguero’s winner in the 93rd minute against Queen’s Park Rangers to snatch the Premier League title from Manchester United in 2012.

'I’ve always said you won’t see anything like it again, and I stick to that,' he says, although he the 'Aguero moment’ as it has become commonly known probably means less to him than it does to others.

He is proud to deliver the words but insists those moments belong to the players, the clubs and the fans, not to him.

Ask about his favourite game from three decades in the Premier League and Tyler instinctively pulls Liverpool’s 4-3 comeback win against Newcastle in 1996 from the thrillers he has called.

His own footballing background, meanwhile, could hardly be any further from the Premier League’s glitzy, moneyed elite.

Tyler has always supported Woking and played as an amateur for Corinthian-Casuals. 'The law was you couldn’t get paid,' he says. 'We were on expenses only and they weren’t dodgy expenses. If I went on the tube to Leytonstone, I got the tube fare repaid and no more.

'I played for five years at that level and never got a penny because that was the rule. I played my last game in 1973 and within two years’ they got rid of it because so many people were bending the rules. An opposition player told me their team were on £75 a game.'

Tyler reflected on his time in the game as a player, coach and commentator with Daily Mail Sport's Matt Barlow

He was famously on commentary for Sergio Aguero's title-winning moment in 2012

From a cricketing family, Tyler was on the books at Surrey where he twice served as 12th man and lived for a time with Bob Willis, who became one of England’s greatest fast bowlers after moving on to Warwickshire.

His manager for a time at Casuals was Surrey legend Micky Stewart, who had also played for the famous amateur football club before turning professional at Charlton. In those days it was possible for the multi-talented to hold down a decent career in two sports.

An afternoon in Tyler’s company is just as likely to involve digressions into non-league football, where he worked as an assistant to Alan Dowson at clubs including Woking and Hampton & Richmond, as it is into the Premier League.

He might regale you with a story about Arsene Wenger and the time, on the way to the gantry at Wigan Athletic, he slipped deeper than he realised into long conversation with the then Arsenal boss about rioting in Paris and almost missed his pre-match slot.

And he might pivot from there into Wenger’s fierce rivalry with Sir Alex Ferguson. 'I have seen Arsene very, very grumpy,' says Tyler. 'When he lost the FA Cup semi-final when Dennis Bergkamp missed the penalty and Ryan Giggs scored.

'I have never seen a manager so angry because he knew he had handed over not only an FA Cup final place but also the domination they enjoyed at that time. They had done the Double in 98 and he felt that was not only about losing a match but losing their psychological edge over their greatest rivals. He was livid. Talk about winning and losing with dignity.'

But there’s every chance he will reminisce about the time when, as a schoolboy Woking supporter in the terrible winter of 1962-63 he was rewarded for volunteering to paint the stands with an invitation to travel on the team bus to an Amateur Cup tie at Lydbrook Athletic.

'We left Woking at seven on the morning of the match for a two o’clock kick-off in Gloucestershire and by nine we were digging the bus out of a snowdrift on the A4,' says Tyler. 'We got there at four, no floodlights, and they had marked the lines on the snow with blue soap powder but there was no way we could play. We turned around to go back, got stuck in Cheltenham and had to stay for the night.'

The only other footballing image on display in Tyler’s home is a photograph of him and Dowson celebrating as the final whistle confirmed their Hampton & Richmond side as Isthmian League champions in 2016.

Tyler has had a hugely varied career, all the way from grassroots level right to the top

Tyler even worked as an assistant coach to Alan Dowson at several Non-League clubs

TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE

After collecting the trophy, Tyler jumped into his car, drove north and less than 24 hours later was at the King Power Stadium to see Leicester crowned champions of England.

'The greatest fairytale story in the Premier League,' as he says. 'I had sampled that in a tiny non-league way, then taken those feelings with me to Leicester where it was multiplied a million times, but I could tell the world a tiny bit about how wonderful they must be feeling.'

The range of his experience is vast. From amateur football in the 60s, through regional television and ITV to Sky’s Premier League revolution. He commentates regularly and coaches at Woking’s academy and has written a book.

It is a wonderful compilation of 110 essays, the reflections on his lifetime in football. 'The random thoughts of a football obsessive,' as he likes to call it.

TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE

Sports.title: Vincent Kompany to RETURN to Bayern dugout less than a month after collapsing at training ground: Club chief reveals 'meningeal irritation' has fully 'healed'
Sports.content:
Vincent Kompany to RETURN to Bayern dugout less than a month after collapsing at training ground: Club chief reveals 'meningeal irritation' has fully 'healed'

Bayern Munich's chief executive has confirmed Vincent Kompany is expected to return to the dugout on Friday, less than a month after collapsing at the club's training ground.

Kompany collapsed on October 23 while watching Bayern's Under-23 side and reportedly suffered from seizures.

The 40-year-old, who suffered a dislocated shoulder in the fall, underwent tests in hospital which determined that a 'meningeal irritation' had been the cause of his collapse.

If left untreated meningeal irritation can become meningitis. The meninges are the membranes around the brain and spinal cord.

Kompany was discharged from hospital the following week to continue his recovery at home.

The Belgian coach is now set to return to the dugout when Bayern face Cologne on Friday, with Kompany due to also address the media tomorrow morning.

Vincent Kompany is set to return to the Bayern Munich dugout for their Bundesliga match on Friday

Kompany's return was officially confirmed by Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen.

'Yes, Vincent is in pretty good spirits. I ran into him today,' Dreesen told German outlet Abendzeitung.

'The meningeal irritation has healed. He has already undergone shoulder surgery.'

Kompany had led training for the first time since his collapse earlier this week, with his arm reportedly in a sling following his shoulder injury.

He had missed five matches during his recovery with Bayern winning two and drawing against Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga.

The German champions also beat Atletico Madrid in the Champions League in his absence, as well as progressing in the DFB Cup.

Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks had overseen the first team during his recovery.

Danks previously worked as Kompany's assistant at Anderlecht before deputising for Dean Smith and Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa and Michael Carrick at Middlesbrough.

Kompany has missed five matches following his collapse at Bayern's training ground on October 23

Bayern had stressed they wanted to give Kompany as much time as required to recover before returning to work.

The German giants play eight matches in the next month, including two matches in the Champions League, before the Bundesliga takes its winter break.

Reports had emerged after Kompany's collapse that club officials had been concerned by his irregular eating habits, as well as barely exercising, drinking excessive amounts of coffee, and taking on too much work.

Bayern sporting director Max Eberl dismissed the claims last month, reiterating that Kompany's illness had been the cause of his collapse rather than his workload.

Sports.title: Leicester City AXE controversial deal with unlicensed gambling company after sponsor sparked fan fury by appointing 'international porn star' as ambassador
Sports.content:
Leicester have decided to end their deal with controversial sponsors BC.GAME six months ahead of schedule.

Fans expressed fury and dismay earlier this month after the club's unlicensed gambling shirt sponsor appointed an 'international porn star' as its new ambassador.

Now Leicester have opted to conclude the partnership – in a move welcomed by supporters. A statement on Wednesday read: ‘The decision follows constructive discussions between both parties in recent days, during which we recognised our differing commercial priorities moving forward.

‘We would like to thank BC.GAME for its support throughout its two-and-a-half-year association with Leicester City and for the constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement.

‘Supporters who have purchased a BC.GAME-branded replica shirt through official LCFC retail channels within the last 28 days (since 21 October, 2026) can return it for a full refund or exchange (subject to availability) by Wednesday 2 December.’

BC.GAME, an online casino company, had been the Foxes' primary shirt sponsor since the start of the 2024-25 season. They announced a partnership with Russian adult content creator Eva Elfie in a video on X earlier this month.

Leicester City have axed a partnership with BC.GAME, after the gambling shirt sponsor appointed 'international porn star' Eva Elfie as its new ambassador

Leicester confirmed fans who have purchased a replica shirt featuring the sponsor's name within the last 28 days can return it for a full refund or exchange by December 2

Elfie, who has 4.8million Instagram followers, is known in Esports and gaming communities too

In recent years, Leicester’s spectacular decline on the pitch has mirrored the relationship with their supporters.

During the years immediately before and after their stunning Premier League triumph in 2016, it was difficult to find a club more in tune with the fanbase.

But a series of baffling decisions – including the tie-up with BC.GAME – eroded trust between the club and their supporters.

Leicester are now in League One and face a long road back but sensible moves like this one suggest they are at least facing in the right direction again.

Sports.title: Premier League identify SIX key refereeing errors in one weekend as boss Howard Webb prepares to appear in front of clubs after Arsenal blunder
Sports.content:
Premier League identify SIX key refereeing errors in one weekend as boss Howard Webb prepares to appear in front of clubs after Arsenal blunder

The Premier League have ruled that referees made a staggering six incorrect decisions in the latest round of matches as officials endured their worst weekend of the season so far.

It was unanimously ruled that referee Farai Hallam should have awarded Kai Havertz a penalty after he was tugged in the area during Arsenal's victory over Hull City, despite being in an offside position.

That is because the laws state that if a foul occurs before an offside offence, a penalty should be awarded.

Although Havertz was in an offside position, he had not committed an offence as he neither played the ball nor interfered with play.

The key match incidents panel (KMI) said: 'Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded.'

Farai Hallam's decision not to award Kai Havertz a penalty was deemed incorrect by the key match incidents panel

Coventry were wrongly denied a spot-kick in their defeat to Everton after James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair

THE 6 WRONG CALLS 1. Everton vs Coventry City: Frank Lampard's side should have been awarded a penalty when James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair. 2. Everton vs Coventry City: The Toffees' second goal, scored by Thierno Barry should not have stood as the ball was adjudged to have gone into the back of the net off his hand. 3. Arsenal vs Hull City: Kai Havertz was denied a penalty after being dragged down. The referee did not award a spot-kick because Havertz in an offside position. However, that decision was incorrect, as he was not committing an offside offence and a spot-kick should therefore have been awarded. 4. Crystal Palace vs Liverpool: Palace were awarded a penalty in the last minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool after Milos Kerkez and Dario Osario clashed heads in the penalty area. The panel saw this as a natural coming together. 5. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: A penalty was given after Abdoul Ouattara tumbled over. The referee gave a foul against Lewis Cook despite Ouattara stepping across him. 6. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: Marcus Tavernier should have seen a second yellow card for time-wasting.

They did, however, praise the VAR for asking the referee to review the incident on the monitor, even though Hallam stuck with his on-field call after watching it back.

In the same weekend, Tottenham Hotspur complained to Pro Ref after Jayden Bogle's heavy challenge on Mathys Tel's ankle, which forced him off injured.

Spurs felt Bogle should have seen red, particularly after Crystal Palace's Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for a similar incident the week prior.

Reviewing the decision, the KMI panel were split but eventually concluded that the foul lacked 'the speed, force or intensity' to be considered serious foul play.

Two of the five panellists, however, felt that the challenge merited a red card.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace's consolation penalty in the 92nd minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool should never have been awarded.

The KMI panel unanimously agreed the referee was wrong to award a penalty when Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio clashed heads while contesting the ball, with contact inevitable given both players were jumping.

However, VAR's decision not to intervene was supported because it was not a 'clear and obvious error'.

It is the second penalty incident in as many weeks that went against Liverpool after Alexander Isak was wrongfully denied a spot-kick against Arsenal.

On the opposite side of Merseyside, James Tarkowski was fortunate not to concede a penalty for pulling Caleb Yirenkyi's hair during Everton's win over Coventry City, with the score still 0-0 at the time. The panel found that Coventry should have been awarded a penalty while Tarkowski should have been booked.

Last season, that incident would likely have resulted in a straight red card. However, the guidance changed this term with red cards only brandished for excessive force.

Thierno Barry's goal that gave Everton the lead faced scrutiny as three panellists believed it should have been disallowed on the pitch, with the 'balance of probability suggesting the ball accidentally struck Barry's hand before directly entering the goal'.

There were also two incorrect decisions in Bournemouth's victory over Ipswich Town.

Bournemouth defender Marcus Tavernier should have been sent off for a second yellow card in the 96th minute for delaying the restart during their 2-1 win, the panel found. However, it was a close call as the panel voted 3-2 against the decision.

Ipswich's scored penalty was also deemed wrongly awarded, with Abdoul Ouattara stepping across Lewis Cook to win the spot-kick rather than being fouled by the defender.

The KMI panel consists of a representative from the Premier League and Pro Ref alongside three former managers or players and meets after every round of Premier League matches to evaluate significant refereeing decisions.

Ref boss Howard Webb will speak to Premier League clubs at a routine meeting on Thursday

While the panel is not new, this is the first season their findings have been publicly released in Pro Ref's drive for greater transparency and accountability.

Pro Ref boss Howard Webb is due to appear in front of clubs on Thursday at a routine Premier League meeting.

And in more positive news for Webb, he will be able to share that VAR delays are down this season after increasing the bar for interventions.

Meanwhile, the KMI panel have assessed 296 decisions this season - only six of which have been judged to be wrong post-VAR.

Sports.title: Man Utd boss Mauricio Pochettino issues defiant message after meeting stars for first time
Sports.content:
Man Utd boss Mauricio Pochettino issues defiant message after meeting stars for first time

Mauricio Pochettino met some of his new Manchester United players on Wednesday as he officially started work at the club's Carrington training base

View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino started work at Manchester United on Wednesday (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United FC)

Mauricio Pochettino is “not wasting time” after he began work as Manchester United head coach on Wednesday following an overnight flight from the United States.

‌



‌



The Argentinian officially took charge after completing his final duties as United States coach in Cincinnati on Tuesday.

‌



Pochettino, who is understood to have signed a deal until the summer of 2029, flew straight to Manchester and was whisked to the club’s training ground at Carrington to meet United staff and start preparations for Sunday’s Premier League match against Liverpool.

‌



“I have plenty of energy,” Pochettino told United’s website after his whirlwind few days. “It’s a privilege to be head coach of Manchester United. And we are not wasting time. We need to be ready to compete on Sunday.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



“Now it’s not time to think about rest, it’s not time to think about sleep. It’s about being ready and to prepare everything to be sure that we are going to compete in the best condition at Anfield.”

His appointment was announced last Friday, just over 24 hours after United had confirmed the sacking of Michael Carrick following the Red Devils’ worst start to a campaign since 1986.

‌



On Tuesday night, Pochettino asked fans to “give him time” to make United the city’s dominant club again after his last match in charge of the United States. Told by former Manchester City loanee DaMarcus Beasley that “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue” in the TNT Sports US studio after the second leg of the Nations League tie against Haiti, Pochettino responded: “You will see. Give me time.

View 2 Images Pochettino beat Haiti 2-0 in his final game with the USMNT (Image: Omar Vega/USSF/Getty Images)

‌



“The new challenge is a big challenge, but at the same time it’s adrenaline you want to feel.

“We need to add our common sense… we know the situation is not a situation that deserves to be a club like Manchester United, the fan base is amazing.”

‌



Pochettino then gave a very short interview to United club staff after arriving at Carrington. “Very excited to be here,” he said.

“It’s an honour. It’s a privilege to be in this amazing club. Yes, looking forward to start to work.”

‌



He added in a later club video directed at fans: “I am looking forward to meeting you guys. I hear so many good things about you. I hope we bring all the happiness working together and connecting together.

“This is going to be a special season to support and to make our players fight on the field and to get the results that we deserve.”
