World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: US steps up pressure on Iran-backed Hezbollah with new sanctions
World.content:
The US Treasury has accused Hezbollah of using charitable organisations as ‘fronts’ for fundraising.

Share US steps up pressure on Iran-backed Hezbollah with new sanctions on social media

The ‌‌United States has announced new sanctions targeting a group that it says serves as a “front organisation” for the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which Washington considers a “terrorist” entity.

On Wednesday, the US Treasury said it had designated the Wa Ta’awanu Association, named for the Arabic words for “and cooperate”, the first two words of a popular Quranic verse.

It described the organisation as a “Hizballah-affiliated charity that provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services”.

Three people based ⁠⁠in Lebanon were also sanctioned. They include the Wa Ta’awanu Association’s founder, Afif Abdel Rida Chouman, and two businessman brothers, Hassan Khechen and Ibrahim Khechen, accused of funnelling money from Iran to Hezbollah.

Two gold companies the brothers reportedly operate were added to the US sanctions list as well.

The administration of US President Donald Trump framed the added sanctions as part of its overarching effort to dismantle Hezbollah’s financial networks and cut off resources for Iran’s proxies.

“The Iranian regime’s attempts to infringe on Lebanon’s sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Since February 28, the US and its ally Israel have waged war against Iran, on the alleged premise that a military offensive was necessary to prevent Tehran from gaining nuclear weapons.

Iran, however, has long denied such ambitions, claiming its uranium enrichment programme is instead for civilian energy infrastructure.



Hezbollah, one of Iran’s regional allies, has been designated a “foreign terrorist organisation” in the US since 1997.

In Wednesday’s statement, the US Treasury accused civilian charitable organisations and humanitarian assistance efforts of channelling “outside donor funds toward Hezbollah’s terrorist activities”.

While Trump earlier this month claimed the conflict with Iran was “effectively over” from a military standpoint, US forces struck Iran’s Qeshm Island this week.

The US also continues to maintain a naval blockade, as well as an effort — dubbed Task Force Iron Gate — to prevent Iran from receiving supplies by land or the Caspian Sea.

To support that effort, the US aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt recently arrived in the Middle East.

Hours before Wednesday’s designations, the US military published a new advisory saying that it would treat ships receiving cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as an attempt to evade its blockade. It warned it could take action against such vessels.

Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) forum that the US would keep imposing “devastating” economic costs on Iran.

Hezbollah has denounced previous US sanctions, calling them an “attempt to intimidate the free Lebanese people”. It added that such economic penalties would have “absolutely no practical effect” on its “strategic choices”.

World.title: Iraq sentences six French nationals to life in prison for joining ISIL
World.content:
Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year.

Share Iraq sentences six French nationals to life in prison for joining ISIL on social media

An Iraqi criminal court has sentenced six French nationals to life in prison for joining the ISIL (ISIS) group, state media reported.

The Karkh Criminal Court delivered the sentencing on Wednesday with representatives from the French embassy in attendance, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported, citing Iraq’s judiciary.

“With these six sentences, the total number of those convicted in this case has reached 16, all of whom are French nationals,” the judiciary said in a statement cited by INA.

All but one of the 16 convicted were sentenced to life. The court sentenced one defendant to 15 years in prison last month.

Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year and charged with belonging to the armed group, which controlled large parts of both countries between 2014 and 2017.

In February, Iraq received more than 5,700 ISIL detainees from over 60 countries after the United States transferred them from Syria, following years of detention in prisons run by Kurdish-led forces.

For years, Iraqi courts handed down hundreds of execution orders and life sentences to people convicted of “terrorism” offences, including foreign fighters. However, some rights groups denounced the trials as rushed and lacking due process.

Among the foreign fighters sentenced on Wednesday was Thomas Barnouin, a 45-year-old Frenchman, who said during his trial that he travelled to Syria convinced he had a religious duty and did not know ISIL would carry out attacks in France, according to AFP.



The ISIL group swept across Syria and Iraq in 2014, committing massacres and forcing women and girls into sexual slavery.

Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over the group in 2017, and Kurdish-led forces supported by Washington defeated ISIL in neighbouring Syria two years later.

Iraq is nonetheless still reckoning with the group’s legacy, with mass graves being uncovered and testimonies of its brutality still to be investigated.

World.title: US lawmakers push to raise minimum wage to $25, end tipped pay system
World.content:
Public support for raising the minimum wage grows, with 78 percent of voters saying it was an important election issue.

In Washington, DC, a group of lawmakers has ramped up calls to increase the United States federal minimum wage and eliminate the subminimum wage, otherwise known as the tipped wage.

The group of 17 lawmakers, which includes current and newly elected House members, is calling for passage of the Living Wage For All Act, which has been languishing since it was introduced in April.

The legislation’s original lead sponsors include Representative Delia Ramirez of Illinois, Representative Jesus “Chuy” Garcia, also of Illinois, and Representative Analilia Mejia of New Jersey.

The bill aims to gradually raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, with different timelines depending on the size of the employer.

Brad Lander, a congressman-elect from Brooklyn, New York, who says he will join the bill as a co-sponsor when the next congressional session begins in January, told Al Jazeera: “Doing it federally is the right way to go. Tying it into broader legislation that raises the minimum wage for all workers is a great approach.”

For larger employers — those with more than 500 employees nationwide or at least $1bn in annual revenue — the increase would be completed by 2031. Smaller employers would have until 2038.

After that, the minimum wage would be maintained at two-thirds of the US median hourly wage, with annual adjustments to preserve that ratio.

The bill would also eliminate the separate subminimum wage for tipped workers, currently $2.13 an hour. Under the existing framework, employers can count workers’ tips towards their minimum-wage requirements.



While several states have raised their own minimum wages, the federal rate remains $7.25 an hour, where it has stood since 2009. Washington, DC, has the highest minimum wage of any US jurisdiction, at $18.40 an hour, followed by Washington state at $17.13. However, 20 states do not have a minimum wage higher than the federal rate. Those states include Texas, Georgia and Iowa.

Laws governing the subminimum wage also vary across states. Seven states require employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage before tips, including Alaska, California and Nevada.

Others, including New York, have higher tipped cash wages than the federal rate but allow employers to take a tip credit, meaning they can pay workers less than the standard minimum wage as long as their tips make up the difference.

In New York, minimum wages vary by region. The rate is $17 an hour in New York City and its surrounding suburbs, and $16 an hour in the rest of the state.

For tipped workers outside the food service industry, the minimum cash wage is $14.15 in the New York City metropolitan area and $13.30 elsewhere in the state. For restaurant workers, those rates are $11.35 and $10.70, respectively.

The distinction is a point of contention for Lander.

“All workers deserve a raise. The 45 million working people who make less than $20 an hour deserve a raise, and the tipped subminimum wage is inexcusable at this point,” he said.

A long-term fight

The subminimum wage has long been viewed as a legacy of racial and economic inequalities that disproportionately affected Black Americans. When Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act in 1938, establishing the first federal minimum wage, it excluded categories of workers in domestic and agricultural occupations, which disproportionately employed Black Americans.

Congress extended federal minimum-wage protections to restaurant and other service workers in 1966. But rather than requiring employers to pay tipped workers the full minimum wage, lawmakers established a separate tipped minimum wage, initially set at 50 percent of the standard federal rate. Employers could count customers’ tips towards the rest of a worker’s minimum-wage obligation. In 1996, Congress froze the federal tipped cash wage at $2.13 an hour, where it remains today.

The purchasing power of the standard federal minimum wage has also changed drastically. Adjusted for inflation, the $7.25 minimum wage in 2009 would be worth $11.32 today, meaning it has lost 36 percent of its purchasing power.



The federal minimum wage’s purchasing power peaked in 1968, when the rate was $1.60 an hour. Adjusted for inflation, that peak would be worth significantly more than the current minimum wage, representing a loss of roughly 53 percent in purchasing power.

The push to raise wages also has public support. A new poll released on Wednesday by One Fair Wage, an organisation that has long campaigned to eliminate the subminimum wage, found that 78 percent of voters considered raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour an important factor in their vote in the recent US midterm elections, where Republicans were dealt massive losses with the cost of living a key issue for voters.

“Washington has allowed the federal minimum wage to become increasingly disconnected from the economic reality facing American families,” Saru Jayaraman, president of One Fair Wage, said in a statement.

The push for the Living Wage For All Act comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in the new Congress.

The last major attempt to raise the federal minimum wage came during former President Joe Biden’s first year in office. Democrats sought to increase the rate from $7.25 to $15 an hour through the Raise the Wage Act of 2021, which was included in the original proposal for Biden’s American Rescue Plan.

Ultimately, the effort failed after the Senate rejected a motion to waive budgetary rules that would have allowed the minimum-wage increase to proceed. The March 2021 vote was 42–58, with all Republicans opposed, joined by seven Democrats and independent Senator Angus King of Maine, who caucuses with Democrats.

Although the legislation failed, Biden raised the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $15 an hour in 2022 through an executive order. President Donald Trump revoked that order in 2025.

World.title: Floodwaters submerge cars and parking lots in Florida town
World.content:
Floodwaters submerge cars and parking lots in Florida town

NewsFeed Floodwaters submerge cars and parking lots in Florida town

Floodwaters turned streets and parking lots into rivers in Davie, Florida, inundating roads, swallowing parking spaces, and leaving drivers facing dangerous conditions. Broward County has declared a state of emergency.

World.title: US Defence Secretary Hegseth reveals military partnership on Venezuela trip
World.content:
Pete Hegseth says the agreement will include joint training and intelligence sharing with the Venezuelan military.

United States Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth has announced a new agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.

The Pentagon chief made a surprise visit to the Venezuelan capital of Caracas on Wednesday, becoming the latest in a series of high-level officials under US President Donald Trump to travel to the South American country.

During his stop, Hegseth revealed that the deal would include intelligence sharing and joint training for the two countries’ militaries.

“We see this as a reestablishment of our defence partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries,” he said.

Their shared aim would be “to stabilise Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all”, Hegseth added.

Hegseth was hosted by interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who has led the government since her swearing-in on January 5. His trip was not previously announced by the Pentagon.

The Trump administration has exerted heavy influence over Rodriguez and her government after abducting former President Nicolas Maduro during a military attack on January 3.

Rodriguez was previously Venezuela’s vice president. Trump has justified the attack as a law enforcement effort designed to force Maduro to “stand trial on American soil”, charging him with weapons- and drug-related crimes.

After the operation, Trump also said he planned to “run” Venezuela, and he told The Atlantic magazine that Rodriguez could “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she refuses to comply with US demands.



Since then, he has worked with the Venezuelan government to extract concessions on US priorities such as energy development and military cooperation.

Critics have accused the US of reducing Venezuela to a vassal state and exploiting its resources while leaving Maduro’s government largely intact.

Under Maduro, the Venezuelan state was accused of human rights abuses including torture, arbitrary imprisonment and extrajudicial killings.

Still, Trump has held up Venezuela as a model he would like to see replicated in other countries, like Iran and Cuba.

In Wednesday’s remarks, Hegseth said that the South American country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner”.

Rodriguez hailed the agreement as a “resumption of the technical-military relationship between both countries”, and she expressed hope that their cooperation could be “brought to its highest possible level”.

Hegseth is also set to meet with officials in Colombia later on Wednesday as part of a trip to the region.

Colombian Defence Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora said on Tuesday that the US would deliver a C-130 Hercules military aircraft, as the US steps up military involvement across Latin America.

Hegseth has faced pressure to step down from his role, following a midterm election in which the US-Israel war on Iran contributed to Republican losses across the country.

A key member of Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth has championed the war, as well as efforts to weaken rules of engagement designed to limit civilian casualties.

Hegseth narrowly avoided a recent impeachment effort in the US Congress this month. The sponsor of that effort, outgoing Republican US Representative Thomas Massie, cited the Iran war as well as a campaign of military strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels off the coast of Latin America.

The boat-strike campaign has killed an estimated 244 people and has been denounced as extrajudicial killings by legal experts.

World.title: What does Israel’s new ground offensive mean for Palestinians in Gaza?
World.content:
Israeli tanks advance beyond the ‘Yellow Line’, forcing Palestinians to flee again as Gaza faces a deepening humanitarian crisis.

Share What does Israel’s new ground offensive mean for Palestinians in Gaza? on social media

Israeli forces have launched a ground operation in central Gaza, advancing west of the line they withdrew to under last year’s ceasefire and forcing Palestinian families, many of whom had already been displaced, to flee their homes once again.

The operation, the first major ground offensive publicly announced by the Israeli military since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, follows a warning by the United States-backed Board of Peace that the 13-month-old agreement risks collapse. In a report to the United Nations Security Council, the board accused Israel of restricting aid and delaying the deployment of Palestinian police, and Hamas of continuing armed activity and taxing goods entering Gaza. Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”.

What happened in central Gaza on Wednesday?

Israeli tanks and bulldozers advanced towards Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south route, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij refugee camp, Al Jazeera correspondents reported. Palestinians fled those areas, amid heavy gunfire and artillery shelling.

The Israeli military body overseeing civilian affairs in the occupied Palestinian territory, known as COGAT, said the army had closed that stretch of Salah al-Din Street and told residents to stay away until further notice. The army hasn’t said how long the operation will last.

An Israeli attack on al-Mughraqa killed one person and wounded several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera. Separate attacks in Deir el-Balah, Nuseirat and Gaza City killed three more people.



“We fear this may be the start of a broader operation and that displacement will begin anew, as we have not yet recovered from the effects of the previous war and displacement,” Mahmoud al-Saafin, a 27-year-old resident of Bureij, told the AFP news agency.

The areas targeted in the operation lie west of the “Yellow Line”, where Israeli troops pulled back to under the first phase of President Donald Trump’s plan, leaving them in about 53 percent of Gaza. Israel has, however, continued to move that line gradually, and it now encompasses around two-thirds of the enclave. More than two million Palestinians live in the rest, mostly in tents.

Why does Israel say it launched the operation?

The military told AFP it had launched “a precise operation” west of the line “to remove a threat” posed to the Israeli army, adding that “there is Hamas infrastructure in the area, adding it was responding to Hamas ceasefire violations.

“We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip,” the army said.

Israel says Hamas has been regrouping and rearming, and it has stepped up attacks. On Saturday, an Israeli attack killed Samir Abu Younis, the Qassam Brigades’ Rafah commander.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel won’t withdraw until Hamas is dismantled. “If tensions escalate on the various fronts, we are fully prepared to seize additional territory, evacuate local residents and incorporate it into Israel’s permanent security perimeter,” he said.

How have Palestinian groups, including Hamas, responded?

Hamas called the operation and the forced evacuations northeast of Nuseirat “a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement”, and urged mediators to “intervene immediately”.

It accused Israel of “systematically” squeezing Palestinians into a narrow area of Gaza, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s caretaker government of escalating to escape its domestic crises.

Hamas also condemned the Board of Peace for having “unacceptably equated the occupation’s ongoing aggression with the suffering of the Palestinian victim”.

The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine called the operation a “prelude” to a wider escalation aimed at forcibly displacing Palestinians.

Has Israel violated the Gaza ceasefire before?

Israeli forces have kept up near-daily attacks, shelling and home demolitions. Gaza’s Ministry of Health says they have killed 1,658 Palestinians and wounded 6,000 since the ceasefire began. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in the same period, the Reuters news agency reports.



On Tuesday alone, Israeli fire killed six Palestinians, including a six-year-old boy, Gaza’s civil defence agency and hospitals told AFP.

Aid remains restricted. About 100,000 tents are waiting to enter Gaza, held up by crossing closures and lengthy Israeli security checks, the International Organization for Migration says.

Where does the ceasefire stand?

The ceasefire halted major fighting, but the rest of the plan, covering Israel’s withdrawal, reconstruction and Hamas’s disarmament, has stalled. Hamas agreed in July to a roadmap to give up its weapons and hand over governance. Israel rejected it.

Israel also hasn’t let the board’s technocratic administration start work in Gaza. That has held up an international stabilisation force, The Associated Press news agency reported.

The board spelled out what failure would mean. “Should it collapse, there would be no road map to return to, no administration to deploy and no enabling environment to rebuild.”

World.title: Pew Research: Islam on track to become world’s largest religion by 2035
World.content:
The report projects steady increases for both Christianity and Islam from 2020 to 2070.

Share Pew Research: Islam on track to become world’s largest religion by 2035 on social media

Islam will soon be the world’s largest religion, taking Christianity’s place by 2035, according to the Pew Research Center.

The research organisation assessed the Muslim population’s expected growth in a report released on Tuesday, which projected that both groups will see their numbers increase over the next few decades.

However, the Muslim population will “simply [grow] at a faster pace,” the report said.

The projection analysed 201 countries and territories, accounting for 99.98 percent of the population, and spanned the geographic distribution and future changes of seven religious groups and affiliations – Muslims, Christians, Jews, Hindus, Buddhists, and others – from the years 2020 to 2070.

The results are part of the Pew-Templeton Global Religious Futures Project, which seeks to analyse religious change and its impact on the world.

The organisation stressed that the findings are “not intended to predict all the ways the world could change” as several other events might occur that could impact a group’s religious affiliation, such as socioeconomic circumstances, natural disasters, and wars.

Baby boom

According to the report, Muslims give birth to the highest number of children, one of the factors that Pew says make them the world’s fastest-growing religious group.

Fertility rates were found to be 3.1 children per Muslim woman, while Christians, with the second-highest fertility rate, had 2.5 children per Christian woman.

A generation can typically replace itself with a fertility rate of around 2.1 children per woman.



Both groups are expected to “keep pace with the world’s overall population growth”, according to Pew.

Muslims could gain up to 1.6 billion people through natural population change, compared to 792 million people for Christians.

Estimated losses

Muslims are expected to have much smaller losses in their community than Christians leaving or converting religions.

“The difference between the number of people who join and leave Islam is expected to result in a loss of 8 million people during the projection period, [whereas] for Christians, the net difference is a projected loss of 105 million people,” the report said.

Those who choose to depart from Christianity may not identify with a religion afterwards, including atheists and agnostics.

However, the research finds that Islam’s projected growth is not the result of people converting from Christianity: the number of Muslims projected to convert to Christianity is only “slightly greater” than the number of Christians expected to become Muslims.

Country dynamics

Between 2020 and 2070, “most of the growth in the world’s Muslim population is projected to occur in places where Muslims already make up a majority of the population”, said Pew.

By 2070, Muslims will make up 95 percent of the population in the Middle East-North Africa region. Meanwhile, in the Asia-Pacific region, Muslims are expected to surpass the religiously unaffiliated.

Muslims were the majority religious group in 53 countries in 2020. An additional 1.2 billion Muslims are expected to live in these countries by 2070, representing 74 percent of the projected growth of the global Muslim population.

For instance, Pakistan’s Muslim population is expected to double from 227 million in 2020 to 461 million in 2070. The country will become the world’s largest Muslim population, overtaking Indonesia, Pew said.

Christian growth will also be concentrated across 120 countries where Christians were already the majority of the population.

Overall, the population of Christians in these countries is forecast to rise by 630 million, representing 92 percent of global Christian growth.

World.title: Putin’s nuclear briefcase makes surprise appearance at China summit
World.content:
NewsFeed Putin’s nuclear briefcase makes surprise appearance at China summit

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s nuclear briefcase, which can be used to authorise a nuclear strike, was spotted at the APEC summit in China. It was being carried to a meeting by a naval officer, according to footage aired by Russian state TV.

World.title: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
World.content:
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.

The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.

With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

The BBC's defence correspondent Jonathan Beale reports from near Kupyansk, where he went underground with the 13th Khartiia Operational Brigade.

Read Jonathan Beale's dispatch from the front line.

World.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
World.content:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground â accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

World.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
World.content:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

World.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
World.content:
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in more than a year on Wednesday, as they prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.

After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.

Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the war in Ukraine could be discussed.

However the main focus during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

World.title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
World.content:
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

World.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a masterpiece, say critics
World.content:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

World.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl found along French motorway in 1987
World.content:
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in SuÃ¨vres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother â tested in an unrelated case â matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor AnaÃ¯s Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.

French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.

El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.

Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.

World.title: William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
World.content:
On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.

During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UKâIndia bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".

The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.

Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UKâIndia partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".

When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.

The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".

The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.

The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.

World.title: Nigerian govt approves establishment of public relations university
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has approved the establishment of the University of Public Relations and Leadership in Gudi, Nasarawa State.

The president announced the approval on Wednesday while delivering an address on the fourth day of the ongoing World Public Relations Forum in Abuja.

Mr Tinubu, who was represented by Vice-President Kashim Shettima, said the institution would contribute to human capital development and provide opportunities to train a new generation of communication leaders equipped to respond to the demands of a rapidly changing global environment.

“In this regard, I am pleased to formally approve and support the establishment of the University of Public Relations and Leadership, a first-of-its-kind initiative designed to advance specialised education, research, professional development and leadership training in public relations, strategic communications and related disciplines.

“Establishing this specialised institution represents a forward-looking investment in human capital and the future of the communication profession. It will provide opportunities to develop a new generation of communication leaders equipped to respond to the demands of a rapidly changing global environment,” he said.

He commended leadership of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), the Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation, and the Nasarawa State Government for their collaboration and commitment towards making the university a reality.

The president urged relevant stakeholders to support the institution to ensure that it develops into a centre of excellence with national, continental and international recognition.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I encourage all relevant stakeholders to work together to ensure the university develops into a centre of excellence with national, continental and international recognition,” he said.

The university approval comes amid the federal government’s efforts to halt the proliferation of higher institutions in the country, referencing concerns about inadequate funding, duplication of academic programmes, under-utilisation of existing facilities and declining standards of education.

In August 2025, the Federal Executive Council (FEC), presided over by President Tinubu, approved a seven-year moratorium on the establishment of new federal universities, polytechnics and colleges of education. The Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa, said the government wanted to redirect resources towards strengthening existing institutions, improving infrastructure and addressing shortages of academic staff.

The government subsequently extended the restriction to private tertiary institutions in March 2026, making the president’s latest announcement particularly significant.

However, the University of Public Relations and Leadership is a project of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), rather than a conventional federal university. The institute had earlier in July 2025 signed a memorandum of understanding with the Nasarawa State Government for the establishment of the institution in Gudi, Akwanga Local Government Area. The state government reportedly provided 101 hectares of land for the project.

Aside from the policy implications, the proposed institution is expected to provide specialised academic and professional training in public relations, strategic communication and leadership, areas that have become increasingly important in the digital age.

Public relations professionals play a significant role in shaping public perception, managing institutional reputations, communicating government policies and building trust between public institutions and citizens. With the increasing spread of misinformation and disinformation, particularly through social media, specialised training could help produce professionals better equipped to promote credible information, manage communication crises and strengthen public engagement.

The NIPR has said the project is intended to bridge the communication gap between leaders and the public while deepening the practice and development of public relations globally.

Call for investment opportunities

Mr Tinubu also urged delegates, particularly those from other countries, to explore investment opportunities in Nigeria.

“Distinguished delegates, as you participate in this forum, I invite you to take a second interest in Nigeria beyond the conference programme. Look beyond the discussions in the hall and discover the opportunities that our country offers.

READ ALSO: Tinubu receives state police bill after approval by all 36 State Assemblies

“Explore our investment potentials: vibrant entrepreneurial ecosystem, creative industries, rich cultural heritage, tourism assets and the ingenuity of our people – the can-do spirit. Of the ten unicorns in Africa, six are in Nigeria: Flutterwave, Opay, InterSwitch, Moove, Moniepoint. That Nigerian spirit, that resilience, we are loud.

“I’m a swashbuckling capitalist. Africans are by nature a humble and self-effacing people, but Nigerians, no. I beg to disagree. We are loud. We are confident, and of course, we are extremely hardworking people. Nigeria is a country of enormous possibilities. We’re a nation of diverse cultures, talents and ideas, with a youthful population, a dynamic private sector and a strong determination to build a more prosperous future,” he added.

Mr Tinubu predicted that Nigeria’s population would surpass that of the United States by 2050, making it the world’s third most populous country, with an estimated 440 million people.

He also praised Nigerians for their achievements in business and other fields, referencing the country’s representation among the world’s wealthiest Black people.

“One out of every four black men is a Nigerian. By 2050, one out of every three black men will be a Nigerian. We will surpass the United States and become the third most populous nation on earth, with a population of 440 million people. And by the end of the century, Nigeria will be the most populous nation on earth. So we have every reason to play Nigeria. I encourage you to engage with our institutions, interact with our businesses.

“The richest black man on earth is a bloody Nigerian. The second richest black man in the world is another bloody Nigerian. The third richest black man in the world is also a bloody Nigerian. I encourage you to engage with our institutions, interact with our businesses, establish vocational relationships and explore opportunities for partnerships and investment. Nigeria goes beyond the stories we tell and what you read on the social media.

“The most outwardly mobile immigrant community in the United States are the Nigerian Americans. Sixty per cent of them have college degrees. So Nigeria goes beyond 419. Nigeria is much more bigger than that. We want you to leave Nigeria, Prof Justin Green, not only with new professional knowledge and friendships, but also with a deeper appreciation of our country and a renewed interest in its prospects. We hope that your experience here will encourage you to return, invest, collaborate, and become ambassadors of Nigeria’s positive story,” the president said.

World.title: Consent, not defence in sex with minors, police warn
World.content:
The Police Command in Lagos State has warned that sexual intercourse with anyone below 18 constitutes a felony punishable by life imprisonment under the state’s Criminal Law.

SP Abimbola Adebisi, the police spokesperson in Lagos, gave the warning in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria in Lagos on Wednesday, while highlighting measures to prevent child sexual abuse and protect minors.

“Consent was not a defence in cases involving sexual intercourse with a child, irrespective of whether the offender described the child as a girlfriend or boyfriend.

“The law recognised anyone below 18 as a child and criminalised sexual intercourse with such an individual, regardless of gender,” she said.

The spokesperson advised parents to introduce sex education early, particularly when children began communicating their needs and interacting with others.

She said children should be taught about their bodies, how to identify their private parts and understand that nobody had the right to touch them inappropriately.

According to her, parents should also explain the difference between appropriate and inappropriate touching to help children recognise potentially abusive situations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ms Adebisi, a police superintendent, urged teachers and school guidance counsellors to intensify sensitisation and provide age-appropriate sex education, stressing that parents had the primary responsibility for educating and protecting their children.

She also called on community members to remain vigilant and report suspicious situations involving minors to their parents to ensure their safety.

The spokesperson advised parents to be cautious about individuals granted access to their children, including domestic workers, caregivers and others entrusted with their supervision.

She urged parents to regularly monitor their children’s activities and interactions with such individuals and understand their experiences while in their care.

Ms Adebisi further emphasised the need for open communication between parents and children, urging parents to create an environment where children could freely share their experiences without fear of being dismissed or reprimanded.

She said parents should listen attentively to their children and encourage them to speak out whenever they experienced or noticed inappropriate conduct or anything that made them uncomfortable.

According to her, such openness will give children the confidence to report suspicious behaviour and enable parents to take timely action to prevent sexual abuse.

World.title: Electricity worker stabbed to death over power disconnection
World.content:
The Benin Electricity Distribution Company (BEDC) says five suspects have been arrested in connection with the killing of its worker, Oscar Eze, in Umunede, Delta, on Monday, over electricity disconnection.

The Acting Managing Director of BEDC, Jonathan Lawani, disclosed this on Wednesday in Benin during a news conference at the company headquarters.

Mr Lawani alleged that Mr Eze, a 38-year-old staff member, was stabbed to death for carrying out an official assignment in the community.

The incident, he alleged, occurred after the deceased disconnected a property over an outstanding electricity bill of nearly N300,000.

According to him, some people allegedly traced Mr Eze to a house in the community and stabbed him repeatedly, leaving him dead at the scene.

Mr Lawani said the disconnection was carried out in line with the regulatory framework governing electricity distribution.

“The only instrument approved by NERC to demand payment from those who refused to pay their monthly electricity bills is disconnection,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The BEDC boss condemned the killing, stressing that electricity workers should not be attacked for performing their official duties.

“The fact that we come to your house to demand payment for the service we have rendered, irrespective of your dissatisfaction with our service, does not give you the right to attack,” he said.

Mr Lawani said the company’s management visited the Assistant Inspector–General of Police’s office, the Divisional Police Officer in Umunede and the scene of the incident on Tuesday.

He disclosed that while five suspects had been arrested, others were still at large.

The acting managing director said the deceased left behind a son from an earlier marriage, a wife he married four months ago and an elderly mother.

He called on the Delta State Government to provide adequate security for electricity workers, warning that continued attacks could threaten BEDC’s operations in the state.

“We believe that the government should provide an enabling environment for people to work, and for a critical sector like electricity, we should be protected,” he said.

Mr Lawani said the company would pursue the case until justice is served.

“We cannot recover his life. We can never take his life back to his people but one thing is that we must get justice, for him,” he said.

State governments urged to protect electricity workers

Also speaking, Abel Enechaziam, head of Maximum Demand Customer and acting chief commercial officer of BEDC, urged state governments to protect electricity workers across the states where the company operates.

READ ALSO: UCH installs new power substation amid recurring electricity crisis

Mr Enechaziam said the company could no longer tolerate attacks and harassment of personnel providing electricity services.

“We cannot continue to tolerate this kind of event. It is very sad,” he said.

He urged the public to stop molesting and harassing service providers in the electricity sector.

He advised customers, dissatisfied with BEDC’s services, to use the company’s complaint channels or approach the relevant electricity regulatory authorities for redress.

He urged electricity consumers to resolve disputes through established channels rather than resort to violence against workers.

(NAN)

World.title: PREMIUM TIMES editor-in-chief Musikilu Mojeed, lawyers, others honoured at Gavel International awards
World.content:
PREMIUM TIMES Editor-in-Chief, Musikilu Mojeed, and late journalist and publisher, Oladotun Oladipo, were among the recipients of awards at the 2026 Gavel International Annual Lecture and Awards in Lagos on Tuesday.

Mr Mojeed received the Ernest Sesei Ikoli/Gavel International Media Achievement Award in recognition of his work in journalism, investigative reporting and media development, as well as his mentorship of young journalists.

In a letter dated 14 September, the organisers commended his professionalism and commitment to public-interest journalism.

They also cited his leadership at PREMIUM TIMES, contribution to online journalism, role in establishing the Guild of Corporate Online Publishers (GOCOP) and presidency of the International Press Institute (IPI), Nigeria.

The award is named after Ernest Sesei Ikoli, a pioneer Nigerian journalist and the first managing director of the Daily Times.

Mr Oladipo received a posthumous Distinguished Merit Award for his contributions to ethical and credible online journalism. His wife, Taiwo, collected the award on his behalf from Maureen Chigbo.

Mr Oladipo founded The Eagle Online and worked with Newswatch, The Punch, Nigerian Tribune, Nigerian Compass and The Sun. He was also politics editor of The Punch and served as GOCOP president from 2017 to 2021.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He died in Lagos on 25 August, aged 56, after nearly three decades in journalism.

Other award recipients included senior lawyers Bayo Ojo, Olisa Agbakoba, Tayo Oyetibo, George Etomi, Kayode Filani and Iniruo Wills.

The event, held at the OPTS Hall of the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Alausa, Ikeja, featured a lecture by retired Court of Appeal Justice Oludotun Adefope-Okojie on the role of the judiciary in Nigeria’s electoral process.

Speaking on the theme, “Electoral Process in Nigeria: Managing the Boundaries of Judicial Intervention”, Mrs Adefope-Okojie urged courts to intervene when political parties breach their constitutions or violate electoral laws.

“The courts must no longer refuse to intervene where political parties violate their own constitution and ‘rubbish’ the Electoral Act. They must intervene to sanitise the system,” she said.

She cautioned, however, against courts declaring candidates who lost elections as winners. Where the lawful winner could not be established, she said, a fresh election should be held to allow voters decide the outcome.

Mrs Adefope-Okojie said 1,209 petitions were filed over the 1,280 elective positions contested in the 2023 general elections, but only 103 succeeded. She said the high number of petitions reflected a lack of confidence in the country’s electoral process.

She also pointed to disputes arising from flawed party congresses, the imposition of candidates and unlawful substitutions as sources of election litigation.

Citing the Supreme Court’s 30 April 2026 decision in PDP v. Sule Lamido, she argued that courts should not use the doctrine of party autonomy as a reason to avoid examining alleged breaches of party constitutions and electoral laws.

The retired justice also raised concerns about the burden of proof in election petitions. She said petitioners often face difficulties proving irregularities polling unit by polling unit and securing the testimony of electoral officials.

She called for clearer rules on electronic evidence, particularly evidence from the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and the INEC Result Viewing Portal. She said uncertainty over what amounts to communication failure could complicate disputes over the electronic transmission of election results.

Mrs Adefope-Okojie outlined four approaches to electoral justice: corrective, protective, substitutive and abdicative. She described corrective justice as addressing electoral wrongs and protective justice as ordering a fresh election where the rightful winner cannot be established.

She said substitutive justice occurs when courts declare candidates who did not receive the voters’ mandate as winners, while abdicative justice describes situations where courts decline to examine credible allegations of malpractice because of procedural or evidential obstacles.

She urged judges and election petition tribunal members to protect voters’ rights and remain within the limits of their judicial responsibilities.

“The Constitution places sovereignty in the people and makes the Courts the guardians of that sovereignty, not its holders,” she said.

She stated that the aim of electoral adjudication should ultimately be to make court intervention less necessary by ensuring that elections are decided by voters.

“The final aim of electoral adjudication should be its own decline: a democracy in which elections are won and lost at the ballot box, not in the courtroom,” she said.

The chairman of the occasion, Anthony George-Ikoli, SAN, said the judiciary had a duty to protect electoral integrity without taking over the responsibilities of voters and electoral bodies.

“The judiciary must neither become an alternative electoral commission nor abdicate its responsibility as the ultimate guardian of electoral legality. That is the delicate boundary we are here this morning to interrogate,” he said.

He noted that judicial restraint should not prevent judges from addressing electoral violations, just as their willingness to intervene should not lead to overreach.

“Judicial restraint should not amount to judicial retreat, just as judicial courage should not degenerate into overreach,” he said.

Another speaker, Femi Falana, SAN, called for reforms to electoral litigation to reduce the burden on the Supreme Court.

He proposed a return to the previous arrangement for appeals in governorship election disputes and criticised the different appeal procedures for presidential and legislative election petitions. He said efforts to address the problems had stalled since 2011.

Gavel International publisher, Mustapha Ogunsakin, praised Mrs Adefope-Okojie’s judicial career, including her role in a 2005 tribunal set up to investigate security breaches at the Ikeja High Court.

He said the tribunal’s report was commended by Bola Tinubu, then governor of Lagos State, and helped establish a framework for court security in the state.

Gavel International, a legal and justice news platform, began its annual lecture series in 2015.

World.title: Motsepe arrives Abuja for 48th CAF Ordinary General Assembly
World.content:
The President of the Confederation of African Football, Patrice Motsepe, arrived in the Federal Capital, Abuja, on Wednesday to a rousing welcome ahead of Saturday’s 48th CAF General Assembly, which Nigeria is hosting.

Mr Motsepe was received on arrival at the Presidential Wing of the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport by the Chairman of the National Sports Commission, Shehu Dikko; Mr Motsepe’s Special Advisor and former NFF President Amaju Pinnick, CAF Secretary General, Samson Adamu, CAF’s Project Lead for both the OGA and the CAF Awards Christian Emeruwa, Nigeria’s Project Lead for both events Ademola Olajire, and other top CAF Management and staff members.

His private jet touched down at the airport at 5:51 p.m., and his entourage immediately left for the Transcorp Hilton Hotel, where all VVIPs, delegates, CAF Management and Staff, invited Guests and other stakeholders are lodging for Saturday’s General Assembly.

It is the first time in 17 years that Nigeria is hosting the CAF General Assembly – the biggest gathering of football administrators and stakeholders in the African continent, bringing together the leaders and managers of the Confederation of African Football, CAF Executive Committee members, Presidents and General Secretaries of all of CAF’s 54 Member Associations, special guests from FIFA including the FIFA President and General Secretary, special guests from other Confederations of FIFA, and other stakeholders of the game globally.

This year is also the first time that one country is hosting both the General Assembly and the CAF Awards – which is the biggest football-centred awards ceremony in Africa, and brings together the best actors of the past (legends) and present, as well as CAF chieftains, guests and stakeholders.

The CAF Awards will take place in Lagos on Wednesday, 2nd December

While the OGA is scheduled for the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre, the CAF Awards will take place inside the expansive Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, formerly known as the National Theatre.
