World.title: CCB official testifies on Useni’s controversial acquisition of London property linked to Ozekhome
World.content:
An official of the Code of Conduct Bureau (CCB) has shared fresh findings regarding the late Jeremiah Useni’s London property, which is at the centre of the criminal trial involving senior lawyer Mike Ozekhome, who is facing charges of forging documents to claim the house.

Testifying as a prosecution on Wednesday, CCB official, Raaji Babatunde, pointed out a discrepancy between Mr Useni’s acclaimed value of the property and the official value quoted in a UK property tribunal’s judgement given last year in a legal dispute over the ownership of the asset.

According to Mr Babatunde, an assistant chief Superintendent with the CCB, while Mr Useni “put the figure for the acquisition of the property at £79,000 in 1992”, the tribunal judgement in London disclosed the purchase price of the property that year as £200,000.

Also, the CCB official, who said he processed Mr Useni’s asset declaration as incoming senator representing Plateau South in 2015, testified that the late military general acquired the assets with an amount of money beyond his earnings as a public officer.

These details add another layer to the controversy that has characterised the property since it became a subject of public attention last year.

The London property, held under shadowy ownership for decades, is at the heart of the forgery case instituted against Mr Ozekhome and the late general’s son, Ponfa Useni.

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) filed the charges after the lid on the mess surrounding the property was blown open in a London property tribunal judgement.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In the trial, Mr Ozekhome and Ponfa face charges of impersonation and forgery of a Nigerian passport presented before a London tribunal to support Mr Ozekhome’s failed bid to claim the London property.

The older Mr Useni, who died in January 2025, acquired the property at No. 79, Randall Avenue, London NW2, United Kingdom, under the fictitious name Tali Shani in 1992.

This was during his active years as a military officer when he took political offices, including the FCT minister, under the military regime.

His purported attempt to transfer its ownership of the London property to Mr Ozekhome allegedly led to the presentation of documents, which the property tribunal in London found to be forged to support the false identities of Tali Shani.

On 27 February, the office of the EFCC arraigned Messrs Ozekhome and Mr Useni’s son, Ponfa, on 12 counts of forgery and impersonation.

According to the charges, the defendants conspired in 2020 alongside the late Useni, a retired general, and made a false Nigerian passport with the number A07535463 and the name Tali Shani, supporting it to be issued by the Nigeria Immigration Service, to claim a property in the United Kingdom.

Similarly, the prosecution charged them with “using a false passport to facilitate the claim of the property.”

The prosecution also alleged that Mr Ozekhome helped Ponfa Useni to impersonate Tali Shani in 2020. Together, they allegedly created a fake “Irrevocable Power of Attorney” to help Mr Ozekhome claim the property.

They denied all the charges.

Process of asset declaration

Led in evidence on Wednesday by the Director of Public Prosecution of the Federation (DPPF) Rotimi Oyedepo, Mr Babatunde said he personally attended to the late general when he went to the CCB to declare his assets in 2015.

The witness said the late Mr Useni cited salaries and sale of property as the source of the funds for the purchase of the disputed property.

Two years after Mr Useni’s asset declaration, Mr Babatunde said he was directed by his superiors to analyse the asset declaration form.

He said the amount of money paid for the acquisition of the property “was far in excess of what is fairly attributed to the income of the public officer and his position.”

Mr Babatunde said Mr Useni declared £18,000 as his annual income, while he claimed to have acquired the property for £79,000 in 1992, although the UK tribunal judgement put the value at £200,000.

He said he wrote a request to the Revenue Mobilisation and Fiscal Commission (RMFC) and got a response as well as a net-worth analysis, which Mr Oyedepo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), submitted as evidence.

He also presented the order and decision of London’s first-tier Tribunal Property Chamber Land Registration in the case between Tali Shani and Mr Ozekhome.

Summarising the CCB’s findings on the property, the witness said, “Because of the inconsistency we noticed between the asset declaration form and the judgment of the tribunal, specifically the price of the acquisition of the property and the owners of the property, while the declarant confirmed that he is the owner. The judgment of the London Court named Tali Shani as the owner.

“Secondly, the record from RMFC places a substantial gap between the lawful income of the late Jeremiah Useni and the value of the property.”

Due to the disparity, the CCB got the property documents in the United Kingdom, and the judgment of the London court, and “the property was confiscated to the Federal Government of Nigeria,” the witness testified.

Defence pokes holes into prosecution’s case

Under cross-examination by Mr Ozekhome’s lawyer Paul Erokoro, a SAN, the witness said he told the EFCC his findings but did not write a statement. He also said he was not sure if the EFCC officer who questioned him wrote down any statement.

He also could not recall the name of the officer or the time and date he was questioned.

Mr Babatunde also said he did not know the late Mr Useni’s rank in the military. He insisted that the general made the declaration as an incoming senator in 2015.

He said he did not issue the late general the acknowledgement slip of the asset declaration form but insisted that he attended to him.

Mr Babatunde acknowledged that the issuing authority on the asset declaration form is Sam Saba.

The witness also said the original asset declaration form was in safe custody in the strong room in the office of the CCB’s chairman.

Mr Erokoro then asked the witness to show the court the letter the CCB wrote to their legal partner to obtain the London Court’s decision; the witness said it was in the office.

However, he said he could not remember the name or address of the lawyer. He also denied knowing the value of the pounds to naira as at 1992.

The witness affirmed that the late Mr Useni had shares, stocks and bonds.

Thereafter, trial judge Chizoba adjourned the case till 23 November.

Highlights of previous testimony

The first prosecution witness, a Nigerian Immigration Service (NIS) officer, testified in March that a passport with the name Tali Shani was fake.

Akim Aridegbe, a principal staff officer to the Comptroller-General of the NIS, said the passport was not issued by the NIS.

Despite the passport sharing features of a genuine copy, it has no record in the NIS database, Mr Aridegbe said.

A forensic examiner, Bamaiyi Mairiga, also told the Court that the passport with the name Tali Shani was forged.

Backstory

Mr Ozekhome’s prosecution in Nigeria stemmed from a London Tribunal’s judgement that blocked him from claiming a property in North London in September 2025.

In August 2021, Mr Ozekhome sought to transfer the property to his name, claiming it was a gift from a man who presented himself as Tali Shani in appreciation for legal services.

But this was challenged in September 2022 by Westfields Solicitors, claiming to represent “Ms Tali Shani,” who insisted she was the registered owner of the property since 1993 and had never signed any transfer.

Ruling on the dispute, Judge Paton of the UK Tribunal ruled that the house was secretly bought in 1993 by the late Mr Useni, former Nigerian Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, using a false identity.

According to the tribunal, Mr Ozekhome’s steps to claim the property were built on a network of fraud, impersonation, and forged documents. Still, it concluded that the late Mr Useni, former Minister of FCT, was the genuine purchaser of the property in 1993.

Similarly, the London tribunal uncovered fraudulent Nigerian identity records, including a passport, a National Identification Number (NIN), and a Tax Identification Number (TIN) allegedly generated with the connivance of corrupt officials at the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), the Immigration Service, and the Federal Inland Revenue Service.

In November 2025, CCB obtained an order of the Federal High Court in Abuja to freeze the property on the basis that it was shadily acquired by Mr Useni.

The CCB reported to the court in a filing in January that the property remained unclaimed weeks after a newspaper publication invited anyone with a legitimate claim to it to step forward.

The court subsequently ordered the property’s final forfeiture to the federal government.

Meanwhile, the Legal Practitioners’ Privileges Committee has since placed Mr Ozekhome’s SAN rank under suspension pending the outcome of his ongoing trial.

World.title: ‘Not for endorsement,’ Peter Obi clarifies meeting with US lawmakers
World.content:
The 2027 presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has clarified that his recent meeting with members of the US Congress in Washington, DC, was not to seek political endorsement ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Mr Obi, a former governor of Anambra State, made the clarification in a post on his X handle on Wednesday.

There were reports suggesting that the NDC candidate’s recent meeting with the US lawmakers was intended to get them to endorse him.

But the former governor, in the X post, insisted he did not characterise his meeting with the lawmakers as an endorsement of his political aspirations.

“The primary purpose of the visit was to engage with congressional leaders and other influential American stakeholders, exchange perspectives, and discuss matters related to Nigeria’s development, the welfare of our citizens and, most importantly, the consolidation of our democracy,” he said.

Mr Obi stressed that he was especially concentrating on strengthening democratic institutions, advancing accountability, and ensuring that Nigeria’s electoral process produces elections that are free, fair, transparent and credible.

“These matters should concern every Nigerian who is committed to our country’s future.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I consider engagements of this kind valuable, and I encourage other Nigerian political leaders, especially those seeking public office, to pursue similar discussions with international stakeholders,” he stated.

“Our democracy can be strengthened through constructive dialogue, the exchange of experiences and a shared commitment to credible elections.”

The NDC faulted what he termed “inaccurate interpretations” of his meeting with the US lawmakers, stressing that Nigeria’s democratic future should not be distorted by such interpretations.

“My mission centred on Nigeria, its people and the future of our democracy- not on endorsing any individual,” he added.

World.title: Nigeria destroys 1,000 illicit weapons, takes total destroyed to 20,000 – Official
World.content:
The National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons (NCCSALW) says it has destroyed approximately 20,000 illicit, decommissioned and unserviceable weapons since its establishment.

The centre disclosed this on Wednesday in an X post after destroying another batch of approximately 1,000 weapons at the Muhammadu Buhari Cantonment, Giri, Abuja.

The exercise, conducted through burning and subsequent smelting, is part of the federal government’s efforts to curb the proliferation of illicit firearms and prevent recovered weapons from returning to criminal circulation.

The centre said the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, noted at the exercise that illicit weapons continued to fuel terrorism, banditry, kidnapping and communal conflicts across the country.

It added that Mr Ribadu stressed the importance of properly documenting and accounting for recovered weapons before their destruction to prevent diversion and re-entry into circulation.

According to the centre, the NSA reaffirmed the federal government’s commitment to an intelligence-led, multi-agency approach to tackling insecurity, including strengthening border security, disrupting criminal financing networks and deepening international cooperation.

It said Mr Ribadu also highlighted the centre’s engagement with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to identify external sponsors and funding sources behind illicit arms trafficking.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In his remarks, the Director General of the NCCSALW, Johnson Kokumo, a retired deputy inspector general of police, said the centre had recovered 22,377 illicitly acquired, obsolete, decommissioned and unserviceable weapons since its establishment.

He said the latest exercise brought the total number of weapons destroyed to approximately 20,000.

Mr Kokumo said the destruction programme was designed to ensure that recovered firearms were permanently removed from circulation rather than returned to the weapons market through diversion or other channels.

He credited the Nigeria Police Force with accounting for 11,907 automatic firearms and locally fabricated weapons destroyed under the programme.

He also acknowledged the contributions of the Nigerian Armed Forces, State Security Service (SSS), Nigeria Customs Service and other security agencies to weapons recovery efforts.

The destruction exercise comes amid persistent security challenges involving armed groups and criminal networks across Nigeria, including insurgency in the North-east, banditry and mass kidnappings in the North-west and parts of the North-central region, as well as communal violence in several states.

The proliferation of small arms and light weapons has remained a major concern for Nigerian security authorities, with illicit firearms frequently recovered during military and police operations against insurgents, bandits and other armed criminal groups.

The NCCSALW was established under the Office of the National Security Adviser to coordinate efforts to control the proliferation and misuse of small arms and light weapons in Nigeria.

World.title: More Nigerian varsities make global list, few break into top 500
World.content:
By Joseph Erunke

Abuja—Nigeria has expanded its presence in the global university rankings, recording its highest-ever number of institutions in the Times Higher Education, THE, Interdisciplinary Science Rankings, even as the country struggles to push more universities into the world’s top 500.



The latest 2027 ranking saw 27 Nigerian universities make the global list, a 50 per cent increase from the 18 institutions ranked in 2026.



However, the country’s growing numerical presence has not translated into stronger representation among the world’s leading institutions.

While the number of Nigerian universities participating in the exercise continued to rise, only two made it into the global top 300, against five in the previous editio

Similarly, seven Nigerian institutions featured in the top 500, compared with eight in 2026.

Amid the mixed performance, Covenant University, Ota, Ogun State, retained its position as Africa’s leading institution in interdisciplinary science, placing joint 49th globally to remain the continent’s only university among the world’s top 50 for the second consecutive year.

The private university also maintained its lead over Egypt’s Cairo University, which placed joint 52nd globally, reinforcing Nigeria’s capacity to produce globally competitive institutions, despite persistent funding and research infrastructure challenges.

Chairman of the Nigerian Tertiary Education Ranking Advisory Committee, NiTERAC, Professor Emeritus Peter Okebukola, who disclosed the results in a statement issued in Abuja yesterday, described the growing participation of Nigerian universities as encouraging but warned that the country must move beyond increasing its numbers to improving its actual performance.

The 2027 ranking, released on November 18, assessed 1,058 universities across 102 countries and territories.

It measured institutions’ capacity to fund, support and deliver research cutting across scientific disciplines.

According to Okebukola, Nigeria’s performance represents a significant expansion from the 19 universities ranked in the maiden 2025 edition, while another seven institutions were accorded Reporter status after submitting data.

This brings the total number of Nigerian universities participating in the 2027 exercise to 34, compared with 30 in 2026 and 27 in 2025.

He said Nigeria had climbed from 16th to 11th position globally in terms of the number of ranked universities, retaining its second position in Africa behind Egypt, which has 37 institutions.

Despite the progress, the ranking exposed the difficulty Nigerian universities face in translating increased participation into improved research competitiveness.

Under the latest assessment, Covenant University emerged as Nigeria’s highest-ranked institution, followed by Landmark University, Omu-Aran, which occupied the 251–300 global band.

Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, and the University of Ilorin were placed in the 351–400 band, while the University of Calabar, University of Lagos and University of Nigeria, Nsukka, occupied the 401–500 category.

Ladoke Akintola University of Technology, Obafemi Awolowo University and the University of Benin completed Nigeria’s top 10, placing within the 501–600 band.

Okebukola, former Executive Secretary of the National Universities Commission,NUC, particularly applauded Ahmadu Bello University and the University of Calabar for their remarkable improvement.

ABU moved from the 601–800 band in 2026 to the 351–400 category in the latest ranking.

, while the University of Calabar climbed from the 601–800 band to the 401–500 category.

Eight Nigerian universities also made their debut in the global ranking. They are the Federal University of Technology, Minna; Michael Okpara University of Agriculture, Umudike; Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi; University of Jos; Rivers State University; Babcock University; Bells University of Technology; and Nile University of Nigeria. Osun State University equally returned to the ranking after a year’s absence.

Of the 27 Nigerian universities ranked, 14 are federal institutions, seven state-owned, while six are privately-owned.

Explaining the factors behind Nigeria’s relatively weak showing in the upper brackets, Okebukola identified inadequate funding for interdisciplinary science research, insufficient dedicated research facilities, weak administrative support and the absence of institutional policies encouraging collaboration across scientific disciplines as major constraints.

He explained that the THE ranking uses 11 performance indicators grouped into three broad pillars: inputs, processes and outputs.

While inputs account for 19 per cent of the assessment and processes 16 per cent, outputs carry the highest weight at 65 per cent.

According to him, many Nigerian universities recorded poor scores in the inputs and processes categories, particularly in research funding and the institutional structures required to promote collaboration across disciplines.

Okebukola commended the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, for prioritising the global competitiveness of Nigerian tertiary institutions and establishing NiTERAC to coordinate efforts towards improving the international standing of the country’s universities.

World.title: Doctors risking heart disease through overwork, sleep deprivation – Experts
World.content:
… Warn of burnout, stroke risks, seek healthier work environments

By Chioma Obinna

Health experts yesterday expressed concerns that Nigerian medical doctors are exposing themselves to increased risks of cardiovascular diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, through excessive workloads, sleep deprivation, chronic stress and failure to undergo regular medical checks.



The experts, who spoke at the Annual General Meeting/Scientific Conference of the Medical and Dental Consultants’ Association of Nigeria (MDCAN), Federal Medical Centre (FMC), Ebute-Metta, Lagos tagged: “ Your Body, Your Responsibility: A Personal Guide to Cancer Risk Reduction for Physicians, lamented that physicians, despite their knowledge of healthy living, often neglect their own health while attending to patients.



They called for a deliberate shift towards preventive healthcare among doctors, warning that professional dedication should not come at the expense of their lives.



Speaking at the conference, Chief Consultant Cardiologist at the Lagos State University Teaching Hospital, LASUTH, Dr Folashade Daniel, said doctors must consciously balance their professional responsibilities with adequate rest, exercise, healthy eating and routine medical examinations.



Daniel, who spoke on protecting the hearts of physicians, said: “I don’t think physicians can balance their work, healthy living, and their mobility. It has to be intentional.”



She noted that doctors sometimes work for extended hours, leaving little time for personal health, but stressed that they must make deliberate efforts to recover and maintain healthy lifestyles.



“First of all, know that your life is not just, your life doesn’t just entail your job. You are a person, you have a family, and you have responsibilities. Yes, to your patients, but also to your family, to yourself,” she said.



According to her, doctors should make adequate rest, relaxation, healthy eating and physical activity essential parts of their routines, rather than treating them as optional activities.



She advised physicians with a family history of cardiovascular disease to exercise extra caution and make annual health checks a priority.



“Take your birthday, for example, your one anniversary, to do a check-up. And then look up all the results with a colleague. Don’t just be your own doctors. Let somebody look at what you have, the results you have done, and give you advice as need arises,” Daniel said.



The cardiologist also urged government to strengthen policies that promote healthier food choices and safer working environments.



She identified excessive salt, preservatives and trans fats in food, particularly from repeatedly used frying oil, as concerns requiring stronger regulation.



Daniel further recommended accessible spaces for physical activity in workplaces, including walkways, trees and encouragement for workers to use stairs where appropriate.



She said access to affordable medicines and wider coverage of the National Health Insurance Scheme was equally important in preventing and managing cardiovascular diseases.



On the consequences of excessive working hours, she warned that sleep deprivation and prolonged shifts could expose doctors to additional health risks.



Earlier, Chairman of MDCAN, FMC Ebute-Metta, Dr Lucky Okpetu, said the theme was chosen because physicians frequently advise patients to adopt healthy lifestyles but fail to practise the same advice themselves.



“We found out that physicians hardly take care of them. They themselves don’t look after their hearts. They indulge in things they are not supposed to. They advise their patients to do the right thing. But they do not do what they tell the patients to do,” he said.

Okpetu, a consultant haematologist, urged doctors to have personal physicians and undergo regular medical examinations.



“The ideal thing to do is, as a physician, you must have your own physician. You have to see your physician regularly,” he said.

He listed kidney function, blood sugar and other necessary medical tests among the routine checks doctors should undertake, adding that lifestyle choices remained critical to cardiovascular health.



Speaking, the Medical Director and Chief Executive Officer of FMC Ebute-Metta, Dr Saheed Ogunme, also challenged physicians to make patients’ health and well-being their foremost consideration while strengthening collaboration between hospital management and consultants.



He stressed that healthcare delivery was a collective responsibility and that no single professional could claim credit for successful patient outcomes.



“If a patient comes to our hospital, has a successful surgery and goes home, it’s not the doctor or consultant that has done this alone. It’s the other people too, who participate in the care of that patient,” he said.



Ogunme also urged doctors to pay attention to their own health, noting that physicians often have no personal doctors to consult when they become ill.



The conference also examined the role of artificial intelligence in reducing workload and addressing manpower shortages in the health sector.



Also, Professor of Medicine and Chairman, Medical Advisory Committee, FMC Ebute-Metta, Prof. Adebowale Adekoya, said AI could help reduce burnout by automating routine documentation and administrative tasks.



He cited ambient scribe technology, which can listen to conversations between healthcare professionals and patients and convert them into clinical documentation.



“AI can listen to conversation between the doctor, the nurse, and their patients. And then transcribe that using voice to text, using language models,” he said.



However, Adekoya warned that doctors must verify AI-generated information before using it in patient care. “Although the responsibility of making sure that it’s accurate still lies with the caregiver of reading it before posting it,” he said.



He also cautioned against applying AI tools developed using foreign population data indiscriminately to Nigerian patients, insisting that local data must inform medical technologies used in the country.



“The responsibility is on us now to generate our own data,” he said.



Chairman of the occasion, Prof. Oluwatoyin Ashiru, urged medical professionals to protect their physical and emotional well-being, warning that exhausted and distressed doctors could struggle to provide the quality of care expected of them.



He challenged professional associations to protect the welfare of healthcare workers, strengthen institutional partnerships and ensure that professional disagreements did not undermine patient care.



His message was clear: doctors must protect themselves while protecting others.

World.title: Foursquare G.O. tasks graduands on integrity, national development
World.content:
By Olayinka Latona

The General Overseer of the Foursquare Gospel Church in Nigeria, Rev. Sam Aboyeji, has charged graduating students of LIFE Theological Seminary, Ikorodu, Lagos, to uphold integrity and sound biblical doctrine as they prepare to preach the Gospel and contribute to society.

Aboyeji gave the charge at the institution’s 2026 graduation ceremony, where he urged the graduands to see their graduation not as an end but as a stepping stone to greater responsibilities in God’s service.

Speaking on the theme of the ceremony, “Trailblazers,” and drawing from Titus 2:7-8, the cleric said the credibility of their future ministries would depend largely on the integrity of their personal lives.

He said: “You have been equipped with knowledge and skills that must now find expression in faithful service to God and humanity. I charge you to distinguish yourselves as trailblazers whose lives exemplify the sound doctrine you have received.”

Quoting Apostle Paul’s admonition to Titus, Aboyeji urged the graduates to be examples of good works, demonstrating integrity in doctrine, reverence, incorruptible speech and soundness of character.

He warned against compromising biblical truths in the face of challenges, urging them to remain courageous, steadfast and diligent in their ministerial responsibilities.

“Be courageous in breaking new ground, steadfast in the face of challenges, uncompromising in matters of biblical truth, and diligent in the discharge of your ministerial responsibilities,” he said.

Reminding the graduands that service to God was a sacred responsibility requiring accountability to the Creator, the General Overseer urged them to remain worthy ambassadors of LIFE Theological Seminary and vessels of honour in their respective fields of assignment.

Also speaking, the Chairman of the Governing Council of LIFE Theological Seminary, Rev. Joe Ameh, urged the graduating class to distinguish themselves as trailblazers and uncompromising ambassadors of Christ in a society increasingly challenged by moral decay and corruption.

Ameh said the graduates were expected to demonstrate the values of Christianity and apply their theological training in addressing contemporary issues in a rapidly changing society.

He said: “As trailblazers, those of you graduating today are expected to be ardent and passionate in distinguishing yourselves before a world characterised by normlessness and anomie. You are expected to be pathfinders in blazing the trail that should characterise the essence of being Christians with a fair measure of theological education in responding to contemporary issues in a fast-evolving setting.”

The seminary council chairman also decried what he described as pervasive corrupt practices threatening the nation’s God-given assets and resources.

He, however, urged the new ministers to remain steadfast and uphold Christian values despite pressures to compromise their standards.

“Despite these pervasive corruptive tendencies, you are to be different in words and conduct and indeed be zealous to propagate sound Christian values irrespective of pressures to compromise our Christian standards,” he said.

World.title: Blindness: Eritrea, 10 others eliminate trachoma from Africa as Nigeria lags
World.content:
By Sola Ogundipe

Eritrea has become the 11th country in the World Health Organisation (WHO) African Region to eliminate trachoma as a public health problem, raising hopes of ending a neglected tropical disease (NTD) that continues to threaten the sight of millions of people across the continent.

The achievement, validated by WHO, places Eritrea among 11 African countries that have successfully tackled the disease through sustained public health interventions, improved access to treatment, hygiene promotion and community mobilisation.

Eritrea joins Algeria, Benin, Burundi, Eritrea, The Gambia, Ghana, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Senegal and Togo as the African countries that have received WHO validation as the number of countries that have achieved elimination globally stands at 34.

Eritrea is also the 66th country globally and the 23rd in the WHO African Region to eliminate at least one neglected tropical disease.

According to WHO, Eritrea achieved the milestone, following two decades of sustained interventions targeting the disease, particularly in remote rural communities where poor access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare had fuelled its spread.

Eritrea’s success followed nationwide surveys conducted between 2006 and 2020, which helped identify affected communities and guide the rollout of interventions across the country.

The government subsequently implemented WHO’s recommended SAFE strategy, a combination of surgery for advanced cases, antibiotics to clear infection, facial cleanliness to limit transmission and environmental improvements, particularly better access to water and sanitation.

A notable feature of the campaign was its community-led sanitation approach, which delivered significant public health gains despite limited external funding.

Health workers deployed digital tools for data collection and mapping to identify affected populations, track disease patterns and direct resources to hard-to-reach communities.

In a congratulatory message, WHO Director-General, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, “I congratulate the Government and people of Eritrea on this historic achievement. After two decades of determined effort, Eritrea has consigned trachoma as a public health problem to history. This is a victory for the communities most affected by this devastating disease, and a powerful example of what sustained national commitment can achieve.”

On his part, WHO Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, said Eritrea’s achievement demonstrated the impact of political commitment, community participation and effective partnerships in tackling neglected tropical diseases.

“I congratulate Eritrea on this historic public health milestone. It shows what is possible through sustained political commitment, community leadership and strong partnerships. Eritrea’s achievement brings us closer to a world free from the suffering caused by neglected tropical diseases and sends a strong message of hope to other African countries working towards trachoma elimination,” he stated.

WHO Representative to Eritrea, Dr Mary Stephen, said: “This success belongs first and foremost to the people of Eritrea. The elimination of trachoma as a public health problem is the result of strong national leadership and ownership, and collaboration between communities, the Ministry of Health, the Fred Hollows Foundation, development partners and health workers across the country,” she said.

While Eritrea has secured WHO validation, Nigeria is making significant progress towards eliminating trachoma, although the disease remains a public health challenge in some parts of the country.

The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare disclosed that 11 local government areas (LGAs) remained to achieve elimination status out of 134 previously identified endemic LGAs.

The country has stopped mass drug administration (MDA) in 116 LGAs after they met the WHO elimination threshold, representing approximately 87 per cent progress towards eliminating the disease in affected areas.

Director and Programme Manager of the National Trachoma Programme, Nicholas Olobio, said Nigeria had also performed more than 100,000 surgeries for trachomatous trichiasis, the advanced stage of the disease that can cause irreversible blindness.

Nigeria’s progress has been hindered by the implementation of WHO’s SAFE strategy, supported by mass antibiotic distribution, eye surgeries, hygiene promotion and improved access to water and sanitation.

Trachoma is among the 21 diseases and disease groups covered by WHO’s Neglected Tropical Diseases Roadmap 2021–2030, which seeks to accelerate prevention, control, elimination and eradication efforts, particularly among populations living in poverty and underserved communities.

The disease is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis and spreads through contact with eye and nasal discharge from infected people. Repeated infections can cause scarring of the inner eyelid, forcing the eyelashes to turn inward and scratch the eyeball. Without treatment, the condition can cause irreversible blindness.

It disproportionately affects poor and underserved communities, particularly those with inadequate access to clean water, sanitation, hygiene facilities and essential healthcare. Despite significant global progress, the disease remains a public health challenge in parts of the world.

Although Africa has recorded substantial progress, it remains the continent most affected by the disease. The global target for eliminating trachoma as a public health problem is part of WHO’s neglected tropical diseases road map for 2021 to 2030.

World.title: How tech engineering lands Ghenewede NATE honours
World.content:
By Islamiyyah Adekanbi

Engr. Goodluck Idele’s decades of engineering work, including his involvement in building and delivering vessels for the Nigerian Navy and oil and gas companies, have earned him a Fellowship Award from the Nigeria Association of Technologists in Engineering, NATE.



Idele was inducted as a Fellow at a ceremony held on Thursday, November 12, at the Dr. Obi Wali International Conference Centre, Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

The award recognises his professional achievements and contributions to engineering. His work on vessels for clients in Nigeria and abroad reflects the technical expertise and commitment to quality that NATE cited in honouring him.

NATE is an affiliate member of the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria, COREN.

The ceremony brought together guests from academia, government, the engineering profession and the oil and gas industry.

Idele’s fellowship marks a milestone in a career spanning several decades and recognises his service to engineering practice.

World.title: Eyesan seeks more opportunities for women in petroleum sector
World.content:
By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja

The Commission Chief Executive, Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), Mrs. Oritsemeyiwa Eyesan, has called for greater opportunities for women in the petroleum sector.

Eyesan made the call on Wednesday while speaking on the topic, “Breaking Barriers,” at the 2026 Women in NNPC Limited (WIN) in Abuja, under the theme, “Powered by Her.”

She asked women to also prioritise competence, resilience and continuous learning as critical tools for breaking barriers.

A statement by the Commission said Eyesan urged women not to be discouraged by delayed promotions, stressing that professional growth requires patience, perseverance and commitment to excellence.

Sharing her personal experience, Eyesan disclosed that she spent eight years in the same position without promotion but remained committed to her career.

Eyesan also emphasised the importance of involving men in conversations about gender inclusion and women’s advancement, noting that some of the major milestones in her career were made possible by men who recognised her competence and provided opportunities.

“I was appointed the first female Head of Strategy, not by a woman, but by a man who believed in my competence. I was also appointed as the first female EVP Upstream, NNPCL, by a man who believed in my competence, and today I stand as the first female CCE of NUPRC by Mr President, who is a man who believes that I will deliver,” she said.

Acknowledging the gradual increase in opportunities for women in the industry, the NUPRC boss called for more deliberate efforts to achieve meaningful representation, advocating at least 25 per cent participation of women in leadership and decision-making positions.

“Is it happening at the scale we want? Not quite, we need more. At least one in four. Not just because we want to make up the numbers but because we think we bring value to the table,” she said.

The NUPRC boss also commended the Group Chief Executive Officer of NNPC Limited, Mr Bayo Ojulari, for the WIN initiative, describing it as a valuable platform for positioning young women for greater opportunities and leadership roles in the oil and gas industry.

She noted that the Nigerian oil and gas industry was recording significant progress through collaboration between the regulator, NNPC Limited and other industry operators.

World.title: UAC completes sale of 43% stake in DP World Logistics
World.content:
By Peter Egwuatu

UAC of Nigeria Plc has completed the sale of its 43 per cent equity interest in DP World Logistics Limited, formerly known as MDS Logistics Limited, to 22 Plus Invest Limited, a member of the Tropical General Investments (TGI) Group.

Ayomipo Wey, Company Secretary and Group General Counsel of UACN, disclosed this in a statement sent to the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) on Wednesday.

The transaction, which was completed on November 18, 2026, followed approval by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC).

The company said the development followed its earlier announcement on September 24, 2026, of an agreement to sell its shareholding in DP World Logistics as part of its divestment plans.

Commenting on the completion of the transaction, UAC Group Managing Director, Fola Aiyesimoju, expressed satisfaction with the successful conclusion of the divestment.

He also appreciated the DP World team for its contributions to the UAC Group over the years, while wishing DP World and 22 Plus Invest a successful partnership and continued progress in their future business operations.

Similarly, Vice Chairman of TGI Group, Farouk Gumel, welcomed the completion of the acquisition, expressing optimism about the partnership with DP World.

Gumel said the partnership would focus on advancing a shared vision for Africa’s trade and logistics sector, particularly by strengthening supply chains, improving regional connectivity and creating long-term value for customers and economies across the continent.

He added that the acquisition marked a new phase for DP World Logistics under its new ownership and was expected to support efforts to strengthen logistics operations and trade connectivity across Africa.

World.title: American strategist denies receiving $4.5m for Tinubu interview
World.content:
By Nwafor Sunday Polycarp, Online News Editor

American political strategist and media personality, Diana London, has denied receiving $4.5 million from the Nigerian government for her recent interview with President Bola Tinubu.

London, in a post on her X account on Wednesday night, described the allegation as a smear campaign, insisting that neither the Nigerian government nor anyone else in the country paid her the reported sum.

She said her visit to Nigeria was to interview Tinubu for a documentary and to see the country for herself.

“I unequivocally deny the claim that Nigeria’s government nor anyone else in Nigeria paid me $4.5 million. I went to Nigeria to interview President Tinubu @officialABAT for parts of a documentary and see Nigeria for myself.

“This SMEAR CAMPAIGN can make noise, but can’t change the facts or stop me from speaking the truth,” she wrote.

The denial comes amid controversy surrounding her interview with Tinubu at the Presidential Villa, Abuja, on Tuesday, and reports alleging that she was linked to a $4.5 million lobbying arrangement involving the Nigerian government in the United States.

Former Vice President Atiku Abubakar had called on the Presidency to clarify whether the interview was connected to the reported lobbying contract and disclose the details of the arrangement.

In a statement issued on Wednesday by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, Atiku said US filings identified London as a consultant to DCI Group AZ, a firm reportedly engaged by the Nigerian government through Aster Legal.

He said the filings indicated that DCI Group received a $4.5 million retainer but maintained that the Presidency should clarify whether the interview formed part of the contract.

Atiku demanded the publication of the contract, details of the payment and the release of the full, unedited recording of the interview.

He also questioned the nature of the engagement, arguing that the Presidency should establish whether the encounter was an independent journalistic exercise or part of a government-funded publicity arrangement.

The former vice president further asked the government to disclose who authorised the payment, the source of the funds and whether public money was involved.

The controversy followed London’s earlier social media posts praising the security partnership between Nigeria and the United States under Tinubu and US President Donald Trump.

In one of the posts, she described Nigeria as the United States’ greatest ally in Africa, saying the security cooperation between both countries was producing results and could create further economic and trade opportunities.

She also expressed appreciation for the opportunity to work with individuals representing Nigeria in efforts to strengthen relations between the Trump administration and the Nigerian government.

However, the posts were subsequently deleted, while London restricted access to the comment section of her X account following criticism from Nigerian social media users.

The development prompted further questions about her engagement with the Tinubu administration and the reported $4.5 million lobbying arrangement.

London’s latest statement is her first direct public response to the allegation that she received the money.

Meanwhile, the Presidency has yet to publicly clarify whether her interview with Tinubu was connected to the reported lobbying contract.
