World.title: Trump's team scrambles to calm U.S. fears over tech outages
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After U.S. President Donald Trump brushed aside the past week's series of tech outages, members of his administration are ramping up their efforts to try to reassure the American public that there is no reason to panic.

Officials are rejecting speculation that there's any link between the IT incident that triggered the grounding of 20,000 flights across the U.S., the two-day shutdown of Microsoft services, trouble with online transactions at U.S. banks or the National Security Agency's classified communications network going offline — all within the space of six days.

Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, led the Trump administration's push to calm fears on Wednesday, telling a House committee on homeland security that the outages were neither connected nor the result of cyberattacks.

"I understand the timing of ​these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people ​should ask us these questions," Clayton told lawmakers in the hearing on worldwide threats, which had been scheduled well before the outages began.

"Based on what we know today, after a ​great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. ⁠They are not a co-ordinated ⁠or state-sponsored attack."

In response to the outages that have disrupted work and travel for hundreds of thousands if not millions of Americans, prompting widespread anxiety about what could be going on, Trump has been mostly silent. When he has spoken out, he has downplayed them.

WATCH | 'It's fine,' says Trump, asked if he's concerned about tech outages: Repeated U.S. tech outages fuel concern, Trump says 'it's life' | Duration closed caption 3:00 Major tech outages on U.S. air travel, banking and security systems are fuelling concern about how secure the country's infrastructure really is, but officials say there is no evidence the incidents are part of a co-ordinated cyberattack.

Asked by a reporter Tuesday if he was concerned about the outages, Trump said, "No, it's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine."

But Trump's insistence that everything is fine — delivered from Manila where he was attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit — appeared to do little to ease nerves in the U.S.

'People are feeling insecure'

Katherine Clark, the No. 2 Democrat in the House as the party's whip, chastised Trump for his response.

"It is a shocking moment when the American people are feeling insecure, when they are wondering about how they can be sure that their families are going to be safe ... and instead they're getting comments like that from the commander-in-chief," Clark told reporters on Capitol Hill on Wednesday.

Even Trump's former press secretary wasn't thrilled with the message. Now in her role as a pundit on Fox News, Karoline Leavitt urged the White House to be transparent with the American people and try to "calm the temperature."

Operating without a press secretary for the past three months — aside from the short-lived tenure of Katie Zacharias — the White House is relying on members of Trump's cabinet for getting out its message on the technical outages. The results have been mixed.

WATCH | Trump's top officials face questions over string of tech outages: Trump officials grilled over massive tech outages | Duration closed caption 5:17 There's been a wave of tech outages across the U.S. in recent days, disrupting everything from flights to emails. On Capitol Hill, top intelligence and security officials faced tough questions about what's causing the outages — and whether they're connected.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who testified at Wednesday's hearing alongside Clayton, faced questions from lawmakers — some Republican — skeptical of the official explanations for the outages.

"Have you ever in all of your years in D.C. seen this many technology outages during this short of a period of time?" asked Republican Congressman Eli Crane of Arizona.

"Absolutely not," Mullin replied, and floated the need for better communication from companies doing upgrades that could trigger such outages.

Crane wasn't satisfied.

"How can you guys, with confidence, sit here and tell us that, 'Hey, these aren't cyberattacks. These are actually just a bunch of patches and old networks'?" Crane asked next.

"We have gone out to each one of those individuals, we've used our tools and we have no evidence that this is a co-ordinated cyberattack," Clayton replied.

WATCH | A cybersecurity expert offers answers: What's up with all the tech outages in the U.S.? | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 10:59 Officials from the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft, banks and the National Security Agency blame technical glitches for recent widespread outages that have affected numerous customers in the United States and abroad. Cybersecurity expert Chester Wisniewski offers his analysis on the recent incidents.

Apparently signalling the administration's concern about its response to the outages, Vice-President JD Vance abruptly cancelled his scheduled appearance Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook event because he was needed at the White House for meetings.

There are reports that some U.S. consumers are responding to the outages by stocking up on essentials.

An analyst note from investment bank Mizuho Securities raised its forecast for Costco stock because of a jump in purchases of emergency preparedness products, Bloomberg reported.

Costco says the trend started in late October, before the outages.

The company noticed an increase in purchases of such items as "rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, batteries and similar items seemingly in response to a variety of concerns on social media," Costco chief financial officer Gary Millerchip said in an email to Bloomberg.

Jordan Rae Kelly, who served as the National Security Council's director for cyber incident response during Trump's first term, says to some extent it doesn't matter whether the outages are the result of technology failures rather than cyberattacks.

"That really misses the point because the consequences have still been incredibly severe," Kelly told CNN on Wednesday.

She said it's crucial that U.S. officials start talking about what guardrails are needed to try to prevent such significant outages in the future.

"The fact that these failures are getting such widespread attention is going to make those conversations come to the forefront and that's really important," Kelly said.

Alex Hamerstone, a director at U.S. cybersecurity consulting firm TrustedSec, believes these sorts of outages will not only continue to occur, they'll likely accelerate with the growing frequency of tech updates.

"Unfortunately, you see those types of things happen with upgrades," Hamerstone told CBC News. "When you're rushing to update things or patch things, that's where a lot of issues come from."

World.title: Cadets being told to stand down as Canada adds billions to defence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian military has put a halt to most cadet training in various parts of the country because of ongoing budget restraint within the Department of National Defence.

The halt involves weekend training and participation in competitions and will last until the end of the fiscal year in March. Weekly parade nights, however, will continue at least for the time being.

Internal emails, obtained by CBC News, outline the decision and paint a picture of an organization struggling to manage the impact of the Defence Department's cuts to operations and support funding.

The Ottawa Citizen was the first to report on the restrictions involving the cadet program. The news was confirmed by a subsequent leak of emails to CBC News.

"Due to the current fiscal environment, all cadet activities are paused for the remainder of the current fiscal year, ending 31 March 2027, with the exception of weekly parade nights, which may continue at this time," said one leaked email quoting Lt.-Col. Raphael MacKenzie, who commands Ontario's Regional Cadet Support Unit (Central).

No one at the Defence Department was immediately available to comment on the leaked documents.

In mid-October, CBC News was the first to report on the department's internal belt-tightening, which is a knock-on effect from cuts mandated in previous federal budgets.

Department expected to find $459M in savings

The Defence Department has been given tens of billions of new funding by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney. It has been told to focus that extra cash on priority areas, including the purchase of much-needed combat equipment.

At the same time, DND is subject to the demand for operations and maintenance reductions announced by the Trudeau government in 2023 and enacted in the 2024 federal budget.

Those reductions, according to the latest federal budget, are significant.

DND is expected to find $459 million in operational savings this fiscal year, and another $459 million next year.

Last week, CBC News reported on how a reserve unit in southwestern Ontario limited paid participation in Remembrance Day activities because of the budget restraint.

There are also unconfirmed reports of full-time reservists having their three-year contracts cancelled with less than 30 days' notice.

That runs contrary to the latest federal budget's departmental plans report, which downplayed the impact of the internal restraint.

"No job losses are anticipated as a result of these reductions," said the budget report, recently tabled in Parliament.

The department and the Canadian military remain in "a period of growth, supported by significant long-term defence investments that continue to strengthen operational readiness, capabilities and the civilian and military workforce needed to deliver them," the report said.

WATCH | Budget watchdog on defence spending: Defence will enter the 'top rank' of government spending: PBO | Duration closed caption 9:11 On Tuesday the Parliamentary Budget Office announced the government could spend as much as $163.6 billion by 2035 on the Canadian military. The fiscal watchdog added that the economic impact such a drastic increase in defence spending will have on federal finances and the Canadian economy is yet to be determined. Power & Politics speaks to Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan.

Conservative defence critic James Bezan said the reserves and cadets are bearing the brunt of the restraint and the budget chaos makes a mockery of the Liberal government's pledge to invest in defence.

"Mark Carney and the Liberals can't be talking out of both sides of their mouths, saying that they're investing in the armed forces and then cutting operations," Bezan said.

"That reduces our readiness. The Carney cuts are having real impacts on the day-to-day operations of the Canadian Armed Forces."

The restrictions on cadet activities took effect immediately in Ontario, while similar measures will come into force on Nov. 21 in British Columbia.

A separate email detailing the restraint in the B.C. region said that cadet leadership is trying to preserve activities that directly support the conduct of weekly training at corps and squadrons and that remains "our priority."

The commanding officer of the Pacific region plans to conduct town halls on Nov. 19 and Nov. 23 to further explain the decision.

"We recognize that this direction will come as a surprise to most and will be disappointing to cadets, families and your teams who have invested considerable time and effort in planning activities for the year ahead," said the second email, dated Nov. 16.

"We share that disappointment. These are not measures that would be taken if the resources were available to sustain the program as planned."

World.title: Nearly 300,000 people sign petition demanding U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's removal
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More than 285,000 people have signed a petition asking the federal government to remove U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra from Canada.

The petition accuses Hoekstra of making public statements that have undermined Canadian and U.S. relations and says he described the 2025 Canadian federal election campaign as "anti-American."

The petition says Hoekstra accused Canada of interfering in U.S. domestic politics while making repeated statements on Canadian politics "inconsistent with diplomatic protocol."

The petition closes to new signatures on Wednesday and most of those who signed live in Ontario or British Columbia.

Now that the petition has received more than the mandatory 500 signatures it needed to proceed, former Green Party leader Elizabeth May can present it to the House of Commons.

Once it's presented to the House, the government has 45 calendar days to respond.

World.title: She says Russell Brand sexually assaulted her when she was 16. She's waiving her anonymity to speak out
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details of abuse. It may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

Mia Latter has decided to waive her legal right to anonymity and speak publicly about her teenage relationship with disgraced actor Russell Brand.

The 37-year-old British woman says Brand sexually assaulted her while they were dating when she was 16 and he was 30.

Victims of alleged sexual offences in the U.K. are afforded lifelong anonymity. But in the wake of Brand's high-profile rape trial, Latter says she felt compelled to go on record to advocate for changes to the country's age-of-consent laws.

"That would never have happened if my parents had been able to stop the relationship dead in its tracks to begin with," Latter told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "They had nowhere to go. The police wouldn't have been able to help them."

In the U.K., people who are 16 and older can consent to sexual activity with an adult of any age who is not in a position of authority over them.

Latter is working with the Close the Consent Gap campaign, which advocates a "staggered" age of consent in which it would be an offence for a person over 20 to engage in sexual activity with a person aged 16–17, unless the age difference is no more than three years.

LISTEN | Interview with Mia Latter: As It Happens 6:44 Mia Latter says Russell Brand sexually assaulted her when she was 16. She wants the U.K. to change its age of consent

Brand, 51, was convicted this month on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison. He continues to deny all allegations against him .

Latter's allegations, which were not part of the trial, are under police investigation.

'I told him my age'

Latter, who now lives in California, says she was shopping at Leicester Square in London when she first met Brand. She recognized him from his appearances on MTV.

"I told him my age before we ever went on a date, and he didn't have a problem with it for one moment," she said.

"My mum went to Brand and asked him not to see me. And she wanted to look him in the eye and talk to him about this. And he just was quite defiant and looked at her and just said, 'And what?' Because he knew there was nothing she could do."

Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault. He's maintained his innocence behind bars. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

The U.K.'s Ministry of Justice says the Law Commission has been tasked with reviewing the country's consent laws.

“Adults abusing imbalances of power, influence or vulnerability to exploit young people is unacceptable and we will always look at what more can be done to protect young people," a ministry spokesperson said.

"Our immediate focus remains on tackling exploitation, supporting victims and ensuring perpetrators are brought to justice."

In Canada, the age of consent is 16, but a 16- or 17-year-old cannot consent to sexual activity if they are dependent on their partner, their partner is in a position of power over them or the relationship is deemed "exploitative."

'Love bombing'

When Latter and Brand first started seeing each other, she says he was very romantic.

"Lots of poetry and, you know, over-the-top declarations of his intentions and how special I was and all of this stuff," she said.

She says she now recognizes this as "love bombing," an abuse tactic that Western University's Learning Network for gender-based violence defines as "a way of exercising control through overwhelming displays of affection, gifts, and praise."

They dated for three months and toward the end of that period, she says he sexually assaulted her. She described the assault as an oral rape.

WATCH | Times columnist on Brand's conviction: Russell Brand sentenced: The CBC's Andrew Nichols talks with columnist Katie Glass of The Times | Duration closed caption 7:22 The British actor and comedian was sentenced in a London court today to 10 and-a-half years behind bars. He was convicted last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.

London's Metropolitan Police Service confirmed it launched an investigation into Latter's allegations in January, but says the Crown Prosecution Service advised that "further information was needed before a charging decision could be made."

“We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor," the police said in an email. "However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”

A Crown Prosecution Service spokesperson said it will "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”

CBC reached out to Brand for comment through his lawyers, but did not receive a response.

Why she decided to go on record

Latter previously spoke about her experience under the pseudodyn "Alice" in a 2023 Sunday Times investigation and the subsequent Times/Channel 4 podcast, Dispatches.

During Brand's pre-trial hearing, defence lawyer Ian Winter KC called Dispatches "a work of fiction" and questioned whether the women featured in the documentary actually exist.

That's why Latter decided to go on record.

"It suddenly clicked in my head," Latter said. "I was like, well, I'm a real person and Russell knows who I am.'"

Winter's law firm, Cloth Fair Chambers, did not respond to a request for comment.

The lawyer has since reported himself to his professional regulator after he had a public confrontation with a Sunday Times reporter following Brand's conviction.

Since she first revealed her identity on Saturday in the Times , Latter says she's been on the receiving end of cruel and defamatory comments from Brand's supporters.

But she says she has no regrets.

"I've just been reading the stories that women are sending to me — and that parents are sending to me, and teachers and social workers and foster carers — about the children that are between the ages of 16 and 18 in their lives that they can't protect," she said.

"That's what's really pushing me forward, and it's also reinforcing to me that I did the right thing in going public. Because this is clearly a much bigger issue than even I could have imagined."

World.title: 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy,' Carney says of ongoing trade talks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that Canada is willing to sign a mutually beneficial deal with the Americans, but if U.S. President Donald Trump can't agree to those terms, then Ottawa will continue on its current trajectory: Aggressively diversifying away from the United States.

Speaking virtually to the Dealbook summit from China as he wound down his nine-day trade mission to Europe and Asia, Carney said Canada continues "to have a series of issues" when it comes to trade with the U.S.

While there has been some progress, "we're not there yet" on putting pen to paper on an agreement, Carney said.

Canada is trying to get the Trump administration to lift or reduce its punishing Section 232 tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum, softwood lumber and other products.

These tariffs have caused job losses and shuttered plants, imperilling what was once one of the closest bilateral relationships in the world.

Canada is also driving for Trump to lift the 50 per cent tariffs he levied on a grab bag of Canadian products, apparently retaliating for Canada's countermeasures on some U.S. goods that were imposed after the president first launched his trade war last year.

Carney met with Trump in China on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit — a conversation he described as "reasonably direct" but one that didn't produce a trade breakthrough.

With the prospect of a U.S. trade deal uncertain, Carney said Canada's talks with China have gone "exceptionally well" and are "very rational," and he has secured meaningful market access for Canadian commodities in return for allowing a relatively small number of Chinese EVs to be imported at lower tariff rates.

As part of his Asian tour, Carney also brokered two free trade deals in a single day with the Philippines and the 11-nation ASEAN bloc, which combined represent a $6-trillion market.

Canada is also on the cusp of a free trade deal with India within the next three months, Carney said.

WATCH | Carney brokers agreements with the Philippines, ASEAN: Carney brokers 2 free trade agreements with the Philippines, ASEAN | Duration closed caption 2:40 Prime Minister Mark Carney brokered two free trade agreements — slated to be signed next year — that will dramatically slash high tariffs on Canadian exports to the Philippines and the 11-member ASEAN bloc in a continued attempt to diversify trade away from the U.S.

Altogether, Canada currently has free trade access to economies with some two billion people, he said, and that number will soon reach three billion.

"We'd like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy," Carney said.

Asked if the U.S. midterm results changed anything for Canada — the Democrats won both houses of U.S. Congress in a landslide — Carney said, "No, is the short answer."

Carney arrives at the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Monday, ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. (Pedro Pardo/Getty Images)

Carney said the only thing that will improve relations between the two countries is a U.S. reversal of anti-Canada trade actions that are designed to destroy key sectors of the economy.

"What will change views is policy decisions that are taken and that will stick," he said. "It will take action as opposed to intent."

But even then, Carney said the government doesn't want to slide into an old pattern of ever-deeper economic integration with the U.S.

Canada doesn't want to be "coerced" or "subjugated" by the U.S., or any other major power, anymore, he said.

The overarching goal of his trade policy — brokering associate membership with the European Union and thawing relations with China — is to secure Canada's long-term sovereignty, Carney said.

WATCH | Canada's ties with China not a 'top issue' for Trump, Carney says: Canada's ties with China not a 'top issue' for Trump, Carney says | Duration 2:00 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from China on Nov. 18, said Canada and the U.S. have different types of trade relationships with Beijing, adding that in the 'hierarchy of issues' between Canada and the U.S., China is not 'the top issue at all.'

Asked about Trump's October assertion that the U.S. "holds all the cards" in its dealings with Canada, Carney was dismissive.

"Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us," Carney said, relaying his commitment to double non-U.S. trade in 10 years.

"I'm not saying the transition is easy. It's not — there are challenges there."

Conservative MP Adam Chambers, the party's industry critic, meanwhile criticized Carney's decision to draw closer to China and pitch warmer relations with the Asian economic superpower as an alternative to securing a U.S. deal.

"If the prime minister thinks it's smart to play chicken with a U.S. administration that has a lot of leverage and harm it may choose to impose on Canada — the government should be very careful about doing that," he told reporters on Parliament Hill.

World.title: First Nations health watchdog investigating how Sask. boy lost use of small intestine after routine surgery
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan's First Nations Health Ombudsperson is investigating how a Regina boy lost the use of his small intestine after a routine surgery for appendicitis.

Sheldon OneBear Rosebluff, 4, is now in critical condition at the Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon. He requires a small intestine transplant.

On Wednesday, his family and First Nations leaders held a media event to discuss the case and ongoing concerns about how Indigenous people are treated by the provincial health-care system.

First Nations Health Ombudsperson Dianne Lafond said she launched an investigation into Rosebluff's medical ordeal after the boy's family filed a complaint. Lafond said she can't discuss the details of Rosebluff's situation until the investigation is complete.

"Nothing is black and white and some cases are very complex," Lafond said on Wednesday. "When a child goes in for a simple procedure and will now be in the health-care system for years … you've got a lot of different factors at play."

The Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) confirmed it is conducting its own review of the care Rosebluff received in hospital.

Kristin Lerat is Rosebluff's biological aunt and has been his caregiver for about three years. She described Rosebluff as a talkative boy who likes to build forts, dance and drum.

"A happy, energized boy. And this has taken the richness out of not only his life, but our lives too," Lerat said.

In September, Rosebluff had a successful surgery in Regina for appendicitis. He appeared to be recovering well until Oct. 24, when he suddenly turned ill and was taken back to hospital, Lerat said.

He had a blockage in his bowels and required surgery. After two surgeries in Regina within days, he was airlifted to Jim Pattison Children's Hospital in Saskatoon, where he eventually had two more surgeries over the course of a week.

"He was critical the whole time, but his body just couldn't handle that many surgeries," Lerat said.

Something happened that "killed" his small intestine and he now requires a transplant, Lerat said.

Sheldon One Bear Rosebluff, 4, seen here in an undated photo prior to his medical ordeal. (Submitted by Kristen Lerat)

The SHA declined to comment on Rosebluff surgeries and his condition due to privacy legislation.

But the SHA is conducting a review of the care Rosebluff received and "what might have occured," according to a statement emailed to CBC.

"Patient safety and the delivery of high-quality, patient-centred care remain top priorities for the SHA, and we take patient safety concerns very seriously," SHA chief medical officer Dr. Rashaad Hansia said in the statement.

"Social Work supports are in place to assist in liaising with the family and coordinating with partner agencies, and we are commit[ted] to ensuring these interactions and supports are provided in a culturally respectful way."

Lafond did not provided a timeline for the ombudsperson investigation, but said more details will be released once it is complete.

Cowessess First Nation Chief Erica Beaudin attended the media event to support the Lerat family.

"We are not here to denounce the health-care system or the people in it," Beaudin said.

"What we're talking about is how we must recognize when we must do better.… For us, treaty is not a land acknowledgement. It is action."

The First Nations Health Ombudsperson is an independent office established by the Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations to investigate complaints about the health-care system.

In October 2025, the ombudsperson said her office had received about 500 complaints since opening in 2023. About 64 per cent of the cases derived from complaints and issues associated with the services of the Saskatchewan Health Authority.

The boy's family is also concerned about being sidelined for important medical decisions. Lerat said the social services ministry took over decision-making for Rosebluff's care once the boy's condition turned critical.

"It was me and the doctors making the decisions. Now it's the ministries and the doctors making decisions," Lerat said. "So if we get a doctor that does not believe in our traditional ways, what does that look like?"

The Ministry of Social Services provided a statement to CBC.

"Due to provisions in The Child and Family Services Act, the Ministry of Social Services is unable to confirm involvement with a family or speak to specific details of any case," it said.

World.title: Women's rugby players fight to save team after Bishop's University cuts varsity program
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Women’s rugby players at Bishop's University in Sherbrooke, Que., say they were left in tears and shock when they were told on Monday the team would no longer receive varsity support or funding beyond this school year.

According to the university, the decision was taken by its board of governors following a year-long review.

“It really felt like being stabbed in the chest,” said Tessa Brosseau, who moved from Vancouver to attend the university in Quebec’s Eastern Townships.

"The reason that I'm at Bishop's is because of Bishop's women's rugby,” said the fourth-year student. “It means everything. It means my life.”

Claudia Croteau and Abigail Burns, both rookies from Alberta, also moved across the country to play for the varsity rugby team.

WATCH | Bishop’s university women’s rugby players blindsided by varsity program cut: Bishop’s University drops women's rugby and men's lacrosse — blindsiding athletes | Duration closed caption 2:14 Bishop’s University is cutting two of its varsity sports programs, stating it wants to focus its resources on fewer teams so that those that remain can receive the necessary support to stay competitive.

The young women say they think of each other as family now, bonded together by all the hard work and sacrifices they've each made to be part of the team — including countless hours of training during early mornings, late nights and rainy practices.

Fighting to keep their rugby dreams alive

The school suggested the team could continue as a club. But the players don’t see that as an equivalent replacement.

“None of us came here to play club rugby,” said Brosseau. “We came here to potentially be prospects for the national program."

Universities with a varsity team can be a pipeline to get onto the national roster. The prospect of that is particularly appealing to young female athletes now, as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world.

Being a varsity team means more amenities, as well, including access to coaching and medical staff. It's also the last level before being able to play professionally.

LISTEN | Women's rugby team not giving up on keeping varsity status: Quebec AM 11:10 Bishop’s University rugby players speak out against decision to cut varsity program Bishop’s University is ending its women’s varsity rugby program after the 2026-2027 academic year as part of a plan to concentrate funding on other teams. Quebec AM guest host Gordon Lambie speaks with women's rugby players Rylee Fletcher and Emy-Jade Audet to find out what this means for them.

The players are not willing to let go of that dream without a fight.

They’ve launched an online petition that’s garnered more than 6,000 signatures, and are considering fundraising in hopes of reversing the board’s decision.

If a solution can’t be found, Croteau admitted that she and other rookies are contemplating transferring schools as a last resort, in order to be able to still play rugby at the varsity level.

“Yes, we love Bishop’s,” she said, “but what makes Bishop’s so amazing is rugby."

'Women’s sports deserve to grow, not disappear'

In its explanation of the decision to cut the varsity program, the university acknowledged it was facing “significant financial pressure.”

However, the team says it was never consulted to help address that challenge. Nor has it been informed of what criteria was considered when taking the decision, which the university has said is final.

Rylee Fletcher, who’s in her fourth year at Bishop’s, is hoping to bring wider attention to what she calls a "devastating" decision.

“At a time when women’s sports are gaining long-overdue recognition, investment, and support, it is incredibly discouraging to see opportunities for female athletes being taken away,” she said.

“We believe women’s sports deserve to grow, not disappear.”

The team finished last this season, but the players believe the future of the team is still bright. (Courtesy of Bronwyn Chénard)

Bishop’s University has said the school has chosen to concentrate its resources on fewer varsity teams to better support their needs.

" This decision reflects financial and operational sustainability, competitive fit and the resources each sport requires. It does not diminish the value of women’s rugby or the people who play it," a school representative said in an emailed statement.

Bishop's plans to keep four women’s and four men’s varsity teams. They include both basketball and golf teams, as well as men’s football and rugby, and women’s hockey and soccer.

Men's lacrosse team also cut

In addition to Bishop's women's varsity rugby team, the men’s varsity lacrosse team has also been cut.

The Canadian University Field Lacrosse Association (CUFLA) said in a statement that it hasn't officially been notified of the decision, but considers it to be a "significant setback" to its efforts of reversing the trend of Canadian student athletes choosing American universities to pursue their education and lacrosse careers.

The CUFLA says it has noticed a "significant increase" in Canadian student athletes returning from universities in the U.S. over the past several years to continue their pursuits at Canadian institutions.

"Lacrosse is increasingly becoming a driver of university enrolment, making the decision by Bishop's University particularly difficult to understand," the CUFLA said.

Last year, McGill University cut 25 club and varsity teams across 15 sports, including women’s rugby.

Concordia is now the only English-language university with a varsity women’s rugby team in Quebec.

World.title: Competition Bureau examining marketing practices by Gap, Old Navy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal Competition Bureau is moving ahead with an investigation into whether clothing giants Gap and Old Navy are violating marketing regulations by making potentially false or misleading claims in their advertising.

The competition watchdog has been granted a court order for information it says will help it determine whether the retailers are supplying customers with genuine regular prices when advertising items as on sale.

It is also examining the retailers' use of so-called urgency cues — messages such as ''Selling Fast'' or ''Only a Few Left'' — that pop up on their sites while consumers are browsing.

In an email to CBC News, the bureau clarified that while the use of such claims is not prohibited, it can raise concerns under the Competition Act about whether they are creating a false or misleading impression to potential shoppers about a product's popularity or availability.

"The growing online marketplace provides a venue where fake urgency cues can easily be promoted," a spokesperson for the bureau said. "It's important that consumers shop wisely, and that businesses do not use pressure tactics that mislead consumers."

Old Navy and Gap are both owned by Gap Inc. and operate both online and bricks and mortar stores nationally.

CBC News has reached out to Gap Inc. for comment about the investigation.

The bureau says it took action after it saw a surge in complaints last year about allegedly inflated regular prices. At the time, it published a warning to remind businesses of their obligations under the Competition Act.

It adds that its ongoing investigation has yet to find any instances of wrongdoing.

World.title: “Basic food stuffs exempt from sales tax:” De la Espriella on tax reform bill
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella rolled back his government’s plan to impose sales tax on basic food stuffs in an attempt to seek approval for his tax reform in Congress.

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella said that “basic household goods will be exempt from VAT. I made that clear from the very beginning.”

Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo and Finance Minister Miguel Gomez last month announced the introduction of a 19% sales tax on basic food stuffs and the creation of a mechanism that would allow the poor to recover this money.

The radical proposal was necessary to prevent Colombia from defaulting on debt, said Gomez.

However, “after several analyses, they adjusted the proposal to protect the basic food basket, which required a greater effort on the part of the government,” the president said Sunday.

De la Espriella’s tax reform, which will have to pass before December 16, got stuck in Congress after the coalition Liberal Party said they wouldn’t support taxing the basic food basket.

Also the far-right Democratic Center party opposed the measure, which almost immediately triggered calls for a national strike.

The president suggested that he would cut expenses he blamed on the leftist “criminal organizations” that won the 2022 elections with former President Gustavo Petro.

My true tax reform is the fight against corruption, against the criminal organizations that squandered the state’s resources for so many years. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“There is still a lot to do, but you can’t fix that disaster in three months,” said De la Espriella.

Contrary to campaign promises to reduce the State apparatus, De la Espriella proposed a 2027 budget that increased state spending.

On top of that, the government has been talking to the International Monetary Fund about a credit line that would support his increased spending.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: A Letter from Havana Times
World.content:
18 years, seven days a week, from Cuba despite everything

Photo por Nester Nuñez

By Circles Robinson

Dear Readers,

In October we reached our 18th anniversary of nonstop daily reporting, commentary, diaries, and photography centered on Cuba, while also covering Nicaragua, Venezuela, and other Latin American countries.

Most of our contributing writers and photographers are in Cuba, documenting the extraordinarily difficult times they are living through. From Pinar del Río, Havana, Mayabeque, Matanzas, Camagüey, and Holguín they tell us of their days spent juggling scarcities of every kind. Yet these talented writers choose to take the time to be part of this online media project. In the coming weeks, some of them will tell you in their own words why.

The Havana Times family also includes others who help make the publication possible with their writing, editing, and technical support from Venezuela, Panama, Nicaragua, Brazil, Chile, Canada, Switzerland, Spain, and the United States.

We are not a large publication, with no salaried staff, but the reader survey we conducted in May, in which many of you participated, showed us that you have a high regard for the credibility of our work. That means a great deal to us. The results also told us that most of you feel Havana Times gives you a good picture of life on the ground in Cuba and a better understanding of the complexities of the country’s politics and the challenges it faces. That is exactly what our combined effort sets out to do.

I continue editing and publishing Havana Times out of a personal commitment to our writers and photographers as well as a love for both Cuba and Nicaragua, where I lived for many years. In this increasingly polarized world, I remain committed to a kind of journalism that emphasizes empathy and ethics while avoiding extremism.

I’m also happy to know that people from different countries who read Havana Times before traveling to Cuba have written to us after returning home to say the publication gave them an introduction to the country; this helped them better understand what they encountered and, thus, get more out of their trip. Many continue reading afterwards. Knowing that our work can serve readers in this way is deeply gratifying.

Our hope is to continue providing this service in the coming year and beyond. Later this month, we will launch our all-important annual reader fundraising campaign. If you also believe in the importance of independent journalism and care about the people and countries we cover, I hope to have your support.

Read more from Circles Robinson here on Havana Times.

World.title: Financing an Apartment in Brazil
World.content:
A condominium in Curitiba, Brazil

By Osmel Almaguer

HAVANA TIMES – I have a Cuban friend who managed to finance a place of his own through Brazil’s Minha Casa Minha Vida [“My house, my life”] Program. I remember writing about that while trying to explain the different ways an immigrant can purchase a property.

That was a more or less a year ago. My friend’s success inspired me to try it as well. He’s in the middle of his financing, which ends in 2028, and I just received an email offering us our own financing.

That doesn’t mean it’s going to work out. We’ve agreed to move forward with the process and learn more about the proposal, and now we’re waiting for a response from the real estate agency, to find out if there are any available units based on our ranking.

If the answer is yes, we’ll begin a series of in-person meetings with the real estate agency to work out the details before signing the contract.

First, they’d give us a full presentation of the project, including the projected construction timeline. After that, we’d discuss the contract details and payment terms.

We don’t yet know the total price of the apartment, but we do know that the condominium project is located in the Cajuru neighborhood, just a few minutes from downtown. I did some research, and it’s a residential area with excellent prospects for continued growth, so from a financial standpoint, it could be a good investment.

I’ve already mentioned that I firmly believe in this approach to managing our finances because, after all, if we spend our whole lives moving from one rental to another, we’ll never own a home of our own – but will still end up paying hundreds of thousands of Brazilian riais [note: 5.87 riais = $1 US].

Just to give an example, in the four years I’ve been in Brazil, I’ve already spent about 60,000 reais (approximately $12,000) on rent, which is equivalent to one-fifth of the value of a small apartment.

Minha Casa Minha Vida is a government program that subsidizes affordable housing for low-income families. Through this program, in combination with another program called Casa Curitibana, we could receive a subsidy of up to 30,000 reais ($6,000) to cover part of the down payment, with the remainder divided into monthly installments until the condo is completed.

A project of this kind raises several concerns. For example, having to pay the monthly loan installments alongside our current rent for two or three years. Construction interest accrues over the waiting period, causing the monthly down payment installments to rise from an initial 600 reais ($120) to as much as 2,000 reais ($400).

The size of the apartment is also a bit discouraging—only 34 square meters.

As an asylum seeker, I don’t have legal status that would allow me to finance an apartment; however, a driver’s license serves as legal identification, and it is possible to obtain one easily by paying between 1,500 and 2,000 reais (between $300 and $400).

For a family that lives paycheck to paycheck, all these expenses—even though they’re only possible thanks to programs like Minha Casa Minha Vida—mean it’s important to carefully calculate and manage every decision, because even the slightest slip-up could leave us in a bind.

Read more from the diary of Osmel Almaguer here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Wednesday, November 18, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

NSA Claims “Temporary Degradation” Behind Outage of Classified Internal Network

Nov 18, 2026

The National Security Agency — the largest spy agency in the U.S. — says a “temporary degradation” is behind an outage of its classified internal network. The network, known as NSANet, has been down since at least early Tuesday morning, and some NSA staff have been unable to access their workplace systems, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for personnel. U.S. officials tell CBS News that so far there is no evidence of a cyberattack.

Apple and Google Hit by Widespread Service Outages

Nov 18, 2026

Apple on Tuesday confirmed widespread service outages on many of its iPhone apps, including Apple Pay and iCloud. Meanwhile, thousands of Gmail users reported disruptions that Google later said were not related to any broad internal system interruptions. This comes amidst a series of other disruptions to air travel, banking and technology infrastructure, including a massive outage at Microsoft last week that disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries.

Nvidia’s Board of Directors Reportedly Not Considering Bringing Back Jensen Huang as CEO

Nov 18, 2026

Nvidia’s board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO. That’s despite Huang releasing a statement that he would be”honored to return as CEO.” Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO, in light of his affair with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. This comes as Jensen Huang is expected to testify behind closed doors on December 1 before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence ​Committee.

Xi Personally Greets Trump on Tarmac in Shenzhen, Breaking Precedent

Nov 18, 2026

Chinese President Xi Jinping personally greeted President Trump on the tarmac when he landed in Shenzhen earlier today for the APEC summit, breaking precedent. After Trump stepped off Air Force One, he and Xi shook hands and hugged each other. The two leaders are set to hold a historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.

Alaska’s Former Democratic Congressmember Peltola Defeats Incumbent GOP Senator Sullivan

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: X/MaryPeltola

In Alaska, former Democratic Congressmember Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola becomes the first Indigenous woman from Alaska elected to the U.S. Senate. She won with 50.1% of the vote to Sullivan’s 45.8%. Her win brings the Democratic majority in the Senate to 56 seats. Peltola posted this message on social media after the race was called.

Sen.-elect Mary Peltola: “I’m so grateful you’ve put your trust in me, Alaska, and I’m ready to get to work. The future is full of opportunities for us to make Alaska a better place across the state. I’m looking forward to working hand in hand with all Alaskans over the next six years. Thank you again.”

Settlers Kill 72-Year-Old Palestinian Grandmother in the Occupied West Bank

Nov 18, 2026

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers killed a 72-year-old Palestinian grandmother and wounded at least 10 others in an attack on the outskirts of Jericho. The woman was identified as Fadda Mohammed Fheidat. She was standing outside of her home when settlers began shooting at her and her family members, fatally striking Fheidat in the head. This is a witness.

Ahmed Aref: “We went outside the house after hearing the children shouting. Then everything escalated. The settlers started shooting. I was inside the house with the elderly woman. We went downstairs, and she was behind me. She stopped at this spot, and I walked past her. I looked back and thought she was still standing, but when I looked again, I found her lying on the ground with blood coming from her head. Look, her blood is here on the road.”

Israeli settlers have recently violently moved into Jericho, seizing several Palestinian homes.

In related news, the United Kingdom has sanctioned eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, as well as a settler group blocking humanitarian aid to Gaza.

Meanwhile, Australia has imposed sanctions on three Israeli individuals and four Israeli organizations for their role in expanding illegal Israeli settlements and settler violence in the West Bank.

Guardian: IDF Uploaded 3.5 Million Photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s Platform

Nov 18, 2026

A new report by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham in The Guardian shows that the Israeli military uploaded 3.5 million photos to Amazon’s Rekognition platform to assist in its facial recognition of Palestinians soon after the invasion of Gaza in 2023. Face recognition technology is routinely used at Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank, and images captured at checkpoints have been used to surveil and target Palestinians.

Israeli Lawmakers Elect Matan Kahana as Speaker of Knesset in Blow to Netanyahu

Nov 18, 2026

In Israel, lawmakers have elected Matan Kahana, an ally of opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, as speaker of the Knesset. It’s a major defeat for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose candidate lost the race for speaker. Kahana was backed by both Jewish-led opposition parties and Arab-led parties.

U.N. Warns Fighting Is Worsening Health Crisis in Taiz, Yemen

Nov 18, 2026

The U.N. warned Tuesday that fighting and road closures are worsening the health crisis in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz, where water supplies meet just 8% of residents’ needs. Hospitals report thousands of cases of acute diarrhea, along with suspected dengue and cholera. This is a government employee in Taiz.

Mansour Mohammed: “We are in a situation, in a suffocating crisis, in a suffocating crisis. This siege has caused a suffocating crisis among all citizens. They can’t live, can’t get out and can’t get in. They sit silent inside and can’t earn a living.”

WaPo: Brazil Police Probes If MAGA Donor Group Linked to Vance Illegally Interfered in Brazil’s Presidential Election

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: Emily J. Higgins

The Washington Post reports Brazil’s Federal Police is investigating whether Rockbridge Network, a conservative donor group co-founded by Vice President JD Vance and Chris Buskirk, illegally interfered in the Brazilian presidential election in order to favor far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino ordered the investigation after the heated runoff between Bolsonaro and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Dino cited allegations by a political activist named Renan Santos, who himself ran for president in the election and said he allegedly received messages from a Rockbridge intermediary searching for a conservative candidate that the MAGA donor group could back in the Brazilian presidential election. The probe also follows complaints by Lula’s Workers’ Party of possible U.S. interference. Flávio Bolsonaro fled to Florida last month after losing the election. He faces multiple criminal investigations back in Brazil.

AP: Immigrant Children Held in Cold, Sunless Rooms for Up to a Month

Nov 18, 2026

The Associated Press reports that immigrant children in the custody of Customs and Border Protection are being detained in cold, sunless rooms for up to a month at a time — far exceeding the legal limit of 72 hours. A legal motion filed by several advocacy groups also revealed immigrant parents held across CBP facilities in the Texas and California southern borderlands have reported widespread due process violations, including phone calls with lawyers that were restricted to less than five minutes. The parents have described being detained with their children in freezing rooms with cement floors while the lights are kept on day and night, making it hard for the children to sleep.

146,000 People Participate in Nationwide Protests in France

Nov 18, 2026

In France, about 146,000 people participated in peaceful protests across the country over the rising cost of living. High school and university students joined some private sector workers on Tuesday in the latest nationwide protests. This is a health worker.

Health worker: “We are paid a miserable amount. That’s one of our demands. We can no longer survive. I speak with my colleagues. It’s impossible to make ends meet at the end of the month. We can no longer do so, even though we have a salary. Our salaries as health workers is nearly minimum wage.”

Egyptian Writer Abdelrahman ElGendy Blocked from Entering the U.S.

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: Abdelrahman ElGendy

The Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy has been blocked from entering the U.S. and is unable to attend this year’s National Book Awards. He is a finalist for the nonfiction award for his book “Huna” about his time as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy may also be ineligible for the prize since the National Book Awards rules require authors to be a U.S. citizen, a permanent U.S. resident or “maintain their primary, long-term home in the United States.” ElGendy currently lives in Europe, though he had lived in the U.S. for three years. He fled the U.S. last year fearing he would be arrested by ICE over his opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and criticism of U.S. relations with Egypt.

Bahraini Human Rights Activist Nabeel Rajab Dies at 62

Nov 18, 2026

Bahraini human rights activist Nabeel Rajab died of a heart attack Tuesday in Turkey at the age of 62. Rajab led the Bahrain Center for Human Rights and became a leading voice of Bahrain’s 2011 pro-democracy uprising. He was jailed repeatedly, spending more than six years in prison. He was most recently arrested in 2016 for criticizing Bahrain’s role in the war on Yemen and was released in 2020. He later fled to Turkey fearing rearrest. Nabeel Rajab spoke to Democracy Now! back in 2014 about his role in pro-democracy protests in Bahrain.

Nabeel Rajab: “I urge American people to pressure the American government, through your member of parliament, through your congressman, to change the situation, to ask the American government not to support dictators.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Bedbug Epidemic in Sancti Spiritus, Cuba
World.content:
Forces the Provincial Court to close

Amidst cardboard, bags, household waste, and abandoned furniture, there appear mattresses that residents identify as infested. / 14ymedio

The infestation has spread to police stations, prisons, public buildings, and homes, while residents improvise remedies to prevent the insects from invading their houses.

Por Mercedes García (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – “Don’t sit down, there are bedbugs.” The warning, given by a police investigator to a citizen who came to file a complaint, sums up an infestation spreading throughout the city of Sancti Spíritus, one that no longer distinguishes between neglected homes, spotless households, and government offices. The insects have found shelter in furniture, mattresses, and public spaces, while residents desperately search for ways to keep them from entering their homes.

Ramón, a self-employed businessman who recently experienced an attempted robbery at his business, has had to visit the First Police Unit several times to follow up on his complaint. Each time, he tells 14ymedio, the investigator has advised him to remain standing. According to his account, the infestation affects the lobby, the holding cells, and other areas where detainees, officers, and visitors come together.

“While I was outside the station waiting, I also heard that the mattresses in Nieves Morejón prison are just as badly infested,” Ramón adds. Two women waiting to be seen to were describing the situation involving a family member imprisoned at that facility. “The prisoners would rather sleep on the floor because the beds are crawling with bedbugs,” the man says.

The alarm has also reached the Provincial People’s Court, whose headquarters had to close because of a bedbug infestation. This would not be the first time. Employees and people familiar with the building’s operations say that services had previously been suspended because of the same problem, but a higher-level order forced them to resume without removing the affected furniture.

This time, they say, the insects were visible to people arriving to conduct business. Some visitors turned around as soon as they noticed them; others preferred to wait standing rather than risk carrying an unwanted passenger home in their clothing. Finally, a decision was made to close the premises again.

For residents on the block, the problem does not end behind the Court’s doors. They fear the insects will spread from one building to another and turn their homes into another source of infestation. “It’s not easy; you lose everything. A mattress costs more than $200, and that’s where you get your rest,” says one resident, who is also worried about clothing and other belongings that could be affected.

Household ingenuity is attempting to make up for the lack of solutions. Some people place cloths soaked in bleach near their entrances and keep their shoes inside plastic bags. One grandmother in the area has gone even further: she placed all four legs of her bed inside cans containing a little kerosene. “I can’t afford to buy a new mattress, so this is what I came up with,” she explains. These are desperate measures that do not guarantee the elimination of the insects and may introduce additional health and safety risks.

The problem is not limited to the city center. In the Garaita area, a heavily traveled road between the El Parque and Kilo 12 popular councils, piles of garbage have become part of the landscape. Soviet-inspired apartment buildings and prefabricated homes stand alongside one another, housing families with widely varying economic circumstances.

Among cardboard, plastic bags, household garbage, and abandoned furniture are mattresses that residents identify as infested. Their presence is especially concerning because rummaging through discarded items to recover usable belongings has become an everyday practice. A mattress thrown out onto the street can end up transferring the problem to another home.

Fighting bedbugs is also beyond the financial reach of many households. Specialized products are difficult to find, and many are imported from other countries at prohibitive prices for people earning government salaries. City residents also question the effectiveness of the cypermethrin fumigation treatments offered by sanitation services. They say they have to pay substantial amounts for these treatments without always obtaining results.

Bedbugs can appear even in carefully cleaned spaces. They are transported among personal belongings and hide in cracks, seams, and furniture. In Sancti Spíritus, however, the combination of persistent infestations, inadequate treatments, and economic hardship threatens to turn a household nuisance into a collective problem. While institutions close their doors and families improvise barriers, the insects continue finding places to settle.

Translated by Regina Anavy for Translating Cuba.
