The investigation centers on a public meeting Chaves led on Nov. 4 at the high school in Turrúcares, a district of Alajuela. Several ministers, government officials, members of the Alajuela Municipal Council and community representatives attended.

At the meeting, Chaves presented a package of projects for the district, including a technical high school, a CEN-CINAI childcare center, care centers for older adults, sports facilities, and repairs to national routes 721 and 136 and their bridges. He made the investments conditional on the Municipal Council withdrawing lawsuits that seek to annul the land-use permits for a landfill planned at the Bajo Pita property in San Miguel de Turrúcares.

When Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez said staff would assess land for the technical school, Chaves instructed that the work not begin while the municipality’s lawsuits remained in place. The value of the package has been reported differently. Chaves announced works valued at about 6 billion colones (about $13.4 million). The Presidency has since cited a figure of about 100 million colones (about $223,000) in infrastructure projects.

The landfill would be built by Empresas Berthier EBI de Costa Rica, which the government has promoted as an environmental technology park. The Municipality of Alajuela granted the project’s land-use permits more than a decade ago but later moved to annul them through lesividad proceedings, arguing the project conflicts with the canton’s zoning plan.

Investors linked to the Canadian company Berthier EBI and to Bajo Pita S.A. then filed an arbitration claim against Costa Rica at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID). Chaves told residents the state faces potential exposure of up to $150 million and that the municipality’s lawsuits weaken Costa Rica’s defense.

He also attached a deadline. Chaves said the offer would be withdrawn once the government had to pay for the country’s legal defense in the arbitration, a cost he estimated at 2 billion colones (about $4.5 million), with the process starting Dec. 2.

No signed agreement guaranteeing that the investors would withdraw the arbitration was presented at the meeting. Legal specialists Álvaro Sagot and Nicolás Boeglin have questioned Chaves’s reading of the case, arguing that the state has legal defenses available and that the claim may be time-barred.

Chaves has rejected accusations of extortion, saying his intervention was intended to warn of the economic consequences the country would face if it lost the international case. No response from Chaves to the opening of the criminal case had been published as of Wednesday morning.

Lawmakers from the National Liberation Party, the Social Christian Unity Party and the Broad Front accused Chaves of blackmail the day after the meeting. An opposition motion condemning his statements, filed Nov. 9, was rejected 31 to 24, with the ruling Pueblo Soberano party voting against it.

In Alajuela, the decision rests with the council. Council president Jorge Arturo Campos described the offer as a trade-off and said residents should take part in the decision, while Chaves rejected a popular consultation and said the council’s 11 members should decide. Two weeks after the meeting, Campos said the council had received no formal request to vote on the landfill and had nothing on its agenda. Turrúcares residents have protested at council sessions and want the court challenges kept in place.

Influence peddling carries a penalty of two to five years in prison under the Law Against Corruption and Illicit Enrichment in Public Service. Any prosecution would face an additional hurdle. As a minister, Chaves holds immunity from prosecution, meaning the Supreme Court’s full bench would first have to approve a request to lift it before the Legislative Assembly votes, where 38 votes, a two-thirds majority, are required.

A separate request by prosecutors to lift his immunity, in a case over alleged parallel financing of his 2022 presidential campaign, has been stalled for months by vacancies among substitute justices on the Constitutional Chamber. The dispute unfolds as the waste disposal capacity tightens. Olivier Álvarez, president of the Association of Chemical Engineers and Allied Professionals (CIQPA), said in remarks published Wednesday that three or four of Costa Rica’s seven active landfills are months, not years, from the end of their useful life, and that the Greater Metropolitan Area needs a new disposal site.

Álvarez said 55% to 60% of household waste is organic and roughly 20% could be recycled if kept clean, and he called for a model that recovers more material rather than one that depends on finding new places to bury garbage. Prosecutors have not said when the preliminary investigation might conclude.

World.title: Costa Rica Traffic Jams Doubled in a Year – Half the Roads Now Back Up
World.content:
If your drive across the Central Valley feels slower than it did a year ago, the numbers back you up. Traffic jams on Costa Rica’s roads doubled in intensity in 2025, and half of all road segments measured now back up at least once, according to the 2026 National Competitiveness Index.

The index, published Nov. 13 by the Council for the Promotion of Competitiveness (CPC), counted 117.6 jam reports for every 100-meter (328-foot) stretch of congested road. The year before, the figure was 57.4. The jam data comes from the State of the Nation Program, which draws on Waze reports shared through the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT). Of the road segments the index evaluated, 50.1% recorded at least one jam, the highest share since the series began.

The waits are getting longer, too. Drivers now lose an average of 207.4 seconds, or about three and a half minutes, on every congested 100-meter segment. CPC economist Andrés Fernández put it in starker terms. He said the average time drivers spend per kilometer (0.62 miles) of jammed road rose from about 30 minutes to about 35 in the latest edition.

Taken together, those figures pushed the index’s road connectivity score from 60.7 to 56.6 out of 100. The 4.1-point drop is the steepest since the series began in 2021. The worst-connected areas are mostly in and around the capital. San José, Escazú, Curridabat, Belén, Montes de Oca and Santo Domingo rank among the most congested, along with Corredores in the southern zone. The area of San José scored just 40.9 out of 100 on road connectivity.

The longest delays, however, turned up on the central Pacific coast. In Garabito, the area that includes Jacó, drivers lose up to 11.9 minutes for every 100 meters of congested road, the highest figure in the country. Heredia averages 5.9 minutes, while Sarchí has the shortest delays at about two minutes.

Fernández said congestion is heaviest in the Greater Metropolitan Area and on the approaches to the ports. Travel times to Puerto Caldera and to Daniel Oduber International Airport in Liberia both reached their highest levels in the index’s history. Over the past five years, 62 of the 82 areas lost ground on road connectivity, while 20 improved. Cartago, Vázquez de Coronado and San Isidro saw the sharpest declines, while Buenos Aires, Carrillo and Guatuso improved the most.

The smoothest traffic is found in Turrubares, Puriscal, Bagaces and Acosta. Congestion weighed on an otherwise improving national picture. Costa Rica’s overall competitiveness score rose 2.4 points to 58.6 out of 100, but the CPC identified worsening traffic and a 41.5% drop in real per-student investment in school infrastructure as the main factors limiting further gains.

For anyone who drives here, the index puts numbers to what the daily commute already suggests. Jams are more frequent, they cover more of the road network and they last longer than at any point on record.

World.title: Costa Rica Ties Worst Defeat in Its History With 7-0 Loss to Argentina
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national soccer team lost 7-0 to Argentina on Tuesday night in Córdoba. The result ties the worst defeat in the team’s history. The friendly at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes, which kicked off at 5 p.m. Costa Rica time, was effectively over by halftime. Argentina led 4-0 at the break and scored three more after the restart. Costa Rica had less than a third of the possession and rarely reached the attacking third.

The score matches Costa Rica’s 7-0 loss to Spain at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and a 7-0 defeat to Mexico in 1975. It is also the heaviest loss of Bryan Ruiz’s short time as head coach. Nico Paz opened the scoring in the eighth minute. Julián Álvarez doubled the lead in the 35th, Paz added his second three minutes later and Álvarez made it 4-0 just before halftime.

Franco Mastantuono replaced Paz at the break and scored in the 48th minute. Alexis Mac Allister made it 6-0 in the 78th after Costa Rica lost the ball deep in its own half. Mastantuono completed his brace two minutes from the end of regulation time.

Argentina finished as runner-up at this year’s World Cup and is playing without Lionel Messi, who has retired from international football. Lionel Scaloni’s side came into the match after a 2-1 loss to Uruguay in Buenos Aires four days earlier. Defenders Mariano Troilo and Aaron Anselmino made their senior debuts in the second half.

At his post-match news conference, Ruiz called it a very hard defeat that showed the gap between the two teams. He said the scoreline left little to add, that there was no justification for the performance and that he and his staff took responsibility. Ruiz said Argentina exposed his team in every part of the game and deserved the win. He admitted he made a mistake by having his side play out from the back. He also said he played some players out of their usual positions, including Andrey Soto, because he wanted to test him.

The coach said his staff will review every player in detail after the international window to decide who stays in the squad. He said he did not regret scheduling Ecuador and Argentina, because his players needed to see what competing at that level demands. In his view, Costa Rica is still far from it.

Tuesday’s loss ended a difficult trip to South America that began Friday with a 2-0 defeat to Ecuador in Quito. Ruiz called that performance very acceptable by comparison. Ruiz, a former national team captain, became interim coach on Sept. 28 after Argentine coach Fernando Batista was dismissed.

The Costa Rican Football Federation later named him permanent coach for the cycle leading to the 2030 World Cup. He also played in the 2022 defeat to Spain, coming off the bench with Costa Rica already 4-0 down. Midfielder Celso Borges started both matches.

Reaction at home was harsh. Commentators and sports pages across Costa Rica called the performance humiliating and questioned whether the team was ready for opponents of Argentina’s level. Costa Rica did not qualify for the 2026 World Cup, and Ruiz’s rebuild is aimed at 2030. Costa Rica has still never beaten Argentina, and Ruiz now has a long review ahead before the team plays again.

World.title: Costa Rica’s $9.8 Billion Banco Popular Has Had No Board Since July
World.content:
Banco Popular, Costa Rica’s fourth-largest financial institution by assets, has operated without a seated board of directors since July 31, and the banking regulator is now urging lawmakers to tighten the rules for who can sit on it. In a letter dated Oct. 9, Hazel Valverde, head of the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (Sugef), asked lawmakers to strengthen the legal requirements for the bank’s directors, including suitability, professional experience, technical knowledge, honorability and independence of judgment.

The regulator warned that governance weaknesses at systemically important institutions, a group that includes Banco Popular, Banco Nacional, Banco de Costa Rica and BAC, could affect the entire financial system. The stakes are large. Banco Popular reported 4.42 trillion colones (about $9.84 billion) in assets and 1.10 trillion colones (about $2.45 billion) in equity at the end of September. Dollar figures in this article use the Central Bank reference sell rate of 449.04 colones for Nov. 18, close to the record lows the dollar has hit this year.

Under the bank’s governing law, only the board can approve the annual budget and certain internal rules. The terms of all seven directors expired July 31, and the board had already stopped meeting after two members resigned on June 29 to join the boards of other state banks.

The bank’s internal audit office warned in August that management cannot take decisions reserved for the board. In September, the bank’s corporate general management cautioned that the 2027 budget, internal regulations and the external audit contract were at risk. The Comptroller General’s Office stated on Sept. 25 that budget approval is a power the board cannot delegate.

Sugef also recommended that lawmakers stagger the board’s terms. Today all seven seats run on four-year terms that expire at the same time. Banco Nacional and Banco de Costa Rica instead name directors to eight-year terms split across two administrations, three seats in one and four in the next. The regulator said that when every term ends at once, a bank can lose significant institutional knowledge and face long periods without a working board.

The government has moved to fill the gap. The Executive Decree allows the Governing Council to appoint, on an interim basis, the four directors and four alternates normally chosen by the bank’s Workers’ Assembly. Together with the three directors the Executive already names, that would complete the seven-member board.

The decree, signed by First Vice President Francisco Gamboa Soto, Minister of the Presidency Rodrigo Chaves Robles and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla, limits the government to candidates the Workers’ Assembly has already preselected. The assembly’s integration commission said last week that it had sent its shortlist to the presidential offices. As of early Wednesday, no appointments had been announced.

The leadership gap follows a turbulent stretch for the bank. On Sept. 11, Sugef lifted Banco Popular out of “financial irregularity,” a status tied to weaknesses in board governance, and placed it at normality level 3. In that resolution, the regulator rated the board’s suitability a 3 on a scale of 1 to 4, where 1 is best.

The bank’s numbers remain solid on paper. Conglomerate profit through September reached 26.4 billion colones (about $58.9 million), up roughly 47% from a year earlier, and capital adequacy stood near 22%, well above the 10% minimum. Loans sent to judicial collection, however, nearly doubled to 67.3 billion colones (about $149.9 million) from 34.1 billion colones (about $76 million).

Sugef’s letter responded to a legislative committee reviewing a bill that would fund non-contributory pensions with half of Banco Popular’s employer contribution, one of several proposals touching Costa Rica’s strained pension system. The regulator said board requirements should be examined as part of a broader review of the bank’s sustainability.

Banco Popular’s press office said the bank will respect the authorities’ decisions and that any changes will follow legal procedure. It described the interim appointment measure as relevant because it would allow a board to act on matters that cannot be decided today.

Banco Popular is one of the institutions many here use for savings, loans and currency exchange. How quickly the government seats an interim board will determine whether the bank can approve its 2027 budget on time, while the regulator’s proposals now sit with lawmakers already weighing a crowded economic agenda.

World.title: US Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years. What It Means for Costa Rica Travel
World.content:
The United States is no longer considered measles-free. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced today that the virus has circulated continuously in the country for more than 12 months, ending a status the US had held since 2000. If you fly between the US and Costa Rica, this is not a travel ban. It means measles now spreads inside the US on its own, rather than arriving mainly with travelers from abroad, so your chance of running into it on a trip north is higher than it has been in a generation.

The US has recorded more than 5,000 confirmed cases so far in 2026, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That is more than double the 2,289 cases in all of 2025 and the highest count since 1991. PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa said vaccination remains the main way to protect yourself. He said the US is taking steps to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response.

Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles-free status, and Guatemala could follow when its 12-month review period ends on Dec. 23. Daniel Salas, a former Costa Rican health minister who now leads PAHO’s immunization program, said Mexico’s measures have sharply cut cases but warned that as long as transmission continues, so does the risk.

Costa Rica is in a different position, it has had no endemic measles transmission since 1999, and as of September health authorities had investigated about 190 suspected cases this year and confirmed five, all imported or linked to an imported case. None was fatal.

Christian Valverde, the Health Ministry’s director general, has said national vaccination coverage against measles is above 94%. PAHO considers 95% the level needed to keep the virus from taking hold, which is why every imported case gets a fast response. If you are heading to the US, Mexico or another country with an active outbreak, you can get a measles booster before you go.

The Health Ministry opened the traveler booster to anyone 15 and older, and Health Minister Mary Munive said doses are available at Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) health centers and at private clinics. Get the shot at least two weeks before you leave. The vaccine needs that time to build protection, and it is the timing the Health Ministry recommends. More than 24,000 travelers had received a booster by September.

Not sure you are covered? Costa Rica’s routine schedule gives two doses, at 15 months and at four years. Adults who have lost their vaccination card, or who were vaccinated before records went digital, are the people doctors most often advise to get another dose. Watch for symptoms for up to three weeks after you get back. Measles usually starts with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, followed a few days later by a rash that spreads from the face downward. Early on it is easy to confuse with other fevers circulating in Costa Rica, such as dengue.

If you think you have measles, call your EBAIS or clinic before you go in, so staff can keep you away from other patients. It is one of the most contagious diseases known, and a person can spread it for several days before the rash appears. The Americas as a whole lost its measles-free status in November 2025, after Canada passed 12 months of continuous transmission. A country can win the status back once it shows 12 consecutive months without endemic spread.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Rent-to-Own Homes With Up to 100% Financing
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Housing and Human Settlements (MIVAH) is drafting a rent-to-own model for families who can afford a monthly payment but lack the savings for a down payment or cannot prove to a bank that they can repay a loan. Housing Minister Guillermo Carazo said the model, known in Spanish as leasing habitacional, would add a rental stage of about five years before a mortgage is formalized.

Under the proposal, a trust or real estate fund would buy the property. When the home is a new apartment, the developer would be paid and exit the deal. The future buyer would then sign a lease with a purchase option, with the sale price fixed from the start, and pay monthly rent comparable to a regular lease. Part of that rent could be set aside as savings toward the down payment, although Carazo said whether that happens, and how much, would depend on each institution’s product.

At the end of the rental period, the tenant could exercise the option and take out a mortgage, subject to the lender’s approval. Carazo said the payment record built during those years would show the lender that the household can sustain a loan payment, lowering the bank’s perceived risk.

That record could also raise the share of the price a lender is willing to finance. In the minister’s example, a borrower initially offered 80% of the appraised value could reach 95% or even 100% after four to five years of proven payments, shrinking or eliminating the down payment.

Ideally, Carazo said, the rent would be close to the future mortgage payment so lenders can confirm affordability. The rental period would not be rigid and could be extended if a family’s circumstances change, for example if one partner loses a job and the household needs to delay the purchase or drop the plan.

Public and private banks, mutual housing associations, cooperatives and the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (SUGEF) are involved in the discussions. Each authorized institution would design its own product under a common legal framework set by a new law. MIVAH expects to have a draft bill early next year, which it will discuss with the Executive Branch before sending it to the Legislative Assembly. Carazo stressed that all conditions would need to be clear to buyers from the outset.

Carazo said developers believe the model would boost home and apartment sales. He offered a preliminary estimate of a 20% to 30% increase, while acknowledging the figure is difficult to calculate. The proposal targets a wide gap. A study by the University of Costa Rica’s Graduate Program in Architecture, the Federated College of Engineers and Architects (CFIA) and the organization Gestionando Hábitat found that 81.4% of renter households, about 279,890 families, face total exclusion or significant restrictions when seeking formal home financing.

Costa Rica has no specific legal framework for rent-to-own housing, although some lease-with-purchase-option arrangements already exist. A previous bill to regulate the model did not become law. Key details remain open, including interest rates, eligibility requirements and what would happen to savings built into the rent if a family walks away before buying. Those terms will depend on the products lenders design and on the final text lawmakers approve.

World.title: ODPEM audit finds expired food, insect-infested supplies and millions in unaccounted donations
World.content:
Auditors inspecting warehouses holding Hurricane Melissa relief supplies found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables and 15 unopened containers that had not been recorded in the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) inventory, exposing serious gaps in how the agency accounted for and safeguarded donated goods.

The findings are contained in an October 2026 compliance audit by the Auditor General’s Department, tabled in Parliament on Tuesday, which also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were not included in the donation schedules maintained by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM).

During a physical inspection of Warehouse 3 on June 18, 2026, auditors found that the 359 boxes of crackers had best-before dates ranging from March 4 to 10, 2026. Insects were also observed on the packaging of some consumable items, raising concerns about the conditions in which relief supplies were being stored.

The discovery came despite ODPEM having spent $450,000 on fumigation at the warehouse in May. The work was completed on May 14, but insects were still observed during the auditors’ inspection the following month.

The audit also revealed that concerns about pests at the facility had been raised months earlier. In an email dated March 23, 2026, ODPEM’s logistics manager informed the administrator that approximately 200 bags of rice at the warehouse were heavily infested with weevils.

The email warned that the infestation posed a significant risk to the condition of the remaining stock and could cause further deterioration if it was not addressed promptly.

However, auditors found that rice remained in storage about three months after the infestation had been reported. During their stock count, they recorded 20,400 packs of rice, contained in 204 bags, with each bag holding 100 packs.

The Auditor General said this pointed to weaknesses in storage conditions and the system used to ensure older supplies were distributed before newer ones, rather than being solely a question of whether the fumigation had worked.

Although ODPEM had arranged for the warehouse to be fumigated, the presence of insects during the June inspection raised questions about the effectiveness and lasting impact of the treatment. The auditor general recommended that the agency obtain an assessment to determine whether the affected items were suitable for consumption.

The inspection also exposed a basic problem with the agency’s record-keeping. ODPEM did not provide auditors with store records showing the quantities of goods that should have been in Warehouse 3. This meant the auditors could not compare what they physically counted with the supplies recorded as received since November 2025 or those distributed during the period under review.

The problems extended beyond the condition of goods in storage.

During a separate physical inspection at Warehouse 2 on September 4, 2026, auditors found 15 unopened containers and other items that had not been valued or entered into ODPEM’s records.

The audit also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were absent from the donation schedules supplied by the agency. The value was based on the cost, insurance and freight figures that auditors could identify from the documents provided.

The auditor general said the discrepancies showed that ODPEM’s schedules did not provide a complete account of the donations received, limiting its ability to demonstrate that all shipments had been properly identified, recorded and valued.

The report recommended that ODPEM reconcile its customs clearance records against its donation schedules, identify and record the omitted shipments, and open, value and enter the 15 containers and other unrecorded items into its inventory.

The findings are particularly significant because similar problems had been raised in the Auditor General’s 2024 performance audit of ODPEM.

That earlier audit identified poor stock rotation, limited storage space and staff shortages, as well as unsuitable storage conditions that exposed relief supplies to mould, excessive humidity, water damage and pests. It also found that obsolete and damaged items were being stored alongside regular relief supplies.

ODPEM had informed the Auditor General in April 2024 that estimated losses of relief items amounted to $3.9 million.

In its response to the latest findings, ODPEM acknowledged the need to strengthen its procedures for receiving, issuing, counting and tracking stock, as well as managing expiry dates. The agency said the unprecedented scale and pace of the hurricane response had placed extraordinary pressure on its existing administrative systems.

It told auditors that it had begun improving warehouse records, revising receipt and issuing forms, updating inventory registers and introducing more regular inspections and stock checks.

In its September 2026 response, ODPEM also acknowledged that some of the weaknesses arose from gaps in staff knowledge and understanding of the requirements governing the management of public resources. It said it would provide targeted training, update procedures and strengthen supervisory checks.

The agency further said it had introduced periodic stock checks and the practice of distributing older supplies before newer ones.

The auditor general recommended that ODPEM establish stronger controls for monitoring the condition and expiry dates of relief supplies, carry out regular physical stock counts and ensure that every donation is supported by records showing what was received, stored and distributed.

Under the agreed targets, ODPEM was to have expiry procedures and a register in place by December 31, 2026, while the assessment of infested stock was due by November 30, 2026. The agency also committed to completing the reconciliation of shipments and recording the unopened containers by December 31, 2026.

The auditor general acknowledged the exceptional conditions under which ODPEM operated following the Category 5 hurricane, which struck Jamaica on October 28, 2025, but said the scale of the response made proper controls over donated resources even more important.

World.title: Reggae Boyz edged by Mexico in Nations League quarter-final
World.content:
Jamaica's defender #02 Miguel Freckleton reacts at the end of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final second leg football match between Mexico and Jamaica at the BBVA stadium in Guadalupe, Nuevo Leon state, Mexico on November 17, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz were edged by Mexico on away goals after losing 1-0 to El Tri in the quarterfinal return leg at the BBVA stadium in Monterey, Mexico on Tuesday.

A first half goal from Jesus Corona was the difference on the night, levelling the scores at 3-3 on aggregate, but the Mexicans won based on the two away goals they scored in Saturday’s first leg 3-2 loss.

Jamaica, ranked 66th in the world, spectacularly led the first leg tie 3-0 before Mexico rallied late at the National Stadium in Kingston to reduce the deficit.

In addition to being eliminated from the Concacaf Nations League, Jamaica will now have to attempt to qualify for the Gold Cup though the play-offs.

Tuesday’s win was the first for Mexico’s newly appointed coach Rafa Marquez in six games.

Jamaica had several chances in a frenetic first half, the best in the 25th minute when they caught Mexico on a break with goalkeeper Raul Rangel caught outside the 18-yard box. But, despite getting past the defender, Renaldo Cephas tripped up and was overtaken by a fast recovering defender.

At the other end, Jamaica managed to keep out Mexico which had made several changes to the team that started in Kingston. Goalkeeper Jahmali Waite made a brilliant save in the 13th minute, parrying a header from Roberto Alvarado for a corner.

However, the Boyz had no answer for a well struck left footer from Corona, starting for El Tri for the first time since 2022, from just on the edge of the 18-yard box into the low left hand corner of Waite’s goal in the 35th minute.

The second half failed to rise to the intensity of the first 45 minutes and, despite throwing a number of attacking players into the fray, Jamaica failed to get the goal that would have seen them create one of the biggest upsets in Concacaf football.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: SICK!
World.content:
.

DELAYED admission and treatment, late diagnosis, a lack of treatment, long waiting lists, and discourteous staff are among the 1,045 cases of patient complaints registered at hospitals across Jamaica’s four regional health authorities (RHAs) since July this year.

Just over 10 per cent of the complaints have been cleared up.

These are among the findings of a troubling review of Jamaica’s public health-care sector which was made public on Tuesday by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton following a statement in the House of Representatives.

The conclusions are contained in a 50-page Ministry of Health and Wellness report, titled ‘Institutional Performance Review’.

Vowing to be open and transparent, Tufton ordered the review earlier this year. The minister had, during his contribution to the 2026/27 Sectoral Debate on May 12, committed to holding public health institutions to clear standards of governance, financial accountability and performance. He committed to report transparently, on progress and ensure that accountability is reflected in the experience of patients.

On June 19, the health ministry implemented the Accountability Framework (MAF) Scorecard, which rates 13 entities against 18 governance and accountability indicators, and the Client Care Connect (CCC), which managed 1,045 client feedback cases across the four RHAs within the first quarter of the current financial year.

Together, the two instruments answer two questions: Are the institutions well-run, and are they serving people well?

The review found that, in terms of access to service, patients typically complained about waiting lists, delayed admission and treatment, limited service availability, inadequate resources, limited service availability, difficulty obtaining appointments and specialist care.

Worryingly, in terms of quality of clinical care, patients complained about delayed diagnosis and treatment, patient management and clinical decision-making, as well as poor management of deteriorating and high-risk patients.

In terms of communication, patients were dissatisfied with inadequate explanations, poor information sharing, delayed responses to enquiries, and inappropriate verbal or non-verbal communication.

Unprofessional behaviour, poor customer service and lack of responsiveness also irked patients. Additionally, they were ticked off by what they perceived to be a lack of courtesy, disrespectful treatment, along with inadequate privacy considerations for them and their families.

According to the review, access to services was the leading category of complaints in every RHA, while quality of clinical care ranked second.

“Communication, professional conduct, and rights, respect and dignity were the other principal themes. Together, access, quality of care, professional conduct and rights, respect and dignity make up about 77 per cent of complaint references nationally,” the review stated.

It also noted that complaints, which make up the bulk of client feedback, are concentrated in a small number of hospitals. Five hospitals, roughly one-fifth of the public hospital network, generate 52.2 per cent of all cases; the top eight generate 64.1 per cent; and the top ten 69.1 per cent. It highlighted that Cornwall Regional Hospital and Kingston Public Hospital — being referral hospitals — naturally had most cases because they saw most patients.

In terms of service points, the accident and emergency departments, outpatient clinics, medical wards, surgical services and maternity services were the most frequently mentioned areas in all four RHAs for client complaints. “These are the highest-volume, highest-contact areas,” the review explained.

“Their recurrence across every region indicates that the issues are systemic, not isolated to individual facilities, and that improvements in patient flow, communication and responsiveness in these areas will have the greatest effect on client experience nationally,” it added.

The review also addressed why only 10.6 per cent or 111 of the 1,045 cases were closed during the quarter, pointing to explanations provided in reports at the regional level. Factors included: Delays in receiving investigation reports and responses from service areas; difficulty obtaining complete documentation and supporting records; high active caseloads and increasing demand for complaint management services; delays in implementing and verifying corrective actions; resource constraints affecting investigation and follow-up; and cases requiring multidisciplinary review before resolution.

“Delayed closure limits the ability to identify quality problems, conduct root-cause analysis, implement corrective action and prevent repeat complaints,” the report said.

It explained that closure performance is therefore treated in the report as a measure of management responsiveness, not merely of caseload.

The report also identified recurring quality problems that suggest systemic rather than individual causes. They include: Barriers to timely access; communication, engagement and navigation challenges; weaknesses in assessment, escalation and management of high-risk patients; deficiencies in clinical documentation and records; weak compliance with clinical and administrative standards; gaps in care coordination; inconsistent investigation and case management; weak monitoring of corrective actions; workforce capacity and oversight constraints; as well as data quality and reporting deficiencies.

According to the report, improvement initiatives were already under way. These include a structured review to strengthen investigation quality and organisational learning in addition to a review of complaints to strengthen patient safety and clinical governance.

Meanwhile, the health and wellness ministry has already piloted a family care presence programme in two hospitals to improve communication, family engagement and patient experience. It also has in place mental health consent and restraint reviews — a new policy guidance on patient rights, governance and accountability. The ministry also recently launched a channel for clients to submit feedback directly to RHAs.

World.title: Listed companies, foreign subsidiaries dominate Business Leader Award nominees
World.content:
Long-serving Observer Business Leader Selection Committee member Gassan Azan (right) shares a light moment with his best friend Gordon “Butch” Stewart at the Jamaica Observer Business Leader luncheon in 2012. The award programme has been renamed in Stewart’s honour and is set for December 13, 2026 at AC Hotel Kingston.

Publicly listed Jamaican companies and locally managed subsidiaries of overseas firms dominate the nomination list for the Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award that is currently under consideration.

There are 10 corporate nominees for the award which is seeking to identify and highlight the companies operating on Jamaican soil that provide the most wholesome and progressive environment for their workforce. Specifically, the theme of the award is ‘Business Leader: Employer of Choice’.

In an inauspicious outcome, no privately held Jamaican-owned organisation made it on the list of 10 nominees, a handful of genuine prospects for nomination having declined to participate in the programme.

The search for the list of potential nominees for this prestigious award had a disproportionately low representation among local private firms once the pool was reduced to the top 25 firms. These are the companies that had a real shot at being one of the 10 nominees. All 10 are survivors of a brutal culling process from a broad initial list of 60, then 40. They were further reduced to a group of 25. The members of this group were all considered potential nominees for the award, with 10 of them ultimately emerging as candidates to go forward.

They were selected after all 25 were asked to submit answers to a 42-question survey that was a deep dive into their industrial relations practices.

Of the 25 companies that were short-listed for the more rigorous probe, only five were privately held Jamaican enterprises. Four of the five declined to participate in the programme and so did not complete the questionnaire.

Only one publicly listed Jamaican firm declined, while three failed to meet the deadline for submitting their responses.

The questionnaires that were sent to the companies demanded significant executive time for completion under a compressed timeline. Some categories of local companies were specifically excluded from being considered for the award. Most notable is the Sandals/ATL Group which is owned by the Gordon “Butch” Stewart’s children, and whose nomination would, therefore, represent a profound conflict of interest. Companies owned by members of the Award Selection Committee were also ruled out for consideration. These are:

· Manpower and Maintenance Services Limited, owned by Audrey Hinchcliffe;

· MegaMart/Bashco Limited, owned by Gassan Azan;

· Paymaster Jamaica, owned by Ambassador Audrey Marks;

· Sterling Asset Management, owned by Charles Ross; and

· Tropical Tours Limited, owned by Fred Smith.

The other judge is Ian Neita, former managing director of Yellow (Pages) Limited.

Additionally, to qualify for consideration, companies were required to have a minimum of 300 full-time employees.

Workers at all 10 companies that have been nominated will be surveyed as part of the final evaluation process to determine the winner in December.

The Jamaica Observer will begin releasing the names of the nominees on Friday when the first of 10 stories will be published both online and in print.

The ‘Business Leader: Employer of Choice’ will be announced on Sunday, December 13, at a gala presentation and dinner at AC Hotel Kingston on Lady Musgrave Road.

The programme has been named in honour of Gordon “Butch” Stewart, the founder of the Sandals/ATL Group of which the Jamaica Observer is a subsidiary.

The first-ever Business Leader Award presentation was on December 11, 1996, two days outside of 30 years to the day when the 2026 award will be held.

The award is promoted by the Jamaica Observer whose name it carried for 30 years until the formal rebranding to the Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award earlier this month.

World.title: Runkus’s faith rewarded with Grammy nom
World.content:
Runkus .

When Billboard named Runkus’s Supernova among its 50 Best Albums of the Year in June, the recognition offered an early indication of the heights the Portmore-born entertainer’s latest body of work could reach. Sharing the coveted list with projects from international heavyweights including Drake, Bruno Mars, Kehlani, and Jill Scott, the reggae artiste was already making an impression well beyond Jamaica’s shores.

“Straight out of Portmore, Jamaica, Runkus might have the best album from the Caribbean Diaspora this year,” the publication declared at the time.

Five months later, that early endorsement has been followed by an even bigger milestone, with Runkus earning a Grammy nomination for Best Reggae Album.

For the entertainer, however, the news was not entirely unexpected.

Having invested considerable time and effort into the project, he submitted it with confidence in what he had created, trusting that his faith would carry it the rest of the way.

“Nothing is promised in life ennuh, but I submitted knowing I had put out the best, and so I hoped for the best in return. I did the work and we know the Almighty say it’s faith and works, so we put in the work and we had the faith. It worked out,” he told the

Jamaica Observer. on Monday after the 2027 Grammy nominations were released.

While the nomination represents a first for Runkus as a solo artiste, it is not his first experience being associated with Grammy-recognised work. He has previously contributed to albums by fellow reggae artistes, but receiving the nod under his own name has brought a different level of satisfaction.

“This is my first nomination in the sense of a solo project. I have been a part of other projects before, contributed to records on Protoje and Jesse Royal’s albums in the past, but this one is my first nomination as Runkus, and it’s an overwhelming feeling of joy,” he said.

The entertainer, whose given name is Romario Bennett, added that he was particularly honoured to find himself among this year’s nominees, acknowledging the calibre of artistes and projects represented in the category.

Beyond the personal achievement, the nomination carries a much deeper significance for Runkus.

Supernova, he went on to say, was not created in isolation, but brought together contributions from several people he considers family, including his late father, veteran entertainer Determine, whose musical influence remains an important part of his journey.

“This is not just my first nomination, it’s also my dad’s as well. He is on the project. Also on the project is my uncle who is incarcerated, my 20-year-old brother, my bredren dem who I consider brothers, and so this project and the nomination is extra special. I earned this alongside family,” he said.

The opportunity to celebrate his father through the nomination is particularly poignant for Runkus, who believes Determine’s contribution to music cannot and will not be limited by accolades. He shared that, although his father’s name may not have been attached to the kind of international recognition now being afforded to

Supernova, he holds his musical accomplishments to the highest regard.

“My dad did exactly what the Almighty willed him to do. Even though there is no accolade attached to my dad’s name, he became one of the greatest artistes I have ever seen,” he said.

It is a sentiment that speaks to the broader meaning of legacy for Runkus, as it also provides an opportunity to acknowledge the people, experiences, and musical foundations that have helped shape him.

He was also keen to address some of the misconceptions surrounding the Grammy selection process, noting that the recognition is not simply a reflection of an artiste’s commercial popularity or record sales.

Runkus urged critics to pay greater attention to what the latest nominations represent for Jamaica’s music industry, instead of becoming caught up in debates about which artiste is more deserving or how many times an individual has been nominated.

“The Grammys is something people don’t understand. It’s peer-based and it’s not as easy as some would have it. It’s not about popularity; it’s not about sales,” he explained. “I believe people want to see people win and, ideally, new people. But what I would say is to pay close attention to this year’s nominees, because they’re all Jamaicans, and that in itself speaks volumes.

“So we can talk about who and how many times someone is nominated, or we can choose to focus on the fact that Jamaica is up,” he continued. “It’s Jamaica all the way, so more honour to all the nominees. I’m excited to keep making music, and I’m sure all the nominees feel that way.”

For Runkus, the nomination is also motivation to continue exploring his creativity. He said his approach to music remains rooted in consistently finding inspiration in the world around him and transforming his experiences into songs.

“If anyone knows me, it’s always work for me… So there’s definitely more work to be done. I’m a youth from Portmore, Jamaica, and we a do it big,” he declared.

Runkus is among six Jamaican artistes nominated in the Best Reggae Album category for the 69th annual Grammy Awards. Joining him are Buju Banton for Too Too Bad, Chronixx for Exile, Ziggy Marley for Brightside, Protoje for The Art of Acceptance, and Shaggy for Lottery.

The nominations represent another significant showing for Jamaica’s reggae fraternity, bringing together established Grammy winners, previous nominees, and a new generation of musical voices.

The winners will be announced on February 7, 2027.

World.title: SYGNUS COURTS LENDERS TO HIT US$1-BILLION TARGET
World.content:
(Photo: Dacx Productions)

SYGNUS Credit Investments Limited (SCI) expects to announce a second multilateral financing partnership within weeks and is in talks with two other development lenders, as it looks to secure a larger bank credit line to fund private-credit deals across the Caribbean.

Jason Morris, co-founder and chief investment officer of Sygnus Capital, told investors and analysts on SCI’s November 16 earnings call that the forthcoming partner would finance SCI directly. The company is still working towards term sheets with the two other institutions. Morris did not name the incoming lender or disclose the size and terms of the facility.

“We’ve cracked the glass ceiling, so to speak, by getting a partnership with IBD Invest, and as you’ll see, in hopefully days or weeks’ time, we have a second multilateral financing partner that will finance SCI directly,” Morris said.

SCI’s first multilateral partnership dates to June, when it agreed to guarantee an uncommitted revolving working capital facility of up to US$10 million from IDB Invest for Sygnus Investment Bahamas. SCI is also an anchor investor in the Bahamas vehicle, which provides financing against businesses’ receivables.

Morris said backing from several development lenders would expand the pool of capital SCI can invest and strengthen its case when it approaches banks.

“Once we have two, three, four multilaterals, which will increase SCI’s ability, our pool of capital, it will also increase SCI’s ability to perhaps, soon enough, get access to a credit line from a bank that wants to do business in the Caribbean,” Morris explained during the question and answer segment.

SCI wants to build up US$100 million in capital available for investment, preferably with a large share in revolving credit lines. That would give it room to draw funds as deals close and borrow again as it repays the lines. At September 30, the company held US$11.16 million in cash and short-term instruments available for investment, with about US$2.45 million in undrawn revolving credit lines. It received the equivalent of US$13 million from its Class J and Class K perpetual preference-share offer during the quarter and said it expected the remaining proceeds after quarter-end.

The continuous drive for funding comes as SCI aims to lift cumulative private-credit deployment across its platform to US$1 billion by June 2030. Morris said SCI and its Puerto Rico business, Acrecent Financial, had deployed more than US$683 million to date and that he would like to reach the target about a year early. He said the platform would need to originate and deploy at least US$100 million annually. At the time of the call, he put the platform’s portfolio at about US$332 million.

SCI financed US$4.11 million in new investment commitments in the September quarter, roughly in line with US$4.10 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, Acrecent deployed US$26.44 million over the same period, including deals originated in the previous quarter.

Morris noted that several SCI transactions had reached final documentation, with deployment likely to pick up later in the financial year.

Net profit attributable to SCI shareholders rose 14 per cent to US$3.62 million for the quarter, helped by higher net interest income, lower fair-value losses and stronger foreign exchange gains. Total investment income of the firm slipped 1.1 per cent to US$5.19 million, while net investment income fell 9.7 per cent as operating expenses rose.

World.title: PRO PUSH
World.content:
Shikiri Douglas (left) of Arnett Gardens FC tries to take a shot as Nickela Thomas of Los Perfectos FC closes in during the Jamaica Women’s Premier League (JWPL) first-leg semi-final match at JFF/Captain Horace Burrell Centre of Excellence on May 16, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WHILE the Jamaica Women’s Premier League (JWPL) is still in its early stages, Professional Women’s Football Jamaica Limited (PWFJL) Chairperson Christina Hudson believes it is making encouraging progress towards its goal of paying players in future seasons.



Prior to 2025, the women’s top flight was managed solely by the Jamaica Football Federation. However, that model changed with the establishment of the PWFJL, which is responsible for the league’s development, management and commercialisation.

The JWPL has secured record sponsorship over the past two seasons and has attracted further financial support ahead of the upcoming campaign including a US$100,000 ($15 million) grant from FIFA’s Women’s League Development Programme.

The PWFJL played a key role in developing the JFF’s five-year Women’s Football Strategic Plan, launched in June, which identified a fully professional league and player salaries as major objectives.

Hudson told the Jamaica Observer there’s still a long way to go, but that she believes the goal is within reach.

“I think that we are closer because the more costs that we are able to take on from the clubs, it frees them up to be able to put more towards their player development side of their business and that can include professional contracts,” she said.

“I think we’re not quite there yet. We’re still an amateur league; it will take baby steps. But each year that we are able to give back more to the clubs and help them be more financially stable, the closer it brings us to being able to have a league that is truly professional.”

The 12-team JWPL is set for its earliest start yet when the 2026/2027 season gets under way on December 5, with Hudson hoping to make that the norm in future years.

“December to May is supposed to be the correct time for the league,” she said. “Last year, we started late only because of Hurricane Melissa, so we had some delays on that front and the season was actually cut short from a six-month calendar to only three months and was pushed to the new year just because the clubs may not have been fully ready to go, especially the ones that were located in Montego Bay. So we’re actually reverting to the original planned calendar that begins in December and runs through to May for a full six months.”

JFF President Michael Ricketts told the

Observer this month that Hudson and her team at the PWFJL have been doing “extremely well” and have done “an excellent job in marketing and commercialising the premiership”.

While the PWFJL has overseen growth in financial support, attendance and viewership, Hudson says the organisation is focused on further development.

“[Planning] becomes easier in the sense that we know what to expect and we know there are certain things that have to get done off of our checklist that don’t change season to season,” she said. “However, we’re not trying to maintain the status quo. We’re trying to improve the product that we’re putting out year after year, so there is a bit of pressure on us to deliver more each season, more for our clubs, as well as more for the fans that we’re hoping to engage throughout the season.”

When the season kicks off in a few weeks, the Reggae Girlz could have already secured their place at a third-straight FIFA Women’s World Cup, once they beat Costa Rica in the Concacaf W Championship quarter-finals in Texas next week Friday.

Hudson believes that would provide a major boost to the JWPL’s success this season.

“I cannot wait for that to happen. I’m immensely proud of our Reggae Girlz and all that they have accomplished and I think for young players, seeing a pathway forward for themselves and seeing themselves in this Jamaican team will be very powerful in getting young girls interested in playing,” she said. “But I think it will also motivate our existing players to [realise] this is a level that they can truly reach if they keep working hard and getting seen by the right people.”

The 2026/27 season will have more on the line as the champions will be able to compete in next year’s Concacaf Champions Cup following all 12 clubs completing mandatory club licencing.

World.title: Fired up!
World.content:
There are more than 1,500 Church’s Texas Chicken locations in over 20 countries.

CHURCH’S Texas Chicken says it remains on track to open 10 restaurants in Jamaica in five years after its first two Kingston locations beat sales projections.

This was the update provided by Anthony Sabga-Aboud, director at Global Brands Limited, during the official opening of its second location at Parade Square, in downtown Kingston. Global Brands Group of Companies is the franchise holder for the Church’s brand in Trinidad & Tobago, St Lucia, St Kitts and Jamaica.

“So, we are on track to hit our goal of 10 locations in five years. This is our second location, and we are actively looking at other sites,” Sabga-Aboud explained on Monday.

The new downtown location saw the company invest more than US$1 million to transform the property at the corner of King Street and South Parade. The company then hired 70 new employees, while creating a space that meets the Church’s brand and improves disability access.

With the company securing two locations in under two years, the Trinidadian businessman noted that his team is in active discussion with several property owners about opening new stores next year.

“We’re very excited about this [Parade] location and we think it’s going to be an iconic location for us,” he said.

The Church’s brand returned to Jamaica in December 2025, nearly two decades after it last operated on the island. Global Brands made a similar investment in its first Jamaican location, at Mall Plaza on Constant Spring Road, where it hired 60 employees.

The re-entry to the Jamaican market broke several global records according to Watson George, the Global Brands executive responsible for the Church’s Texas Chicken brand. That Mall Plaza store broke metrics such as customer count, transaction count and even sales for the first-day opening of a new Church’s location. There are more than 1,500 Church’s locations in over 20 countries.

“In fact, that [Mall Plaza] opening in that market was the best opening globally,” George added.

The Parade Square location also broke a regional record as it’s now the largest Church’s restaurant in Latin America and the Caribbean. The available space on the property also gives the team more room to expand the operations as it adjusts to the downtown environment.

Although the company intends to expand across the island, focus will be placed on Kingston and St Andrew; Portmore and Spanish Town, St Catherine. Deandra Jones is the country manager for Church’s in Jamaica while Dane Swaby is the restaurant general manager for Mall Plaza location.

“We are proud to be part of downtown Kingston, proud to be creating jobs for Jamaicans and proud to bring that great taste. This is only the beginning of our Jamaican journey, and we think that the future is extremely bright,” George added in his remarks.

Aside from the new jobs created, George also pointed to the various suppliers and contractors who are benefiting from the continued expansion of the brand in Jamaica. Jamaica Broilers Group Limited, Wisynco Group Limited and Massy Gas Products Limited all supply each Church’s brand with various inputs needed to serve their customers. Massy Gas Products is a subsidiary of Trinidadian conglomerate Massy Holdings Limited.

The success of Church’s in Jamaica continues to reinforce Global Brands’ confidence in the Jamaican economy which was significantly impacted by Hurricane Melissa in October 2025. The positive reception from customers and speed to launch the second Church’s location reinforces the demand from the Jamaican public for different quick-service brands.

Global Brands currently operates several food brands such as Pizza Boys, Wok ‘n Roll, Rituals Sushi and Rituals Coffee House across the Caribbean. Rituals Coffee House operates at Village Plaza, adjacent to Mall Plaza.

“It’s been very, very positive. It’s a great country. A great economy. You know, we want to keep growing and keep being part of the community,” Sabga-Aboud reiterated.

Church’s Texas Chicken is currently owned by private equity firm High Bluff Capital, with the brand receiving an injection of capital by Golub Capital in July 2026. The company signed an agreement in April 2026 to open 600 or more restaurants in China over several years. Church’s Texas Chicken was founded in April 1952 by George W Church Sr.

World.title: EPP moves to suspend Serbia’s former ruling party
World.content:
Aleksandar Vučić speaks during a pre-election rally of his Serbian Progressive Party in Belgrade on March 24, 2017. | Andrej Isakovic/AFP via Getty Images

SNS will have 12 months to deliver on the EPP’s demands, or face expulsion.

The center-right European People’s Party leadership decided Wednesday to suspend the Serbian Progressive Party, the political home of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić.

The move comes after the Serbian party, also known as SNS, lost the October 2026 general elections, ousting Vučić, its de facto leader and the country’s president for nine years.

The decision, seen by POLITICO, will need ratification by the EPP’s Political Assembly on Dec. 7-8. After that, the SNS, which has associate member status because Serbia is not an EU country, will have one year to deliver the reforms demanded by the political family. If it does not meet the demands by then, it risks expulsion from the group, as reported earlier in POLITICO’s European Parliament Insider WhatsApp channel.

World.title: Burnham’s 10-year plan lined up for Dec. 17 publication
World.content:
It is the last date that he could publish the plan while sticking to his pledge, since it is the final sitting day of parliament before MPs’ Christmas recess.

The person with knowledge of the conversations called it a “terrible decision,” since it would give MPs and the public little time to digest Burnham’s vision before the festive season.

A second person with knowledge of the conversations said that the date was not set in stone.

Downing Street declined to comment.

An early draft for the plan has been circulating in Whitehall, and officials expect it to have around a dozen sections or chapters, including on Britain’s place in the world.

In key areas, though, it is more likely to outline a broad vision than granular detail. This includes the future for England’s water sector, more details of which are set to follow in a cross-government spending review in 2027.

Burnham has a mounting in-tray of issues to get through in the next month. Before Christmas, the prime minister has pledged to outline long-term options for moving closer to the EU, respond to two major reviews on reforming welfare benefits, and spell out more details of his plan to move power and resources to England’s regions.

World.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is here. The EU has 6 reasons to pay attention.
World.content:
The game lands in a vastly different world than the one the previous version entered in 2013, one where EU regulators are trying to protect kids from harmful online content and handle the onslaught of AI. Here are six reasons an EU policy maven should pay attention to all the fun and games:

1. It's a European game, sort of

The Grand Theft Auto series was originally made by two Scottish programmers, David Jones and Mike Dailly, at a Dundee game studio called DMA Design. The rights to the series were later sold to an American company, Take-Two Interactive, in the late 1990s, although its subsidiary Rockstar Games still has large offices in Edinburgh.

Meanwhile, the EU's right to claim a Scottish success story as its own lapsed with the 2020 EU-UK withdrawal agreement.

A young man plays Grand Theft Auto IV on the game's day of release on April 29, 2008 in London. | Cate Gillon/Getty Images

European leaders worried about the bloc's declining competitiveness are turning to a number of policy solutions to encourage innovation, from new funding mechanisms to changes in public procurement rules.

2. EU rules may be on gamers' side

Prior to the game's release, gamers were concerned that GTA VI's online version would include the same micro-transactions and in-game currency that fans say are making games "dull and repetitive." The game being released today won't have these features, although a later online version might.

The European Commission is proposing new rules to curb the use of these features by kids, or at least make them more transparent, because Brussels says they encourage spending. The gaming industry says these proposed rules under the Digital Fairness Act will be catastrophic for EU businesses.

World.title: EU Commission accused of withholding emails on killing patent law
World.content:
It was “unbelievable” that there were “zero emails on this highly-politicized, economically-relevant procedure,” Carsten Zatschler, Wölken’s lawyer, said at the EU's General Court.

“All of this apparently happened without any form of electronic communication,” Zatschler said. “That’s quite simply not credible.”

In February 2025, the Commission announced it was withdrawing plans for a standard essential patents (SEPs) regulation on the licensing of patents, saying there was no “clear signal of support” from co-legislators. Negotiations between the European Parliament and EU countries were ongoing at the time. The proposal was officially killed in July that year.

The proposal had triggered a fierce lobbying battle between patent holders — including Nokia, Ericsson, Qualcomm and Huawei — and companies that license their technology, from phone makers to carmakers.

The withdrawal was announced on the same day that Vance met with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at an AI summit in Paris, where they discussed AI, Ukraine and transatlantic ties. The timing prompted questions in the European Parliament about whether their conversation played a role in quashing the proposal.

Zatschler asked: “Why was it surprisingly withdrawn? Whether a meeting between Ursula von der Leyen and U.S. Vice President JD Vance played a role, that's obviously not something we need to discuss here.”

World.title: German government recruits World Cup hero Philipp Lahm to teach financial literacy
World.content:
Philipp Lahm receives the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany in Berlin on Oct. 1, 2025. | Gerald Matzka/Getty Images

The former international full-back will take part in a program teaching financial literacy to young Germans.

Philipp Lahm, the former international defender who captained Germany to victory at the 2014 World Cup, has been tapped by his country's government to tackle another challenge: helping young Germans find the best savings account.

Lahm will become a "financial education ambassador" alongside actress Tomomi Themann, the ministry announced Wednesday. Both will work pro bono.

“As an ambassador for financial education, I want to highlight its value in making informed choices about how we live our lives, and do my part to make it accessible to society at large,” the ministry quoted him as saying in a press release.

World.title: France’s Philippe steps up attacks on Le Pen and Mélenchon as his poll numbers slide
World.content:
Philippe, who served as President Emmanuel Macron’s first prime minister, also challenged Le Pen and Mélenchon on Europe and foreign policy, arguing they are hiding their ambitions to deliver “a slow Frexit” or “brutal break with Europe.”

Philippe was once seen as the best-placed moderate to beat Le Pen, but he has slumped in the polls, which now show the far-right Le Pen and far-left Mélenchon advancing to the runoff next spring. Doubts about Philippe have also spread among his close allies since the summer.

His struggle has put French moderates in a bind, as no one among the glut of candidates crowding the race has distinguished themselves from the pack. Centrist former prime minister Gabriel Attal and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau have also lost ground in recent polls. Macron, who remains unpopular, cannot seek a third consecutive term.

There are also two relative newcomers to the race: Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner and Cannes Mayor David Lisnard.

“Philippe is falling, and there’s only one end; he’ll hit the ground,” said a centrist former minister who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. Riner’s candidacy “has finished off the job and killed the center,” they added.

Attal, Retailleau and Lisnard met Tuesday to hammer out a deal to organize a primary that would give a single candidate the best chance of advancing to the runoff. While they agreed to hold the contest in January and stage a few televised debates, they have not agreed on who should participate, Retailleau and Attal’s campaign teams told reporters.

Philippe has repeatedly said he would not take part in a contest that would likely deepen divisions. But it will be difficult for him to ignore the primary if preparations accelerate and he continues to fall in opinion polls.

World.title: Wie Björn Höcke die Geschichte umdeutet
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Björn Höcke nutzt den Volkstrauertag für eine gezielte Provokation und präsentiert stark überhöhte deutsche Opferzahlen zu Flucht, Vertreibung und alliierten Luftangriffen. Die AfD fordert einen Schlussstrich unter die NS-Vergangenheit, doch wie funktioniert diese geschichtspolitische Umdeutung genau, und auf welche fragwürdigen Quellen stützt sich die Partei dabei?

Mit dem ehemaligen Fußballweltmeister Thomas Berthold schickt die AfD zudem einen Kandidaten für das Amt des Bundespräsidenten ins Rennen, der offenkundig Verschwörungserzählungen und Reichsbürger-Thesen verbreitet: Von Schattenmännern, die die Welt regieren, bis hin zu bizarren Gesundheitstipps.

Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren, wie die AfD mit gezieltem Geschichtsrevisionismus eine neue nationale Identität stiften will. Zudem beleuchten sie, warum die Personalie Berthold die Zerrissenheit der Partei offenlegt und welche strategischen Ziele die Parteispitze mit solchen Nominierungen verfolgt.

Den WELT-Artikel von Frederik Schindler über Björn Höckes Rede vom „deutschen Volkstrauertag“ gibt’s hier.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

World.title: Moldova summons Russia’s envoy over multiple drone incursions
World.content:
Maia Sandu looks on during a meeting at the European Commission in Brussels on Nov. 16, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

“This is what the ‘peace’ promoted by the Kremlin looks like,” fumed Chișinău’s foreign ministry.

Moldova’s foreign ministry summoned the Kremlin’s ambassador-designate in Chișinău, Oleg Ozerov, on Wednesday morning after Russian drones violated the country’s airspace.

Seven drones entered Moldova’s airspace Tuesday afternoon, the country’s defense ministry said, including one over the capital Chișinău. At least five of them crashed on Moldovan territory.

“This is what the ‘peace’ promoted by the Kremlin looks like: attack drones flying over the capital of a free and sovereign state,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. “Russia does not respect the Republic of Moldova or its people and is putting their lives at risk.”

World.title: Alleged Russian agent arrested for spying on Silicon Valley tech firm
World.content:
A Russian national has been arrested in California on suspicion of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided support to Ukraine, US officials said on Wednesday.

 

Igor D'iu faces charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, operating as a foreign agent without notifying US authorities, stalking and fraud.

"Igor D'iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major US technology company," Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.

Rozhavsky said D'iu used "physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence."

US Attorney Craig Missakian said the company was targeted because of its "assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."

"We will not tolerate any efforts -- by foreign governments or otherwise -- to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," Missakian said.

What does the indictment say?

According to the indictment, D'iu travelled from Turkey to Mexico in June 2026 before being smuggled into the United States, where he allegedly communicated with his Russia-based co-conspirators via Telegram.

They allegedly instructed him to gather information on company employees and visit a coffee shop near its Palo Alto office to "photograph their laptop screens while they worked."

FBI agents found $18,000 (€15,500) in cash, a fake US passport under the name "Hugo Landry Johns" and two Russian passports during an October raid on D'iu's home in East Palo Alto, according to the Justice Department.

If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the US attorney general, five years for conspiracy, five years for stalking and one year for fraud.

He is scheduled to appear in federal court on 24 November.

World.title: Bukele confirms airstrike on Haitian gang leader Jeff's luxury mansion
World.content:
The president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, confirmed on Wednesday that his forces had attacked and destroyed the luxurious mansion of one of the main leaders of Haiti's criminal gangs, known as "Jeff" Larose. For now, it is not clear whether the leader was killed in the strike or whether he was even in the house when it was bombed.

 

Bukele posted a video on the social network X showing images of Jeff posing in front of his mansion, followed by Salvadoran helicopters that approach the building and open fire. The footage shows several columns of smoke rising above the property.

"My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières," the president wrote, referring to the 1803 battle that helped secure Haiti's independence from France and make it the world's first black republic.

Thousands of Haitians took to the streets of Port-au-Prince for the second day in a row to celebrate the operation and chant the Salvadoran president's name. "Jeff is a criminal and I hope he is dead. We asked for help and Bukele answered us," said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old vendor.

Jeff Larose, also known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa or Taliban, leads a gang that has controlled the community of Canaan, north of Port-au-Prince, for years. According to Haiti expert Diego Da Rin of the International Crisis Group, speaking to AP, it is one of the country's most structured criminal organisations and one with the greatest territorial control.

Related Haiti formalises security pact with El Salvador as thousands march in support of Bukele

The strike comes after Salvadoran forces also attacked the residence of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, on 8 November. The two leaders were allies and are considered two of the main criminal bosses in the capital.

Salvadoran deployment endangers civilians

Bukele deployed about 2,500 troops to Haiti last month, after four Salvadoran soldiers were attacked on 18 October in gang-controlled territory and went missing.

The use of helicopters and explosive drones has made it possible to step up operations against criminal organisations, but it has also increased the risk to the civilian population.

Experts warn that one of the main challenges remains keeping control of the territories that have been retaken and preventing the gangs from taking reprisals against residents.

World.title: Data watchdog probes massive Deutsche Bank leak of 15M files
World.content:
Following the massive data breach that leaked over 15 million internal records, the office of the commissioner for data protection in Hesse has said on Wednesday that it has launched a probe into Deutsche Bank.

 

Alexander Rossnagel, the data protection commissioner, said he will check whether the bank had appropriate data protection measures and if the leak was reported in a timely fashion.

"I am investigating whether Deutsche Bank promptly notified the affected individuals," Rossnagel said.

Whistleblowers leaked internal documents to a group of international media, revealing that the bank had reportedly ignored repeated internal warnings about money laundering, corruption or sanctions violations.

Among the bank's clients are Russian oligarchs, US President Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Deutsche Bank CEO admits errors

"When you look at the events today, you naturally question whether something could have been done differently," CEO of Deutsche Bank, Christian Sewing, told German newspaper Handelsblatt.

"Looking back, you can always say that at a certain point in time you might have been able to prioritise differently," Sewing told Handelsblatt.

When asked whether he took internal warnings seriously, Sewing refuted: "During the customer review, I asked whether a private customer needs the same complex process as a large company with 300 subsidiaries," Handelsblatt reports.

"That doesn't mean I wanted to put risks aside."

A blow to Deutsche Bank's reputation

Although Deutsche Bank said the matters "date back many years" and that it had reinforced its controls, the leak has dealt consequential damage to the bank's reputation, sending its share down.

The bank claims it proactively informed the appropriate authorities about the leak and that testing found no account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed.

While the probe won't investigate the documents, it will assess the technical and organisational measures put in place to judge if they were appropriate.

World.title: US Defence Secretary announces military cooperation in surprise Caracas visit
World.content:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela on Wednesday, state TV reported, during an unexpected visit to Caracas.

 

Hegseth was received by Venezuela's interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, in the capital ahead of a planned visit to Colombia later Wednesday.

"We see this as a renewal of our defence partnership and an opportunity for our two great armed forces to work together," Hegseth said, according to footage broadcast by VTV, Venezuela's state television channel.

The trip, which had not been publicly announced by the Pentagon, marks another step in the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas following the capture in January of Nicolás Maduro.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, meets Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez at Miraflores Palace in Caracas, Venezuela, on Wednesday, 18 November 2026. (Miraflores presidential press office, via AP)

What does the agreement include?

The cooperation agreement announced by Hegseth and Rodríguez provides for the resumption of technical and military cooperation between Washington and Caracas, which had been suspended for years amid deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries.

According to the Venezuelan leader, one of the main objectives is to strengthen the training of Venezuelan armed forces personnel through joint training and cooperation programmes. Rodríguez said the initiative would help improve the military's preparedness to respond to shared threats.

The agreement also aims to improve the operational equipment available to Venezuelan forces and provide access to new technologies. So far, neither government has provided details on the timeline for implementing the agreement, the resources to be allocated or the specific mechanisms through which cooperation will take place.

Washington and Caracas strengthen ties

Rodríguez took power after Maduro was captured, although her continued leadership of the country remains shrouded in uncertainty. Her interim mandate expired in July and there is still no announced date for the next presidential election.
