World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 – Dates, Locations and Opening Hours
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas market season will begin on November 20, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru.

The main markets in the city centre will follow on November 28, when the Christmas tree in Old Town Square will also be illuminated for the first time.

Markets and Advent events will take place across the Czech capital, from the historic centre to neighbourhoods such as Vinohrady, Smíchov and Karlín. While some will close on Christmas Eve, others will remain open until January 6, 2027.



Prague Christmas Markets 2026 – Full Schedule

Náměstí Míru | Nov 20 – Dec 24 |

Náměstí Republiky | Nov 25 – Dec 24 |

Tylovo náměstí | Nov 26 – Dec 24 |

Anděl, Smíchov | Nov 27 – Dec 31 |

Mariánské náměstí | Nov 27 – Jan 6 |

Old Town | Nov 28 – Jan 6 |

Wenceslas Square | Nov 28 – Jan 6 |

Jiří z Poděbrad Square | Nov 28 – Dec 23 |

Karlínske náměstí | Dec 6 |

When Will the Christmas Tree in Prague Be Lit?

The Christmas tree in Old Town Square will be illuminated for the first time on Saturday, November 28, marking the opening of Prague’s main Christmas market.

According to organiser Taiko, the tree will be installed on November 23 and 24. This year’s Norway spruce comes from Šimonovice in the Liberec Region. It is approximately 60 years old, stands 23 metres tall and has a trunk circumference of more than two metres.

After the Christmas season, apprentices from Jarov Secondary Vocational School will process its wood into products for social organisations in Prague.

Where to Find the Main Christmas Markets

Old Town Square

November 28, 2026 – January 6, 2027

Daily, 10:00–22:00

Prague’s largest Christmas market will feature wooden stalls selling decorations, handicrafts, gifts and traditional seasonal food. The Christmas tree and its lighting ceremony will once again be the main attraction.

Wenceslas Square

November 28, 2026 – January 6, 2027

Daily, 10:00–22:00

Located a short walk from Old Town Square, the market will offer Christmas decorations, gifts, handicrafts and refreshments.

Náměstí Míru

November 20 – December 24, 2026

Daily, 10:00–20:00

The first Christmas market of the season will open around the Church of St Ludmila. Stalls will sell Advent wreaths, candles, decorations, sweets and seasonal refreshments.

Anděl

November 27 – December 31, 2026

Daily, 8:00–20:00

The market in Smíchov’s pedestrian zone will remain open until New Year’s Eve, making it one of the few locations operating after Christmas.

Other Christmas Events in Prague

Several additional events will take place during Advent.

– Bavarian-Czech Advent Market: November 27–29 at Chotek Palace, with regional food, nativity scenes, woodcarving demonstrations and workshops.

– Christmas Craft Markets: December 5–6 at Výstaviště Praha, featuring around 150 artisans. Admission is free.

– Lemarket: December 11–13 at Galerie Mánes, showcasing Czech designers, independent brands, fashion and handmade gifts.

– New Town Advent: December 13 at the New Town Hall, with craft stalls, workshops, performances and free admission.

World.title: Chinese National Circus to Make Czech Debut in February 2027
World.content:
The National Circus of China will perform in the Czech Republic for the first time in February 2027, bringing its production ZENSATION: Grandmasters of Balance to Prague, Brno and Ostrava.

The show combines traditional Chinese acrobatics with contemporary stage production, drawing on an artistic tradition that dates back more than 2,000 years.



Titled ZENSATION: Grandmasters of Balance, the production brings together some of the circus’s best-known acts in a programme featuring performers trained at China’s leading circus academies.

Many have spent most of their lives mastering acrobatic disciplines, with years of intensive training behind the precision and control required for each performance.

The programme is designed as a retrospective of the Chinese circus, revisiting celebrated routines that have received awards at international festivals and attracted audiences around the world.

Rather than relying on elaborate visual effects, the production puts the emphasis on the performers themselves, highlighting balance, coordination, physical strength and precision.

Its approach combines established acrobatic techniques with a contemporary presentation, placing the human body and its capabilities at the centre of the show.

The production is directed by Raoul Schoregge, artistic director of the Chinese National Circus in Europe. Under his direction, the show brings together highlights from the circus’s long history in a format intended to appeal to both established fans of acrobatics and audiences encountering the tradition for the first time.

The February 2027 tour will visit three cities:

– Ostrava – February 2027

– Brno – February 2027

– Prague – February 2027

Tickets are available here.

World.title: Could You Crack the Case? English-Language Detective Game Comes to Prague
World.content:
On November 29, The Globe Bookstore & Café will host The Edenmoor Case, an interactive detective game that challenges teams to solve a fictional crime by examining evidence, questioning witnesses and putting their theories to the test.

Set in 1928 in the fictional town of Edenmoor, Louisiana, the game invites participants to step into the role of investigators.

Armed with an initial case file, players must uncover what happened, determine who can be trusted and build a convincing case before their time runs out.



Unlike traditional escape rooms, The Edenmoor Case does not rely on elaborate physical sets or theatrical performances. Instead, teams gather around a table and conduct their investigation through a digital platform, accessible from a laptop, tablet or smartphone.

The platform allows players to explore different locations, question witnesses, examine documents and uncover new leads. But the information they encounter is not always straightforward. Witness accounts may contradict one another, seemingly important details can lead nowhere, and a single overlooked clue could change the direction of an investigation.

Much of the experience unfolds through discussion between team members. Players compare their findings, challenge one another’s assumptions and decide which leads are worth pursuing.

With limited time and multiple possible interpretations of the evidence, reaching a shared conclusion becomes part of the challenge.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Edenmoor Case | Detective Game Prague (@edenmoor.case)

The game also introduces a competitive element. Several teams investigate the same crime simultaneously, working with identical evidence and under the same two-hour time limit. Each team must submit its conclusions, with the challenge focusing on the strength of the investigation rather than simply who finishes first.

Designed for groups of two to eight people, the English-language experience offers an alternative to traditional group activities in Prague. Friends, couples and colleagues can take part together, while individual participants are also welcome to register.

The next session takes place on Sunday, November 29, at The Globe Bookstore & Café, Pštrossova 6, Prague 1. Doors open at 4:00 PM, and the investigation begins at 5:00 PM.

Tickets cost 300 CZK per person in advance or 330 CZK at the door.

Registration and further information are available at www.edenmoor.eu/prague. Updates and a closer look at the game can also be found on Instagram at @edenmoor.case.

For private group bookings and enquiries, contact [email protected].

World.title: Samosas, Biryanis and Tandoori: Three Reasons to Visit Ekant in Prague
World.content:
Karlovo náměstí is not usually the first place people think of when planning a dinner out in Prague.

It is central, but it lacks the restaurant scene of neighbourhoods such as Vinohrady or Karlín. There are plenty of reasons to pass through, but perhaps fewer to stay for dinner.

Ekant Indian Restaurant is one of them.



The restaurant serves a broad menu of North Indian dishes, from curries and tandoori specialities to biryanis, samosas and freshly baked naan.

If there are two things worth ordering, they are the samosas and the biryanis. The latter are a particularly good alternative to the usual curry-and-rice combination, while the samosas make an easy choice to start a meal.

The menu also covers chicken, lamb and seafood dishes, alongside a sizeable vegetarian selection. Vegan options are available, too, and the restaurant can accommodate certain dietary requirements on request.

There is plenty of choice, whether you are visiting for a quick lunch, a relaxed dinner or a meal with friends. The restaurant has a casual dining room, with table service, takeaway and delivery available.

World.title: Need a Plumber or Electrician in Prague? This App Can Help
World.content:
Finding a reliable plumber, electrician, cleaner or handyman can be time-consuming, particularly for foreigners living in the Czech Republic who may not know where to look or whom to contact.

A Czech platform called Helplii aims to make the process easier by bringing customers and local service providers together through a single online marketplace.



Instead of searching through multiple websites, social media groups or personal recommendations, users can describe the job they need done and post a request through the Helplii app. Local professionals can then respond with offers, allowing customers to compare prices, availability and reviews before deciding whom to hire.

The process is designed to cover everything in one place. Once an offer has been accepted, customers can communicate directly with the provider through the app, share details and photos, and arrange the work. Payments are also handled through the platform.

Helplii covers a wide range of everyday services, including plumbing, electrical work, home repairs, cleaning, furniture assembly, gardening, moving assistance and pet sitting.

The platform also lists services such as IT support, accounting, tutoring, photography and translation.

According to the company, its marketplace currently covers more than 25 service categories and 16 cities and towns across the Czech Republic.

The platform focuses primarily on freelancers and small businesses, although larger service companies can also register. To offer services in the Czech Republic, providers must have a registered business identification number (IČO).

Helplii also includes several features intended to make transactions more transparent. Providers submit their own prices, customers can review ratings and feedback from previous jobs, and communication takes place within the app. Phone numbers remain hidden until an offer is accepted.

For service providers, the platform offers another way to find customers without having to rely entirely on advertising or personal contacts. They can receive requests matching their skills and availability, submit their prices and build a reputation through customer reviews.

Helplii is available for both iOS and Android devices.

World.title: West Ham Star Tomáš Souček Launches English Autobiography in Prague
World.content:
Tomáš Souček has presented the English edition of his autobiography at the British Embassy in Prague, with the book set to reach UK readers ahead of Christmas.

British Ambassador Matt Field welcomed the West Ham United midfielder to Thunovský Palace on Monday, November 16, for the launch. The event marked the next step for the autobiography, which was first published in the Czech Republic a year ago.

The English edition will be titled Tomáš Souček – My Story and will initially be available through West Ham’s official fan shop. Souček said the decision to translate the book had been made from the beginning, with the aim of making it accessible to supporters in England.



“I’m living a second life in England. My children are growing up there, and I feel right at home. That’s why I’m so happy we can bring this book to West Ham fans. I have an incredible connection with them, and they deserve it,” Souček said to Prague Morning.

The launch also featured an unusual alternative to the traditional champagne toast. Instead of pouring sparkling wine over the book, Souček and Field blew bubbles above its cover, referencing West Ham’s pre-match tradition and the club anthem I’m Forever Blowing Bubbles.

“In England, seeing a bubble blower means seeing West Ham. Besides, I’m not really a fan of being doused in alcohol. Bubbles are a much better fit for this book,” Souček said.

Field, meanwhile, recalled watching the Czech midfielder lift the UEFA Europa Conference League trophy in Prague in 2023.

“I’ve been a fan ever since. I know he’s scored more goals in the Premier League than any other Czech footballer. But apparently, that wasn’t enough for him, so he decided to write a book, too. As a diplomat, I can only hope he doesn’t decide to try his hand at my job as well. That would start to look like a hat-trick,” the ambassador joked.

The autobiography was written by Souček together with football journalists David Čermák and Jan Palička. It covers both his professional career and personal life, including his struggles with insomnia and depression at different stages of his football journey.

The English edition includes an additional chapter covering West Ham’s relegation season, the disappointing World Cup campaign in the United States and Souček’s return to football after a serious ankle injury.

World.title: Furiant Is Back: Prague’s Czech Sweets Pop-Up Reopens November 27
World.content:
Furiant, the Czech pastry pop-up that attracted long queues and sold out daily during its first run, will reopen on November 27 at its original location inside the Parnas restaurant.

The project brings together Jiří Matějka, former head pastry chef at Karlín’s Eska and Café Slavia, and Jozef Onderka, owner of Café Slavia, SmetanaQ and the Forbína cocktail bar.



Their idea was to create a modern Czech confectionery focused on traditional sweet dishes rather than the croissants and French-style pastries found in many of Prague’s newer bakeries.

When Furiant first opened in October 2025, the response exceeded expectations. Operating from Thursday to Sunday, the pop-up sold out every day, sometimes closing earlier than scheduled.

The team initially struggled to keep up with demand, choosing not to increase production at the expense of quality.

Matějka developed the concept after several years working in Berlin, where he began to miss traditional Czech sweets. His experience at Eska and abroad helped shape an approach that combines familiar dishes with contemporary pastry techniques and carefully selected ingredients.

The menu puts the spotlight on Czech sweet meals, including semolina porridge, rice pudding, plum dumplings, pancakes and buchtičky se šodó (small sweet yeast buns served with vanilla custard).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Furiant (@furiant_prague)

One of Furiant’s defining characteristics is its deliberately limited menu, which changes regularly according to the season and availability of ingredients.

The kitchen works with Czech flour, dairy products from the Struhy farm, chocolate from the Herůfek family and locally sourced poppy seeds, which are ground on-site.

The reopening will give Prague residents another opportunity to visit the pop-up at Parnas, overlooking the Vltava River and Prague Castle.

World.title: Prague Unveils New 70-Metre Velvet Bridge on Kampa Island
World.content:
Prague has unveiled a new public artwork on Kampa Island, marking the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution.

Created by Czech-born artist and illustrator Petr Sís, the 70-metre-long ceramic mural traces key moments in the country’s history from the founding of Czechoslovakia in 1918 to the fall of communist rule in 1989.

The installation, known as the Velvet Bridge, was originally conceived as a gift to Prague for the 30th anniversary of the Velvet Revolution in 2019.



Its completion was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and administrative obstacles, but the project finally reached its conclusion on November 17, 2026, exactly 37 years after the demonstrations on Národní Street that helped bring down the communist regime.

Sís, who emigrated from Czechoslovakia and has lived in the United States for decades, returned to Prague for the unveiling ceremony.

The artwork occupies a previously unused wall along the Vltava River, facing Střelecký Island. The same location hosted the project’s original presentation in 2019.

Twelve scenes from Czech history

The design takes inspiration from Charles Bridge, with 12 symbolic images set beneath its arches. Together, they portray important moments and figures associated with Czech democracy, independence and the struggle for freedom.

Portraits of two former presidents replace the traditional bridge towers. Václav Havel appears at one end, while Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, the first president of Czechoslovakia, stands at the other. Both figures also appear in individual scenes along the structure.

The images draw heavily on Sís’s own books, including The Three Golden Keys, in which the artist revisits Prague through the perspective of someone living in exile, uncertain whether he would ever return, and The Wall: Growing Up Behind the Iron Curtain, his account of childhood in communist Czechoslovakia.

The theme of freedom runs throughout Sís’s work. During the unveiling, music from the 1960s played from the artist’s personal vinyl collection, including the Beatles’ Yellow Submarine, which also features in the mural.

The Velvet Bridge cost approximately CZK 5 million to create. Its construction involved hand-painted ceramic tiles produced by a workshop in Portugal.

The project was financed by 16 donors. The finished artwork has been donated to the City of Prague, with its future maintenance entrusted to the Technical Administration of Communications.

World.title: Hungary among EU’s worst countries for gender equality, new report reveals
World.content:
Hungary is among the lowest-ranking European Union countries in the gender equality index published by the European Institute for Gender Equality (EIGE), along with Cyprus and Czechia, the institute’s report published on Wednesday shows.

EU gender equality progress remains slow

The Gender Equality Index tracks progress on gender equality across the EU. It brings together 27 indicators from all Member States across six areas of life: work, money, knowledge, time, power and health. The data is combined into a score from 0 to 100, where 100 means full gender equality, showing where gaps remain and where policy can have the greatest impact.

According to the annual report, the European Union scored 64.5 points on the scale measuring gender equality, an improvement of just 0.9 points compared with the previous year and of 5.6 points since 2020. The results show that progress remains extremely slow, and improvement in one area does not necessarily go hand in hand with advances in others, the report said.

France leads the ranking with 74.8 points, ahead of Sweden, Denmark and Spain.

Meanwhile, Hungary is among the 14 member states that improved their results but whose gap relative to the EU average widened further. This group also includes Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Romania and Slovakia. By contrast, 13 member states, including Czechia, Poland and Austria, improved while narrowing their gap to the EU average.

Decision-making remains the weakest area

Europe-wide, the area of decision-making remains the weakest of gender equality and modest improvements are largely thanks to quotas required by law. In seven member states, women already fill at least 40 percent of the seats on the boards of the largest listed companies.

Progress elsewhere is considerably slower, however. In education, a setback has been measured since 2020 in 11 member states, while in health, progress has essentially stalled.

Also, significant differences remain between women and men in the sharing of child-care and family responsibilities.

Gender equality could boost the EU economy

According to EIGE’s research, promoting gender equality could increase per-capita EU GDP by 6.1 to 9.6 percent by 2050 and could contribute to the creation of as many as 10.5 million new jobs.

PM Magyar calls for historic breakthrough in women’s rights

In what he called a “historic breakthrough” in the protection of the rights of women, Prime Minister Péter Magyar recently called on parliament to support the government’s related aims, including ratification of the Istanbul Convention. He asked the parliamentary groups to agree that decisions regarding women’s lives, bodies and futures should be made in consultation with them, and to adopt the package together “on behalf of the entire nation”.

World.title: Hungary moves to end tobacco wholesale monopoly introduced by the Fidesz government
World.content:
The Magyar government has proposed ending the exclusive tobacco wholesale and supply rights held by the National Tobacco Supply Company, opening the market to competition from 1 June 2027.

Hungary to shake up tobacco wholesale

The move would dismantle a key part of the tobacco distribution system established under the Fidesz government, although the state-controlled retail network of national tobacco shops would remain in place for now.

The bill, submitted to parliament late on 17 November, would terminate the company’s concession without compensation. Tobacco shops would be able to source their products from multiple suppliers, provided those businesses hold the necessary excise licences.

Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy said the government wanted to end a system in which business interests linked to former transport and investment minister János Lázár had benefited from substantial profits without meaningful competition.

Government challenges decade-long concession

The National Tobacco Supply Company received its exclusive distribution rights in 2015, without a public tender, under a concession originally intended to last 20 years. Between 2015 and 2025, it generated HUF 67.3 billion in profit, of which almost HUF 64 billion was paid out in dividends, according to figures cited by Vitézy.

The company recorded HUF 11.4 billion in profit in 2025 alone, distributing the entire amount to its owners. Vitézy argued that the arrangement had effectively guaranteed the company revenue while exposing it to limited commercial risk. The government also questions whether awarding the exclusive rights without a competitive tender complied with Hungarian and EU competition rules.

Under the proposal, the company would still be allowed to supply tobacco shops, but would lose its monopoly. The government says this means there is no justification for compensation.

New rules for margins and suppliers

As Telex wrote, the legislation would also change how retail margins are calculated. Instead of being linked to the full price of tobacco products, margins would be based on the amount remaining after VAT and excise duty are deducted.

The proposed margins for retailers would range from 38 to 43 per cent for cigarettes, 25 to 32.5 per cent for rolling tobacco and 28 to 36.5 per cent for heated tobacco products. The government says the new calculation would prevent tax increases from automatically boosting guaranteed earnings for distributors and retailers.

Other obligations concerning stockholding, deferred payments and the transfer of product ownership would also be removed, allowing commercial partners to negotiate their own terms. Fines for irregular sourcing would be reduced substantially, from the current HUF 5 million–500 million range to HUF 150,000–10 million.

Political dispute over market opening

The proposal has prompted criticism from former prime minister Viktor Orbán’s office. His spokesman, Bertalan Havasi, accused the government of selling off Hungarian economic interests to foreign businesses, claiming the reform could transfer control of tobacco distribution abroad. Vitézy rejected the criticism, arguing that the monopoly had created an artificial profit centre for selected business interests.

The retail concession system, introduced in 2013 and frequently criticised over the allocation of licences, is not being abolished by this proposal. Its future is still under review by the economy ministry. The new wholesale system is scheduled to take effect on 1 June 2027, when the existing concession would end.

World.title: Polish foreign minister delivers blunt message to Hungarians: ‘I hope anti-Ukraine propaganda stops brainwashing people’
World.content:
Poland’s Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has expressed hope that Hungarians will no longer be subjected to anti-Ukraine propaganda, arguing that Russia’s war against Ukraine also threatens Hungary’s security. Speaking ahead of his visit to Budapest, he criticised former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s approach to Russia and questioned how the Hungarian politician had moved from liberal politics towards the far right.

In an interview with Hungarian news outlet HVG published on Wednesday, Sikorski discussed the future of Polish-Hungarian relations, Ukraine’s EU accession, and the possibility of restoring trust between Hungary and its European partners. He is visiting Budapest on Thursday, where he is scheduled to meet Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán.

Sikorski hopes Hungary will change its attitude towards Ukraine

Reflecting on Hungary’s previous efforts to slow Ukraine’s EU accession process, Sikorski said disagreements with candidate countries were perfectly normal and could be resolved through negotiations.

However, he drew a distinction between legitimate concerns and using bilateral disputes as hostile political tools.

Hungary has the right to demand guarantees concerning the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, he acknowledged. Poland also expects neighbouring countries to respect minority rights, pointing to areas where place names appear in Polish, German and Lithuanian.

Nevertheless, he warned that such concerns should not become an instrument of political hostility.

Anita Orbán and Radoslaw Sikorski in May 2026. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

Sikorski also criticised the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of Orbán’s previous government, saying that blaming Ukraine for the war was difficult to reconcile with Hungary’s historical experience.

He referred to the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, when the Soviet Union brutally crushed the country’s uprising against communist rule.

“I hope that people in Hungary will no longer have their brains washed with anti-Ukrainian propaganda and, like the Poles, will recognise that Russia’s brutal attacks against Ukraine also affect them,” the Polish foreign minister told HVG.

‘I don’t understand Orbán’s transformation’

Sikorski also reflected on his long-standing acquaintance with Viktor Orbán. The two politicians studied at the University of Oxford, and Sikorski remembers the Hungarian politician as a liberal.

He admitted that he still struggles to understand Orbán’s subsequent political transformation and shift towards the far right.

“Prime Minister Donald Tusk and I defended Viktor Orbán within the European People’s Party for much longer than others,” Sikorski recalled.

However, reports concerning corruption eventually became a breaking point even for those who had previously supported the Hungarian leader.

He also questioned Hungary’s relationship with Moscow during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, saying that some contacts between the previous Hungarian government and Russia had undermined trust among European partners.

According to Sikorski, the tone of certain conversations suggested a degree of closeness with Moscow that Poland considered inappropriate.

Anita Orbán and Radoslaw Sikorski in May 2026. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

Poland welcomes a fresh start in relations with Hungary

Despite the tensions of recent years, Sikorski expressed optimism about the future of Polish-Hungarian relations under the new government.

He welcomed the revival of the Visegrád cooperation and praised Hungary for removing obstacles concerning several issues important to Poland, including reimbursements from the European Peace Facility and assistance provided to Ukraine during the early stages of the war.

He also welcomed Hungary’s decision, alongside Poland, to allow Ukraine to open its EU accession negotiation clusters.

Sikorski said political dialogue between the two countries was already intensive and positive, adding that Warsaw wanted cultural and economic relations with Budapest to return to normal.

Asked whether seven months since Hungary’s elections had been enough to restore trust among EU and NATO partners, he stressed that member states must cooperate in good faith and balance their national interests against the broader interests of the European community.

He acknowledged that this had not always happened under Hungary’s previous government.

While the Polish minister did not suggest that all differences had disappeared, his remarks indicate that Warsaw sees an opportunity for a significant improvement in bilateral relations.

His Budapest visit and meeting with Anita Orbán will offer another opportunity to turn that political goodwill into closer cooperation.

World.title: Romania’s far-right AUR could turn Orbán’s political dream into reality – but what would happen to Transylvanian Hungarians?
World.content:
Romania’s rising far-right AUR party is gaining political influence and reviving anti-Hungarian rhetoric, which raises concerns about the future of the country’s Hungarian minority. However, experts warn that the biggest danger of a potential AUR-led government might not be the immediate closure of Hungarian schools or cultural institutions, but a more subtle strategy: bringing the Hungarian minority’s political representatives under its control.

The Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), led by George Simion, has emerged as Romania’s largest opposition force. After joining forces with the Social Democrats (PSD) to bring down the Bolojan government, the party has gained influential positions in parliament, the Court of Accounts and the public media leadership.

Although AUR presents itself as an anti-establishment movement, its growing cooperation with the PSD suggests it is increasingly interested in becoming part of the political system. Simion is reportedly preparing for the 2028 elections, hoping to secure a place in government.

In an analysis published by Telex, journalist Péter Cseke and sociologist Tamás Kiss of the Romanian Institute for Research on National Minorities examined the party’s ambitions, its similarities with Viktor Orbán’s former political model and the implications for Transylvanian Hungarians.

Why is AUR becoming so popular?

According to Cseke, AUR’s greatest appeal is its anti-establishment message rather than its nationalist provocations. The party uses slogans such as “God, homeland, family, freedom”, presenting itself as an alternative to the political elite that has dominated Romania for decades.

Kiss identified two major factors behind its rise: the ultraconservative movement that developed around Romania’s 2018 family referendum, which helped build connections between the party and the Orthodox Church, and the social consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic. During the crisis, many people working in insecure jobs and Romanians employed in Western Europe felt abandoned by the state. AUR successfully channelled their frustration, distrust of institutions and opposition to vaccination.

The experts also see similarities between AUR’s political strategy and the model Viktor Orbán built in Hungary after 2010. Its economic programme combines tax cuts and deregulation with economic nationalism and demands for greater state control over strategic industries.

Kiss described this approach as a form of authoritarian neoliberalism. Like Fidesz, AUR seeks to strengthen domestic business interests against foreign capital. However, this could leave the very people who support the party economically vulnerable, as keeping domestic businesses competitive may depend on low wages and weak worker protections.

Don’t miss this: Hungarian communities in Romania fear losing local representation under proposed administrative reform

Anti-Hungarian rhetoric could give the struggling RMDSZ a lifeline

AUR has recently intensified its attacks on the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (RMDSZ), including proposals to abolish the alternative electoral threshold that helps the Hungarian party enter parliament. Another controversy involved an initiative to change the Romanian spelling of the Transylvanian resort name Băile Balvanyos.

Paradoxically, these attacks could benefit the RMDSZ politically.

The Hungarian party has faced difficulties following its unpopular participation in government and the electoral defeat of its main political ally in Budapest, Viktor Orbán. With Orbán no longer in power, AUR also has fewer reasons to moderate its rhetoric out of consideration for Hungary’s government.

Cseke believes the renewed nationalist attacks are breathing political life into the RMDSZ, which can use fears about the future of Hungarian minority rights to mobilise its voters ahead of the 2028 elections.

An AUR government might not close Hungarian schools – but the real danger could be greater

The experts agree that an AUR-led government would pose serious risks to Romania’s democratic institutions and its Hungarian minority. However, Kiss cautioned against assuming that the party would immediately launch an all-out assault on Hungarian schools, cultural organisations and minority representation.

He identified two separate dangers. The first would be the erosion of democratic checks and balances and the establishment of a more authoritarian political system. This would be particularly damaging for national minorities, whose rights depend heavily on democratic safeguards.

The second, more unexpected scenario concerns the future of the RMDSZ itself.

Rather than dismantling Hungarian institutions, an AUR government could seek to incorporate the Hungarian political elite into its own power structure, offering positions and financial support in exchange for political loyalty.

Kiss compared this potential strategy to Serbia under President Aleksandar Vučić, where the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (VMSZ) has retained its institutional presence while becoming integrated into the governing system through political patronage.

In this scenario, the RMDSZ could remain in place, but gradually lose its independence and become a partner serving an increasingly authoritarian government.

Therefore, the most troubling possibility is not necessarily that Hungarian institutions would disappear, but that they could survive in name while losing their ability to represent the community independently.

World.title: Good news for Hungary’s fuel security, bad news for drivers: What’s happening to oil supplies?
World.content:
Hungary has restored its strategic oil reserves to the European Union’s required 90-day level after they were slashed by half earlier this year to support the introduction of protected fuel prices. The development should strengthen the country’s fuel supply security, although motorists may have to wait longer for relief at the pumps, as diesel remains significantly more expensive across Europe.

The Ministry of Economy and Energy (GEM) announced that Hungary’s crude oil and petroleum product reserves had returned to the equivalent of 90 days of imports by the end of October. According to the Hungarian Hydrocarbon Stockpiling Association (MSZKSZ), this is the first time since February that the country has reached the required level.

Hungary replenishes oil reserves ahead of schedule

In March, the government released a substantial portion of its strategic reserves to help introduce protected fuel prices, causing the available stocks to fall by approximately 50%. The Minister of Economy and Energy subsequently set a deadline of the end of June 2027 for replenishing the reserves.

However, the latest figures show that Hungary has managed to restore the required stockpile considerably earlier than planned.

The ministry stressed that the replenished reserves would once again serve their original purpose: protecting domestic consumers and ensuring security of supply, rather than supporting fuel price policies.

The composition of the reserves has also changed. Last month, diesel stocks decreased slightly as part of a stock rotation programme, while crude oil reserves increased. The MSZKSZ plans to replace a significant portion of the stored crude oil with newly produced, winter-grade diesel and petrol before the end of this year.

Three developments strengthening Hungary’s fuel security

The restored reserves are not the only positive development for Hungary’s energy security.

First, the US administration has extended Hungary’s exemption from sanctions related to purchasing Russian energy products until March 2027. This provides additional room for the country to maintain its existing energy supply arrangements.

Second, the AV3 unit of the Danube Refinery (Dunai Finomító) returned to full capacity in October after a year of restoration work. The refinery’s renewed operation should also support domestic fuel production.

Third, the International Energy Agency (IEA) expects the global oil market to move towards a surplus from the end of 2026. Its latest forecast suggests that supply could exceed demand, potentially easing pressure on international oil prices.

Diesel prices remain a concern despite improving global supply

Despite these encouraging developments, European motorists are still facing expensive diesel.

According to the IEA, global oil supply has exceeded demand for the first time since the start of the military conflict involving Iran. Nevertheless, diesel prices in Europe remain around 77% higher than before the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

There has been some improvement in recent weeks. The North Sea Dated crude oil benchmark has fallen by 32% from its early October peak, while European diesel prices have dropped by 11% over the same period.

However, the agency continues to warn about the risk of diesel shortages. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure could further complicate supplies, while ongoing fighting around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait continues to create uncertainty over global shipping routes.

The IEA sees the faster release of emergency reserves as one possible way to cover potential shortages in the coming months, until international hydrocarbon trade returns to more normal conditions.

For Hungary, restoring the mandatory 90-day reserves is an important step towards greater energy security. However, it does not automatically mean cheaper fuel for drivers, particularly while European diesel markets are under pressure.

World.title: Nuclear accident risk in Ukraine rising as Russia attacks power supplies, experts warn
World.content:
The risk of a nuclear accident in Ukraine is increasing as Russian attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure intensify ahead of winter, nuclear safety regulators representing 38 countries have warned.

Russian attacks threaten the power supplies nuclear plants rely on

In a joint statement issued on Monday, the organisations urged Moscow to stop targeting nuclear facilities and the electricity infrastructure essential to their safe operation. They warned that prolonged power cuts could undermine the ability of nuclear plants to keep radioactive fuel cool, potentially increasing the risk of a meltdown.

The warning comes as Ukraine’s electricity grid faces mounting pressure from Russian drone and missile strikes on power stations, transmission lines and substations. The system has already been weakened by nearly five years of war.

Nationwide blackout could affect nine reactors

Per Strand, head of the Heads of the European Radiological Protection Competent Authorities (HERCA) and the Heads of the Nordic Radiation Safety Authorities (NORA), told Reuters that Russian attacks had become more dangerous in recent weeks, with drones carrying larger payloads and using more precise targeting systems.

He identified a nationwide blackout affecting all nine of Ukraine’s nuclear reactors simultaneously as the worst-case scenario. Such an event could create a serious risk of radioactive releases, he warned. Even when a reactor has been shut down, its nuclear fuel continues to generate heat and requires cooling. A reliable electricity supply is therefore essential for maintaining safety systems and preventing overheating.

Strand said the situation could still be prevented if Russia faced sufficient diplomatic pressure to halt attacks on energy infrastructure. If the strikes continue, European countries will need to coordinate their emergency preparations for a possible nuclear incident.

Zaporizhzhia plant remains particularly vulnerable

Ukraine has four nuclear power plants, and three of them are operational. Together, they provide around 80 per cent of the country’s electricity consumption this winter. The fourth facility, Zaporizhzhia, is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and remains under Russian control, close to the front line. Its reactors are shut down, but the site still depends on electricity from Ukraine’s grid to operate cooling equipment and other essential safety systems.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday that military activity had destabilised Ukraine’s electricity network during the previous week, forcing some operating reactors to reduce their output. They also said that Zaporizhzhia had lost its external power supply 27 times since February 2022. During these cases, the plant has had to rely on emergency diesel generators. Since late March, it has depended on a single external power line.

The joint warning was issued by HERCA, the Western European Nuclear Regulators Association (WENRA) and NORA, which together represent 38 countries, including all EU member states, the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Japan. The regulators stressed that attacks on nuclear facilities and supporting infrastructure must stop to prevent a potentially severe accident.

World.title: New to Budapest? Here are 10 ways to make friends and find your community
World.content:
Moving to Budapest can be exciting, but building a social life from scratch is not always easy. You may meet colleagues within days of arriving, yet still struggle to find someone to spend a Friday evening with a few months later. Fortunately, the Hungarian capital has plenty of communities where newcomers and expats can meet people, make friends and discover shared interests.

According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), 255,443 foreign citizens lived in Hungary on 1 January 2025, accounting for 2.7% of the population. With international communities continuing to grow, there are plenty of opportunities to connect with people who may be going through the same experience.

But how do you turn a pleasant conversation at an event into an actual friendship? Research by Jeffrey Hall, a communication researcher at the University of Kansas, suggests that it takes around 50 hours together to move from acquaintances to casual friends, approximately 90 hours to become friends and more than 200 hours to develop a close friendship. In other words, showing up just once is unlikely to be enough.

The good news is that Budapest offers numerous recurring events, many of them conducted in English. International Socializing in Budapest, for example, organises weekly Saturday evening meet-ups at Kovász Kultúrbár, giving newcomers an easy way to meet other internationals without having to prepare anything in advance.

Prefer something more interactive? Board Games in English meets twice a week at different venues, while Casual Board Games and Beers offers a more relaxed Tuesday evening gathering. Sport enthusiasts can join communities such as Running Latte Club, which organises regular social runs followed by coffee or drinks, or WeMove Budapest, which brings internationals together through sports, hikes and other activities.

There are also options for book lovers, Hungarian language learners and anyone looking to spend an evening away from their phone. From silent reading sessions to guided hikes outside the capital, there is something for different interests and comfort levels.

Want to find the right group for you? Our sister publication, Hungary Insider, has put together a practical guide to 10 Budapest communities, including their meeting schedules, locations, membership information and participation fees. It also shares useful tips on how to turn those first encounters into lasting friendships.

World.title: Orbán’s foreign trips cost Hungarian taxpayers EUR 13 million – luxury hotels, Michelin-starred dinners and football matches included
World.content:
Hungarian taxpayers footed a bill of HUF 4.8 billion (EUR 13 million) for 327 official air trips involving former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and his delegations between 2015 and 2025, newly obtained government records reveal. The figures also expose the soaring cost of accommodation, while some of the most expensive trips included luxury hotels, lavish meals and even visits to football matches.

The detailed figures were obtained by investigative news outlet 444.hu following a lengthy legal battle with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. The ministry initially refused to release the records, prompting the outlet to take legal action. It eventually won the case in June this year and received the documents at the end of October.

According to the data, the ministry contributed public money to 327 flights over the ten-year period, with the total expenditure reaching HUF 4.8 billion. This covered not only air travel but also accommodation, daily allowances, catering, car rentals and other expenses. Importantly, the figures do not include flights operated by the Hungarian Defence Forces’ Falcon aircraft, meaning the actual cost to taxpayers could have been considerably higher.

Hotel bills soared in recent years

Brussels was by far the most frequent destination, with Orbán making 74 trips to the Belgian capital. These visits cost the ministry a combined HUF 550 million. His five trips to the United States came to another HUF 380 million.

One of the most striking findings concerns accommodation costs. Between 2016 and 2021, the ministry’s annual hotel bills remained below HUF 100 million on average. However, they exceeded HUF 300 million in 2022. By 2025, the government had spent almost HUF 450 million on accommodation for Orbán and his delegations – nearly as much as during the entire six-year period from 2016 to 2021.

The five most expensive trips listed in the documents offer a glimpse into how public money was spent.

Viktor Orbán poses with a Hungary scarf, with the image saying “The Hungarians are off!” The caption of Orbán’s Facebook post reads: Watch out, Germany! Photo: Viktor Orbán / Facebook
