1. Vietnam and Singapore: HUF 180.4 million

Orbán’s September 2017 trip to Vietnam and Singapore topped the list. Accompanied by a government and business delegation, he held talks and attended an economic forum. The Singapore programme also included a visit to the National Orchid Garden, where he placed a plaque bearing the name Dendrobium Viktor Orbán next to one of the flowers.

More than HUF 150 million went on flights alone, while accommodation in the two countries cost a further HUF 15 million.

The records even list some relatively minor purchases: umbrellas worth HUF 24,000 and a cooler bag costing HUF 16,000. Meanwhile, the Fullerton Hotel in Singapore recorded HUF 4 million in hospitality expenses.

2. Argentina: HUF 159 million

In December 2023, Orbán travelled to Buenos Aires to attend the inauguration of Argentine President Javier Milei. The three-night visit cost Hungarian taxpayers HUF 159 million.

Almost HUF 46 million was spent on travel, while accommodation at the Thames Plaza Hotel and the Four Seasons accounted for another HUF 73 million.

The records also show HUF 12 million in catering expenses and HUF 7.5 million for room hire and hospitality at the hotels. One working meal for the delegation took place at Michelin-starred restaurant Don Julio. The bill came to HUF 1.27 million, with a further HUF 145,500 paid in tips – also from public funds.

Other items included half a million forints’ worth of flags and HUF 90,000 spent on mineral water.

3. Qatar: HUF 131.9 million

Orbán travelled to Qatar to watch both the semi-final and the final of the 2022 FIFA World Cup. He combined the two visits with trips to Brussels and Bucharest, leaving Qatar after the semi-final for EU-related meetings before returning to Doha via the Romanian capital for the final.

According to the ministry’s records, the two visits cost HUF 131.9 million, of which approximately HUF 126 million was classified as accommodation.

The released documents do not reveal exactly who stayed in which hotels, despite the substantial amount involved.

At the time, 24.hu asked the government about the official nature and accounting of the football-related trips. Before the final, government spokesperson Bertalan Havasi said Orbán had been invited by FIFA and was attending as an official guest. However, he did not answer further questions submitted after the match.

4. Washington and Palm Beach: HUF 127.1 million

During his March 2024 visit to the United States, Orbán attended an event organised by the Heritage Foundation in Washington before travelling to Florida to meet then-presidential candidate Donald Trump.

The trip cost HUF 127.1 million, including HUF 61.5 million in accommodation. At the Eau Palm Beach Resort & Spa, a single day’s consumption was billed at HUF 11.5 million. Another HUF 2.4 million was charged at a club called Club Colette.

Car rental accounted for HUF 9.6 million, while gifts worth HUF 271,000 were purchased at the Mar-a-Lago Club, located at Trump’s estate.

Orbán’s daughter, Flóra Orbán, also accompanied him. At the time, Havasi explained to 24.hu that the former prime minister’s wife could not travel, so their daughter stepped in to accompany her father. According to the spokesperson, Flóra’s travel expenses were paid for personally by Orbán.

5. Beijing and Shenzhen: HUF 106.5 million

Orbán’s October 2023 visit to China included participation in the Belt and Road Forum, a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and talks with Chinese officials. He also visited Shenzhen, where he met the founder and chairman of BYD and toured Huawei’s headquarters.

Accommodation was the biggest expense, with HUF 65 million paid for stays at the InterContinental in Shenzhen and the luxury Bvlgari Hotel in Beijing.

At the Beijing hotel, the delegation also incurred almost HUF 2 million in room hire and HUF 3.7 million in working meals. In total, nearly HUF 13 million was spent on meals for the delegation during the trip.

Football trips alone cost taxpayers more than HUF 280 million

A separate investigation by 444.hu examined how much public money was spent on Orbán’s passion for football.

According to the records, the Foreign Ministry paid for at least part of nine football-related trips between 2016 and 2026, with the total exceeding HUF 280 million. These included journeys to watch Hungarian teams play and attend major international matches.

Accommodation was once again the biggest expense, accounting for HUF 180 million. Actual travel costs came to HUF 79 million, while government airport lounges cost another HUF 8.3 million. Other expenses, including taxis, parking and restaurant bills, totalled HUF 10.3 million.

However, this is not the complete picture either. Several matches Orbán is known to have attended do not appear in the ministry’s database. Some trips were reportedly made using Hungarian Defence Forces aircraft or private jets, meaning their costs may have been covered elsewhere.

Examples include the 2018 Champions League qualifier between Vidi FC and Ludogorets, as well as the club’s Europa League group-stage matches against Chelsea and PAOK.

Some trips remain unexplained

The documents also contain several journeys whose purpose 444.hu was unable to establish. One example is a trip between Vienna and Lisbon from 31 October to 4 November 2016. The only recorded expense was a HUF 278,000 bill for a government lounge at Vienna Airport, with no further details available about the programme.

When asked about several such trips, Havasi offered little explanation, telling the outlet: “These are government records, held by the government. Please contact the relevant ministries.”

World.title: Turkish Court Hands Imamoglu New Jail Term, Political Ban
World.content:
A Turkish court on Wednesday sentenced jailed Istanbul Mayor and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu to two years and one month in prison and imposed a political ban on him over alleged vote-rigging at the Republican People’s Party, CHP, congress in 2023.

Eight other defendants, including the New Party’s Istanbul provincial chair, Ozgur Celik, received the same sentence, while three others were acquitted. The bans will not take effect unless the convictions are upheld on appeal.

Celik criticised the proceedings, pointing to the acquittal of Izmir Mayor Cemil Tugay, a former CHP politician who recently joined President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP.

“It was said that Ozgur Celik and Cemil Tugay were distributing money to delegates,” Celik told the court. “Cemil Tugay is acquitted, while Ozgur Celik receives a prison sentence and a political ban. What kind of dual system of justice is this? Does someone in this country have to betray their cause and defect to the AKP to be cleared by a court?”

The New Party was founded in July by Ozgur Ozel and 90 other lawmakers who left the CHP after a court annulled the 2023 congress that elected Ozel chairman and reinstated his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu.

Wednesday’s ruling is the second prison sentence carrying a political ban imposed on Imamoglu. The first sentence was for insulting a public official.

Imamoglu is meanwhile on trial in the much larger Istanbul Municipality corruption case.

Prosecutors accuse him of leading a criminal organisation and committing offences including bribery, fraud, money laundering and bid-rigging, seeking 2,352 years in prison.

Imamoglu and the New Party deny all the accusations. The trial, involving more than 400 defendants, remains ongoing.

World.title: Vukovar Remembers 1991 Victims as Croatia Renews Call for Serbia’s Cooperation
World.content:
Vukovar’s wartime hospital staff led the procession this year. Of more than 1,000 people working there before the aggression started, only around 250 remained alive when the city fell under occupation. On November 20, 18 members of the hospital staff were killed at Ovcara farm near the city, alongside 182 other victims.

The Siege of Vukovar was the bloodiest battle of the Croatian War of Independence. The city was razed to the ground by artillery attacks that lasted for three months, and following the collapse of its last defences, mass killings of prisoners and the wounded from the hospital took place. However, those three months bought time for Croatia to organise its defence against the Yugoslav People’s Army, JNA, which served as an instrument of Slobodan Milosevic’s regime in Belgrade.

This secured Vukovar its heroic status in the creation of the modern-day Croatian state.

World.title: Long-Expected Day in Serbia’s Parliament Ends in Frustration
World.content:
From early in the morning, the Assembly’s first floor, housing the conference and press room, was filled with journalists from various media outlets, not only Serbian, but from the Western Balkans, the UK, Russia, Slovenia and Germany.

Rows of cameras lined the space, with reporters interviewing MPs as they passed by, while others broadcasted live from parliament.

The back entrance was reserved for journalists, who queued together, from young and visibly excited students of journalism from the Faculty of Political Science in Belgrade, to prominent figures, such as Zoran Kesic, a well-known political satirist and TV figure, who was filming a live blog for YouTube.

Many of them greeted each other as they entered the Assembly, calmly and politely, as if this was something that happened each day. In reality, for such a large number of journalists to enter the building was a rare occurrence. According to media outlet N1, more than 350 media representatives were accredited to cover the constitutive session of parliament.

“The parliament’s press office told me they had never received so many accreditation requests before, and that some media outlets had applied for accreditation for the first time, including outlets they had never even heard of,” Dimitrije Gasic, an editor at the Kompas portal, who came to parliament to cover the session, told BIRN.

Before the session opened, Aleksadar Vucic, surrounded by MPs from the now opposition United Serbia list, addressed the media in the lobby of the Assembly following an attack on an MP,.

Lidija Vukicevic, an actress and a parliamentary candidate for the United Serbia list, was doused with yogurt as she entered parliament, which turned into an event that the SNS used against its parliamentary opponents throughout the day.

A visibly agitated Aleksandar Vucic claimed that his SNS MPs had been subjected to verbal and physical attacks, while police had failed to intervene. He alleged that the attack was organised and accused the Students’ List of being behind it.

Appearing increasingly irritated by journalists’ questions, which he refused to take, and by some who whistled at him, Vucic announced that he would only speak to the media after the parliamentary session had ended.

The United Serbia parliamentary members left the conference room, while journalists fled to the entrance of the gallery for a chance to record and photograph the start of the session.

Entry was regulated by the Assembly staff who denied entry to digital journalists without professional cameras.

Nevertheless, journalists were visibly enthusiastic, particularly those who had been labelled as “opposition” journalists by the previous government. For many of them, it was a rare opportunity to feel welcome in parliament, with the SNS no longer holding a parliamentary majority.

At the start of the constitutive session, MPs voted to establish a committee to verify the mandates of the new MPs, with 244 voting in favour and one abstaining. The committee comprised Drazen Draskovic and Petar Mito from the Students’ List, and Vjerica Radeta from the United Serbia list. Presiding MP Stojan Radenovic then announced a one-hour break.

During the break, members of the Students’ list mostly stayed on the first floor in the cafe, or giving interviews. Members of the United Serbia list could not be found.

Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and university professor who headed the Students’ List in the elections, expressed pride in the student movement’s victory, saying they had eagerly awaited this day.

“I hope the constitutive session of such an important institution will proceed as it should. We will do everything in our power to ensure that it takes place through civilised dialogue, and I hope that we will elect a new Speaker of parliament very soon, perhaps even today, as this is the first step towards achieving the goals that lie ahead,” he told BIRN.

“I will act in accordance with the rules and procedures of the National Assembly of Serbia and respect the dignity of this institution, so that it becomes what all Serbian citizens would like to see in the future. I therefore call on all MPs, both from the Students’ List and other parliamentary groups, to conduct themselves with dignity and in a manner befitting a civilised society,” Srdanovic added.

Tihomir Stanic, a renowned actor whose birthday was on the same day, told BIRN this was the best way to celebrate his birthday.

“This is the greatest reward for me, because I believed in the students from day one and knew I would support them unconditionally, even when I did not always understand their decisions.

“This is the beginning of a major institutional struggle to build on the victory these young people have achieved. The fact that 2.4 million people voted for the Students’ List shows that expectations are high, and we are ready to meet them,” Stanic said.

“It is truly remarkable that we achieved such a convincing and fantastic victory under such unequal conditions,” he added.

“Now that we have the legal framework and institutions, and can make decisions by majority vote, everything will be incomparably easier and clearer. We know how much citizens expect from us, but that does not frighten us. On the contrary, it encourages and excites us,” he continued.

Session without a conclusion

World.title: Serbia’s Criminal Police Chief Detained for Alleged Torture
World.content:
Belgrade’s First Basic Court on Tuesday night ordered up to 30 days’ detention for Marko Kricak, head of Serbia’s Criminal Police Directorate, UKP, for alleged torture and ill-treatment of ten people in the government building’s garage in August 2025.

The prosecution suspects he and nine other police officers inflicted severe pain and suffering on ten people through force and threats in order to obtain information, intimidate and unlawfully punish them.

The alleged incident took place between August 14 and 15, 2025, from 10:30 p.m. to 1 a.m., in the government garage on Nemanjina Street in Belgrade. Kricak was serving in the Interior Ministry’s Unit for the Protection of Certain Persons and Facilities. The nine other suspects were questioned on November 5.

On November 6, a court in Belgrade ordered up to 30 days of detention for nine current and former employees of Serbia’s Interior Ministry, including the commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Igor Zmiric, over allegations of abusing and torturing students and others inside the government building following protests in August 2025.

Kricak was questioned by prosecutors on Tuesday, after which they requested that he be remanded in custody, citing concerns that he could influence witnesses, interfere with the investigation or destroy evidence. Prosecutors also pointed to the seriousness of the alleged offence and the public concern it had generated.

The Belgrade’s First Basic Court investigation is ongoing, with prosecutors expected to question the ten alleged victims and other witnesses.

At least 15 people were detained in the garage beneath the government building on the night of August 14, 2025, amid anti-government protests, BIRN reported.

BIRN obtained statements given to prosecutors by four of the detainees and spoke to five others, who reported being beaten, threatened with sexual violence and death and having their personal belongings destroyed. The human rights organisations Amnesty International and Civil Rights Defenders warned that the alleged abuse could constitute torture and a violation of international law.

Over nearly two years of mass protests, several protesters have accused Kricak of excessive use of force. Student Nikolina Sindjelic alleged that Kricak threatened her with rape while she was detained in the garage beneath the government building in August 2025.

Kricak is already in detention over a different case. On November 3, the Higher Court in Belgrade ordered his detention over allegations of abuse of office and torture linked to the investigation of a murder at a Belgrade restaurant in May 2026.

Kricak and Bosko Sekulovic, head of the Crime Suppression Service, are suspected of abusing their official positions and failing to perform their official duties during the investigation. Kricak is also suspected of physically abusing a suspect in the murder case.

World.title: In Croatia, 35 Years On, Vukovar is Restored, But Still Divided
World.content:
Vukovar has been rebuilt. Of the town that was virtually razed to the ground, only a few traces remain to remind people that a war was ever fought there. Its urban infrastructure has been restored, and it has gradually regained its former appearance.

“Externally, everything that could be done has been done. Now the question is what can be done – or, more precisely, whether there is a will to do it internally,” Puhovski says, touching on a sensitive subject.

Puhovski believes that the issue of commemorating victims from the ‘other side’ should also have been addressed.

“Something will have to be done regarding the graves of the ‘other side’. This is a task that still lies ahead for everyone – all the more significant and difficult because almost no one within the Croatian majority perceives it as a serious undertaking,” Puhovski says.

Drawing a parallel, he notes that in the 1970s, 25 years after the Second World War, quiet, informal and secret negotiations took place between Yugoslav diplomats and non-governmental organisations in Germany on the maintenance of German soldiers’ graves in Yugoslavia.

“In Yugoslavia at the time, there was no great emphasis on democracy or human rights. Yet an atmosphere emerged, driven primarily by the formation of the European Union, suggesting that such matters should be left in the past,” Puhovski explains.

For years, Milorad Pupovac, president of the Independent Democratic Serb Party and the political representative of Croatia’s Serb community, laid wreaths in the Danube on November 17 to commemorate Serb civilians who perished during the Croatian war.

Following considerable opposition, he decided in 2024 to discontinue the practice at that location.

Looking to the future, Puhovski hopes the situation will improve. He is a cautious optimist.

“These processes do not follow a linear path. Elsewhere, such issues might fade over time, but here, they tend to resurface. I anticipate a process of normalization – one that is constant, yet frustratingly slow and incremental,” Puhovski says.

He notes that developments in Vukovar tend to follow a similar zigzag pattern.

“I believe that some things will gradually begin to settle down. However, it seems to me that the key descriptor here – one that needs to be reiterated – is ‘frustratingly slow’.”

World.title: Letter from Brussels: EU Learns How Explosive Balkan Music Can Be
World.content:
Many of the European Commission bureaucrats who spend their days in the cold offices of this massive institution’s buildings here may now have to warm up their work atmosphere with some music from the Western Balkans, and not for entertainment purposes.

After an unfortunate incident at the recent Enlargement Forum 2026, some of them will be translating the lyrics, trying to understand which song is politically acceptable, which is not, and why. It may be the most useful homework anyone in the EU enlargement business has been given this year.

At the weekend, a Slovenian band was commissioned to entertain the guests at the Forum, and decided to play one song from each country in the enlargement group. For Kosovo, they chose a Serbian nationalist song. They played only the melody, but the big screen showed the title in Serbian and introduced it as the song representing Kosovo.

Anyone from the region knows the words: Kosovo as an eternal and holy Serbian land that will never be given up. The song, ‘Oj Kosovo, Kosovo’, was written in 1989, inspired by the celebrations of the 600th anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo. For those who claim to know the region, that anniversary needs no footnote: it was the moment that crowned the rise of Slobodan Milosevic. And everyone in Brussels should and must know what happened next.

World.title: Handouts or Highways? Critics Question Kosovo’s Infrastructure Strategy
World.content:
In November 2021, the mayor of Gjilan/Gnjilane, Alban Hyseni, vowed that a highway connecting the southeastern Kosovo town with the capital, Pristina, would be finished by 2025, within the four-year term in government won by the Vetevendosje party he belongs to.

Two years later, in mid-2023, Vetevendosje leader and Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said the road would open within the year; when that didn’t happen, he included it in a list of projects slated for completion in 2024.

Kurti was sworn into office again in September this year, but still the Pristina-Gjilan/Gnjilane highway is not ready. It will be less than 50 kilometres long, but only half has been built.

And the price tag keeps going up. It now stands at 183.7 million euros, more than double the cost initially planned in 2018, when the project was launched.

The highway is indicative of a broader issue when it comes to major infrastructure projects in Kosovo, experts say. Too often, they are dogged by delays and spiralling costs, yet the government keeps touting its ‘capital investment’ spending.

This month, Finance Minister Hekuran Murati announced an unprecedented level of capital investment spending for the coming year - 1.07 billion euros.

But according to a BIRN analysis of the data, only 16 per cent of that is new money - the rest is money that should have been spent in 2026, but wasn’t.

World.title: Serbian Court Seeks Arrest of Kosovo Serb Kingpin Radoicic
World.content:
The Higher Court in Belgrade has ordered Milan Radoicic’s detention and that an arrest warrant be issued for him for violating a measure prohibiting him from leaving his place of residence, according to media reports on Tuesday.

Radoicic failed to report to Belgrade’s Savski Venac police station on November 15, when he was required to confirm that he was still at his registered place of residence, as ordered by the court.

The businessman and former vice-president of the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista party, who is seen as a ‘kingpin’ operator among Serbs in northern Kosovo, is under investigation over an armed attack on the Kosovo village of Banjska/Banjske in September 2023.

The Higher Court in Belgrade confiscated his passport in 2023, and warned that detention may be imposed if he violated the terms imposed on his freedom of movement, which included not leaving his place of residence. He was ordered to appear at a police station twice a month.

Belgrade Higher Prosecutor’s Office questioned Radoicic in September 2023 about allegations that he had obtained large amounts of weapons and took them to northern Kosovo, where an armed Serb group was involved in the deadly shootout with Kosovo police in Banjska/Banjske on September 24 that year.

Prosecutors allege that Radoicic “procured weapons, ammunition and explosive devices” in Bosnia, “which were delivered to him in the city of Belgrade”.

They claim Radoicic “transported and stored [the weapons] in unspecified locations” in Kosovo and “hid them in abandoned buildings and forests”. In the ensuing shootout in Banjska/Banjske, a Kosovo policeman was killed. Three of the gunmen also died.

In September 2023, Radoicic said he took sole responsibility for the shootout, while he described as a “defence” operation against the Kosovo authorities, without the knowledge of his political party, Srpska Lista, or the Serbian authorities in Belgrade.

However, he also denied guilt during the investigation.

World.title: Bulgarian prosecutors charge 11 over participation in ‘s Parliament approves amendments to the Foreigners Act’s Parliament approves amendments to the Foreigners Act
World.content:
The Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office said on November 18 that it was charging 11 individuals, including four minors, with participation in a far-right racist organiation in Plovdiv calling itself the “Ku Klux Klan”.

The statement said that a 32-year-old individual has been charged with leading the “Ku Klux Klan organisation – Plovdiv Division”, with 10 members, from January 2025 to November 16 2026.

The organisation aimed to preach and incite discrimination, violence and hatred based on race, skin colour, origin, nationality, ethnicity and sexual orientation through speech, print, electronic information systems and otherwise, a crime under the Criminal Code.

The Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office is also charging 10 identified members of the organisation – men, including four minors aged 16 and 17, with participation in the same structure.

The statement said that on November 17, a joint special operation was carried out in the city of Plovdiv by the Interior Ministry and State Agency for National Security under the leadership of the Plovdiv District Prosecutor’s Office.

During searches and seizures in the city of Plovdiv and the town of Rakovski, at 14 addresses – homes and adjacent buildings inhabited by members of the structure, and in two motor vehicles, various material evidence was found – books, notebooks, badges, clothes with specific symbolism, telephones, masks, swastikas and other items proving affiliation with the far-right racist organisation.

The flag of the Plovdiv structure was also found at one of the addresses.

It was established that its members gathered from January 2025 to November 26 in various public places in the city of Plovdiv, including in restaurants.

The accused alleged leader was detained for a period of up to 72 hours by order of the supervising prosecutor.

The existence and activities of the organization became known during the investigation into the murder of 37-year-old Georgi Kuzev on Mladeshki Hulm in the city of Plovdiv on August 4 2026, the statement said.

Kuzev was murdered by a group of youths who adhered to extremist views.

The Ku Klux Klan is a US white supremacist group founded in 1865. In the 19th and 20th centuries, members were linked to extreme racist violence.

World.title: Bulgarian prosecutors charge 11 over participation in ‘s Parliament approves amendments to the Foreigners Act
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Parliament voted on November 18 to approve the second and final reading of amendments to the Foreigners Act, tabled by the Cabinet after it adopted them in July.

The amendments bring Bulgarian law in line with European Commission directives.

Employers will be required to pay compensation to foreign nationals if they lose access to the labour market through no fault of their own but due to their employer’s actions.

When foreign citizens who have the right of long-term residence in Bulgaria lose their employment due to the fault of the employer, not only must they receive compension, they will be able to register with the employment bureau and during this period their right of residence will not be revoked.

The amendments introduce an obligation to conclude a written contract setting out the rental conditions for accommodation provided by the employer to seasonal workers.

Foreigners employed as seasonal worker will pay health insurance for the duration of their stay in Bulgaria in order to have access to healthcare.

Through changes to the transitional and final provisions of the law, the deadline for issuing personal documents for Bulgarian and foreign citizens was reduced.

The deadline for issuing personal documents, including identity cards, passports and driver’s licences, is reduced from 30 to 20 days.

The fast order remains three days, and the express order will now be eight hours from the time of request.

The amendments were drafted because of the need to transpose into Bulgarian law a 2024 EU directive on a uniform application procedure for third-country (meaning, non-EU) nationals for a single permit to reside and work in the territory of an EU member state and on a common set of rights for third-country workers legally residing in a member state, the Bulgarian government information service said in July after the Cabinet adopted the amendments.

The objective of the proposed amendments and supplements is to achieve compliance between the national legal framework and the EU legal framework with regard to the Pact on Migration and Asylum, and in particular to determine the authorities for the screening procedure and to determine the tasks to be performed by other relevant state structures, the government information service said.

World.title: European Commission sets up new EU Sanctions Office, appoints new EU Sanctions Envoy
World.content:
The European Commission (EC) said on November 18 that it has created an EU Sanctions Office.

The purpose of the offrice is to bring together the Commission’s expertise on the entire sanctions lifecycle, from policy design to implementation, enforcement, and anti-circumvention, including outreach to and engagement with third countries, according to the statement.

The EC has appointed Lars Danielsson as International Special Envoy for the Implementation of EU Sanctions.

Danielsson will take up the position on February 6 2027, when the mandate of the current Envoy, David O’Sullivan, ends.

Danielsson, a career Swedish diplomat with extensive diplomatic and EU experience, held senior positions in the Swedish Prime Minister’s Office, including as State Secretary for International and EU Affairs, and most recently served as Sweden’s Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the EU from 2016 to 2023.

A central part of the new Office’s work will be to support the EU Sanctions Envoy, whose role is key to the EU’s efforts to prevent circumvention and work with partner countries, the EC said.

The Envoy engages with third countries to reduce the risk that EU sanctions are bypassed notably through alternative trade routes, financial channels, or procurement networks.

EC President von der Leyen said: “EU sanctions are a central part of our response to Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine”.

“With each package we are eroding the foundations of Russia’s war economy. But to be effective, they must be fully implemented, rigorously enforced and protected against circumvention. And that is why we are creating the EU Sanctions Office, to strengthen our capacity and ensure the impact of all our sanctions regimes,” Von der Leyen said.

The statement said that this approach will ensure the role of sanctions coordination for the EU vis-à-vis member states and third countries and is relevant for all sanctions regimes, in particular Russia and Belarus but also Iran, North Korea, Syria, and hybrid and organised crime.

“It will support member states with faster compliance guidance, data sharing, and economic and technical analysis to ensure harmonised implementation and enforcement of our sanctions,” the EC said.

As the demands on designing and implementing sanctions evolve, strengthening the Commission’s capacities and structures is essential, it said.

The scale and complexity of these measures have also shown the need for stronger coordination, closer cooperation with member states, and deeper engagement with international partners, the Commission said.

(Photo of Lars Danielsson: Swedish government)

World.title: EC proposes 45 billion euro in additional financial support for Ukraine in 2027
World.content:
The European Commission (EC) adopted on November 18 a set of legislative proposals to provide up to 45 billion euro in additional financial support to Ukraine in 2027, helping to address the country’s estimated 70 billion euro financing gap for next year, the EC said.

These proposals follow the EU’s 90 billion euro Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027 and reaffirm the Union’s continued commitment to supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia’s ongoing war of aggression, the statement said.

The legislative package consists of:

A proposal establishing an Instrument for Coordinated Support to Ukraine, providing a new loan of up to 45 billion to be financed by borrowing in capital markets;

A proposal to amend the current Multiannual Financial Framework Regulation enabling the EU budget to guarantee the new loan; and

Incentives for international partners to provide additional financial support to Ukraine via proposals to amend the existing Ukraine Facility and the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism.

EC President Ursula von der Leyen said: “Europe will continue to ensure maximum support to Ukraine and maximum pressure on Russia”.

“We have provided vital support to Ukraine throughout this war. And we will continue to help Ukraine protect its people and infrastructure from Russia’s attacks,” Von der Leyen said.

“And keep schools and hospitals open as Russia rains drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities.”

For 2026, Ukraine’s needs are covered, she said.

“And today we are proposing a further 45 billion euro to cover two thirds of its needs for 2027. Together, with our international partners, we will strengthen Ukraine. For as long as it takes to achieve a just and lasting peace.”

The proposed 45 billion euro support will take the form of a limited-recourse loan. This means that Ukraine will be required to repay the principal only once it receives reparations from Russia.

The proposed support would be structured in two components, with up to 25 billion euro allocated to military assistance and up to 20 billion euro provided as general budget support.

The support will help Ukraine strengthen its defence capabilities, maintain essential public services and sustain its economic resilience, the EC said.

It will also support closer integration between Ukraine’s and Europe’s defence industries.

The budget support will be conditional on Ukraine pursuing reforms, including in the areas of rule of law and anti-corruption which are relevant for the implementation of the interim benchmarks under the Fundamentals Cluster, the statement said

The EU support to Ukraine will be financed through Union borrowing on capital markets. The new loan would be guaranteed by the EU budget headroom. The headroom guarantees the EU financial assistance programmes for Ukraine adopted since 2023 and provides a solid and cost-efficient backing for the loan.

As in 2026, the EU proposes to cover around two-thirds of Ukraine’s urgent financing needs, while continued support from international partners will be essential to meet the remaining needs. To facilitate additional third-country contributions, the Commission is proposing two further amendments as part of the Instrument for Coordinated Support to Ukraine.

First, the Commission proposes to extend the possibilities for using future windfall profits generated by immobilised Russian sovereign assets.

An amendment to the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, would allow these revenues, once the repayment of the previous G7-backed loans disbursed under this instrument has been completed, to contribute to the repayment of new eligible loans provided by the EU and G7 partners.

This would also allow future windfall profits from immobilised Russian assets to contribute to the repayment of the proposed 45 billion euro loan and the existing 90 billion euro Ukraine Support Loan, without changing the principle that Ukraine would only be required to repay the principal once it receives reparations from Russia.

Second, the Commission proposes a new mechanism to facilitate additional EU lending to Ukraine fully backed by guarantees from third countries.

Up to five billion euro in additional EU loans can be implemented through the Ukraine Facility with the financial backing of AAA/Aaa-rated third countries. This would allow international partners to support Ukraine through the EU’s well-established borrowing capacity and delivery programmes with strong safeguards for the Union budget.

The EU maintains its position that Russia must be held accountable for the damage caused by its war of aggression against Ukraine. The Union reserves its right to use immobilised Russian assets to repay the loans, in full accordance with EU and international law, the EC said.

The legislative proposals will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU for consideration and adoption in accordance with the applicable legislative procedures.

The Commission will work closely with the co-legislators and EU member states to ensure that the necessary arrangements are in place to provide Ukraine with timely and predictable financial support in 2027, the EC said.

(Photo: G Schouten de Jel)

World.title: Athens-headquartered Eurobank to acquire Bulgaria’s First Investment Bank
World.content:
Eurobank S.A. and the majority shareholders of First Investment Bank (Fibank) have agreed on the acquisition of Fibank, creating the #1 bank in Bulgaria and a Southeastern European banking champion, Eurobank said on its website on November 18.

Eurobank is to acquire a 65 per cent stake in Fibank, to be followed by a mandatory tender offer for the remaining shares.

Additionally, Bulgarian Development Bank has committed to tender its about 18 per cent stake in the mandatory tender offer, the statement said.

The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to customary regulatory approvals and closing conditions.

The statement said that Fibank is valued at about a billion euro and for the transaction, which is to be entirely cash, Eurobank will pay about 650 million euro for the 65 per cent stake.

Eurobank S.A. is a leading banking group in South Eastern Europe, headquartered in Athens and listed on Euronext Athens and the Cyprus Stock Exchange, the statement said. It holds leading positions in its core markets of Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria.

Fibank is Bulgaria’s fifth-largest bank by asset market share as of September 30 2026 with a strong retail and corporate banking franchise and a comprehensive range of products and services, Eurobank’s statement said.

Following the envisaged combination of Fibank and Eurobank Bulgaria (Postbank), the combined franchise will become the largest bank in Bulgaria by total assets, and deposits, with a market share of 20 per cent as of September 30 2026, the statement said.

The statement said that the transaction represents a further step in the execution of Eurobank’s strategy to strengthen its regional presence and build leading banking franchises across its core markets, combining the number one position in Bulgaria with leading positions in Greece and Cyprus.

“Bulgaria offers a compelling combination of growth, convergence potential and euro-area membership.” Eurobank said.

“Having adopted the euro on January 1 2026, it is one of the euro area’s faster-growing economies, with real GDP growth projected at 2.6 per cent in 2026 – ahead of the EU at 1.4 per cent.”

Fibank was founded on October 8 1993 by Ivailo Mutafchiev and Tseko Minev.

It has been listed on the Bulgarian Stock Exchange since its 2007 IPO, at the time the largest bank IPO in Bulgaria. Fibank is the fifth-largest bank in the country. It operates 115 branches in Bulgaria, a banking subsidiary in Albania and a branch in Cyprus and employs more than 2700 people as of December 2025.

As of September 2026, Fibank reported consolidated total assets of 10.6 billion euro, gross loans of 5.6 billion euro, customer deposits of 8.2 billion euro and tangible book value of 1.05 billion euro. Profit after tax for the first nine months of 2026 amounted to 97 million euro.

Eurobank has been present in Bulgaria since 2002 through Eurobank Bulgaria AD (Postbank), currently the fourth-largest bank in the country. The network comprised 181 retail branches and 11 business and private banking centres, with 3143 employees. The Bulgarian business generated adjusted net profit of 182 million euro in the first nine months of 2026.

(Photo via Fibank’s Facebook page)

World.title: Opposition slams Radev, Yotova for appeasing Putin as ships are sunk off Bulgaria’s coast
World.content:
The policy of appeasing the warmonger Putin — a policy introduced by Prime Minister Roumen Radev and President Ilana Yotova — has brought the war dangerously close to the Bulgarian Black Sea coast, former prime minister and parliamentary leader of opposition We Continue the Change Nikolai Denkov said in a post on Facebook on November 17.

Denkov’s comment came against the background of the latest drone attack on a merchant ship off the coast of Bulgaria, in a series of incidents that Bulgaria’s government refuses to blame on Russia.

Romania’s Maritime Administration said that the November 17 sinking of the Gas Husky was the work of Russia, but Bulgaria’s authorities remained silent on the matter, as they have in all cases of the seven merchant ship attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast since the beginning of October.

Denkov said: “The ‘peace-making’ efforts of Radev and Yotova — which misled hundreds of thousands of Bulgarians during the elections — are yielding results. Just not the kind they promised”.

“In the Black Sea, two more ships have been sunk by Russian drone attacks in the span of just two days. We expect an explanation from ‘Prime Minister’ Radev as to when and exactly how peace will arrive, and when commercial vessels will once again be able to sail safely within our Black Sea economic zone,” Denkov said.



According to Denkov, Yotova must clarify whether her support for the resolution adopted at the 20th Summit of the International Organisation of La Francophonie — which identifies Russia as a military aggressor and reaffirms Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders — signals a shift in how the country’s leadership envisions the path to peace.

In a media statement on November 17, Democratic Bulgaria co-leader Ivailo Mirchev said: “We insist that President Yotova convene the Consultative Council of National Security”.

“There are two reasons. A seventh sunken ship, they still don’t know the reasons for the first sunken ship and who sank it. And secondly, Russia’s request, during the meetings in Abu Dhabi, to restore the geopolitical borders of 1997. If you remember, Bulgaria was not in Nato at that time,” Mirchev said.

Mirchev said that no measures have been taken since the first Consultative Council of National Security. That meeting was held on October 7.

“And not only that – when our allies provided us with a plane to monitor the Black Sea, what the authorities did was not give the order to destroy the drones that sank another ship. As a result, there are currently 421 containers on the Bulgarian coast,” Mirchev said.

Yordan Ivanov, a DB MP and chairperson of Parliament’s committee on transport and communications, said: “We from Democratic Bulgaria insist that the ruling party include in the agenda of the National Assembly this week our proposal for the creation of an interdepartmental unit under the Cabinet security council”.

“It should analyse the economic risks for the state budget and Bulgarian business arising from the crisis in the Black Sea. I recall that more than 20 years ago, a similar unit operated, which constantly assessed the risks to the economy related to difficulties in the transportation of goods. We insist that our proposal be considered this week,” Ivanov said.

The government’s idea is to depersonalise the topic of the attacks in the Black Sea to such an extent that they completely disappear from the airwaves, and we are observing this for the second day in a row, Georg Georgiev, an MP for opposition GERB-UDF and a former foreign minister said.

What the government is doing at the moment is not just irresponsible, it is dangerous, harmful, and when it comes to priorities like connectivity, which Prime Minister Radev boasts about so much, let him look into the eyes of the European partners who will come to Bulgaria and comment on the topic, Georgiev said.

“What security in the most dangerous sea in the world, what trade, what shipping, what connectivity and what middle corridor in the Black Sea, which is more dangerous than the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.

Georgiev said that the question of whose ships are not being asked, the topic of Russia and the topic of security in the Black Sea region and the peace that the government wants are not being raised.

“If Romania already has several drones destroyed, just a few days ago we imposed reservations on the Dublin declaration, which targets an extremely important issue for Bulgaria from 2022, when Russia said that the countries that have joined Nato at a certain point must leave the alliance, Georgiev said.

He said that at the moment there is no talk of shipping security, supplies, trade, tourism, “but only of the statistics that we have rescued people and an operation has been carried out”.

“The propaganda has managed to silence it very successfully, but I can tell the government that with all the forces we have in public communication and media presence, we will not allow it and every time there are such attacks, we will come out and publicise them, because the security of our country is a component of the common security of Europe,” he said.

GERB-UDF MP Hristo Gadzhev said that one of the government’s undisputed successes is that it allowed the Black Sea to become the most dangerous sea in the world.

“The government is acting like an extra who only registers the strikes in our area of the Black Sea, which affects all taxpayers, since rescue operations cost money and pollution affects Bulgarian tourism,” Gadzhev said.

“Unless it is some secret strategy of the government to develop new tourist opportunities next year, such as a drone excursion, watching a live ship sinking,” he said.

The November 17 attack is yet another refutation of the statement by Deputy Prime Minister Ivo Hristov, who two weeks ago told Bulgarian National Television that after the end of the presidential elections, the attacks on the ships had stopped.

“We can note that the attacks stopped after the elections. We will definitely not hide the truth about the attacks, but throwing accusations at anyone could lead us to war,” Hristov – a former MEP who has a long record of pro-Russian statements – said.

The media statements by Bulgaria’s defence and transport ministries about the November 16 and 17 attacks emphasised how the sailors on the two vessels had been rescued. Nothing was said about who was behind the attacks, although it would take remarkable naïveté, incompetence or a yearning to play to a pro-Russian section of the electorate to blame any country other than Russia.

(Photo of the Gas Husky on November 17: Defence Ministry)

World.title: EU autumn economic forecast raises Bulgaria 2026 growth forecast to 2.7%
World.content:
The European Commission’s autumn forecast for the EU economy, released on November 17, projected Bulgaria’s economic growth this year at 2.7 per cent, up from the EC’s 2.5 per cent estimate in its spring forecast in May.

The Commission also lowered its growth estimate for Bulgaria’s economy in 2027 to 2.1 per cent from 2.2 per cent, while also projecting 2.3 per cent growth in 2028.

Bulgaria’s government initially targeted 2.6 per cent growth this year, but the most recent Finance Ministry figures estimate growth at three per cent this year. The country’s draft 2027 Budget package targets 2.5 per cent growth in 2027.

The Commission attributed the projected slowdown in Bulgaria’s economic growth to lower consumer demand (due to high prices), a deceleration in wage growth, as well as reduced investment after the European Union’s NextGenerationEU post-Covid stimulus programme ends in 2026.

Even so, Bulgaria’s projected economic growth both this year and in 2027 is estimated to exceed that of the euro area and the EU as a whole. The Commission forecast 1.2 per cent growth in the euro zone in 2026 and 2027, and 1.4 per cent for the EU economy in both years.

The autumn forecast further increased the EC’s estimate for harmonised inflation in Bulgaria this year, to 4.6 per cent from 4.2 per cent in the spring forecast, projecting a deceleration to 3.9 per cent in 2027 and 3.3 per cent in 2028.

This estimate reflected higher energy prices following the conflict in the Middle East, but the Commission noted that services inflation has also been high, driven by rising input costs, notably for energy and labour.

Regarding Budget balance, the EC projected the deficit to widen to five per cent of GDP this year, before dropping to four per cent next year and rising again to 4.8 per cent in 2028.

Bulgaria’s Finance Ministry, in the macroeconomic framework tabled alongside the 2027 Budget package (adopted by the Cabinet on November 16), projected this year’s deficit at 5.5 per cent and targeted a 3.5 per cent deficit for 2027.

World.title: Second merchant ship in two days sinks off Bulgaria’s coast after being hit by drones
World.content:
A search and rescue mission was mounted on November 17 for the crew of the Gas Husky, the second merchant vessel to sink off Bulgaria’s coast in two days.

The Romanian Maritime Administration said that the ship had been hit by drones, though there was no immediate official confirmation from Bulgarian authorities.

A statement by Bulgaria’s Defence Ministry said that two Air Force Su-25 and a Cougar helicopter were involved in the operation to rescue the crew of the Gas Husky, which sank about 50 miles east of Byala.

A life raft with people had been located at the site, the Defence Ministry said.

The ministry said that the Gas Husky disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and at 8.02am on November 17, an emergency buoy was activated, emitting a signal for a sunken ship.

The Gas Husky, a Liberian-flagged gas transport vessel, had been en route from the port of Alexandria in Egypt to the port of Navodari (Midia), Romania.

On November 16, the Betul 8 sank in the Black Sea off Cape Kaliakra and the mouth of the Kamchia River following a drone strike. All 12 crew were rescued.

The site of the sinking of the Gas Husky is not far from where the Betul 8 went down.

There have been several drone strikes against merchant vessels off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania, with loss of life and some ships sunk. The attacks are widely blamed on Russia.

The total number of such incidents in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea has now reached seven since the beginning of October, when attacks on vessels off the Bulgarian coast began. Bulgarian authorities continue to refuse to name who is behind the attacks.

(Photo: Vessel Finder)

World.title: New Routes and More Flights to Croatia in Winter Schedule
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – New routes and more flights are on the cards for Croatia as part of the winter flight schedule.

Croatian airports are going to be connected by regular routes to 26 markets during the winter flight schedule, which is one more than last winter. Poslovni reports that there will be 35 airlines operating in total, or three more than before. 77 percent of operations are directed abroad with 110 unique routes, representing an increase of three routes, the Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) has revealed.

HTZ collected the flight data for the winter schedule from Croatia’s airports in October. They add that the data shows positive trends continuing in the development of Croatia’s air connectivity with international markets.

“Continuous improvement of air connectivity is one of the important prerequisites for developing year-round tourism and strengthening Croatia’s international competitiveness. It is encouraging that even during the winter we see the arrival of new airlines, the introduction of new international routes, and an increase in the number of flights on a series of existing connections,” commented HTZ Director Kristjan Staničić, emphasizing the importance of connecting Croatia with new markets.

The HTZ highlights international routes such as Air China’s Zagreb – Bucharest – Beijing service, which continues to operate during the winter following its launch in September, as well as Ryanair’s Zagreb – Warsaw (Modlin) route, which will operate twice a week throughout the entire winter. British Airways will launch its Dubrovnik – London flights at the beginning of March 2027.

World.title: Vukovar: After 35 Years, a Mother Finds Her Son’s Remains
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – The siege of Vukovar and the subsequent massacre took place over three decades ago now, but after 35 long years, a mother has finally found her son’s remains.

For 35 long and painful years, the Bataković family didn’t know where Zlatko was. Index reports that they waited for an answer about his fate without a grave on which to place flowers and without the chance to properly say goodbye. After three and a half decades of uncertainty, his remains have finally been found, reports HRT. “When they told me, I felt such relief. Mum will finally get to light a candle at her son’s grave instead of in front of Our Lady,” said his brother Branko.

a quiet young man who grew up on the banks of the danube

Zlatko Bataković was 26 years old when he disappeared in wartime Vukovar. His older brother Branko remembers him as Džala, a quiet and peaceful young man who loved the Danube more than anything. “He would often come back from fishing without any fish. I would ask him: ‘So Zlatko, what do you even do there for 20 hours?’ He would reply: ‘Nothing, I just look at the water, it relaxes me.’ He would go to the Danube like that, sit and it would calm him. I couldn’t understand how someone could lose a whole day just looking at the water,” Branko recalls.

joining the national guard

Soon the time came when he could no longer sit peacefully by the river. In June 1991 Zlatko, together with three other young men from Mikluševci, enlisted in the Croatian National Guard. He had already made the decision and only came to tell his brother he was leaving. “It was the 10th of June 1991 when he told me: ‘Bajo, I’m joining the Guard.’ I asked him why, and he answered: ‘Bajo, better me than you, you’ve got two children, I have to go.’ Even then I didn’t understand it, but he left,” Branko revealed.

their final meeting

His brother last saw him in August, when he came to congratulate them on their wedding anniversary and birthday. That day Vukovar was being bombed and they came to pick Zlatko up. He started towards the vehicle but returned once more to his mother. “He came out. He was wearing a chain with a pendant that said Zlatko – we had bought it for him for his eighteenth birthday. He said to me: ‘I’m going now, I’ll give you all the money. Put it in the passport.’ I told him: ‘I won’t.’ And he answered: ‘You have to, you have to take it.’ He hugged me and kissed me,” his mother Veruška Bataković remembers.

She couldn’t know that she was seeing him for the last time ever. The war was becoming ever more brutal. Croatian defenders on positions around Vukovar were trying to stop the enemy forces. “I remember him telling me: ‘Nothing will come of this. They’ll just keep it as a buffer zone so there won’t be a conflict.’ We never even dreamed that something like this would happen,” says fellow fighter Zdenko Biki.

years turned into decades…

According to witness statements, Zlatko was captured at Ristić’s farm and taken in the direction of Negoslavci. There, his brother Branko says, he was recognised by a man who knew the family, but that did not save his life. “He told him: ‘I know you, you’re Veruška’s son. Why are you here? I’ll let you go home now.’ He took him to the back yard, fired a burst into his back and killed him,” Branko says. The years passed and every new piece of information raised hope. They searched for him among the living, on lists of prisoners and in the stories of returnees. They believed even in things that seemed impossible to others. “We even had information that the Serbs had taken them to the mines in Aleksinac to work. Mum used to dream that Zlatko was alive, that he was working in a mine in Serbia, that he had lost his memory and that he had a wife and two children,” Branko says.

zlatko was finally found, three and a half long decades later

Zlatko’s remains were found two years ago at Petrovačka dola. Branko asked Minister Tomo Medved for only one thing – that the news of the discovery not be published before he personally told his mother. He spent two days gathering the strength for that conversation. “Mum is always watching the TV. The news came at around five and I arrived at four. I called all the children to come in. She was surprised and happy. And then I hugged her and told her. That scream… it cannot be described,” Branko recalls.

For 35 years Veruška had no grave she could go to. In front of the image of Our Lady in the courtyard she lit candles, prayed and waited for the son she had last hugged in August 1991. Now she finally knows where her beloved son is. On his grave reads the name she had spoken in her prayers for decades. Behind the letters remains a life cut short at the age of 26 and a mother who waited decades for an answer. Now that she has received it, she still asks the same question.

“Why him of all people? Zlatko, you shouldn’t have gone. But we couldn’t stop him. That was his fate from birth and that’s that,” concluded Veruška Bataković.

World.title: Croatian Rest Stops Ranked Among the Best in Europe
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – Croatian rest stops have ranked among the best in Europe, coming 7th out of the 23 analysed countries.

A major analysis of rest stops across Europe was recently carried out, with Poland ranking the absolute best, and Sicily the worst. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that numerous areas of road user interest were looked into, whether it’s refuelling, using the toilet or just grabbing a coffee, rest areas are among the key elements of any motorway and travel plan.

Czechvignette.cz, an independent intermediary for the sale of Czech vignettes, conducted a study on the best and worst rest areas across Europe. It ranked as many as 5,363 rest areas along motorways in 26 European countries, based on more than seven million Google ratings and over 300,000 user reviews. The analysis covered petrol stations, classic rest areas and locations that offer both fuel and food. Countries were ranked according to the rating of a typical rest area, that is, the median rating of all ranked rest areas in the country. Only 23 countries with at least 10 ranked rest areas made the list. Finland (8), Ireland (9) and Luxembourg (8) did not have a sufficient number of rest areas.

croatia is positioned among europe’s best

According to the data, Croatia ranks 7th out of 23 countries based on the rating of a typical rest area, with a score of 4.21. It sits just behind Slovenia (4.24) and ahead of Hungary (4.15). Also in the top 10 are Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Romania, Austria, Czechia and Norway.

Toilets are the biggest source of complaints (23 percent), followed by staff and service (14 percent) and prices (10 percent). The highest-rated rest area on Croatian motorways is Krka – West on the A1 motorway in the southbound direction near Skradin, with a score of 4.62. The lowest-rated is Modruš – South on the A1 in the eastbound direction near Josipdol, with 3.82 stars. A typical Croatian rest area has a rating of 4.21 stars, which is the median score of the 90 ranked locations. Of the top 10, eight offer a full range of services. The remaining two (both Krka rest areas) have catering facilities.

Half of the 10 lowest-rated rest areas are located on the A3 motorway, while five of the 10 highest-rated are on the A1. According to the analysis, Karlovac County has three rest areas among the top 10 and two among the bottom 10.

neighbouring italy ranks exceptionally poorly

Looking at Europe as a whole, MOP Rudnik Zachód on Poland’s S19 expressway (near Kraśnik) is the highest-rated, with an average score of 4.72 stars. Poland can boast six of the ten highest-rated rest areas in Europe overall; Bulgaria has two, while Spain and Romania each have one. Returning to the top country on the list, a typical Polish rest area is rated 4.3 stars — the highest average among the 23 countries — while Belgium is at the very bottom with an average of 3.78, just behind Italy (3.79).

When looking at specific locations, the analysis shows that Area di parcheggio Costa Gaia Nord, a rest area on Sicily’s A29 motorway near Alcamo, is the lowest-rated in Europe, with an average score of 2.15 stars. France has as many as six of the ten lowest-rated rest areas. Toilets are the biggest source of complaints across Europe, they account for 23 percent of all written review complaints. Staff and service follow with 14 percent, and prices with 10 percent. Safety, parking, and fuel/EV charging each make up approximately four to six percent of complaints.

World.title: British Airways Cancels Zagreb-London Route as Ryanair Dominates
World.content:
November the 19th, 2026 – British Airways is cancelling its long-standing Zagreb-London route as Ryanair dominates the route from the Croatian capital to Stansted.

The famous British national carrier British Airways has decided to cancel its route between London and Zagreb. This significantly changes the flight offering between the capitals of Croatia and the United Kingdom, according to the portal Croatian Aviation.

British Airways, one of Europe’s largest airlines, is discontinuing the route that connected London Heathrow Airport with Zagreb. Index reports that for many years, this service was part of British Airways’ network and provided a direct link between the two cities, as well as onward connections to international destinations via the London hub. Last winter the airline made the route seasonal and did not operate it from the end of October until the end of March. Although the same arrangement had been announced for this year, flights have now been withdrawn from sale for next summer as well.

ryanair dominates the route – and it’s much cheaper

The market for flights between Zagreb and London has become highly competitive in recent years. Ryanair currently operates on this route, connecting Zagreb with Stansted Airport, while Croatia Airlines maintains a service to Heathrow. Ryanair’s entry has significantly affected market dynamics, especially in the segment of passengers for whom ticket price is the most important factor. Heathrow Airport continues to play a key role for business travellers and those continuing their journeys to other continents via London.

With the withdrawal of British Airways, Zagreb Airport is losing yet another major European carrier. The question arises whether the remaining airlines will be able to compensate for the capacity previously provided by British Airways. This is particularly relevant for direct flights to Heathrow, given that the airport is heavily congested and has no free slots available.

The departure of British Airways is an additional loss for Zagreb Airport, from which Austrian Airlines will also permanently withdraw in the near future

World.title: “I Couldn’t Leave”: The Pregnant Nurse Who Stayed in Vukovar Hospital
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – Zvezdana Pinjuh was very heavily pregnant in November 1991, despite that, she stayed to help the wounded and vulnerable at Vukovar Hospital instead of escaping. “I couldn’t leave”, she recalls.

Nurse Zvezdana Pinjuh was in the advanced stages of her pregnancy back in November 1991, yet she remained in the besieged Vukovar and continued helping the wounded in the local hospital. Index reports that although she had the opportunity to leave the city, she decided to stay with her colleagues and patients. On the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar, she recalled those days in an interview for Dnevnik. “I stayed. I just couldn’t leave. There were very few of us medical staff, and there were a great many wounded. Every day there were more and more. I simply could not allow myself to abandon all of that even though I was pregnant,” Pinjuh recalled.

no water, no electricity, and barely any medical supplies

During the nearly three-month siege of Vukovar, the hospital was one of the few places where the wounded could receive medical help. Around 4,000 wounded passed through it, and the medical staff performed approximately 2,500 operations. Despite the markings of the International Red Cross, the hospital was exposed to shelling every day. On some days as many as 700 projectiles fell on it.

Towards the end of the siege, doctors and nurses worked without electricity, water and basic medical supplies. Despite such conditions, 16 children were born in the hospital during the war, and the medical staff also provided assistance to twenty members of the enemy forces. “The conditions were inhumane, we worked 24 hours a day, there was very little rest. We were thirsty, hungry, exhausted, but we all worked equally. That was a unity that is unimaginable,” Pinjuh recalled.

the massacre after the fall of vukovar

After the defence of Vukovar was broken on the 18th of November 1991, members of the JNA and Serbian forces also entered the hospital. On the 19th of November, numerous wounded, patients, defenders, civilians and members of the medical staff were taken from the hospital. In the following days, crimes against the prisoners followed. Around 200 people taken from the Vukovar hospital were killed at nearby Ovčara. The fate of some of those taken away has still not been clarified, and their families continue to search for the remains of their loved ones to this day.

Pinjuh said that Vukovar has been rebuilt after the war, but that the consequences of the wartime suffering are still deeply present among its inhabitants, especially because of the unresolved fate of the missing persons. “I hope that these newer generations will breathe life back into Vukovar and that it will again be a beautiful city as it once was,” she said. Today marks 35 years since the fall of Vukovar, and the central commemoration will take place with the Column of Remembrance, through which people from all over Croatia will pay tribute to the fallen defenders and civilians.

World.title: Zagreb Ranks Extremely Poorly in Terms of Air Quality
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – Zagreb has ranked extremely poorly in terms of air quality, at the very bottom of the entire European ranking.

Zagreb ranks near the bottom of the European ranking of cities by air quality, according to a new study by the organisation Clean Cities, whose results were presented by the Cyclists’ Union (Sindikat biciklista). Poslovni reports that among the 40 European cities analysed, the Croatian capital took an embarrassing 38th place, with a grade of E and 19.1 points out of a possible 60. Only Bucharest and Athens ranked worse.

The study, titled Free to Breathe, covered air quality and the progress of European cities in developing sustainable mobility. The results reveal a worrying picture: only three cities — Copenhagen, Stockholm and Helsinki – already meet the new European Union limit values for two particularly harmful groups of pollutants — nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) and fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅). This means that as many as 93 percent of the analysed cities still do not meet the new European air quality standards.

zero points for zagreb

A particularly worrying figure concerns Zagreb’s readiness to meet the stricter European standards that are due to apply from 2030. In this category, the Croatian capital scored no points at all. Overall, Zagreb collected 19.1 points out of a possible 60. For current air quality it received 13.6 out of 30 points, while for changes in pollution levels over the past ten years it scored 4.5 out of a possible ten points. It performed even worse in the category of transport policies aimed at reducing pollution. For sustainable mobility measures it received only one point out of a possible ten. Cities were assessed according to four criteria: current pollution levels, compliance with the new EU limit values, changes in air quality over the past decade, and transport and other measures that promote sustainable mobility.

only bucharest and athens are worse than zagreb

The study results show large differences between European regions. While Nordic cities achieved the best results, the bottom of the ranking is mainly occupied by cities in Southern, Central and Eastern Europe. Among the cities with the worst results, in addition to Zagreb, stand out Turin, the wider Milan area, Kraków, Wrocław, Warsaw, Rome, Prague and Budapest. The last two places went to Bucharest and Athens. Athens particularly stands out for its high concentration of nitrogen dioxide. The average value was 37.6 micrograms per cubic metre, the highest among all 40 cities analysed.

london and paris show that this issue can be resolved

Nevertheless, the study also brings positive examples of cities that have managed to significantly improve air quality over the past ten years. Among them are Copenhagen, London, Paris and Stuttgart. Their progress is linked to concrete transport and urban planning measures, such as the introduction of low- and zero-emission zones, the electrification of bus transport, the establishment of school streets, and the construction and expansion of cycling infrastructure. Some cities have managed over the past decade to reduce nitrogen dioxide concentrations by more than a third, and some have come close to a reduction of as much as 50 percent. In this way they have shown that decisive transport policies can deliver significant results in the fight against pollution. How widespread the problem is is also shown by the fact that as many as 37 of the 40 analysed cities exceed at least one of the four new air pollution limit values, while 18 cities fail to meet any of them.

much stricter rules by 2030

With the revised Ambient Air Quality Directive, the European Union is introducing stricter limit values for pollutants that member states must achieve by 2030. The aim of the new rules is to reduce the health risks associated with pollution and to bring European standards closer to the recommendations of the World Health Organisation. Along with the publication of the study results, the Free to Breathe campaign was also launched. Through it, the organisation Clean Cities calls on European cities and national governments to accelerate the implementation of measures for cleaner air. The study results clearly show that Zagreb seriously lags behind a large part of Europe in this area. Given the extremely weak result in the category of transport policies, the city authorities face a major challenge: without more concrete measures to reduce car traffic, develop public transport and encourage cycling, significant progress will be hard to achieve.

World.title: Three Months After the Omiš Fire – Still No Real Answers
World.content:
November the 18th, 2026 – Over three months have now passed since the devastating Omiš fire, yet the public and more importantly those directly affected are still waiting for actual answers.

The catastrophic fire that engulfed the Omiš area on the night of August the 13th to the 14th remains fresh in most people’s minds, particularly for those who were near it. Index reports that six people lost their lives as a result of that specific fire, homes were destroyed, and residents fled directly into the sea to escape the flames. Survivors described the dramatic moments, escaping from blocked roads, and boat rescues for HTV. Three months after the tragedy, they are still seeking answers regarding accountability, the warning system, and reconstruction aid.

fleeing from the flames

For the residents of Omiš and surrounding towns, the night of the fire began with the flames rapidly spreading toward their houses. Goran Lović from Lokva Rogoznica recounted how his wife called him to return urgently because the fire had already caught their building. When he arrived, the fire had spread so much that they could no longer reach their other house, about three hundred meters away, where a minor child was located.

Dubravka Marunčić from Stanići was putting her children to bed when her daughter noticed that the tree in front of the house was red. When she turned around, she realized the fire had already reached them and decided to leave immediately with the children. Gabrijela Baučić from Borak also tried to escape by car with her family, but traffic had almost come to a standstill. “My younger one, David, when he saw the flames in the rearview mirror, turned around and saw it coming close to us. ‘Mum, drive faster, we’re going to burn!’ And you’re just standing still. It’s horrendous.”

Julija Hrstić tried to protect her house by hosing it down with water, but when they lost electricity and water, the family decided to leave. They grabbed their dog and put him in the car, but soon got stuck in a line of vehicles that was barely moving.

clogged roads and an escape into the sea

Marunčić described how cars drove between flames while the wind carried embers. “It was burning on both the upper and lower sides of the road. A rain of embers was falling and it was horribly hot,” she said. When she saw that cars were also burning and people were fleeing from them, she turned toward the sea. There, she got out of the vehicle with her three children and ran toward the shore, where many people were already in the shallows. “We couldn’t breathe. Thick black smoke came down, embers were falling around us,” she recalled.

She also recounted how a young man approached them in the sea and began splashing them with seawater to protect them from the heat. “Just by him being close to me, I felt safe. I calmed down because I knew I could count on him,” she recalled. Soon, boats arrived and began transporting people to safety.

“we could hear people screaming”

Among the people who set out in their boats to help with the rescue was Mario Popovac from Omiš. With a friend, he sailed toward the endangered areas despite extremely poor visibility due to smoke. “We heard screams. We simply drove the boat right in among the people. At 200 or 300 metres from the shore, we couldn’t stand the heat,” he described. They found the first people about three hundred metres from the shore. Popovac says the smoke was so thick he couldn’t even see the bow of his own boat. During one trip, his friend warned him to stop, and in the sea they spotted an elderly man keeping himself afloat by holding onto two empty fuel cans.

“We came across him by chance. It is fortunate, in my opinion, that citizens spontaneously went out to sea,” he said. The evacuation lasted until roughly 04:30 in the morning. Marunčić also mentioned Milan Balić, who came by boat to pick up people on the shore of Mala Luka and, according to her, refused to leave until he had boarded everyone who needed help.

three months since absolute tragedy…

Six people lost their lives in the fire. Among the deceased were two female workers from the same hotel, a retired fire commander, and three members of the same family. Julija Hrstić admits that she is still overwhelmed by emotion today. “A life that is lost cannot be brought back. Neither life nor health for the people who will suffer consequences. When I think about it today, I often feel like crying,” she said. Even three months after the tragedy, residents are raising questions about how the warning system functioned. Baučić claims they did not receive timely evacuation instructions. “No siren sounded, we received no instructions. It was chaos. Nobody knew where to go or what to do,” she said.

Julija Hrstić also wonders why the SRUUK early warning system was not activated. “Could there have been a reaction to alert people? Better a false alarm than for this to happen,” she stated. Residents also pointed out neglected firebreaks and the unavailability of water. Goran Lović claims there were not enough hydrants.

left with no answers

The danger did not end when the fire was extinguished, because landslides are now threatening the area. Baučić, whose apartment burned down, described how her family lost everything in a single night. “In one night, you simply lose everything you’ve built for years. Without a home, a family nest,” she said. She warns about rocks that began falling after the fire and the danger of larger landslides due to destroyed vegetation. Goran Lović warns of the same issue, believing that urgent coastal remediation and state aid are needed because the local community lacks sufficient funds. He also adds that residents estimate the total damage to be higher than the amount mentioned by the government.

Three months after the tragedy, residents are still waiting for answers about the causes of the fire and possible accountability. “There is no information whatsoever about the investigation, accountability, and handling of the situation. We want something to be set in motion so that Omiš never happens to anyone again,” said Julija Hrstić. Lović also demands that authorities explain what happened. “We just want to know what happened, why people lost their lives, why our property is gone,” he stated. He emphasizes that residents feel forgotten and expect concrete help.
