He says the connectivity ministerial was not about EU enlargement. Its main focus was the development of transport, energy and economic links across the region – an area in which Georgia could play an important role because of its geographical position.

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, Georgia’s EU integration process remains suspended, and the country’s position has deteriorated further compared with the previous year. The Commission says the Georgian authorities took no steps during the reporting period to implement the nine recommendations set out as conditions for advancing the country’s EU accession process.

Zakareishvili stresses that international transport and trade routes are constantly changing. A country that does not take part in the relevant negotiations may eventually lose the opportunity to benefit even from its own geographical advantages.

“If Georgia does not take part, someone else will take its place and share the spoils! If you do not show up to a party, the party will go on without you – and someone else will eat the slice of cake that was meant for you,” he says.

In the analyst’s view, Georgia should pay particular attention to the development of a new transport corridor through Armenia, including the so-called “Trump Route”, which could significantly reshape the transport geography of the South Caucasus.

Zakareishvili fears that if Georgia does not actively participate in regional connectivity projects, a significant share of international freight could bypass the country. Georgia would then lose the economic and political advantages built up over decades through its Black Sea ports, railway, pipelines and East-West transit corridor.

The analyst draws a historical parallel with the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan oil pipeline and the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline. He says that, as a result of political decisions made at the time, these projects were routed through Georgia rather than Armenia. But the situation could now change: new transport routes in the region could allow Armenia to become a transit country at Georgia’s expense.

Zakareishvili believes Turkey will play a particularly important role in this process. The development of new routes and the redistribution of transport flows could increase the importance of Turkish ports and Mediterranean routes, affecting the competitiveness of Georgia’s Black Sea ports.

“As long as Georgia has pipelines and ports, and still has a chance to take part somewhere, to get a foot in the door and claim a share – if not a piece of the cake, then at least a seat at the table – it should do so. Otherwise, these processes will move forward without Georgia,” Zakareishvili says.

In his view, the authorities’ refusal to attend international meetings, justified on the grounds of protecting the country’s dignity and sovereignty, could in reality damage Georgia’s economic interests.

“EU candidate status is becoming little more than a formality”

Zakareishvili identifies the Georgian authorities’ decision to suspend political dialogue with the European Union as one of the main reasons for the country’s growing distance from Brussels.

In November 2024, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Georgia would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028. The announcement came after the EU had effectively suspended Georgia’s accession process and stepped up its criticism of the government’s policies.

Zakareishvili believes that instead of meeting the conditions set by the European Union, the Georgian authorities chose political confrontation. He says candidate status alone does not mean progress towards membership: the country must fulfil specific commitments.

The analyst points to Ukraine, Moldova, Albania and Montenegro as examples of countries that continue to implement reforms as part of their efforts to move closer to the EU.

“The European Union did not write an application saying, ‘I want Georgia to join.’ It was Georgia that said it wanted to join the European Union. It is all very well to want to join the EU, but you need to look at its standards, its economy and its relations. The EU’s conditions include judicial reform, de-oligarchisation and many other things that the ruling Georgian Dream party does not like,” Zakareishvili says.

In his assessment, the EU’s declining political attention to Georgia is not limited to deteriorating diplomatic relations. The country could also gradually be left out of regional developments in which its geographical position and transit potential once gave it a significant advantage.

The analyst warns that Georgia’s international role is not determined by geography alone. A country may lie on a transit corridor on the map, but to gain real economic and political benefits, it must take part in the processes shaping the region’s future transport, energy and security architecture. Otherwise, Georgia risks finding itself surrounded by new political and economic partnerships while remaining on the sidelines.

Paata Zakareishvili on Georgia-Russia relations

World.title: Part of Crimean Bridge collapses into sea: what damage to one of Kremlin’s key propaganda symbols means
World.content:
On 17 November 2026, the Crimean Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, was severely damaged in another Ukrainian attack. Video footage and photographs circulating online appear to show a large metal arch and a section of the road deck collapsing into the sea. Both road and rail traffic across the bridge have been suspended.

The attack is particularly significant because the Crimean Bridge is a vital land corridor linking the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed in 2014, with Russian territory. Moscow has also used the bridge to supply its military forces.

For years, the Crimean Bridge was regarded as one of Vladimir Putin’s largest infrastructure projects and a symbol of Russian control over Crimea. Its damage creates several problems at once: it complicates Russian military logistics, increases the cost of supplying Crimea and shows how difficult it is for Moscow to secure one of its most heavily protected strategic assets.

It is important to note that the collapse on 17 November was preceded by an attack on 16 November, which also reportedly damaged the bridge’s structure. This means the bridge has been hit in a series of successive strikes rather than in a single isolated incident.

According to Anton Herashchenko, an adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, the attack involved a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Russian authorities confirmed the attack and the suspension of traffic across the bridge, but have yet to issue an official statement about its collapse.

The Russian outlet Agentstvo reports that federal television channels did not mention the attack on the Crimean Bridge in their morning news bulletins. Instead, they covered strikes on several bridges in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine.

The collapsed Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

What does the collapse of the bridge arch mean from an engineering perspective?

To understand the scale of the damage to the Kerch Bridge, it is important to know how it is constructed.

The bridge is approximately 19 kilometres long and consists of two independent parallel structures: one carries road traffic and the other railway traffic.

Both structures rest on concrete supports. However, the navigable section of the Kerch Strait features large metal arch structures that support the corresponding spans and provide sufficient clearance for ships to pass underneath.

According to reports published on 17 November, a roughly 227-metre-long arch of the road bridge collapsed into the sea, along with the section of road deck connected to it. The adjacent railway arch was also damaged but has not collapsed.

Why does this matter?

The arch is not a decorative feature of the bridge but a key load-bearing element. Its damage means that the load in the affected section can no longer be safely distributed.

This creates several technical problems:

Damage to the load-bearing structure: After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles.

After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles. Risk of damage to adjacent elements: The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans.

The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans. Safety of the railway infrastructure: The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure.

The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure. Possible disruption to shipping: Debris from the collapsed structure could also obstruct the shipping channel used by vessels.

It is important to stress that the collapse of the arch does not mean the entire 19-kilometre bridge has been destroyed. However, one of its most important sections has been damaged. Restoring traffic will require a detailed structural assessment, the removal of debris and the necessary engineering and repair work.

Rebuilding such a large load-bearing element is a far more complex, time-consuming and costly process.

What does the collapse of the Kerch Bridge mean symbolically?

For Russia, the bridge is one of the most visible political symbols of the annexation of Crimea.

When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, one of Moscow’s main challenges was establishing a land link between the peninsula and Russian territory, as the Kerch Strait separates Crimea from Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. By building the bridge, the Kremlin overcame this geographical barrier.

Vladimir Putin personally championed the project. In May 2018, he drove a lorry across the bridge and officially opened its road section. The event was broadcast on Russian state television and became an important part of the Kremlin’s propaganda narrative.

For Moscow, the bridge carried several key messages:

Consolidation of the annexation of Crimea: The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory.

The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory. Putin’s political project: Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities.

Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities. Demonstration of Russian control: The bridge signalled that Moscow intended to maintain a long-term presence in Crimea and had no plans to return the peninsula to Ukraine.

Russia decided to build the bridge in 2014, following its annexation of Crimea. Construction began in 2016. The road section opened on 15 May 2018, while rail traffic began in December 2019.

The bridge is considered one of the longest in Europe. Its construction cost around 228 billion roubles (approximately $3.5–3.8 billion at the exchange rate at the time).

The project involved extensive engineering work. The structure includes supports on both land and underwater, while specially designed high arches allow ships to pass through the navigable section of the strait.

After the first explosion in 2022, the damage to the bridge was seen in Ukraine as an important moral and symbolic victory. At the time, Al Jazeera reported that the attack had heightened the perception of Russia’s vulnerability.

Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

How many times has Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge before?

Before the attack on 17 November 2026, Ukraine had carried out three major successful operations against the Kerch Bridge. Ukrainian officials subsequently confirmed or acknowledged responsibility for them.

The strike on 16 November 2026, which directly preceded the attack on 17 November, should also be treated as a separate incident.

8 October 2022: First major explosion

A lorry travelling across the bridge exploded, damaging several road spans and causing some of them to collapse. The blast also set fuel tankers on a passing railway train on fire. Four people were killed.

Ukraine subsequently acknowledged its involvement in the attack. Repairs to the damaged sections took several months.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge on 8 October 2022

17 July 2023: Sea drone attack

Ukraine attacked the bridge using Sea Baby naval drones. The road section sustained damage, and one of its spans collapsed. Two civilians were killed in the attack, and their child was injured.

Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out the operation.

Sea drone attack on the Kerch Bridge in 2023

3 June 2025: Underwater explosion

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detonated explosive devices near the bridge’s underwater supports. According to the Ukrainian side, the blast had an estimated force of 1,100 kilograms of TNT.

The SBU said the operation had been in preparation for several months and that the bridge’s supports had sustained significant damage. The agency claimed that the structure had been left in a critical condition.

Underwater explosion on the Kerch Bridge in 2025

16 November 2026: Another strike

The Ukrainian drone attack damaged the bridge’s structure. Russian authorities initially described the damage as minor, but traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended and later partially restored.

16 November 2026: Another strike on the Kerch Bridge

What did Russia use the Kerch Bridge for?

For Russia, the bridge was not just a transport link for Crimea’s population. It was also one of the key logistical routes used in its war against Ukraine.

Military role

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the bridge acquired particular strategic importance. It allowed Russia to transport military supplies from its territory to Crimea and then onwards to the occupied regions of southern Ukraine.

These supplies included:

military equipment and armoured vehicles;

ammunition and weapons;

fuel and other military supplies;

military personnel and logistical resources.

The bridge allowed Russian forces to move military supplies relatively quickly from Russian territory to Crimea and then distribute them towards the front line in southern Ukraine.

In March 2024, Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), said Russia had significantly reduced its use of the bridge to transport military equipment following Ukrainian strikes.

According to Maliuk, 42–46 trains carrying weapons and ammunition crossed the bridge every day before the attacks. After the strikes, that number fell to four or five.

Civilian and economic role

The bridge is also an important transport route for Crimea’s residents and tourists.

It was used to deliver:

food;

fuel;

consumer goods;

construction materials;

various industrial products.

The bridge also carried passenger trains and cars travelling between Russia and Crimea.

A prolonged disruption would therefore affect not only military supplies but also everyday economic life in Crimea, the cost of delivering goods and the tourism industry.

The collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge

What alternatives does Russia have?

Disabling the Kerch Bridge does not mean that Russia will lose the ability to supply Crimea altogether.

Moscow can use the land corridor through the occupied parts of southern Ukraine. It links Russia’s Rostov region with the occupied territories of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and Crimea.

However, this route has several drawbacks. It is significantly longer, runs close to active combat zones and is itself vulnerable to Ukrainian strikes.

Russia could also use the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, but it would not be able to fully replace the bridge’s capacity.

Disabling the Kerch Bridge therefore represents a serious logistical blow to Russia, even if Moscow continues to supply Crimea via alternative routes.

Why is this attack significant?

From a military perspective, Russia is losing – at least temporarily – one of its most important transport corridors, which it used to supply its forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine.

From an economic perspective, a prolonged closure of the bridge will increase the cost of supplying Crimea and put additional pressure on alternative transport routes.

From a political perspective, it is another blow to Putin’s project, which has become a symbol of Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

It is also particularly significant that the bridge was considered one of Russia’s most heavily protected strategic assets. It was guarded by air defence systems, maritime barriers and other security measures. Yet Ukraine has managed to strike it repeatedly.

However, the ultimate strategic impact will depend on how long the bridge remains out of service, how severe the damage is to its supports and the adjacent railway structure, and how quickly Russia can increase the capacity of alternative routes.

One thing is clear: the Kerch Bridge is one of the most important symbols Putin has created since the annexation of Crimea. Its repeated damage sends Moscow a clear message: in its war against Ukraine, no infrastructure asset is safe or beyond reach.

World.title: EU foreign policy chief: ‘Syria must withdraw recognition of occupied territories in Georgia and Ukraine’
World.content:
EU foreign ministers have called for closer relations with Syria. However, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that any association agreement with Syria should include a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine, alongside commitments to protect human rights.

Kallas made the remarks at a press conference following a meeting of EU foreign ministers.

According to Kallas, EU member states agreed that maintaining relations with Syria was important. Without EU engagement, other actors would fill the existing political and diplomatic vacuum in the country.

Kallas said the EU was considering signing an association agreement, negotiations on which began in 2008. The agreement would provide a common framework for cooperation between the two sides. At the same time, the EU would begin work on a new mandate to modernise the agreement.

“The question now was the status of the agreement. Negotiations on it took place in 2008, quite a long time ago. So the question arose as to whether we should make changes to it.

“The EU works in such a way that decision-making takes time. That is why the compromise would be to sign the 2008 association agreement. This would give us a framework within which we could work on all the issues that matter to both sides. At the same time, together with the Council, we will begin work on developing a new mandate for a modernised agreement,” Kallas said.

Kaja Kallas

Kallas said EU foreign ministers had called for several key issues to be addressed in the agreement. These include clear conditions on human rights protection and a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine.

She explained that the issue concerned the territories whose independence was recognised by Bashar al-Assad’s regime.

“We are now working in technical groups on the details, both technical and legal, but we are making progress,” the EU foreign policy chief said.

At the press conference, Kallas also commented on the architecture of European security. She said that Russia had been a party to several international agreements that laid the foundations for European security. However, the main problem was not the existence of these documents, but Moscow’s failure to honour its commitments.

In this context, Kallas cited the Helsinki Final Act, the Paris Agreement and the Budapest Memorandum.

“The problem is not with the agreements themselves, nor with Ukraine’s position on this issue. The problem is that Russia violates these agreements and fails to comply with their terms. So the main question is: how can we restore the European security architecture?” Kaja Kallas said.

Background

On 29 May 2018, the regime of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad recognised the independence of Georgia’s occupied regions of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). Tbilisi responded by severing diplomatic relations with Damascus. The EU condemned the decision on the same day, saying it violated international law and the principles of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Assad’s decision followed Russia’s military intervention in the Syrian civil war. Moscow was one of the main supporters of Assad’s government, and Damascus’s move was seen as serving the Kremlin’s interests.

In June 2022, Syria also recognised the independence of Ukraine’s occupied territories of Donetsk and Luhansk. Ukraine responded by severing diplomatic relations with Syria.

Assad’s regime fell in December 2024, and a new government took power in Syria. Against this backdrop, Tbilisi called on Damascus to withdraw its recognition of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

Ukraine restored diplomatic relations with Syria in September 2025. The association agreement now under consideration by the EU could therefore mark a new stage in relations with Syria. However, the territorial integrity of Georgia and Ukraine remains one of the key conditions in this process.

World.title: Old links on Aliyev’s X account redirected users to opposition videos: cyberattack or global vulnerability?
World.content:
Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

On 15 November, links in some old posts on President Ilham Aliyev’s account on X redirected users to videos featuring opposition politicians and bloggers, as well as footage of protests. Most of the posts dated from 2010–2011. The links led to videos featuring Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, and bloggers Mehman Huseynov and Gabil Mammadov.

The posts themselves remained unchanged, but the links they contained began directing users to different pages. The altered links remained accessible for several hours, and users shared the posts across social media.

That evening, the Azerbaijani president’s press service issued a statement:

“Cyberattacks are currently targeting the social media accounts of Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Relevant agencies are taking the necessary measures to prevent these attacks and investigate the incident.”

The statement did not specify which platforms had come under attack, how the attacks were carried out or who was behind them.

Similar incidents affected the accounts of several prominent politicians, government agencies and companies around the world on the same day. This raises the question:

Were the president’s accounts actually hacked, or was the incident the result of a global vulnerability that affected numerous accounts, including those of Donald Trump and McDonald’s?

Trump, Gates and Burger King among those affected by similar incidents

According to a CNN investigation published on 15 November, links in old posts by politicians, government agencies and companies on X began redirecting users to unrelated videos, images and websites over the weekend.

The largest number of such cases involved the personal account of US President Donald Trump. Links in at least 12 of his posts began directing users to other websites. Similar changes affected posts by Bill Gates dating from 2010 and former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau from 2011.

A link in a 2011 Burger King post listing the locations of its restaurants redirected users to a page listing Nazi concentration camps. A link in one of McDonald’s posts led to a page about the 11 September attacks. Similar cases also affected posts by the FBI, the US Department of Defence and former Vice-President Mike Pence.

All the links had been shortened using Bitly, a service that turns long web addresses into shorter ones. The service was widely used on Twitter, now known as X, between 2009 and 2014. According to CNN, Bitly links do not expire, and users with paid subscriptions can change the addresses to which they redirect.

Bitly said it had identified “an issue that allowed malicious actors to reuse some old, inactive links”. The company said it had suspended the accounts used to change the links and deactivated the links themselves. However, Bitly did not say who was behind the activity.

No password required

An attack of this kind does not require access to an account password. The original post remains unchanged; only the destination address of the shortened link changes. As a result, someone clicking a link in a post published by the president 15 years ago ends up on a completely different page.

IT expert Osman Gunduz also believes that the problem stems not from hacked accounts but from a security vulnerability in Bitly’s system. He recommended that government agencies and other organisations check their old links, deactivate potentially dangerous ones and use their own domains wherever possible.

Ari Lightman, a professor of digital media at Carnegie Mellon University, told CNN that many old accounts remain inadequately monitored. He described the situation as “problematic”.

Government agencies have not yet confirmed that the incident involving the president’s account was linked to a Bitly vulnerability. The president’s press service has issued no further statements on the matter.

Who appears in the videos?

The videos feature some of the most vocal critics of the Azerbaijani authorities.

Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, has been under arrest since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of actions aimed at violently seizing power. Karimli rejects the charges, calling them fabricated and politically motivated. The investigation ended in October. If convicted, he faces a prison sentence of 12 years to life. On 12 November, he received the Magnitsky Human Rights Award in London.

Blogger Mehman Huseynov was sentenced to two years in prison in 2017 on defamation charges. He was released in March 2019. Following the incident, Huseynov sarcastically “thanked” the president on Facebook for sharing a video featuring him: “Thank you, Mr President!”

Blogger Gabil Mammadov, who lives abroad, has been convicted in absentia in Azerbaijan. The Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 16 years in prison.

What does “cyberattack” mean?

In the past two months, the Azerbaijani authorities have reported cyberattacks for the second time. On 13 October, more than 100 government websites came under attack. At the time, the State Service for Special Communication and Information Security said when the attack began, which systems it targeted and that its impact had been limited. The agency blamed an unnamed “foreign hacker group”. However, the pro-Iranian group 313 Team, which is believed to operate in Iraq, claimed responsibility. Its members said they had acted in protest against the ban on wearing hijabs in schools.

The statement about the attack on the president’s accounts, however, provided no similar details.

Previous cyberattacks on social media accounts in Azerbaijan have mainly targeted independent media outlets. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, an international press freedom organisation, almost all Azerbaijani-language posts disappeared from Meydan TV’s Facebook page in June 2020. In August this year, eight independent Azerbaijani media outlets operating in exile issued a joint statement. They said a series of coordinated copyright infringement complaints had led to the suspension of several of their Facebook and Instagram accounts.

This time, the incident affected the president’s own account. It remains unclear who changed the links and why they chose opposition videos as the new destinations. Bitly has not disclosed who owned the accounts it suspended.

Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

World.title: First trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping scheduled for November 19
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. The first trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to take place on November 19 at approximately 10:30 a.m. Baku time.

The talks will be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Delegations from all three countries will participate in the meeting, and their composition has already been agreed upon. Meanwhile, work on a draft joint communiqué is still underway.

The duration of the meeting will be determined by the three heads of state themselves.

The talks are expected to take place at the Chinese president's state residence.

World.title: Repsol’s net debt falls 64% to €2.04 billion as cash flow rises
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Repsol’s net debt fell 64.3% year on year to €2.04 billion (€2,038 million) at the end of September 2026, down €1.63 billion from the end of the second quarter, the company said. Cash flow from operations rose 178.6% to €3.53 billion.

Trend’s calculations based on company data show that net debt was 44.4% below the second quarter’s €3,667 million and 54.6% (€2.45 billion) below the €4,487 million recorded at the start of the year. Excluding leases, Repsol had a net cash position of €633 million, compared with net debt of €935 million in the second quarter and €2,546 million a year earlier. Gearing fell by 5.1 percentage points to 6.2% from 11.3%.

Cash flow from operations was 82.4% above the second quarter’s €1,935 million and 2.8 times the year-earlier figure of €1,267 million. Nine-month cash flow rose 68.8% to €6.50 billion. Working capital absorbed €763 million, compared with €108 million a year earlier.

Free cash flow was €2,893 million, 3.4 times the second quarter’s €855 million and the year-earlier figure. It accounted for 82% of cash flow from operations, compared with 67% a year earlier. Nine-month free cash flow reached €4.20 billion, 2.8 times the €1.49 billion recorded a year earlier. Capital expenditures fell 32.7% to €684 million, while divestments dropped to €51 million from €604 million.

Dividends accounted for €601 million, treasury shares for €338 million and dividends to minority shareholders for €174 million during the quarter. Shareholder payouts of €939 million represented 26.6% of cash flow from operations.

Liquidity stood at €11.92 billion, covering short-term gross debt maturities 4.14 times, compared with 5.43 times previously. This implies short-term maturities of about €2.88 billion, compared with €2.20 billion. Cash amounted to €3.93 billion, up 30.8% from the previous quarter.

Compared with December 2025, inventories rose 45.8% to €7.98 billion, receivables increased 49.5%, and payables rose 36.5%, while equity increased 12.1% to €30.97 billion.

World.title: Repsol launches €950 million buyback, lifts January dividend to €0.56
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Repsol has announced a third share buyback program of up to €950 million for 2026 and raised its planned January 2027 dividend to €0.56 per share gross from €0.53, the company said, bringing total 2026 shareholder remuneration to about €3 billion.

"Strong cash generation allows us to launch a third share buyback program in 2026 amounting to 950 million euros," said Josu Jon Imaz, Repsol CEO.

Trend’s calculations based on company data show that the third program is 1.9 times the second (€500 million) and 2.7 times the first (€350 million). The first redeemed 15.8 million shares at about €22.15 each, and the second 17.4 million shares at about €28.78 (up 30%). At the second program’s price, €950 million would buy about 33 million shares, or about 3.1% of the 1,072 million shares in issue.

The second program was completed on October 26, and the 17,375,862 shares redeemed, 1.59% of capital, cut share capital to 1,072,230,472 shares from 1,089,606,334.

The roughly €3.0 billion of 2026 payouts comprises €1.2 billion of dividends (40%), €850 million of completed buybacks (28%) and €950 million of the new program (32%).

The January 2027 payment of €0.56 is 5.7% above the €0.53 approved at the shareholders’ meeting and 1.6% above the €0.551 paid in July.

Repsol’s commitment is to distribute 30–40% of cash flow from operations. Total payouts of €3.0 billion imply annual cash flow of €7.5–10 billion, and nine-month cash flow of €6.50 billion is already 65–87% of that range.

World.title: Azerbaijani and Turkish FMs discuss bilateral relations
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. On November 18, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov held a telephone conversation with his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan.

During the call, the ministers discussed the current agenda of the allied relations between Azerbaijan and Türkiye, prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation in various areas, as well as regional and international security issues.

They also exchanged views on other matters of mutual interest.

World.title: Putin-Trump meeting to take place in China on November 19
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. A bilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump will take place on November 19 in Shenzhen, China, following the plenary session of the APEC summit.

This was announced by Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov.

"We plan to hold a bilateral meeting tomorrow. We are making preparations and hope that the meeting will be useful and substantive. Several representatives from both sides will take part in the discussion," he said.

According to Ushakov, the Russian and U.S. presidents exchanged only a few words during an official reception on November 18, as they were not seated next to each other and therefore had no opportunity to continue their conversation.

He added that the leaders would have more opportunities to talk on November 19 throughout the working day.

A trilateral meeting involving Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is also scheduled for the same day. It is expected to last no more than one hour.

Ushakov also commented on the Russian-Chinese talks held on November 18. According to him, the meeting took place behind closed doors in a friendly and candid atmosphere and represented another stage in the ongoing dialogue between the two leaders.

During the talks, Putin and Xi Jinping discussed key international and regional issues, with particular attention paid to resolving the conflict in Ukraine.

World.title: Turkmenistan, Italy explore expanding cooperation in energy, textiles and agriculture
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 18. Turkmenistan and Italy have discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in energy, the textile industry, trade and agriculture, the Turkmen Foreign Ministry reported.

The issues were discussed at a meeting between Turkmenistan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Ahmet Gurbanov and Eugenio Zoffili, a member of the Italian Chamber of Deputies and Vice-President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, on November 18.

According to the ministry, the sides highlighted the potential for implementing joint projects as part of efforts to strengthen trade and economic ties.

Notably, Italy has long been one of Turkmenistan's most important economic partners in Europe, with cooperation centered on energy, manufacturing and industrial technologies. Italian energy company Eni has operated in western Turkmenistan since 2008 under a production-sharing agreement, while companies including Maire Tecnimont, Danieli, Bonatti, Leonardo and Pietro Fiorentini have participated in discussions and projects related to petrochemicals, engineering, transport and industrial modernization.

Bilateral economic ties have also been supported through regular business forums and high-level political dialogue. During President Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov's visit to Italy in 2019, the two countries held a business forum in Milan that resulted in numerous agreements covering energy, transport, textiles, banking, healthcare and education. More recently, Italy and Turkmenistan have continued to identify energy, transport, agriculture, water management and investment cooperation as priority areas under both bilateral consultations and the Central Asia-Italy dialogue format.

World.title: Tree protestors ordered to pay $150k for failed bid to halt golf course
World.content:
The litigants behind a failed challenge to the North Adelaide Golf Course upgrade have been ordered to pay $150,000 of the state government's legal costs.

The ruling, handed down by Federal Court Judge Natalie Charlesworth on Thursday, comes after the proponents of the case — public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna woman Janette Milera — turned down an earlier $150,000 government settlement offer.

The government's total legal bill was around $450,000 to $550,000, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas has previously said.

Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera had sought to halt the golf course upgrade and its felling of 585 trees, arguing the redevelopment of the North Adelaide park lands breached federal conservation laws.

But Justice Charlesworth ruled against them in October, finding she was not satisfied the plans were "likely to have significant impact on species".

The litigants, who were represented by pro bono lawyers, have since said a government application for costs would "probably" bankrupt them.

Mr Kemp Attrill has raised $132,000 via a GoFundMe for his legal challenge.

His barrister on Wednesday argued the case was "purely in the public interest" and the judge should weigh special circumstances in awarding costs.

The government's lawyer rejected this argument but indicated she would not object to a costs order of $150,000.

World.title: Man in custody after suspicious death of Whitsunday woman
World.content:
A man is in custody over the death of a woman at a home in Queensland's Whitsundays.

Police said they were called to a home at Cannonvale, near Airlie Beach, about 8.45pm yesterday and found a woman with "a number of injuries".

She was declared dead at the scene a short time later.

Police said a man in his 70s, who knew the woman, was taken into custody at the home and taken to hospital.

A crime scene has been established and investigations into the circumstances of the woman's death are continuing.

Whitsunday MP Amanda Camm said in a statement on social media that the community was devastated to learn of the woman's death.

"As police investigate this matter, my heart goes out to the woman's family, friends and our first responders across emergency and health services," Ms Camm said.

World.title: Renters on 'moderate incomes' falling victim to homelessness in Darwin
World.content:
Peter Wishart had a "good job" as a heavy equipment mechanic for more than 30 years, but after a heart attack in 2020, doctors told him to cut back on physical work.

"Best advice was 'just take a break for a while while we try and investigate it'," he said.

After working as much as he could while dealing with ongoing health issues, Mr Wishart became homeless in May this year.

"I found myself at a point where I couldn't afford to keep paying the rent," he said.

Peter Wishart is among the growing number of Darwinites unable to afford rent. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He has been living out of his car in Darwin since then, and said he is still facing a wait of up to seven years for public housing.

"They're accommodating families first, which is fair enough, but six to seven years — I can't last that long," he said.

Annie Taylor, the chief executive of NT Shelter, the Northern Territory's peak body for homeless services, said stories like Mr Wishart's are becoming increasingly common.

Annie Taylor says Darwin is among the most expensive Australian cities for renters. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Darwin is the second most expensive place to rent a house in the country, people don't often know that," she said.

" [Homelessness] is becoming an issue that affects people on moderate incomes. "

Tejinder Singh has provided free meals to Darwin's homeless community through his charity, Sikh Family Food Van, for 16 years.

He told the ABC he has never seen as many people sleeping rough, or so much violence in the homeless community, until recent months.

"I am very scared for them," Mr Singh said.

"Last Sunday in Darwin City, people were fighting each other with a big stone — I've never seen this type of incident in my life."

Tejinder Singh and his family prepare meals for anyone in need around Darwin. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He said the recent closure of Darwin's biggest homeless shelter, YiSSA, has contributed to the chaos.

"It was a good place, they had security and they had cameras," he said.

"If any drama happened [it was confined to] only one place, now drama happens all [over the] city."

Stakeholders have different solutions

Mr Singh said the NT government should continue to crack down on crime and substance issues, which he hopes will help reduce homelessness.

"If the government focus on controlling alcohol and drugs, hopefully we can control these issues," he said.

Tejinder Singh says the NT government needs to crack down on anti-social behaviour. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Taylor believes the best way to reduce homelessness in Darwin is to "just build more houses".

"We need to build housing and we all need to work together to do that," she said.

"Government can do that, community housing providers can do that.

"We also need — along with the social housing — the affordable housing, so that we can accommodate many different types of people."

Data shows rental tenants have hit breaking point New data from Domain shows renters across Australia are hitting their affordability limit.

Unable to find work while being homeless, or pay rent without having a job, Mr Wishart said he was caught in a "catch-22 situation".

After living here for roughly 30 years, he plans to leave the Northern Territory.

"I can't really wait for public housing … so why not," he said.

"Just roll the dice and just see if something better comes up."

World.title: Live: One Nation candidate denies climate change as election campaign rolls on
World.content:
One Nation candidate for Murray Plains Garner Smith has told the ABC he doesn't believe in the science behind climate change.

Asked on ABC Central Victoria Breakfast this morning whether he accepted the consensus of the world's leading climate scientists, he said: "No, I don't actually.

"In fact, as far as I'm concerned, climate change has become nothing more than a mechanism that transfers money and power from the many to the few," he said. "I think there'd be a lot of people out there that'd be absolutely relieved to hear somebody say that."

One Nation candidate Garner Smith (Supplied: Gannawarra Shire Council)

The former mayor for Gannawarra Shire in north Victoria and Nationals Candidate said while he wasn't a scientist, he studied "all the sciences" in high school.

"Got 100 per cent in physics actually when I did my HSC in high school … So I would consider myself to be as scientifically minded as anybody," he said.

Smith also reiterated One Nation's commitment to scrap the proposed VNI West electricity transmission project and said he was not particularly supportive of wind or solar developments.

World.title: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews and gamer acclaim
World.content:
Critics are calling Grand Theft Auto VI a masterpiece after the most expensive game ever created launched overnight.

Launching just past midnight AEDT, many gamers stayed up overnight to play.

As media embargoes were lifted, dozens of reviews were published, delivering almost universal praise.

ABC Good Game Spawn Point host Angharad Yeo said GTA VI "may actually live up to the hype".

Angharad Yeo has so far loved her time with the game. (ABC News)

"It is just so wonderfully crafted, so detailed and immersive to the point where I'm expecting things that I should expect from it," Yeo said.

"I think people will be playing this for weeks, if not months, if not years."

Fans of the series waited 13 years for the latest instalment, and after lengthy delays, there was unprecedented hype and pressure surrounding the release.

Initial reviews dashed fears the game could never live up to that hype.

On Metacritic, a game review aggregating website, GTA VI has a score of 99, a rank shared only by 2023's Baldur's Gate 3 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998).

Players around the world are logging in to to explore Vice City and lose themselves in the world of GTA VI. (Supplied: Rockstar Games)

ScreenHub Australia gave the game four stars out of five, and reviewer Alice Clarke said: "At its core, GTA VI is a pretty good game.

"There are large sections where it is an absolutely epic game, and large sections that are boring and too limited," she said.

"However, after I pushed through the boring parts and it opened up enough to become a proper GTA title, it became worth it."

The world of GTA VI is between 50 to 75 square kilometres, twice the size of GTA V. (Supplied: Rockstar Games)

Former Australian pro-gamer Jamie Skella told ABC News Radio the release was more of a cultural phenomenon than a regular video game launch.

"It's so rich, it's alive," he said.

"They've really added just immense amounts of detail to the non-player-controlled characters, and the voice acting is phenomenal."

GTA VI is said to be the most expensive game ever developed, with an estimated budget of more than $2.2 billion.

Yeo said developer Rockstar Games had likely already made its money back.

"Reportedly, they've brought in $US1.5 billion [$2.21 billion] in worldwide revenue based just on the pre-sales," she said.

Mr Skella said "some 1.5 million Americans are probably skipping work today for it", joining many Australians who have booked time off.

Danny Cotter (right), with fellow GTA fan Hayden, is hoping to finish the game before he goes back to work next week. (Supplied)

Longtime fan Danny Cotter has booked four days off work so he can play it at launch.

"I've got full faith that it's going to blow me away," he said before the release.

Mr Cotter set his Xbox time to New Zealand, allowing him to access it hours earlier than other Australian gamers, and he played it until 4am AEST.

"I just woke up and I'm ready to play all day today," he said.

"I was very, very impressed with the prologue.

"There is a plot point that I will not spoil that I can see making the story and the journey far more emotional at times, which I am excited for."

Jack Hudson loves the new game's role-playing elements. (Supplied)

Jack Hudson also set his system time zone to New Zealand and clocked six to seven hours on the game overnight.

"This iteration of the game I feel ticks so many boxes," he said.

"It's just been phenomenal."

Mr Hudson, who has 5,000 hours in the game's predecessor, GTA V, has loved the role-playing element of GTA VI.

He rates it as a strong 9.5 out of 10 and thanked his boss, Emma Lo Russo, for approving his time off.

Declan Higgins and his wife came home from an outing to wait for the launch. (Supplied)

Declan Higgins said he enjoyed the game so much he had to make a conscious effort to go to bed after 3am.

"It's been so good," Mr Higgins said.

Aussies are calling off work to play GTA6 Australian gamers are taking tomorrow off to play GTA 6 the second it is released.

CBS reported in August that there was even a US Army Unit offering four days of leave to play the game for service people who re-enlisted for a two to six-year term of service.

Mr Skella, asked if it was worth the wait, said his answer could only be: "Hell yeah."

Yeo said there was still "so much to do" in her play-through.

"If previous Rockstar games are anything to go by, there's going to be very, very long legs on this game," she said.

World.title: Aboriginal corporation board goes against rule book to try to cast family out
World.content:
Central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara is in the midst of a factional divide amid questions that a whole family group is not connected by ancestry to the Aboriginal clan.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names of people who have died, used with the permission of their family.

Several board directors are believed to have resigned amid claims that other directors are trying to oust the Dunolly-Lee family from the Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation, known as Djaara.

At two weeks old, Deborah Dunolly was adopted by Djaara man Thomas Clarence Lynch Dunolly and his wife Rosemary Dawn Dunolly.

"My father gave me his name and an identity I have carried with pride ever since," she wrote in a statement to members ahead of the vote.

"My connection to this Country does not just sit with this membership; it has been a part of my life and who I am for as long as I can remember."

The Dunolly-Lee family declined to be interviewed for this story.

The names of respected Aboriginal people adorn a message stick held at Djaara. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

Djaara's chair Rebecca Philips said the board was legally required to maintain an accurate register of traditional owners and, when eligibility concerns arose, put them to a vote by its members.

But members of the Dunolly family group said the Dunolly-Lee family met all the requirements set out in Djaara's rule book about who was a traditional owner, calling the vote a personal attack against the family by other groups.

A special general meeting will take place on Saturday for the roughly 750 Djaara members to vote on whether to cancel the Dunolly-Lee family's membership.

The Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation is the largest registered Aboriginal party by revenue and assets in Victoria, earning nearly $40 million and employing 250 people.

Board proposes membership cancellation

A letter sent by Djaara to its members raised cancelling the membership of 10 people from the Dunolly-Lee family.

"We have noted the underlying disharmony felt by the variation of knowledge, awareness and position on this matter of recognition and eligibility for membership," Ms Phillips wrote.

"They are not a judgement of any person's worth, contribution, family relationships, or sense of belonging within the Dja Dja Wurrung community, as these are independent of membership.

"Notices of intended cancellation were issued, and written objections were received."

Rebecca Phillips is putting the Dunolly-Lee family's membership to a vote. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

The vote on whether the Dunolly-Lee family retains membership will be decided by the organisation's current rule book, the letter read.

But the rule book, finalised in 2013 when Djaara's recognition and settlement agreement was authorised, shows the organisation's full group confirmed the Dunolly-Lee family's rights were inherited from ancestors despite being adopted.

The decision is also backed by minutes from the meeting and emails that specifically mention the Dunolly family's situation.

Deborah Dunolly's statement tells of how her parents were unable to have children of their own and so adopted her and her brother, Thomas.

She also explains how she and her brother were raised within Djaara kinship structures.

Djaara is the largest registered Aboriginal party by revenue and assets in Victoria. (Supplied: Djaara)

Vote goes against rule book, elders say

The board's letter said it was up to members to decide whether they socially recognised and accepted the Dunolly-Lee family members.

Four elders have told the ABC they were "disgusted" by the actions of the board and said they believed Djaara was no longer the gold standard for Aboriginal corporations in Australia.

Uncle Tommy Baksh has spoken out in support of his family members. (Supplied: Uncle Tommy Baksh)

A Djaara elder, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told the ABC the vote to cancel the membership of the Dunolly-Lee family went against the organisation's rule book.

Uncle Tommy Baksh, the elder Dunolly member, said the vote to remove the Dunolly-Lee family had left him angry and shocked.

"It's racism, and they're singling out a family that they don't know the full history," he said.

"To see them go through the ups and downs of the meetings has been emotional and upsetting."

The rule book is the Djaara's primary internal governing document.

The ancestral land of the Dja Dja Wurring in central Victoria. (Supplied: Djaara)

The Dunolly-Lee family has been invited to address the membership at the meeting and make a case for their right to a cultural claim and to remain members.

The Dja Dja Wurrung people are made up of 18 family groups across central Victoria.

Cultural principles and heritage

It was only a year ago that Djaara put a vote to members about who could be a member through cultural claim, with the group deciding to keep to the rule book as it was set out.

A senior Djaara member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of backlash from Djaara's board, told the ABC that in 2025 the board tried to change the rules, including removing cultural adoption, but the majority of members voted to keep the rule book as it was.

Board minutes from last year show the motion to change the rule book was not carried.

Aunty Marlene Burchill supports the Dunolly-Lee family. (Supplied: Marlene Burchill)

Aunty Marlene "Marl" Burchill remembers Thomas Dunolly riding his bicycle from Cummeragunja to spend the day with her mother, Iris Atkinson.

She said going against the rule book to remove the Dunolly-Lee family from the Aboriginal corporation was "pathetic".

"It's just plain spitefulness and jealousy that's taking place here. Bec has overstepped her position as chair," Ms Burchill said.

"They don't know what good governance is."

She said the vote was a personal attack on the Dunolly family by several other family groups, who she claimed did not have legitimate ties to the Djaara people through a distant relative.

Multiple university Indigenous studies faculties declined to speak publicly about the vote and divide in Djaara.

Families' claims under scrutiny

Djaara's rules set out four elements for being considered a Dja Dja Wurrung person.

These are being a descendant by birth or cultural adoption, the person identifying as Dja Dja Wurrung, having an active association with Dja Dja Wurrung business and country, and being accepted by other Djaara traditional owners.

The final point clarifies that being accepted can be achieved by being a member or by meeting the first two elements of birth and cultural adoption, and self-identifying.

Documents show the full group of the organisation in 2013 decided to respect the ancestors' decision about who could claim cultural connection, meaning the Dunolly-Lee family could be a traditional owner, even though their claim is through being adopted.

But the division within the organisation has also raised questions about whether other members are rightful descendants.

The vote will go to Djaara's membership at a special general meeting this weekend. (ABC News: Tyrone Dalton)

Documents question whether some Dja Dja Wurrung members are rightful descendants of Caroline Malcolm, and not her husband's second wife, Maryanne, who was from country further east in the Goulburn area.

The rule book states that Caroline Malcolm's mother was born in 1846 at Menzies Station Loddon, and may have been recorded in the Mount Franklinford 1863 census as residing at Bullock Creek.

It said a Coranderrk Mission burial registry lists Caroline Malcolm's family group as being from the Loddon area.

Ms Phillips is the head representative for the Caroline Malcolm family group — one of 18 family groups that make up the 18 available seats on Djaara's board.

A Djaara member told the ABC that differences between family groups, Ms Phillips's performance as chair and her family group's eligibility, as well as the Dunolly-Lee issue, had driven several board directors to leave.

In a statement, Ms Phillips said claims regarding widespread director resignations were incorrect, adding that the board held a quorum to operate legally.

"Out of respect for our traditional owner community, procedural fairness and member privacy, we will not comment on individual memberships or internal governance matters through the media," she said.

"Our focus remains firmly on delivering outcomes for our members and caring for Country."

Djaara and Ms Phillips did not respond to questions about Caroline Malcolm's family connections.

By law, the national regulator for Aboriginal corporations, the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations (ORIC), can appoint a special administrator to take control of an organisation in serious circumstances.

ORIC states it generally only places organisations into special administration when there is a risk of failure or severe dysfunction.

In a statement, ORIC said it did not make public comment on whether it was considering, monitoring or investigating a particular matter.

"This approach helps ensure the integrity of our regulatory processes and protects the interests of those involved," it said.

World.title: Cummins stands firm despite Bancroft's Sandpapergate allegation
World.content:
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins has responded to Cameron Bancroft's sensational claims that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper in 2018, in a statement through his manager.

Bancroft on Wednesday night released a 4,500-word piece detailing the events of the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa, where he was caught using sandpaper on the ball during a Test in Cape Town.

Last week, Cummins held a 70-minute press conference in the wake of the saga being brought back into the spotlight following the release of Usman Khawaja's memoir, Sabr.

Cameron Bancroft's bomb is Australian cricket's point of no return Cameron Bancroft's statement is the atom bomb Cricket Australia has always feared. For so many of the game's key figures, there is no turning back now.

Cummins maintained he, and the bowling unit, did not know sandpaper was being used on the field.

Bancroft's article on Wednesday directly contradicts Cummins's statement, but the Test captain has maintained his position.

"Pat’s position hasn't changed in eight years," Cummins's manager, Neil Maxwell, said.

"He's been consistent and adamant from day one. Pat feels for Cam, of course. He has been through a lot.

"We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said.

"Pat has rebuilt the Australian cricket team. That 24-year-old in Cape Town resolved to fix the team and spent eight years doing it."

Bancroft said Cummins's press conference last Friday, where the Test captain said any suggestion bowlers knew of the sandpaper use was "utter nonsense", was the catalyst for his tell-all piece.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote in an article that originally appeared in the West Australian before being sent out to all media.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins's press conference."

Darren Lehmann, who was Australian coach at the time of the incident, was commentating for ABC Sport when Bancroft's article was published on Wednesday.

Bancroft said Lehmann was present during conversations about using sandpaper on the ball to help it reverse-swing.

The former coach said he would need to "work through each allegation" before making any comment.

"The allegations … I've got to sit back. It's only just come to light. So I just need to sit back and process all that and work through each allegation. That's what I will be doing over the next few days," Lehmann said on ABC Radio.

"I need to have a really good read of it, don't I? What's been transpired, speaking to people, and just make sure I'm saying what I want to say and answer the questions you want to ask."

Earlier on Wednesday, Cricket Australia (CA) had announced a forum for players to come forward and discuss their recollections and perspectives of the infamous period in Australian cricket history.

However, CA chief executiveTodd Greenberg said the forum was not an investigation, and CA would decide what information from the forum would be made public.

World.title: Adelaide records one of its warmest November nights
World.content:
Adelaide has experienced one of its warmest November nights ahead of thunderstorms and showers across the state on Thursday.

The West Terrace observation station recorded an overnight minimum temperature of 24.5 degrees Celsius, which the Bureau of Meteorology said was rare for November — less than 1 per cent chance of it occurring based on historic averages.

The mercury continued to rise, reaching 27.3C at 3am on Thursday, helped by north-easterly winds bringing warm air from inland.

Despite being unusually warm, the overnight temperature in Adelaide was still short of the historic November minimum of 30.1C in 1922.

Storms are expected for Thursday afternoon across South Australia ahead of a cooler day on Friday, according to the bureau's duty forecaster Robert Urbaniak.

"The showers and thunderstorms will tend to pick up from around 2pm, and then you'll see a stronger band of thunderstorms come through around 8pm," he told 891 ABC Adelaide.

Up to 10 millimetres of rain has been predicted for Adelaide, however Mr Urbaniak said less was likely.

"I wouldn't be surprised if it's on the lower side," he said.

"Some of the weather models have the showers essentially missing Adelaide, but nonetheless the chance for some showers and thunderstorms is there."

CFS volunteers are on alert for potential fire danger. (ABC News: Simon Goodes)

The Country Fire Service will be on alert in the coming days as lightning, northerly winds and reduced rainfall across the state, particularly in the Eyre Peninsula and West Coast, heighten potential fire risk.

"Next couple of days are going to be challenging for I'll say the Eyre Peninsula but more broadly across the state too," CFS commander Stephen Boucher told SA Country Hour

"There is significant lightning bands that are coming across and reduced rainfall so those combinations don't mix as well as some northerly and some strong winds attached to that."

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE updates: Labour hire boss continues evidence as inquiry probes Gap Road project
World.content:
Bernard Kearney, the co-owner of CFMEU-backed subcontractor BK Labour, has admitted to creating fake invoices and submitting them to the industry regulator.

The invoices were submitted to the Labour Hire Authority after it asked why BK Labour paid union boss Joe Myles’ companies more than $127,000.

Bernard Kearney testifies today.

Florence Pugh has hit back at online speculation she has had cosmetic surgery and has been using Ozempic with a fiery Instagram post. Florence Pugh at the 17th Governors Awards at the weekend. Her appearance set off fevered speculation. Variety via Getty Images “A lot of people are pointing out how Florence used to have, like, full beautiful cheeks that made her face super recognisable. Now that her jaw is more defined, her chin is more pointier, her jaws are more sharp, it makes sense why people are wondering if she’s had work done,” the video claimed. On Wednesday Pugh posted a comment below the video noting that she was now 30 and that “body’s (sic) and faces change”.



“It’s not that deep, the fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging (sic) and what’s surgery is disturbing. Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever,” she wrote. Then on Thursday morning (AEDT), Pugh hit back again with a long statement on her Instagram account saying such commentary was “stressful” and she was “disturbed” by it. Florence Pugh (left) this year and (right) last year at the Thunderbolts premiere. “I woke up the other morning and quite a lot of you were discussing my face and body in such a disturbing way. I learnt online that I had been on ozempic? I learnt that I’d had upper bleph? Lower bleph? Filler? Face lipo? Bucal fat remover? Chin surgery? Nose surgery?!



“Yes I’m disturbed. For women who now think I’m something I’m not. For having my body dissected and pointed at again. I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow.” A screenshot from Pugh’s video. Instagram Along with the statement, Pugh posted video to her Story showing her working out, doing push-ups weighed down by a chain and capturing the moment where she managed two chin-ups in a row. The video was captioned, “Ozempic could never”. In her statement, the East of Eden star said she had been “subjected to fat-shaming in the business from the moment I started”. She added that she had “loved every time I get to tell someone to f--- off when they’ve been inappropriate about my weight, and I am not changing that now just because you’ve all said so”.



“I have never been on ozempic. I have NEVER done any face surgery. And don’t EVER say that I didn’t make my own nose, I’ve always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby.” Pugh said she had been on a health kick, going to the gym and changing her relationship with alcohol as she headed towards her 30th birthday. “It’s funny to see you all use reference images from times where I was really mentally unhappy and abusing my body and put it next to the image from the governors (sic) awards the other night where I am happy and truly respecting my body,” Pugh wrote. She also canvassed the many hateful comments she had endured over her career and asked for followers to use her response to the speculation as a “moment of self-reflection”. “I’m not angry at you, I’m angry at the situation that’s been projected on to us. It feels inescapable but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye,” Pugh finished. Health Minister Mark Butler has said his decision to cut nearly all of the plan managers responsible for funnelling billions in government funding to NDIS participants will allow the scheme to function more smoothly.

Just 20 of the 1442 NDIS plan managers will be authorised to work with the scheme’s half a million participants in an attempt by the government to eradicate dodgy operators by accrediting only a limited number of providers.

“There’s no question there are some pretty serious issues that I’ve expressed really serious concern about … We’re determined to get them back under control.”

World.title: ASX slumps ahead of jobs data, Wall Street on longest losing streak since June
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slumps ahead of jobs data, Wall Street on longest losing streak since June Stan Choe Updated November 19, 2026 — 10:22am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has opened sharply lower after a fifth-straight drop for the S&P 500 dragged Wall Street to its longest losing streak since June, with AI stocks continuing to weigh on global indexes. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 105.2 points, or 1.2 per cent, in early trade. Unemployment figures for October will be released at 11.30am AEDT. The ASX fell by 0.7 per cent on Wednesday, its fifth-straight losing session. The Australian dollar is weaker at US67.18¢. Wall Street is on unsteady footing as doubts over AI companies hover. AP The S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent after zigzagging between gains and losses through the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561 points, or 1.1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite added 0.4 per cent. Nvidia was once again was at the centre of Wall Street’s moves. Its stock initially jumped 2.7 per cent after the chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected but that gain was wiped out and it closed 2.9 per cent lower. Perhaps more importantly, it also gave a forecast for revenue in the current quarter that was better than expected.



Related Article Breaking

Insolvency General Pants collapses after years of trouble The question is whether Nvidia’s big growth can continue despite the turmoil created by the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. He had an immense personality that drew attention and investment to AI, and he built Nvidia into a company so big that it helped to fund some of the industry’s growth itself. “Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts after announcing the company’s latest results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.” The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia, though, failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory chips exploded with the AI boom, went from an early rise of 1.5 per cent to a drop of 1 per cent.



CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents access to them out to customers over the cloud, sank 4.1 per cent and has lost nearly a third of its value so far this year. The entire industry has been swinging recently. Besides criticism that AI stock prices simply shot too high in their frenzy, the industry is facing worries that this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections could mean more regulation for it. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of oil companies were heavy weights due to drops for oil prices. ExxonMobil fell 4 per cent, and Chevron sank 4 per cent after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.3 per cent to settle at $US91.95. The drop in oil prices helped to pull yields down in the bond market, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 5.06 per cent from 5.10 per cent late on Tuesday. High yields have made mortgages more expensive to get, which has chilled the housing industry. But they’ve moderated over the last month, and a report on Wednesday said homebuilders broke ground on more projects last month than economists expected.



That helped push stocks of homebuilders modestly higher, and Lennar added 0.7 per cent. Some of the strongest gains on Wall Street came from retailers following their profit reports. TJX rallied 8 per cent after the company behind the TJ Maxx and Marshalls stores reported slightly better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Ernie Herrman said he expects momentum to accelerate through the holiday shopping season. Target climbed 4 per cent following a better-than-expected profit report, which included its strongest quarterly sales gain in roughly five years. Take-Two Interactive Software revved 6.2 per cent higher amid glowing reviews for its latest “Grand Theft Auto” video game.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 16.90 points to 7,323.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561.25 to 50,198.17, and the Nasdaq composite rose 101.50 to 24,429.88. Related Article Opinion

AI Nvidia’s result is gobsmacking, but a sideshow to its CEO spy scandal Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In stock markets abroad, indexes fell in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 sank 1.3 per cent after a report said inflation in the United Kingdom worsened. That could up the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates to get inflation under control. Expectations are high that the Federal Reserve in Washington will raise its own interest rate when it meets next month, after it made no move last month. Notes released Wednesday from the Fed’s latest meeting indicated some officials are considering a larger increase to rates than usual in December.



South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2 per cent a day after dropping to its lowest closing level since February. It’s swung in particular because its market is dominated by two stocks tied to the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.” The encouraging numbers and words coming from Nvidia, though, failed to create lasting gains for the price of its stock or for others across the industry. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory chips exploded with the AI boom, went from an early rise of 1.5 per cent to a drop of 1 per cent.



CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents access to them out to customers over the cloud, sank 4.1 per cent and has lost nearly a third of its value so far this year. The entire industry has been swinging recently. Besides criticism that AI stock prices simply shot too high in their frenzy, the industry is facing worries that this month’s sweeping victories for Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections could mean more regulation for it. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of oil companies were heavy weights due to drops for oil prices. ExxonMobil fell 4 per cent, and Chevron sank 4 per cent after the price for a barrel of Brent crude fell 1.3 per cent to settle at $US91.95. The drop in oil prices helped to pull yields down in the bond market, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury eased to 5.06 per cent from 5.10 per cent late on Tuesday. High yields have made mortgages more expensive to get, which has chilled the housing industry. But they’ve moderated over the last month, and a report on Wednesday said homebuilders broke ground on more projects last month than economists expected.



That helped push stocks of homebuilders modestly higher, and Lennar added 0.7 per cent. Some of the strongest gains on Wall Street came from retailers following their profit reports. TJX rallied 8 per cent after the company behind the TJ Maxx and Marshalls stores reported slightly better earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Ernie Herrman said he expects momentum to accelerate through the holiday shopping season. Target climbed 4 per cent following a better-than-expected profit report, which included its strongest quarterly sales gain in roughly five years. Take-Two Interactive Software revved 6.2 per cent higher amid glowing reviews for its latest “Grand Theft Auto” video game.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 16.90 points to 7,323.63. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 561.25 to 50,198.17, and the Nasdaq composite rose 101.50 to 24,429.88. Related Article Opinion

AI Nvidia’s result is gobsmacking, but a sideshow to its CEO spy scandal Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In stock markets abroad, indexes fell in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. London’s FTSE 100 sank 1.3 per cent after a report said inflation in the United Kingdom worsened. That could up the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates to get inflation under control. Expectations are high that the Federal Reserve in Washington will raise its own interest rate when it meets next month, after it made no move last month. Notes released Wednesday from the Fed’s latest meeting indicated some officials are considering a larger increase to rates than usual in December.



South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2 per cent a day after dropping to its lowest closing level since February. It’s swung in particular because its market is dominated by two stocks tied to the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
