World.title: Explainer: The US has lost its measles elimination status. Could New Zealand?
World.content:
Explainer - More than 25 years ago, the United States effectively stopped measles transmission. This week, it lost its elimination status. How did this happen and could it happen here?

Cases of measles,one of the most contagious viruses there is, have been surging in many countries since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Despite several outbreaks of measles here in New Zealand the past few years, we achieved the elimination of endemic measles cases in October 2017.

US Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. KENT NISHIMURA / AFP

"Measles elimination status" doesn't mean the virus is completely absent, but that a country has interrupted continuous transmission and has a handle on keeping any smaller new outbreaks from spreading.

But that could be at risk as on-time childhood vaccination rates with the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine continue to fall in Aotearoa.

What has happened in the United States?

It was officially announced this week that the United States has lost the measles elimination status it achieved in 2000.

The Pan American Health Organisation or PAHO, a division of the World Health Organisation or WHO, confirmed on Tuesday that the United States, along with Bolivia and Mexico, lost their status "as free from endemic measles transmission, as the virus had circulated continuously in each country for at least 12 months".

Ambra Hawksley holds her son Andrik Hawksley, age 6, while his sister JaeLynn holds his hand as he prepares to get an MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio, at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. JAN SONNENMAIR / AFP

"My first reaction is that this was preventable," said Dr Heather Battles, a senior lecturer in anthropology at the University of Auckland who researches infectious disease, epidemics and pandemics.

"The Covid-19 pandemic did interrupt a lot of routine vaccinations, and not just in the US, so there's been a lot of catching up to do," she said.

"And perhaps there hasn't been the political will to invest in public health to do that work."

Measles cases have been steadily on the rise in the US, with outbreaks in largely unvaccinated communities. The disease is highly contagious and can cause serious and life-long health problems.

Some 7700 people in the US have been infected with measles ⁠and 13 have died since 2025, Reuters has reported.

Among them were several children, including a child in New York who died this month and was the state's first death from the disease in 30 years.

"It's a giant stain on our reputation," Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Centre at the Brown University School of Public Health, told The New York Times.

"Everyone ought to be just utterly disgusted by the willing return back to an age of death and high cost."

This picture released from UNICEF Samoa shows a girl receiving a vaccine during a nationwide campaign against measles in the Samoan town of Le'auva'a. ALLAN STEPHEN / UNICEF / AFP

What does losing elimination status mean?

If measles spreads continuously for at least 12 months, it meets PAHO's criteria for the return of endemic transmission.

According to WHO, it doesn't mean that the US has lost "all capacity to control the disease" or that it's spreading in wild outbreaks throughout the country. But it is circulating widely.

But it "is a significant public health setback because it means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalisation and death," the Pan American Health Organisation said.

The US isn't alone - Canada also lost its own elimination status in November 2025. Meanwhile, countries with wide endemic transmission including Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala have seen the highest measles cases in 2026 so far, according to WHO data.

"Losing a measles elimination status has broader implications than losing a public health designation," Dr Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, director of PAHO, told media.

"It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalisation, and death."

Kollin Hilihetule getting vaccinated at a pop-up clinic in Manukau during a measles outbreak in 2025. RNZ/Jessica Hopkins

Could the loss of measles elimination also happen in New Zealand?

New Zealand has had several outbreaks of measles in recent years but managed to keep its elimination status - for now. But we've been warned.

A 2024 report by the Public Health Communication Centre reported WHO officials saying "New Zealand is at risk of a large outbreak and losing its elimination status, unless immunity gaps are rapidly closed".

"Anywhere where measles vaccination rates drop is potentially in danger of measles outbreaks," Battles said.

New Zealand's childhood MMR coverage has deteriorated since before the Covid pandemic.

On-time delivery of childhood MMR vaccine doses were "suboptimal", a Ministry of Health report on immunisation from 2015 to 2024 found.

More than six in 10 Māori children and half of Pacific children were receiving their first MMR dose late, and the report noted "the risk of repeated outbreaks is concentrated in these populations".

Measles has a devastating history in Aotearoa, Battles has written, with outbreaks that killed many in the 1800s, including thousands of Māori.

"New Zealand's worst measles year in the past century was 1938, with 375 deaths among both children and adults," she noted.

Measles vaccination finally began here in 1969.

There was a large outbreak of more than 2000 measles cases in 2019, and the latest outbreak in New Zealand ran from September 2025 to February 2026 after 48 connected cases were identified. According to the Immunisation Advisory Centre, the response included vaccine outreach with nearly 107,000 MMR doses delivered over four months.

US President Donald Trump's Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has long been sceptical of vaccines. SAUL LOEB / AFP

Has Robert F Kennedy Jr made measles worse?

A big reason for the change in the US status is falling numbers of those taking up the MMR vaccine. As measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to man, it requires about a 95 percent rate of "herd immunity" among the population to keep the spread of infection down.

However, in many parts of America vaccine hesitancy has grown since the Covid pandemic. The spread of misinformation about vaccines has led to a loss of trust in health systems.

US childhood vaccination rates have fallen by approximately 3 percent since 2020, from the 95 percent herd immunity threshold to an estimated 92.4 percent in 2025-2026, according to the American US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has been a notable vaccine sceptic and repeatedly cast doubts on their effectiveness. He has also overhauled many of America's vaccine policies.

Kennedy has publicly endorsed the MMR vaccine but also in a Fox News interview in 2025 made the unsupported claim that the vaccine leads to "deaths every year" and misleadingly said it causes "all the illnesses" of the disease. He has also called it a "leaky vaccine" that wanes and falsely stated it hasn't been "safety tested".

Kennedy has also been criticised for his involvement in allegedly promoting vaccine mistrust during a measles outbreak in Samoa in 2019 that caused 83 deaths, mostly children.

A recent Reuters investigation found childhood vaccinations have sharply dropped during Kennedy's tenure.

However, the CDC, which is overseen by Kennedy, did issue a statement this week that it is "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".

"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection."

A fact sheet for measles sits on a table at a mobile clinic offering free vaccinations on February 6, 2026 in Spartanburg, South Carolina. The clinic offered free MMR vaccinations as the South Carolina Department of Health reported 876 cases of measles earlier in the week, most centered in Spartanburg County. SEAN RAYFORD / AFP / Getty

What can we do to ensure we don't lose elimination status?

Vaccinate, vaccinate, vaccinate.

Health New Zealand says that studies have shown the MMR vaccine is 95 percent effective with a single dose and 99 percent effective with two doses. Given in childhood, the doses should provide lifelong protection.

The MMR vaccine is is free for everyone under the age of 18, and it does not matter what your immigration status is. It is also free if you are 18 and over and eligible for funded healthcare.

"NZ has been fortunate that recent importations have not resulted in significant outbreaks - but without high herd immunity, as long as measles is circulating outside NZ, that remains a risk," Battles said.

Can a country get back to elimination of measles?

It could take years for the US to regain its measles elimination status, health experts say.

"Losing measles elimination status is a setback, but it is reversible," PAHO says. Brazil, for instance, lost its status in 2019 but regained it in 2024 following extensive vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response efforts.

The sweeping cuts of many health and science programmes in the US could be difficult to build back from.

"Trust takes a long time to build, or rebuild," Battles said.

World.title: Wayne Brown says Wellington aligned with US in full-length interview on Chinese TV
World.content:
Audio player for " David Seymour on Wayne Brown's China comments " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics/2680024%2Fwayne-brown-says-wellington-aligned-with-us-in-full-length-interview-on-chinese-tv

David Seymour on Wayne Brown's China comments Midday Report Download MP3 7m

Auckland mayor Wayne Brown has given a long-form interview on Chinese television, where he claimed Wellington was aligned with the US while Auckland supported China.

He also said he was "grinding down" the New Zealand government to make it easier for Chinese visitors to get visas, but "getting rid of the ones that are a bit awkward".

The mayor's six-city tour of China had already attracted controversy, with the US Ambassador to New Zealand, Jared Novelly, suggesting Brown had become too close to the Chinese government.

In a post-trip media interview with Stuff, Brown praised China's approach to economic growth and described democracy as having had its day.

But during a CGTN interview, filmed while he was in China, Brown was asked how he reconciled China being New Zealand's biggest trading partner while the country was a member of the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance and "having to pay allegiance to the US, from the perspective of Wellington at least".

"Wellington's my biggest obstacle," Brown said during the 24-minute long interview.

Video player removed for printing https://www.youtube.com/embed/Osq1rVN4QZY?si=3wAWiC1yoa70ViNC

"I have a very poor relationship with Wellington as a central manager of our country.

"Wellington is probably veered a bit more towards America, but Auckland, the biggest city, is definitely more pro-China. We've got 300,000 Chinese there anyhow."

He said he had suggested selling New Zealand's Five Eyes seat to Japan.

"I can't see anything in it for us.

"I have a very different view from some other central government people. But I'm very popular, and they're not."

During the interview, Brown briefly forgot his role.

"My predecessors were former politicians," he said.

Auckland mayor Wayne Brown. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"I'm quite unusual, coming from nowhere to be a prime minister, uh, no, being the mayor of the biggest city."

He also told the interviewer about his preferred way of governing.

"The former guy before me [Phil Goff] was a former Labour MP, and he ran it [Auckland Council] like government with one party versus the other.

"But I don't have any party. I don't allow party discussions. You've got to make a sensible decision as council on the issues you're facing."

Brown claimed he was influencing the government to ease visa requirements for Chinese visitors.

"I'm slowly grinding my government into making visas easier and easier for Chinese, and we're getting rid of the ones which are a bit awkward. And that's happening."

He was also critical of the Port of Auckland, saying cargo operations should be moved away from the city centre to other Upper North Island ports. He said it did not make sense for Auckland to be "delivering cars in the middle of a city on expensive port land".

"It's bad that you've got trucks right through the middle of the city.

"The land is more valuable for other things than a port. I could build buildings on that or do something different with it."

He said the Ningbo-Zhoushan Port, in eastern China, was "very efficient".

"I would like to send some people here just to check the efficiency of my port.

"If you ask the people who run it, they'll tell you we're wonderful. But I don't actually believe that. I want to have someone independent who actually runs a very efficient port to have a look at what the things are we could do better."

The port was owned by Auckland Council, but governed by an independent board.

Waikato University professor Al Gillespie said there was merit in the comments Novelly made about Brown and his criticism was fair.

However, he said Novelly should not have done so in a public way as it was undiplomatic.

David Seymour. RNZ/Nick Monro

Caretaker Government responds

In response to Brown's comments, Acting Prime Minister David Seymour said New Zealanders had family who had fought to defend democracy, and he said it was a "vastly superior" political system to any other.

Brown "is simply incorrect," Seymour said, calling Brown's position as mayor "not really too different from being the chair of a board of trustees at a state school".

"I suspect commentary and behaviour of this type won't help his chances at re-election…

"If we don't like our government, we should have the ability to put an anonymous pink slip in a box every so often, in our case every three years, and bloodlessly remove a bad government. That is something that our forebears have literally fought for and people are fighting for right across the Russian front of Ukraine today, among other places."

But also, Seymour said the US ambassador's public reaction was "inadvisable".

"I think the most important thing is to just dial it down a notch."

Meanwhile, Otago University China foreign policy expert Associate Professor Nicholas Khoo said Brown was ill-informed and didn't understand the complexities of international politics.

His comments were "problematic because they're simply inaccurate".

World.title: 'Somebody had spoken up': Kiwi's role in Aussie cricket's 'Sandpapergate' scandal
World.content:
A New Zealander has been described as the sole voice of reason in the ball-tampering scandal enveloping Australian cricket.

The latest explosive revelations concerning "Sandpapergate", a furore which began during Australia's tour of South Africa in 2018, shine a positive light on Kate Hutchison, Cricket Australia's media manager at the time.

According to former player Cameron Bancroft, who has poured fuel on the fire by saying the entire Australian team knew about the ball-tampering during the tour and that he had lied about the extent of the plot to protect Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident, Hutchison was the sole dissenting voice.

Hutchison, who now works in a corporate role in Melbourne, is a former New Zealand Rugby communications staffer. She has also held a high-profile role in Swimming Australia.

In a lengthy column published in The West Australian, Bancroft, who was banned along with fellow batsmen David Warner and Steve Smith over the plan to rough up the ball with sandpaper, wrote: "Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening".

"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

Australian batter Cam Bancroft is bowled during the controversial test in Port Elizabeth, South Africa, in 2018. Deryck Foster/Photosport

"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.

"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.

"I cannot speak for Kate's thoughts beyond what I remember her saying and doing. She deserves the opportunity to give her own account.

"But her reaction is important because it completely challenges the idea that nobody had an opportunity to question what was happening.

"We did. I did. And I chose to continue."

Australia captain Pat Cummins. Joel Carrett / Photosport

RNZ has attempted to contact Hutchison. A media contact at her employer RACV, an insurance company, said on Thursday that Hutchison was "not doing media today".

Bancroft, Warner and Smith were the only players banned over the incident but batter Usman Khawaja's recently released autobiography contradicted the conclusion of the initial CA investigation which reignited the controversy.

Compounding matters, captain Pat Cummins, denied in a recently press conference any involvement in using sandpaper and said the allegations in Khawaja's autobiography were "utter nonsense".

Bancroft wrote: "What I saw, experienced and lived with, not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa, is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."

World.title: Outspoken Tongan footballer suspended, calls for overhaul
World.content:
The Tongan men's football team needs a total revamp if it is to compete in the region, a national team player says.

Anthony Likiliki was suspended from the rest of the team's tour of New Zealand last week after his interview with the Oceania Football Center (OFCe), in which he criticised the team's preparation and performances following the 11-0 defeat to East Coast Bays.

Likiliki revealed he had been removed from the remainder of the four-match tour after expressing his dissatisfaction with the team's outing and the methods being employed by the coaching staff.

The OCFe reported that the New Zealand-based player, one of six overseas footballers included in the squad, had previously criticised the tactical approach adopted by head coach Timote Moleni as well as the overall preparation of the national team.

"Of course, and after speaking my mind I am suspended from this whole tour, the standard of this team is just not at the right place," Likiliki told OFCe.

"But I have no regrets. I spoke no lies."

Likiliki described the performance as unacceptable and called for significant improvements in the team's organisation.

His said the coaching staff's tactical decisions were not up to par.

"They have been using this same system that has not worked for years," he said.

"Same ideas, same results."

He said Tonga needs a playing system capable of making better use of the available footballers, particularly those based overseas who had experienced more competitive football environments

He questioned whether the national team's preparation was sufficient to compete against opponents from stronger domestic leagues and regional teams.

The Tongan men's team after their first tour match. Likiliki is standing third from right (11), with coach Timote Moleni, standing far right. Tonga Football

Players voice

Responding to questions from RNZ Pacific on Wednesday, Likiliki said he was speaking on behalf of players who could not speak for themselves.

He said players were unhappy about the environment within the team.

"I understand the local players are afraid to speak their mind with the consequences that comes after it," he said.

"I was brought up in Tonga as a local myself and I totally understand how this management works. They've dismissed me before at youth ages due to missing training for school assignments that I needed to do.

"What I said comes from a place of passion love from the jersey. I'm a local kid who came out a few years ago here to New Zealand and have played semi-professional here."

Likiliki, who is also the strength and conditioning coach for the Auckland University Rugby Football Club, said he was not surprised that he was suspended.

He said "if having standards is a problem with them that says a lot about them not me", adding he stands by what he stated.

"I stand by it that it does not work at all, same formation and same system they've been using to have us lose over and over again against any Pacific teams," he said.

"I understand the gap between what's at home and what's in New Zealand but the players struggle with this system of theirs.

"It's just a mess. When I play their system, I feel as if I've never played football in my life either.

"I did not improve with their system, I improved when I moved here years ago and played the systems New Zealand coaches used to expose my strengths rather than exposing my weaknesses."

Likiliki said there are players who want to play for Tonga "but if this situation with me is problematic, then they are not ready for any higher level player to come with an even higher standard to improve the game".

Follow the rule

Meanwhile, Tonga Football's director of football Jagdish Reddy said the player had been suspended because he did not follow set procedures and systems.

He said they will not discuss the suspension in the media.

"There is an established process that must be followed when concerns or disagreements arise within a National Team environment," Reddy said in response to questions raised by RNZ Pacific.

"Players and officials alike, are entitled to have views and raise concerns, but these matters should be discussed through the appropriate authorities and internal processes rather than through the media.

"This principle is not unique to Tonga. National and professional teams around the world operate within standards of conduct, accountability and team discipline, and TFA is no different.

"For that reason, we will not discuss individual disciplinary matters or internal National Team matters through the media or engage in a public debate regarding this situation."

The Tonga national men's football team undertook a four-match tour of Auckland in the last two weeks.

World.title: US senators push for stronger military space ties with NZ
World.content:
objectives.

United States senators are calling for deeper military space ties with New Zealand.

The Pentagon embarked on 2026 as the 'Year of Integration' of its space efforts with allies and partners.

Nine senators wrote to the Pentagon this week saying further maturation of New Zealand's space programmne and additional investment would advance US national security

objectives.

This would help "ensure allied and partner space superiority by providing opportunities for additional satellite tracking, space surveillance, missile coverage, and communications

redundancies," they wrote on Tuesday (US time).

New Zealand already played a "crucial role" in US Space Command operations running a space-watching hub in Auckland and and supporting partner nation training around the world, they said.

Congressional records show Senator Eric Schmitt [https://www.congress.gov/119/crec/2026/07/13/172/113/modified/CREC-2026-07-13-pt1-PgS3781-2.htm

introduced an amendment] in July for the Pentagon to produce a strategy within six months to enhance US-NZ defence cooperation, including for more shared space and military industrial efforts.

He singled out addressing shared security challenges in the Pacific and the Antarctic.

His amendment was submitted but does not appear to have gone further though it had called for a strategy by the end of 2026.

The senators wrote to the Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink on November 17 asking him to consider extra steps to improve space efforts with New Zealand, "a key Five Eyes partner, where doing so advances US national security interests and strengthens collective capability".

Meink in September publicly acknowledged for the first time the US has deployed weapons in space. The US Department of Defence describes China as its "pacing" or number one threat militarily and in space.

The NZDF's Defence Capability Plan envisages spending up to hundreds of millions of dollars building space and aerospace capabilities, as well as on emerging military technology.

Schmitt's amendment aimed "to expand cooperation on space, and advanced defense capabilities" and assessment of opportunities to expand defence industrial base cooperation, including around aviation, munitions, maintenance and repair "and the integration of New Zealand industry into allied defense supply chains, as appropriate".

New Zealand was quietly added to the US National Technology and Industrial Base several years ago and more recently, joined the US's Partnership for Indo-Pacific Industrial Resilience to boost military industrial supply chains.

The senators' letter talked up existing NZ efforts including in the US-led Combined Space Operations initiative to "protect shared space interests from disruption, denial, or destruction, and promote responsible behaviour".

One of the nine - three Democrats and six Republicans - Republican Deb Fischer chairs a Strategic Forces Subcommittee that covers military space, missile defence and US Space Command.

RNZ reported last month that US Space Command gagged the NZDF over providing the NZ public with information about the Auckland Joint Commercial Operation (JCO) space-watch hub's operations.

The senators referred to the hub, saying NZDF's No. 62 space squadron "plays a crucial role" in it as the Pacific Cell Lead.

"NZDF has also launched experimental payloads into orbit on US satellites, while Prime Minister Christopher Luxon established a dedicated ministerial position for space in 2023.

"The relatively small scale of New Zealand's military space bureaucracy - coupled with the country's geographically advantageous launch and operational environments

and growing commercial space sector - offers considerable avenues for mutual partnership and opportunities to innovate."

Chief of Space Operations General Chance Saltzman visited New Zealand in May, just before he retired, when he signed a "statement of intent" over space operations with NZDF. The senators said, "We believe in the necessity of having ready and capable allies and partners.

World.title: Advocates champing at the bit to revive Horse of the Year event, after troubled run
World.content:
The largest equestrian event in the Southern Hemisphere, a staple of the Hawke's Bay calendar for decades, is facing further uncertainty.

At its peak, 1500 horses and their riders performed in show jumping, dressage and eventing across many disciplines for 55,000 spectators.

But a string of cancellations during the Covid-19 pandemic and Cyclone Gabrielle, and event sponsorship woes in an economic downturn, have left organisers cash-short.

Tim Aitken is the former chairman of the joint venture set up between the Hastings District Council (HDC) and Equestrian Sports New Zealand (ESNZ) to run the event, Horse of the Year (Hawke's Bay) Limited.

But he said the company had "wrapped up", sold assets and dissolved its board in May, after it struggled to get cashflow to run this year's event, and the next one was looking uncertain too.

"Me personally, I'm absolutely gutted, and quite angry about it, to be honest," he said.

"To wind up Horse of the Year (Hawke's Bay) Ltd decision was made at the beginning of the year, if not earlier, so it's been a long time."

What's your experience with the show? Let us know: monique.steele@rnz.co.nz

The Companies Register showed Horse of the Year (Hawke's Bay) Limited, started in 2012, was overdue in its obligation to file its annual return, so the process to remove the company from the registry was initiated by the Registrar of Companies.

Aitken said he had requested documents from the shareholders to complete the dissolution of the company, but was waiting to hear back.

He said it may have been able to make a modest profit if this year's event went ahead, to cover a loss in 2025, but it was unable to secure funding, including from the district council's events fund to attempt it.

"To have no, lose all that support from our shareholders," he said.

"And finding out now that they haven't actually gone out and told anyone that the event's not running anymore, I find that really, really frustrating."

In December last year, when the organisers decided to cancel this year's show, the Hastings District Council told RNZ it was not in a position to extend funding while it still faced substantial Cyclone Gabrielle recovery costs.

Aitken said it was challenging to find a replacement event sponsor once Land Rover pulled out, though the company had previously signalled its decision to exit events sponsorship more generally.

Tōmoana Showgrounds during an event to thank those involved in Cyclone Gabrielle's response and recovery in February 2024. RNZ / Lauren Crimp

He said for an event that had run in Hawke's Bay for more than two decades, it died "a very quiet death".

"It was a huge event for Hawke's Bay. It was the largest question event in the southern hemisphere of its kind, and it's gone."

Is it gone?

But proponents ESNZ and the Hastings District Council were exploring options to allow the event to continue beyond 2028.

New ESNZ chief executive Emily Downes said the organisation was exploring what the future of the event may look like.

"I can reassure you that this is not the end of our biggest national equestrian event, and Equestrian Sports New Zealand has continued to explore what the future of the event may look like."

Downes said the event was deeply valued across the equestrian community and missed by many in its absence.

"We also recognise the immense contribution of all those who have played a role in its success and legacy particularly in the Hawke's Bay region.

"We recognise the strong desire across the equestrian community to see the return of Horse of the Year and are working diligently towards delivering this."

Hastings District Council chief executive Bruce Allan said it was disappointed the show was unable to go ahead this year, and confirmed the management company had been "wound up" following the recent challenges.

"Hastings has a proud history as the home of the event and, while ultimately ESNZ will decide its future, we would love to see that legacy continue at Tōmoana Showgrounds for future generations of riders, supporters and our wider community."

He said HDC purchased the company's equestrian assets for Tōmoana Showgrounds to continue to support events from grassroots to premier level.

"Council is in the final stages of developing the Tōmoana Showgrounds Future Framework, which identifies equestrian events as a core activity for the venue.

"We are continuing to engage with ESNZ to understand its future plans for Horse of the Year and its title classes.

"These discussions will help Council and the Tōmoana Showgrounds Charitable Trust make informed decisions about future investment in equestrian facilities, competition surfaces and supporting infrastructure."

Allan said the event was an important part of Hastings' identity and significant to the wider region.

World.title: Commerce Commission files charges against Air New Zealand
World.content:
The Commerce Commission is filing charges against Air New Zealand under the Fair-Trading Act.

It alleges the airline misled passengers about their rights to compensation when flights were disrupted for reasons within the airline's control.

Delays that would be considered within an airline's control include engineering issues, crew sickness, and operational delays.

The commission said over the past five years, consumers have frequently raised concerns about Air New Zealand.

Its deputy chair Anne Callinan claimed Air New Zealand made statements that led some passengers to incorrectly assume they weren't entitled to compensation, and rejected legitimate reimbursement claims.

Callinan said the commission believed passengers missed out on money they were entitled to under the law.

She said New Zealand's Civil Aviation Act is clear that airlines have a responsibility to reimburse domestic passengers for losses caused by cancellations or delays that are within the airline's control.

World.title: Alexander Zverev officially notified of lawsuit by ex-partner in abuse case
World.content:
Top-ranked tennis player Alexander Zverev has officially been notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals.

The latest legal case alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.

The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with French sports daily L'Equipe earlier this year that "it has been proven that the accusations were false" and "my innocence has been proven".

Zverev's Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement shared with The Associated Press that they were formally served with Patea's lawsuit on Wednesday.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit," Zverev's lawyers said. "If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion" protected by the German constitution.

They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.

Patea's lawyer, Michael Scheele, told The AP that Zverev's claim over his innocence "triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client".

He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.

"Quite apart from the fact that Zverev's claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form," he said. "Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement."

Patea is seeking an order that Zverev not repeat such comments and that he be fined up to 250,000 euros ($408,600) each time he does.

Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing.

The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.

Brenda Patea arrives at court in 2024 after making her allegations against Alexander Zverev. (Getty Images: Jens Kalaene/picture alliance)

Zverev this month ascended to the number one ranking for the first time. He also won his first two Grand Slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin. His next match is on Thursday.

Zverev has not commented on the lawsuit.

It is not the first time that legal affairs have clashed with Zverev's tennis schedule. The settlement with Patea was decided while Zverev was playing the 2024 French Open. He did not appear in court then.

He previously denied abuse allegations from another former girlfriend, Olga Sharypova, who first made the accusations in 2020 and followed up in 2021 with a detailed account in a Slate.com article that was taken down because of a preliminary injunction issued by a German court. Slate said it stood by the article.

The allegations prompted the men's professional tennis tour, the ATP, to investigate her claims.

It ended 15 months later, in January 2023, with the ATP saying there was "insufficient evidence" to substantiate the claims.

AP

World.title: GWS Giants desperate to draft young star
World.content:
It's a sign of the precarious position of Australian Rules Football in Western Sydney that Ethan Matthews' father, Cameron, took to bribing kids to join his son at the Ingleburn Magpies.

"Definitely got lots of players across from softball at times, in rugby league, a few soccer," Ethan told ABC Sport.

"When we were younger, not too much, five, 10 bucks, but then as we started to get a bit older, we started to demand a bit more, so I probably got up to $25, $50 at times, depending on how talented the athlete was."

Bribing kids to play Aussie Rules in rugby league heartland gives some indication about why the GWS Giants are so keen to bring their Academy player through their door in Thursday night's AFL draft.

Ethan Matthews is the most talented product to come out of western Sydney in the Giants' history. (Supplied: Phil Hillyard)

Drafting a gifted Aussie Rules player is important not just for the Giants' playing list but also for the message that they are still trying to sell 16 years down the track: that the club can build a local Aussie Rules culture so that more kids like Ethan Matthews take up the game and follow the Giants.

The job of winning the hearts and minds of rugby league and soccer fans in western Sydney is a constant work in progress for the Giants.

While the Giants made the Grand Final in 2019 only to get thrashed by Richmond, the impact of COVID the following year put a halt to the team's momentum that they're still struggling to recover from.

So, Matthews is much more than the most talented player to come out of western Sydney in the club's short history; he's the poster child for the region and what local boys and girls can achieve.

The Giants are expected to take Matthews with their pick nine, but there's every chance that he could be bid on prior to that, which would mean GWS would have to match the bid.

Ethan Matthews could be one of the top picks at the 2026 AFL Draft. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

The local boy from the village of Appin, south of Campbelltown, would be just the fifth western Sydney local drafted to the Giants since the team entered the AFL in 2012 and the highest draft pick of those by a country mile.

When he's picked, it will be the culmination of a dream for the politely spoken 18-year-old who'll be in Melbourne on draft night.

"I just expected it to be a great get-together with all my family and friends," Matthews said.

"Just a moment to celebrate the journey. It's been a great, not a few years; it's been 10 years now of hard work and effort put in."

Matthews knows that there's every chance another club could snaffle him, but the Giants have given him enough reassurance that he's heading to Sydney Olympic Park come Friday morning.

"They've certainly told me as much as they can; they would love to have me," he said.

"I'm not going to lie and say they aren't my preferred team to go to; [I've] been there since I was 12 and love the Giants very much."

Ethan Matthews with his father, Cameron, mother, Melissa and sister, Ava before the AFL draft in Melbourne. (Supplied)

The journey began even earlier at just four when his footy-loving dad and mad Collingwood supporter took him down to join the Ingleburn Magpies Auskick side.

From there, he progressed through to the Giants' development side in the under-12s to the Academy at 16 and then this year played a starring role for the Giants Talent League side and then the Allies in the National Under-18s Championships.

The highlight for the 186cm left-footer was a best-on-ground game against Vic Country, where he racked up plenty of disposals plus nine score involvements, six tackles and eight marks playing in the midfield.

The highlights of that game were a recruiter's dream as Matthews glided around the field dodging tackles and delivering pinpoint left-foot passes to leading forwards.

"I like to think I'm quite a fundamental and skilful footballer; I like to use my Footy IQ," he said.

Unfortunately, Matthews injured his foot later in the Championships, which brought his season to an end, but not before he picked up the Hunter Harrison medal as the best player from the northern states' academy programs.

And while his close footy mates were following his progress closely thanks to Cameron's bribes, that wasn't the case for his other school friends who were wondering where he'd disappeared to.

"Not too many people, I guess, especially at school, had too much of an idea about a national champs game, and no-one knows where you've been or what you've done, and I've kind of liked that," he said.

"But yeah, all my close friends and all my mates that play footy certainly do know, and I'm lucky enough with Dad bribing people to come across, most of my friends have at some stage played footy with me in younger years and are very interested."

Once at the Giants, Matthews is determined to work hard and break into the team, which is coming off a disappointing 2026 season highlighted by injuries to key players.

"It's going to be very hard to crack into the AFL team," Matthews said.

"So, first [I've] just got to get into the side, but once I do, I reckon I would start on a wing or a half back, and then ultimately in a few years' time I see myself as a midfielder."

Ethan Matthews says he wants to be a role model for young Australian Rules footballers in western Sydney. (Supplied: Phil Hillyard)

Matthews also sees himself as a role model to help grow the game in Western Sydney.

"It's an honour and a privilege, especially to represent this area," he said.

"I'd love to be a role model for many kids, especially out in this area, to keep striving and play footy, and have a dream, I think, being a role model out here would be something very special to me."

Come Thursday night, Matthews will almost certainly be decked in orange and charcoal, and while that's been his destiny for six years, it will mean permanently abandoning his childhood team and first love, Collingwood.

"I definitely love the Giants just as much, but yeah, [I'm a] Collingwood fan," he said.

"Dad signed me up before birth, didn't have much choice there."

World.title: Opetaia's fight with former heavyweight champion called off
World.content:
Jai Opetaia's eyebrow-raising move to heavyweight to fight Deontay Wilder is over after the Australian withdrew from their bout.

The Gold Coast-based Opetaia (31-0) was set to move up from cruiserweight to face former world champion Wilder on the undercard to Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's Cardiff blockbuster next month.

"Fighter to fighter, I know the feeling, and it's frustrating. I've ‌always prided myself on fighting anyone, anyplace," Opetaia posted on social media on Wednesday night.

He rubbished suggestions he'd pulled out of the fight because of Wilder's "big right hand".

"The goal has never changed and still, like I've always said, remains the same. Undisputed," he said.

"They all said I couldn't after signing with Zuffa Boxing, everything always against us, stripped and vacated multiple times … but you watch.

"I'm coming to spoil the party."

The fight was seen as a lucrative, profile-raising option — albeit a risky one given the power of Wilder — to stay busy before a potential cruiserweight clash with David Benavidez next year.

Jai Opetaia (left) and David Benavidez (right) could potentially fight in 2027. (Getty Images: Zuffa Boxing/Ed Mulholland/)

Opetaia's co-promoter Mick Francis said Opetaia had aggravated a hand injury first sustained during his September bout against Noel Mikaelian.

"This is a disappointing setback for Jai, who was looking forward to what promised to be a cracking fight. His focus now is on making a full recovery and continuing his quest to become the undisputed cruiserweight champion of the world," he said.

Benavidez and Opetaia agreed in the ring after Opetaia's last win to face each other next May.

The two-division champion holds the WBO and WBA's cruiserweight belts and will face WBC strap-holder Michal Cieslak in a unification battle next month.

And the WBC had installed the Australian as the mandatory challenger for the winner of that fight.

Opetaia was stripped of his IBF title for fighting for the unsanctioned Zuffa belt he now holds, alongside his enduring Ring champion status.

The Australian beat former WBC champion Mikaelian, who gave up his belt for a shot at Opetaia.

Opetaia remains in a court battle with the IBF to reclaim that belt and, if successful, could walk into a clash with Benavidez with all four major organisations' belts on the line.

Meanwhile, contenders have lined up to replace Opetaia on the card, with Derek Chisora, Richard Riakporhe and even fellow Australian and Tasman Fighters stablemate Justis Huni floated as options.

AAP

World.title: English press slam 'fickle' Aussie cricket fans, tell Cummins to resign
World.content:
For Aussie cricket lovers, they are grim reading.

"Pat Cummins has torched his own reputation over Sandpapergate," screamed the headline on an opinion piece by The Daily Mail's chief sports writer, Oliver Holt, demanding Australia's Test captain resign.

His counterpart at The Telegraph, Oliver Brown, has gone in even harder.

After Cummins held a press conference in which he said he had no knowledge of the infamous 2018 ball-tampering plot, the broadsheet's scribe complained "fickle" Australian fans had been way too eager to believe the star's version of events.

On Wednesday, after multiple more explosive claims had emerged, he lined up the skipper again, writing that his credibility was "in ruins" and likening his denials to Bill Clinton's "I did not have sexual relations with that woman" speech.

Ah, yes. Sandpapergate is providing a bright spot amid the late-Autumn drizzle and gloom for many English cricket fans, media pundits and former players.

Loading...

The scandal, which was reignited earlier this month by passages in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, is big news in Britain.

As the civil war rages Down Under, each day has provided blistering critiques in Blighty's press.

Filing from Perth last week before a one-day match between the old enemies, The Times's chief cricket correspondent, former England captain Mike Atherton, wrote: "Can there ever be a better time to be in this beautiful country than when Australian cricket is tearing itself apart?"

For those wondering, his answer was "obviously, no".

Perhaps Atherton is in a unique position to comment? In 1994, he was accused of ball tampering by using dirt in his pocket to scuff the pill during a Test match against South Africa. He was fined, but has always denied wrongdoing.

Loading...

The Sandpapergate saga deepened on Wednesday when Cameron Bancroft wrote a 4,000-word defence of himself for The West Australian newspaper.

Bancroft was one of the Australian players suspended when the scandal first broke in 2018. Cameras caught him rubbing sandpaper on the ball during the now-infamous match against South Africa.

In the article, he claimed the entire team knew what was going on, and that Cummins's press conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".

Bancroft's bomb Australian cricket's point of no return Cameron Bancroft's statement is the atom bomb Cricket Australia has always feared. For so many of the game's key figures, there is no turning back now.

After its publication, Cummins's management released a statement reiterating the star's position that he had no knowledge of the plot.

Atherton is not the only former England player to have weighed in.

Michael Vaughan has spoken about it, as has Matt Prior, who told England-based magazine The Cricketer he did not believe Cummins and that Australia's other bowlers in the Sandpapergate Test did not know about the ball tampering.

"There is just no way that a conversation wouldn't have been had in any of the dressing rooms that I've played in," he said.

Charlie Banfield has no sympathy for his counterparts Down Under. (ABC News: Alex Parsons)

Around London's famous Oval cricket ground, which is set to host the fifth Ashes Test next year, fans of the sport were critical of the way the scandal was being handled in Australia.

"I think you guys over in Australia, your fans are probably going to be a bit quiet compared to the English fans [when the Ashes start next year]. And to be honest, I think you should be," said England supporter Charlie Banfield, who spoke to the ABC at The Rose pub a short walk from the stadium.

He said Australia had brought the game into disrepute and that the scandal would be unsettling ahead of the Ashes.

"Hopefully, they'll get what's coming to them," Banfield said.

Another cricket fan, Vikrant Kheterpal, was a little more sympathetic.

"Well we don't know whether he [Cummins] is lying, we don't [know] where he's told the truth," he said.

World.title: Bancroft has blown up Australian cricket and there is no going back
World.content:
As it all crumbles around him, Cameron Bancroft does not smile from the ashes.

It was not his goal to bring Australian cricket to its knees, but he will have known it was an unavoidable consequence. Bancroft watched and listened, silent until he felt no option but to speak.

His words are a watershed, across which there is no return. Here is the Sandpapergate story, as plainly and fully as we are likely to get it. And now we know.

Bancroft's confessional essay, coming in at more than 4,500 words, is the most significant moment in Australian cricket since the same man was caught placing sandpaper in his pants.

Umpires speak to Bancroft on the field in Cape Town, 2018. (Getty Images: Gallo Images: Peter Heeger)

To read it is to feel Bancroft's pain and to share in it. There is anger in his words at the perceived betrayal, regret for mistakes made and years lost, despair at the loneliness that came from becoming a pariah within his own community. The same community he feels he sacrificed himself to serve.

Here is Bancroft as Raskolnikov, living the past eight years of his life burdened by his crime, his guilt, that weight only growing greater with each passing day.

Bancroft stands to gain nothing from its telling and will likely lose a lot. His account is captivating and impassioned.

Above all, and this may be the most compelling element, it is detailed. Names are named, specific match scores are recounted and used as justification for motive.

We now know, according to Bancroft at least, precisely when the sandpaper plot was formed, who was involved, how and where he performed the illegal act and how everyone reacted at every juncture.

This is the button Cricket Australia has long feared being pressed, the one which drops the atom bomb on the game, its champions, its mythology, its governance.

Loading...

Just hours before Bancroft's statement, Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg had described a world where differing versions of truth are possible, where everyone has a story to tell and no one account is any more trustworthy or valid or reputable than another.

We don't live in that world anymore. Cameron Bancroft blew it up, and with it all the shades of grey so many key figures have used as camouflage.

Of course, you could still argue it remains the word of Pat Cummins, Darren Lehmann and the bowlers against that of Bancroft, David Warner and Usman Khawaja. There will surely have to be a reaction from those now directly accused by Bancroft, and the tune may be a familiar one.

But who is listening anymore? The cricket loving public of Australia is utterly fed up with this nonsense, this slanging match between men they are supposed to admire, or at the very least support.

Even if Pat Cummins is and has been telling the truth — and to believe that, much of what Bancroft wrote would have to be a lie — who will believe him next time he fronts up and speaks?

The rebuttal from Bancroft was so pointed against Cummins specifically, citing his 70-minute press conference as the inspiration for his statement, that his position as captain of the Australian Test team is now questionable.

It seems Cummins gambled everything on that press conference, and the wrong card may have just come up.

Bancroft and Steve Smith lied about the use of sandpaper at the initial post-play press conference. (Getty Images: Gallo Images: Ashley Vlotman)

The naming of a squad for the Test series against New Zealand was expected this week but has now been pushed into next.

When Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon are all named — just as they were by Bancroft, who marked them each down as knowing participants in the ball tampering in South Africa — will Australia continue to accept them? Respect them?

Perhaps that is unfair. Perhaps they are each as agog at this breakthrough as Bancroft was when Cummins spoke last week.

Perhaps they do still firmly believe "their truth", totally incompatible though it may be with rival truths, existing an indeterminable distance from the actual, verifiable truth, in itself a notion long since given up on.

Greenberg's half-baked amnesty forum, announced in Hobart presumably while the nuclear weapon was being built in Perth, immediately looks quaint to the point of ridicule. In a post-Bancroft world, closed-door honesty sessions aren't convincing anyone.

Loading...

All of which boils down to the wider point, one which has been made painfully clear for the past two weeks: Australians are sick and tired of being taken for fools by the people who play in and run their cricket team.

The lies, the cover-ups, the allegations, the counter-allegations, the statements, the press releases. Wearing us down, eroding trust, chipping away at an emotional connection many Australians develop in childhood and carry with them all their lives.

There was already a case to be made for regeneration of the Australian Test team for on-field reasons, but the carpet has moved so dramatically beneath them that simply carrying on now feels more difficult than ripping it up.

Bancroft has broken through, and one way or another there is no turning back. Scorched earth. Fire as destroyer; or perhaps, with a little luck, as cleanser.

World.title: Bancroft says 'whole team' knew about sandpaper in explosive claims
World.content:
Cameron Bancroft claims the entire Australian cricket team knew about their 2018 sandpaper plot, in an explosive article that will cast another dark cloud over the Test squad.

Bancroft, who with Steve Smith and David Warner was banned over the tactic, said the entire team knew about the plan despite recent claims from current Test skipper Pat Cummins to the contrary.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote in an article that originally appeared in the West Australian before being sent out to all media.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

Steve Smith (right) and Cameron Bancroft acknowledged ball tampering in Cape Town but did not mention sandpaper. (Getty Images: Gallo Images: Ashley Vlotman)

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins's press conference."

In a press conference that lasted more than an hour on Friday, Cummins said former batter Usman Khawaja's assertion that the entire team was in on the ball tampering was "complete and utter nonsense".

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone," Bancroft wrote of Cummins's response.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with — not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa — is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."

In a statement to the ABC, Cummins's agent said:

"Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."

Bancroft said he recalled having several conversations with the bowlers on that tour about how the ball was moving.

"I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough," he wrote.

"I also spoke with Tim Paine, who was in a key position behind the stumps to observe how the ball was moving. I wanted and needed feedback.

Loading...

"How else am I to know if what I'm doing is effective or not if I don't have these conversations with the bowlers bowling with it and the wicketkeeper?

"All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful."

Bancroft also said he had received "wraps and encouragement" from players and coaches regarding his work on the ball, naming former bowling coach David Saker, while also suggesting coach Darren Lehmann was aware of what was happening.

"This event is crystal clear in my mind. Not only for the praise I received. But I also remember a very different reaction," he wrote.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.

"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up."

Bancroft said 12th man Peter Handscomb had rushed out to him to tell him to put the sandpaper away, on direction from Lehmann.

"He [Handscomb] said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now'. And Pete was doing his job after Boof shouted to him on the walkie talkie 'get the f****** sandpaper off Bangers now,'" he wrote.

"In my opinion, if he didn't know, he wouldn't have said that.

"And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now. Once again. WE ALL KNEW."

Speaking on ABC Sport's coverage of Australia's ODI clash with England on Wednesday night, Lehmann said he would take time to read Bancroft's article and form a response.

"It's a lot for everyone, I presume, not just me," Lehmann said.

"There's no point rushing into anything that's said. I just want to make sure I'm really clear which way I'm going."

The explosive article came just hours after Cricket Australia announced it was opening a forum for all players and staff to "share their truth" about what happened in South Africa eight years ago.

However, Warner and Khawaja immediately criticised the forum, with all conversations set to remain private.

"Are we going to get down to what the public want, [which] is the truth?" Warner said.

"Where do we actually end here, because it is upon the board to review what they want to be published. Yes that's a safe space, but is everyone able to talk?

"I would have liked an open public inquiry and the people that were there at the time can come forward and speak."

Cricket Australia released its own statement on Wednesday night, addressing Bancroft's claims.

"We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments," the statement read.

"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.

"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."

'Mortifying' development for Cummins

Loading...

Veteran cricket journalist Gideon Haigh said the Bancroft column put captain Cummins in an uncomfortable position ahead of next month's home Test series against New Zealand.

"I think it's mortifying for him," Haigh told 730.

"We should keep in mind that he was the junior member of that pace ensemble. He maybe didn't feel confident about going against the flow, in the same way that Cameron Bancroft didn't feel confident about going against the flow.

"Bancroft talks about a meeting taking place afterwards where the use of sandpaper was freely discussed and what the team would say, and no-one speaking up, and no-one saying afterwards, 'I didn't know about this.'"

"So Pat Cummins, presumably, remains silent in that meeting, and I guess now he's got to give an account about why."

Haigh said the Bancroft column came from a man who felt he "had carried a great burden" for over eight years.

Out of David Warner, Steve Smith, Cameron Bancroft and Usman Khawaja, Smith is the only player yet to claim all players knew about the plot. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

"It's a statement from a cricketer who really has no reason to lie, in fact every good reason to keep his own counsel about this," Haigh said.

"He feels like a man who has carried a great burden for the past eight and a half years and perhaps there's some relief involved in sharing his story with a wider audience."

Haigh said then-coach Lehmann may have questions to answer given Bancroft's claims in the column that the former Test batsman was aware of the process.

"He even had a story at the end about [coach] Darren Lehmann sending Peter Handscomb onto the field at Cape Town and telling him to get the sandpaper off the field," Haigh said.

"Darren Lehmann denied specifically any knowledge of the [sandpaper] plans to CA's investigators in 2018, so it will be interesting to see if he has any response."

World.title: England wins ODI series as Australia falters in chase after Duckett ton
World.content:
Australia has crumbled to a one-day international series loss to England, with star all-rounder Cameron Green forced from the field after being struck by a bouncer.

Chasing 329 to win the deciding game three in Hobart on Wednesday, the hosts were bowled out for 231 in the 47th over.

Green was substituted out of the game in the 27th over after being felled and left with blood in his mouth following a Gus Atkinson delivery.

Ben Duckett scored a vital 133 for England as the tourists set Australia a big total in the third and final ODI in Hobart. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

The loss came on another turbulent day for Australian cricket, with former opener Cameron Bancroft claiming the whole Test side and coaches knew of sandpaper ball tampering in 2018.

Earlier, Ben Duckett scored 133 off 115 balls to help set the platform for England's big total.

England got off to a flying start but were pulled back through the middle overs by the part-time spin of Matt Renshaw.

Renshaw picked up 3-51, which included a flighted delivery to bowl Joe Root (12) in the 15th over, the scalp of Jordan Cox (12) stumped and Duckett off a top edge in the 39th over.

Matt Renshaw's impressive spin bowling brought three vital wickets for Australia against England in the final ODI in Hobart. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Australia's chase started poorly with openers Travis Head (four) and Mitchell Marsh (one) gone inside the first two overs.

Shifted to No.3 at the expense of Cooper Connolly, Renshaw (55) launched a salvage mission before being caught and bowled by spinner Liam Dawson.

It got worse a few overs later when Alex Carey (37) was run out, leaving Australia 5-115 in the 27th over, before Green (three) was forced off shortly afterwards

Connolly, who had been batting at No.3, managed 29 at No.7 before being bowled by Dawson.

Young England quick Sonny Baker was the pick of the bowlers with 4-45.

Australia, who were beaten comfortably by England in game two, now face a dearth of ODI cricket before the World Cup begins in October.

AAP

World.title: Sydney's Papley banned for three games after roadside drug test
World.content:
Sydney's Tom Papley will miss the Swans' preseason game and the first three matches of the 2027 season after being banned by the AFL over a failed roadside drug test.

The AFL banned Papley for conduct unbecoming, giving the Swans small forward a notifiable adverse finding under the league's Illicit Drugs Policy.

He was also given a suspended $5,000 fine.

NSW Police stopped Papley on November 2 for a roadside licence check.

He was issued with a court attendance notice for driving with a suspended licence, due to an unpaid parking fine.

The Swans player then completed a random drug test that gave a positive initial result. Today, the AFL said the secondary sample had confirmed the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

NSW Police has fined Papley $722, and his licence will be suspended for three months.

Swans culture issue Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich expresses "bitter disappointment" after Tom Papley's drug test result hurls the AFL club back into the spotlight.

AFL COO Tom Harley said the sanction reflected the seriousness of the breach.

"AFL players are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with illicit drug use," Harley said in a statement.

"The player is being held accountable for his actions and has acknowledged he made a grave mistake."

Papley apologised for his behaviour in a statement released by the Swans.

"I am extremely sorry for my behaviour which has caused distress for my family, everyone connected to the Club and broader industry," he said.

"I accept my actions have fallen well short of the standards that is expected of me at this football club, and I will work very hard to win the trust back of everyone in the wider community.

"Road safety is something that affects everyone in our community, and I take full accountability for my mistake.

"I would also like to take this opportunity to thank my wife, my family, my manager Winston, the Club, my teammates, the AFLPA and all those who have supported me over the last fortnight."

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich said Papley understood the sanction and was taking responsibility for his mistakes.

"While we are very disappointed in his actions, he is an important member of the team, and we will work closely with him and the entire AFL program to reinstate the high standards the Club expects of everyone.

"We need to be better, and change must occur."

Tech.title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

Tech.title: Democrats skip a vote on adding Brendan Carr’s adviser to the FCC
Tech.content:
Senate commerce committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-TX) began a meeting Wednesday meant to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee to the Federal Communications Commission with a lopsided dais. To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). To his left were about a dozen empty chairs — every Democratic member of the panel was absent.

Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC, as he did at the Federal Trade Commission. “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said.

“This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party”

But in statements and comments to reporters outside the committee room, Democrats said that the process has been far from normal. Senate committees often vote on nominations to historically independent agencies in bipartisan pairs. Confirming Danielle Thumann Severs, senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to become a commissioner at the agency would put the FCC at four total members — three Republicans and one Democrat, Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez, because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions.

Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. One way to do that would be to renominate Gomez. But so far, the president has not offered any Democratic nominees for the commission. Democrats said they made their concerns clear to Cruz, and added, “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In addition to the procedural concerns, Democrats worry about Thumann’s work as an adviser to Carr, and whether she was truthful about the matters she worked on. In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) detailed his concerns. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and “helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the 2 FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,” Luján wrote. “She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.

Even Cruz admitted concerns with Carr’s handling of Kimmel’s comments in the aftermath of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing. But at Wednesday’s meeting, he said he “emphatically agree[s]” that Thumann had resolved any lingering worries about that. He added that his JAWBONE Act, which the committee previously passed, could directly address First Amendment violations by government agencies of either party. The bill would let individuals sue government officials if they illegally try to compel social media or broadcast companies to remove their speech. Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS), who’d similarly expressed concern over the Kimmel incident, said he found Thumann’s responses on the subject “comforting,” including in a phone call earlier that morning where he said he’d expressed his “serious interest in how the FCC protects and promotes free speech, including free speech on broadcast.” On the call, he said, “she was able to satisfy me once again in her answers, including an explanation for her role at the FCC and her lack of engagement on this type of issue as the FCC made decisions.”

“If she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?”

Speaking to reporters outside of the hearing room ahead of the meeting, Luján accused Thumann of lying to the committee. “The questions that I have is if she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?” he said. Luján said he wants both Thumann and Carr to appear before the committee by the end of the year to answer lawmakers’ questions. Asked if he’d support using the committee’s subpoena power or even pursuing impeachment against Carr when Democrats regain power next year, Luján said his vote to confirm Carr as a commissioner under President Joe Biden is among his biggest regrets, and that while he hopes Carr will testify voluntarily, “everything should be on the table here to be able to get answers for the American people.”

When it came time to vote on whether to advance Thumann’s nomination for a final step of a vote on the Senate floor, all 15 Republicans voted “aye.” That gave Thumann enough votes for her nomination to advance to the Senate floor, where it’s expected to pass along party lines once scheduled. Still, the clerk listed off the names of the 13 Democratic committee members whose seats remained empty. There was no response.

Tech.title: Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

This drastic shift in priorities will likely change what the DCU looks like in the coming years as Skydance attempts to parlay its comics IP into projects that can help it get on top of the $80 billion of debt the company is now responsible for after acquiring WBD. Ellison’s instinct to whip out the A-list superheroes is probably right from a business perspective. Most casual DC movie fans are more interested in stories about the Trinity than obscure characters like Gorilla Grodd. But after two iffy attempts at creating interconnected DC movie franchises, that audience might not have much of an appetite for yet another full-on reboot.

Rather than starting from scratch, DC Studios should probably keep some of the things that worked well during Gunn and Safran’s tenure, like presenting Superman as a compassionate person with a strong moral compass. But if the studio really wants to take this franchise in a new direction that gets people excited, it should also be thinking about tapping into the energy of some of DC’s most successful recent comics. Though the WBD merger prompted Skydance to begin laying off almost 2,000 employees last month, DC Comics — which Skydance gained control of as part of the deal — was reportedly left unscathed because the publishing arm’s business has been performing surprisingly well. Much of that success seems to have been driven by strong sales of comics created by DC’s Absolute Universe imprint.

Image: DC Comics / Mark Spears

Launched in 2024, the Absolute Universe comics reimagine DC’s heroes and villains as wildly different versions of their classic selves. Absolute Wonder Woman is a witch raised in Hell, Absolute Superman first arrives on Earth as a teenager who remembers his childhood on Krypton, and Absolute Batman is a working-class civil engineer rather than a socialite born into immense wealth. The Absolute characters’ worldviews and approaches to enacting justice are all distinct from their mainstream universe counterparts. But as much as the Absolute comics diverge from established canon, they each capture the essence of what makes their central characters iconic pillars of the DC brand.

Wonder Woman aside, there have been so many cinematic portrayals of DC characters based on their classic selves that it has often seemed like Warner Bros. was stuck in a kind of rut. There have been slight stylistic differences between the various big-screen iterations of Superman and Batman over the years, but for the most part, they have all come across as the products of a studio that’s averse to trying new things.

Absolute Batman is compelling because it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics.

That’s part of what made Matt Reeves’ The Batman— which didn’t bother to rehash Bruce Wayne’s tragic origin story — feel somewhat like a breath of fresh air when it debuted in 2022. Robert Pattinson will reprise his role as the Dark Knight in The Batman Part II, but it’s not really clear whether that version of the character will have any bearing on the DCU’s future.

Between Reeves’ Batman films existing in their own universe (similar to Todd Phillips’ Joker features) and Pattinson presumably being busy now that he’s been cast as Amazon’s new James Bond, it doesn’t seem likely that that version of the character will be incorporated into the DCU. Ellison obviously intends to put out more projects featuring Batman, though, and DC Studios could tell a riveting story if it took some cues from the hero’s Absolute incarnation. What makes Absolute Batman such a compelling series is the way it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics. In those books, Bruce Wayne is part of Gotham’s marginalized underclass, while the Joker is a moneyed elite whose villainy is highlighted in the way he manipulates various industries.

Previous Next



1 / 3 Batman taking on crooked cops in Absolute Batman Annual. Image: DC Comics / Daniel Warren Johnson, Mike Spicer, Clayton Cowles

This inversion puts Absolute Batman in a position to operate as a vigilante with a much deeper connection to the ordinary people he has sworn to protect. Monstrous supervillains like Poison Ivy and Bane are still major threats, but the comics also spend time pitting Absolute Batman against more ordinary evils like corrupt police departments infested with white nationalists fixated on terrorizing minorities. Absolute Batman’s progressive political overtones might not gel with Ellison’s personal sensibilities, and the comic’s brutality probably doesn’t align with Latcham’s approach to making films. But Absolute Batman’s phenomenal sales have made it abundantly clear that readers are enjoying these stories, which is likely a big part why DC Studios announced earlier this year that it has plans to produce an animated series based on the comics.
